units.tr: 3. That the Greek and Latin Church for 400 years after Christ used this version alone and approved it, and made translations from it, rejecting others, which have therefore since vanished. Yet it was not of divine authority, which belongs to no version as such.

units.la: 4. Veram τῶν 70. versionem in Origenis Hexaplis conservatam fuisse. Non tamen cum Hebraico codice per omnia concordasse, quod ex triplici causa fuit, scribarum scil. incuria & temeritate, interpretum hallucinatione, & exemplarium Hebraic. varietate. Varias istas lectiones authoritati Scripturae non derogare, &c.
units.tr: 4. That the true version of the Seventy was preserved in Origen's Hexapla. Yet it did not agree in every respect with the Hebrew codex, which came about from a threefold cause: namely, the carelessness and rashness of the scribes, the mistakes of the translators, and the variety of Hebrew copies. These various readings do not detract from the authority of Scripture, etc.

units.la: 5. Versionem quae in Hexaplis erat, non periisse, sed hodie extare, licet in quibusdam vitiatam.
units.tr: 5. That the version which was in the Hexapla has not perished, but is extant today, although in some places corrupted.

units.la: CUm in multorum votis esset, qui sumptus ad imprimenda Biblia nostra Polyglotta contulerunt, ut, quò uberior editionis hujus fructus in omnes redundaret, Alphabeta linguarum singularum una cum Introductione, ad earundem saltem lectionem, in usum tyronum breviter delineata haberent; & si non singularum Lexica & Grammaticas edamus (quae cum a variis authoribus accurate scripta in lucem prodierint, idcirco superuacaneū esset denuò imprimere) saltem rationem de studiis in hisce linguis feliciter instituendis indicare velimus, quosq; libros, Lexica, &c. & Grammaticas, parare sibi debeant: visum est Introductionem hanc brevem ex optimis, quas videre contigit, Grammaticis collectam, cum indiculis authorum, qui ad penitiorem harum linguarum cognitionem maximè utiles sunt, vice prodromi edere; adjectis etiam quibusdam de antiquissima lingua Coptorum seu Ægyptiorum, & de lingua Armenorum, & antiquis eorum versionibus Biblicis, quas licet in hoc opere Biblico non promittimus, jucundum tamen & linguarum studiosis gratum (ni fallor) erit, aliquid de linguis istis & versionibus Scripturæ, quæ in eis extant, degustare. Et, si Deus vitā otium q; concesserit, posthac fortasse aliquid in hisce tentabimus. Cūmq;, licet Tomus primus seu Pentateuchus jam typis impressus in multorū manus, qui impensās & operā suppeditārunt, pervenerit, tantæ tamen molis opus plurīū annorū curriculū postulet, antequām omnibus numeris absolutum prodire possit: Præfationes vero & Prolegomena seu Apparatus, quæ primo Tomo præfigi solent ante totum absolutum perfici non possint, utpote in quibus lectori reddenda sit ratio omnium quæ in Tomis singulis occurrunt, quod, nisi quis spiritu Propheticoafflatus esset, perfectè fieri non potest: Ne tamen spes protracta ægram reddat animam, ut loquitur Sapiens; Pro. 13.12. quædam in genere de instituti operis ratione, linguarum naturā, versionibus & exemplaribus tam impressis quam MSS. quibus utimur, eorūmque antiquitate, & apud Ecclesiam priscam authoritate, & usu, quidq; ex hac Editione præ aliis commodi haberi poterit, breviter delibare constituimus, pleniorem de hisce omnibus tractationem in aliud opus (in quo quæstiones omnes quæ vel de textibus originalibus, vel de versionibus moventur, pro viribus enucleabimus, quōdque Apparatui Biblico refervamus) rejicientes.
units.tr: Since many who contributed money toward printing our Polyglot Bible wished that the fruit of this edition might reach everyone more fully, they wanted alphabets of the individual languages, together with a brief introduction designed for students, so that at least the reading of these languages would be possible. Although we are not publishing lexicons and grammars of each language (these have already been published, accurately written by various authors, so it would be superfluous to print them again), we nevertheless wish at least to indicate the method of studying these languages successfully, and which books, lexicons and grammars, they ought to obtain for themselves. It seemed right to publish in advance this short introduction, gathered from the best grammars we have been able to see, together with a list of authors who are most useful for a deeper knowledge of these languages. We have also added some remarks on the most ancient language of the Copts or Egyptians, on the language of the Armenians, and on their ancient Biblical versions. Although we do not promise these in this Biblical work, it will (unless I am mistaken) be pleasing and welcome to students of languages to taste something about these languages and the versions of Scripture that exist in them. If God grants us life and leisure, we may perhaps attempt something further in these areas later. Now, although the first volume, the Pentateuch, has already been printed and has reached the hands of those who supplied the expense and labour, a work of such great bulk requires several years before it can appear completed in every respect. Prefaces and Prolegomena, or Apparatus, which are customarily placed before the first volume, cannot be finished until the whole is complete, since in them an account must be given to the reader of everything that occurs in the individual volumes, which cannot be done perfectly unless one were inspired by the Prophetic Spirit. Yet, lest "hope deferred make the soul sick," as the Wise Man says [Prov. 13.12], we have resolved to set out briefly, in general terms, the plan of the work, the nature of the languages, the versions and the printed and manuscript copies we use, and their antiquity, their authority and use in the early Church, and what advantage this edition may have over others. We reserve a fuller treatment of all these matters for another work, in which we will, as far as we are able, work out all the questions that arise concerning both the original texts and the versions, and which we reserve for the Biblical Apparatus.

units.la: ¹1. Primo itaq; Lingua una inter omnes homines ante confusionem Babylonicam viguisse, præter Sacras literas Gen. 11.1. agnoverunt etiam Ethnici, ut ex Abydeni testimonio apud Eusebium & Cyrillum, & Sibyllæ apud Josephum, constat. Linguæ autem unitas ut magnum erat humano mano generi indultū beneficium, societatis scilicet vinculum; sic linguarum divisio horrendum erat irati Numinis judicium; societatis enim humanæ dissipatione minabatur: quod necessario eveniret, si tot essent linguæ quot homines, sic enim nec pater filium, nec maritus uxorem intelligere posset; quod ne eveniret, non singulis hominibus, sed singulis potius familiis peculiarem dialectum vel linguam Deum immisisse, quò in unam Coloniam melius coalescere possent, verisimile videtur. In hoc tamen summa emicuit Dei bonitas & providentia, (qui etiam ex malis bonum extrahere novit,) ut homines qui turrim Babylonicam construebant ne dispergerentur, linguarum divisione per omnes terras, quas filiis hominum colendas dedisset Deus, dispersi, earúmq; fructus ubique percipientes, gratâ linguarum harmoniâ Creatoris beneficentiam celebrarent; quód-que primò divinæ vindictæ signum erat, postea nascentis Ecclesiæ exordio, sic Deo volente, magnum esset amoris divini indicium: cùm qui primò linguarum varietatem in hominum animos immisit, ut dispergerentur; idem etiam linguarum donum inter alia χαρίσματα[?] Apostolis aliisque divinâ virtute contulit, ut Ecclesiam per orbem dispersam, palantésque Christi oves, in unum ovile colligerent, & pluribus linguis Τὰ μεγάλεια τῆς θεοῦ[?] prædicarent. Postquam enim Christus Dei filius, qui patris mandata Syro sermone Judæis exequutus fuerat, cœlos conscenderat, Spiritum Sanctum ad discipulos misit, eosque afflatu suo variarum linguarum peritissimos fecit; ut hisce cœlestis militiæ armis, quæ Turris Babylonicæ ædificatoribus ne cœlum arrogantiâ suâ ascendere viderentur, quondam obstiterant, ( principe hujus mundi à gubernaculis dejecto ) terrarum orbis vitus ad Deum Creatorem reduceretur, & Ecclesia, Dei domus, cujus fastigium cœlos omnes exsuperat, iisdem fundamentis æternum duratura ædificaretur.
units.tr: 1. First, then, that there was one language among all men before the confusion at Babel, the Gentiles also acknowledged, besides the Sacred Letters [Gen. 11.1], as is clear from the testimony of Abydenus in Eusebius and Cyril, and of the Sibyl in Josephus. Just as the unity of language was a great benefit granted to the human race, namely the bond of society, so the division of languages was a dreadful judgment of an angry Deity, for it threatened the dissolution of human society. This would necessarily have happened if there had been as many languages as men, for then neither a father could understand his son nor a husband his wife. To prevent this, it seems probable that God sent a particular dialect or language not to individual men but rather to individual families, so that they might more easily unite into one colony. Yet in this the supreme goodness and providence of God shone forth (for he knows how to bring good even out of evil): that the men who were building the Tower of Babel, lest they be scattered, were dispersed through all the lands which God had given the sons of men to inhabit by the division of languages, and, enjoying their fruits everywhere, might celebrate the Creator's beneficence with the pleasing harmony of tongues. And what was at first a sign of divine vengeance would, at the beginning of the rising Church, by God's will become a great token of divine love. For the one who first put the variety of languages into men's minds so that they would be scattered, the same one also bestowed the gift of languages upon the Apostles and others by divine power, among other gifts [charismata], so that they might gather the Church dispersed throughout the world and the wandering sheep of Christ into one fold, and proclaim "the mighty works of God" [ta megaleia tēs theou] in many tongues. For after Christ, the Son of God, who had carried out the Father's commands for the Jews in the Syriac tongue, had ascended into heaven, he sent the Holy Spirit to the disciples and, by his inspiration, made them most skilled in various languages. With these weapons of the heavenly army, which had once stood in the way of the builders of the Tower of Babel, lest they seem to raise themselves to heaven in their arrogance, the prince of this world having been cast from the helm, the globe of the earth was to be restored to God the Creator, and the Church, the house of God, whose summit surpasses all the heavens, was to be built upon the same foundations, to endure for ever.

units.la: 3. Cum vero quod prædicabant Apostoli, postea eodem spiritu afflati Scriptis consignarent, quo doctrina cœlestis posteris perennis esset; linguam Græcam elegerunt Spiritus S. amanuenses, ut omnium aptissimam in qua mysteria salutis toti orbi traderentur, sicut Hebraicam elegerat Deus in qua voluntatem suam Judæis patefaceret: unde maxima linguarum istarum prærogativa præ aliis orta est, ut ex iis seu fontibus, omnes nationes in proprias linguas, tanquam canales, aquam vivam haurirent, & utraque lingua Sancta encomio merito celebrari debeat.
units.tr: 3. When, however, the Apostles, afterwards inspired by the same Spirit, committed to writing what they preached, so that the heavenly doctrine might be lasting for posterity, the Holy Spirit's scribes chose the Greek language, as the most suitable of all in which the mysteries of salvation were to be handed down to the whole world, just as God had chosen the Hebrew language in which to reveal his will to the Jews. Hence arose the great pre-eminence of these two languages over the others, so that all nations might draw living water from these sources, as from channels, into their own tongues, and both languages ought rightly to be celebrated with the praise of being holy.

units.la: 4. Sacra itaque Scriptura, mysteriorum salutis Thesaurus, & sacrum doctrinæ cœlestis scrinium, vel ipsis Apostolorum temporibus, vel paulò post in varias linguas, Syram, scil. Arabicam, Armenam, Ægyptiacam, Indam, &c. testibus Chrysostomo, Hieronymo, Theodoreto & aliis, traducta erat: quas versiones cum Ecclesia per orbem disseminata, veritatis firmamentum & columna, cui oracula Dei concredita sunt, ut textibus authenticis conformes, & omnia ad salutem necessaria dogmata complectentes approbaret; non potuit aptius inveniri medium, quo Sacrorum Codicum tum integritas, tum sensus et vera intelligentia, vel in omnes nationes propagari, vel ab omni labe & corruptela (quæ vel à librariorum negligentia & audacia irrepere possent, vel Hæreticorum & Schismaticorum fraude & astutiâ qui textum corrumpere semper sategerunt ) vindicari possent, quàm versionum istarum cum textibus Originalibus collationem instituere, utráque etiam fideliter collata posteris transmittere : quod enim in una aliqua lingua fortasse efficere possent Hæretici, corruptionem aliquam inducendo, in tam multis longè latéque per orbem sparsis versionibus efficere nunquam potuerunt.
units.tr: 4. Therefore Sacred Scripture, the treasury of the mysteries of salvation and the holy chest of heavenly doctrine, was translated into various languages, Syriac, namely, Arabic, Armenian, Egyptian, Indian and others, either in the very times of the Apostles or a little after, as witnessed by Chrysostom, Jerome, Theodoret and others. Since the Church, spread throughout the world, the pillar and foundation of truth, to whom the oracles of God have been entrusted, approved these versions as conforming to the authentic texts and comprehending all the doctrines necessary for salvation, no more apt means could have been found by which the integrity of the sacred codices, their sense and true understanding, could both be propagated to all nations and be defended against every stain and corruption. Such corruption could creep in either through the negligence and rashness of copyists, or through the fraud and cunning of heretics and schismatics, who always strove to corrupt the text. This means was the collation of these versions with the original texts, and the faithful handing down to posterity of both, once collated. For what heretics might perhaps have accomplished in one single language, by introducing some corruption, they could never accomplish in so many versions scattered far and wide through the world.

units.la: §. 5. Versiones itaque antiquæ præsertim Orientales, tum ratione affinitatis quam habent cum linguis Originalibus, tum authoritatis & usus generalis in primæva Ecclesia, optima sunt media ad verum locisensum in obscuris indagandum, verámque lectionem in dubiis vel depravatis restituendam. Cùm enim Autographa tam veteris quàm novi Testamenti hodiè non habeantur, ad quæ recursus haberi poterit in dubiis & variantibus, quæ occurrunt, lectionibus ; Apographa verò omnia ab hominibus errori obnoxiis exscripta [?]sint, quique infallibilem assistentiam Spiritûs Sancti non habuerint, licèt ut ipsis originalibus conformia essent, quantùm potuit, invigilárit Ecclesiæ diligentia, quin tamen in quibusdam varia lectiones essent, sieri non potuit ; ut ex exemplaribus optimis & vetustissimis clarè constat: ita tamen invigilante Divinâ providentiâ ut in omnibus adsidem & salutem necessariis magnus sit in omnibus consensus, omnéque varietates in rebus minoris momenti reperiantur : qui quidem inter tot versiones consensus, quæ variis seculis facta, & apud tot gentes tantâ locorum intercapedine inter se dissitas, nulloque inter se nexu nisi ejusdem fidei colligatas fideliter servatæ sunt, vel pervicacem suadere possit, doctrinam horum librorum alium Authorem quam Deum non agnoscere, qui tam mirabiliter contra Sathanæ ejusq; satellitum furores, qui sacros hosce Codices non tantum adulterare, sed prorsus extirpare omnibus viribus contenderunt, hactenus eos conservavit.
units.tr: §. 5. Ancient versions, especially the Oriental ones, therefore, both because of their affinity with the original languages and because of their authority and general use in the primitive Church, are the best means for searching out the true sense in obscure passages and for restoring the true reading in doubtful or corrupted places. For since the autographs of both the Old and New Testaments are no longer extant, to which recourse could be had in cases of doubtful or variant readings that occur, and since all the copies have been transcribed by men liable to error, who did not possess the infallible assistance of the Holy Spirit, the diligence of the Church has taken care, as far as it could, that they should conform to the originals; yet it was not possible that in some places there should be varying readings, as is clear from the best and most ancient copies. Nevertheless, under the watchful providence of God, there is great agreement in all matters necessary for faith and salvation, and all the variations are found in matters of minor importance. This agreement among so many versions, made at various ages and faithfully preserved among so many peoples, separated from one another by such great intervals of places and bound together by no connection except the same faith, could persuade even a stubborn person that the doctrine of these books has no author other than God, who has so wonderfully preserved them until now against the rages of Satan and his satellites, who have striven with all their power not only to adulterate these sacred codices but utterly to destroy them.

units.la: 6. In varietatibus autē ut vera lectio eliciatur, quodnam melius vel excogitari poterit medium, quàm optimorum exemplarium & vetustissimarum Versionum collatio, eamq; lectionem quæ cum pluribus, vetustioribus, & melioris notæ libris locisque circumstantiis melius congruit, retinere? Hanc viam iniérunt Hieronymus, Cyrillus, Eusebius, Augustinus reliquique Ecclesiæ antiquæ proceres; eandem Masorethæ Tiberienses in recensendo textu Hebræo, Mercerus, Buxtorfius, &c. in emendandis Targumim; Erasmus, Stephanus, Beza & alii in N.Test. Editionibus Græcis; eandem deniq; inierunt Sixtus 5. & Clem.8. in Græca 70. Vulgataque Latina Editionibus, ut ex Nobilio, Morino, Luca Brugensi aliisque patet.
units.tr: 6. But in cases of variant readings, what better method could be devised for eliciting the true reading than to collate the best copies and the most ancient versions, and to retain the reading that agrees best with the larger number of older and more reliable manuscripts and with the circumstances of the passage? Jerome, Cyril, Eusebius, Augustine and the other leading figures of the ancient Church followed this path. The Tiberian Masoretes did the same in revising the Hebrew text, and Mercerus, Buxtorf and others in emending the Targums. Erasmus, Stephanus, Beza and others did so in their Greek editions of the New Testament. Finally, Sixtus V and Clement VIII followed the same path in their editions of the Greek Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate, as is clear from Nobilius, Morinus, Lucas of Bruges and others.

units.la: 7. Nec tantum ad lectionem veram, sed & ad genuinum sensum indagandum confert versionum antiquarum collatio; quomodo enim ipsa priscæ Ecclesiæ Lumina Scripturā intellexerint, quemque sensum receperint, hoc modo nobis indicant. Cumq; hodie inter tot schismata, quæ Ecclesiam præcipuè Occidentalem miserè dilacerant, omnes Scripturam pro se allegent, deque Scripturæ vero & genuino sensu lis tota fit & controversia; per versiones ubique receptas totius fere Ecclesiæ, ta locorum quam temporis ratione Catholicæ judicium um in promptu habemus, quæ de locis controversiis sensum suum nobis aperit: cujus judicio qui se submittere nolit, profectò se nullo judicio præditum esse offendit, & vix hominis nedum Christiani nomine dignus erit; qui enim omnem veteris & Catholicæ Ecclesiæ fidem derogat, nul-lam sibi relinquit. Æquissimi enim habendi sunt arbitri, nulloque partium studio in trans-versum abripi possunt, qui longè retroactis seculis ante lites & controversias nostras exortas vixerunt, sacrumque depositum, quod ipsi à majoribus per manus acceperant, fideliter nobis reliquerunt.
units.tr: 7. The collation of ancient versions helps not only to discover the true reading but also to search out the genuine sense. For they show us how the bright lights of the early Church understood Scripture and which sense they accepted. Today, amid so many schisms which wretchedly tear apart the Church, especially in the West, everyone appeals to Scripture in his own favour, and the whole dispute is over the true and genuine sense of Scripture. Through the versions received everywhere by almost the whole Church, both in place and in time, we have at hand the judgment of the universal Church, which opens up to us its sense on controverted passages. Whoever refuses to submit to that judgment shows that he has no judgment at all and is scarcely worthy of the name of man, let alone of Christian. For whoever detracts from the faith of the old and catholic Church leaves himself no faith at all. Those who lived long before our disputes and controversies arose must be regarded as the fairest of judges. They cannot be swept sideways by any partisan zeal, and they have faithfully handed down to us the sacred deposit which they had themselves received from their elders.

units.la: 8. Utilissimum itaq; gravissimumq; erat Decretum Concilii Viennensis sub Clemente 5 celebrati, ut in Academiis essent linguæ Hebraicæ, Arabicæ, & Chaldaicæ Professores publici; qui linguas istas docerent, & libros ex ipsis in linguam Latinam transferrent, ad fidei propagationem, & infidelium faciliorem conversionem.
units.tr: 8. Therefore the decree of the Council of Vienne, celebrated under Clement V, was most useful and weighty: that in the universities there should be public professors of the Hebrew, Arabic and Chaldee languages, who would teach these tongues and translate books from them into Latin, for the propagation of the faith and the easier conversion of unbelievers.

units.la: 9. In seculo hoc nostro, quo literæ humaniores quasi revixerunt, maximo Ecclesiæ commodo & cum æterno ipsorum honore laborarunt viri longè doctissimi in editionibus Bibliorum, unà cum versionibus quibusdam antiquis; inter quas præter Bombergi editiones plures Venetiis, Buxtorfii Basileæ, Vatabli Parisiis, Munsteri, Hutteri & aliorum, maximè eminent, & palmam reliquis eripuerunt, 1. Complutensis, 2. Antuerpiensis, 3. nupera Parisiensis.
units.tr: 9. In this our age, when the humane letters have, as it were, come back to life, very learned men have laboured, to the great benefit of the Church and to their own everlasting honour, on editions of the Bibles together with certain ancient versions. Among these, besides the editions of Bomberg at Venice, of Buxtorf at Basel, of Vatablus at Paris, and of Münster, Hutter and others, three stand out most and have carried off the palm from the rest: (1) the Complutensian, (2) the Antwerp, and (3) the recent Parisian.

units.la: 1. Complutensis labore ac studiis Theologorum quorundam Complutensis Academiæ, impensis verò Cardinalis Ximenii Archiepiscopi Toletani, sex voluminibus comprehensa Anno 1510. in lucem prodiit, complectens praeter vetus Testamentum Hebræum, & Vulgatam Latinam, versionem 70 interpretum Græcam cum translatione Latina, Onkelosi Chaldaicam Pentateuchi cum translatione Latina, Testamentum Novum Græco-Latinum, & Apparatum, in quo quædam Grammaticæ, Lexica, indices, &c.
units.tr: 1. The Complutensian, produced by the labour and studies of certain theologians of the University of Alcalá, at the expense of Cardinal Ximenes, Archbishop of Toledo, appeared in 1510 in six volumes. Besides the Hebrew Old Testament and the Latin Vulgate, it contains the Greek version of the Seventy with a Latin translation, the Chaldee Pentateuch of Onkelos with a Latin translation, the Greek-Latin New Testament, and an apparatus in which there are some grammars, lexicons, indexes and so on.

units.la: 2. Antuerpiensis priori multo perfectior tum versionum quarundam accessione, tum typorum, & chartæ elegantia ac splendore, 8 voluminibus comprehensa, quam sumptibus Philippi Regis Hispaniarum (unde Biblia Regia vocantur) summa fidelitate & cura edidit Arias Montanus Anno 1572. qui Complutensibus addidit 1 Chaldaicam Paraphrasim in reliquum vetus Test. cum versione Latina. 2. Interlinearem versionem tam veteris quàm novi Testamenti. 3. Syriacos N. Test. libros, tam Syriacis, quàm Hebraicis characteribus descriptos opera Guidonis Fabritii Boderiani, cum Apparatu magno, in quo varia Lexica, Grammaticæ, cum tractatibus quibusdam ad meliorem textus intelligentiam, varia quædam lectiones, indices, &c.
units.tr: 2. The Antwerp edition, far more perfect than the earlier one both through the addition of some versions and through the elegance and splendour of its type and paper, was published in eight volumes, with the greatest fidelity and care, at the expense of Philip, King of Spain (whence it is called the Royal Bible). Arias Montanus edited it in 1572. To the Complutensian he added: (1) a Chaldee paraphrase of the rest of the Old Testament with a Latin version; (2) an interlinear version of both the Old and the New Testament; (3) the Syriac books of the New Testament, written in both Syriac and Hebrew characters, the work of Guido Fabritius of Bodeor, with a great apparatus containing various lexicons, grammars, some treatises for a better understanding of the text, various readings, indexes and so on.

units.la: 3. Parisiensis in 10 magnis Tomis prodiit, An. 1645. impensis viri clarissimi D. Michaelis de Jay, qui licet vir privat°, animo tamen excelso & plane Regio propriis sumptibus opus edidit, quo a primis literarum incunabulis non vidit orbis, Ecclesia omnibusque Theologiæ & literarum studiosis, utilius; ut quod Biblia Regia, quæ Orbis miraculum a quibusdam dicebantur, multis parafangis superet, idque non tantum typorum & chartæ bonitate & magnificentia, sed adjectis aliis quibusdam antiquis Monumentis nunquam antehac evulgatis; Samaritano (scil. Pentateucho cum versione Samaritana, toto etiam veteri Test. Syriaco; Et tam veteri quam novo Arabico. Dolendum vero Apparatum & Prolegomena,cum Appendice in ultimum tomum rejecta, quæ ad operis complementum pertinebant,ex dissidio eorum qui operi præfuerunt,adhuc desiderari;quodque editiones quas protulit hæc ætas limatiores, quam quæ in Complutensi & Regio opere erant, non secuti sint : de quibus post hac plura.
units.tr: 3. The Parisian edition appeared in ten large tomes in 1645, at the expense of the most illustrious Michel de Jay. Although he was a private individual, with a lofty and truly royal spirit he published the work at his own cost. Since the first beginnings of letters the world, the Church and all students of theology and literature have not seen anything more useful than this work. It surpasses the Royal Bible, which some called the wonder of the world, by many leagues, and this not only in the goodness and magnificence of its type and paper but also through the addition of certain other ancient monuments never published before: the Samaritan Pentateuch with a Samaritan version, the whole Old Testament in Syriac, and both the Old and New Testaments in Arabic. It is to be lamented, however, that the apparatus and prolegomena, together with an appendix which were thrown into the last tome and which belonged to the completion of the work, are still lacking because of the quarrel among those who presided over the work. Also, they did not follow the more polished editions that this age has produced, which were not in the Complutensian and Royal works. More on these things hereafter.

units.la: 10.Cum ante[?] nihil simul inchoatū & perfectū sit, ut olim Orator, & pigri sit ingenii contentum esse his quæ ab aliis inventa sunt, ut ait Seneca. Epist. 8. nemo nobis vitio vertet si de nova editione Bibliorum cogitemus, præsertim cum non sic nova cudimus, ut vetera destruamus, ut Hieronym. Epist. ad Chromatium. Salvo itaque omnium honore qui prioribus editionibus insudarunt, quorum labores omnes pii & doctissimi[?] semper magni æstimabunt, Editionem molimur (favente Deo) prioribus perfectiorem usuique studiorum magis accommodatam; quæ licet tam variis antiquis versionibus, aliisque quæ in prioribus non habentur, auctior[?], quam exemplarium optimorum delectu Bibliis prioribus longe accuratior sit, multo tamen minori pretio constabit: De qua paucis in præsentiarum lectori rationem reddimus.
units.tr: 10. Since nothing is perfect from the start, and, as the orator said of old, it is the mark of a lazy mind to be content with what others have discovered, as Seneca says (Epist. 8), no one will blame us if we think about a new edition of the Bibles, especially as we do not forge new things in order to destroy old ones, as Jerome says (Epist. to Chromatius). Therefore, with full respect for all who have laboured on the earlier editions, whose labours all pious and most learned men will always esteem highly, we undertake (God willing) an edition more perfect than the earlier ones and better suited to the use of study. Although it is richer in the various ancient versions and other materials not found in the earlier editions, and is far more accurate than the earlier Bibles through a choice of the best copies, it will cost much less. We give the reader a brief account of it for the present.

units.la: 11. Primum sibi locum merito vendicat Textus Hebraicus; linguam enim hanc Deus primis parentibus infudit, suamque voluntatem in hac hominibus primo patefecit, unde a plerisque omnium antiquissima censetur: licet inter Patres Theodoretus, inter recentiores Maronita, Myricaus, aliique primas dent Chaldaicæ; quidam etiam linguam primam, quâ ante Diluvium homines untebantur, nullibi proprie extare, sed ejus reliquias in omnibus linguis reperiri volunt, ut magnus ille literarum Dictator H. Grotius, Annot. in Gen. 11.
units.tr: 11. The Hebrew text rightly claims first place. For God infused this language into our first parents and first revealed his will to men in it, whence it is judged by most to be the most ancient of all. Although among the Fathers Theodoret, and among more recent writers the Maronite and Myricaeus and others, give the first place to Chaldee, and some want the first language, in which men spoke before the Flood, not to exist anywhere properly, but its remains to be found in all languages, as the great dictator of letters, H. Grotius, holds (Annotations on Genesis 11).

units.la: 1. Controversiam istam hic nostram non facimus, de qua reliquisq; quæ ad Hebraicas literas, puncta, Textumque pertinent, alibi dicemus. Hoc à plerisque pro certo sumitur, quod cum à Creatione ad captivitatem Babylonicam per annos circa 3400. durasset, vulgaris esse desiit, nec ullibi vernacula fuit. Judæi enim à captivitate reduces, cum 70 annis inter Assyrios mixti essent, linguam ex Hebraica & Chaldaica seu Syra mixtam in patriam intulerunt: unde fit quod nullibi hodie nisi in veteris Test. libris extet sermo puré Hebraicus. Quod si quis objiciat Jacobi posteros quibusdam annorum Centuriis in Ægypto vixisse, linguam tamen suam puram conservasse: sciendum est, Hebraicam majorem cum Chaldaea quam cum Ægyptiaca habere affinitatem, ideoq; facilius cum Chaldaea commutari posse; praeterea in Ægypto simul habitabant Hebræi integram posfidentes terram Goschen, cum in Assyria & Babylonia dispersi essent singùli inter dominos suos, quorum lingua uti necessario cogebantur. Observatione etiam dignum est illud doctissimi Brocharti, (qui multa de linguis antiquis nobis supeditavit) Babylonem semper Hebraicæ linguæ fatalem fuisse, tum ob linguarum confusionem ibi factam, tum quod Judæi captivi ibi linguam patriam dedidiscerint. Nil etiam mutationi magis obnoxium esse quam linguas, quæ in perpetuo fluxu sunt, ostendit in Historia Latinitatis Melchior Inchoferus, omniáque regna Occidentalia clarè demonstrant. Quantum Hetrusca & Latina hodierna ab antiqua recesserint, ex inscriptionibus & Tabulis Eugubinis Hetruscis literis antiquis exaratis, & ex columnis rostratis, quas nemo adhuc explicavit, cuivis constat; quantaque ex variarum gentium sinitimarum confluxu oriantur corruptelæ, in omnibus Europæ linguis quotidiè conspicimus, ut bene observat doctiss. Kircherus. Idcirco linguæ omnes, quas libri scripti à communi clade non servant, vicissitudini, ut omnia humana, semper obnoxiæ sunt, & singulis seculis insignem mutationem subeunt.
units.tr: 1. We do not raise here the controversy over this, nor the other questions which concern the Hebrew letters, the points and the text; we shall speak of them elsewhere. It is taken as certain by most that, having lasted from the Creation to the Babylonian captivity for about 3400 years, it ceased to be the common language and was nowhere the vernacular. For the Jews returning from captivity, having been mixed for seventy years among the Assyrians, brought into their homeland a language mixed of Hebrew and Chaldee or Syriac; whence it comes that today pure Hebrew speech is found nowhere except in the books of the Old Testament. But if anyone objects that the descendants of Jacob lived in Egypt for some centuries yet preserved their language pure, it must be known that Hebrew has greater affinity with Chaldee than with Egyptian, and so could more easily be exchanged for Chaldee. Moreover, in Egypt the Hebrews lived together, possessing the whole land of Goshen, whereas in Assyria and Babylonia they were scattered, each among his own masters, whose language they were necessarily compelled to use. It is also worth observing what the most learned Bochart (who has handed down to us much about the ancient languages) said: that Babylon was always fatal to the Hebrew language, both because of the confusion of tongues made there and because the Jewish captives there unlearned their native tongue. Melchior Inchofer, in his History of Latinity, also shows that nothing is more subject to change than languages, which are in perpetual flux, and all the Western kingdoms clearly demonstrate this. How far the modern Etruscan and Latin have departed from the ancient is known to everyone from inscriptions and from the Eugubine Tables written in ancient Etruscan letters, and from the rostral columns which no one has yet explained. And how great corruptions arise from the mingling of neighbouring peoples we see every day in all the languages of Europe, as the very learned Kircher rightly observes. Hence all languages which written books do not preserve from the common ruin are, like all human things, always subject to vicissitude, and undergo a notable change in every age.

units.la: 12. De Hebraica tamen, ut observant quidam, hoc maximè notandum, eam esse omnium purlissimam sine ulla vocum peregrinarum mixtura, quæ in Chaldæa & Syra frequentissima; esse quoque Chaldaicâ multò simpliciorem, ideóque antiquiorem, cùm Chaldaica multa vocabula inter se diversissima ad unicam radicem Hebraicam reducantur.
units.tr: 12. Some writers observe that the Hebrew language, above all, should be noted as the purest of all, without any mixture of foreign words, such as are very frequent in Chaldee and Syriac. It is also much simpler than Chaldee and therefore older, since many Chaldee words that differ widely from one another are traced back to a single Hebrew root.

units.la: 13. Antiqua autem hujus-linguæ elegantiam & utilitatem prædicare idem ferè esset ac Soli facem accendere. Elegantiam ejus suprà Græcam & Latinam fusè ostendit Erpenius eleganti de hac lingua oratione, orat. scil. 3. p. 106, 107, &c. Juásq; veneres habere, maximè dum de sacris agitur, quas cætera linguæ exprimere non valent, nõrunt omnes: vix ulla est lingua ex hac non prognata, ut in reliquis linguis Orientalibus clarum; imò pleráq; Græca Themata originis esse Hebraicæ ostendit idem Erpenius dictâ oratione: literárumque tum nomina tum ordinem in Alphabeto, in omnibus ferè linguis, ab Hebraâ fluxisse, demonstrant Acrosticha vetustissima in Psalmis, & Hieremiæ Threnis.
units.tr: 13. To proclaim the ancient elegance and usefulness of this language would be much the same as lighting a torch for the sun. Erpenius has set out its elegance at length, above Greek and Latin, in his elegant oration on this language, namely Oration 3, pp. 106, 107, and following. Everyone knows that it has its own graces, which other languages cannot express, especially when sacred matters are under discussion. There is hardly any language that is not descended from it, as is clear in the other Oriental languages. Indeed, Erpenius shows in the same oration that most Greek roots are of Hebrew origin. The most ancient acrostic poems in the Psalms and in the Lamentations of Jeremiah demonstrate that both the names and the order of the letters of the alphabet came from the Hebrew in almost all languages.

units.la: Utilitatem vero longe maximam esse dubitari non potest, cum Deus ipse humanum genus hac lingua primo allocutus sit, fœdusque quod cum Judæis pepigit hac lingua confirmari voluerit; adeo ut ad veteris Test. sensum indagandum non tantùm utilis sed & necessaria sit ejus cognitio, imò nec Græca τῶν 70. versio, nec versiones Latinæ sæpè intelligi possint sine archetyporum inspectione: unde S. Hieronymus inter patres, ob hujus linguæ peritiam, multò fœlicius assecutus est genuinum Scripturæ sensum, quàm alii qui nec doctrinâ nec ingenio ipsi erant impares.
units.tr: But the usefulness of the language is far greater, and it cannot be doubted. God himself first addressed the human race in this language, and he willed the covenant he made with the Jews to be confirmed in it. So the knowledge of it is not merely useful but necessary for understanding the sense of the Old Testament. Indeed, neither the Greek version of the Seventy nor the Latin versions can often be understood without inspecting the originals. For this reason St. Jerome, on account of his skill in this language, attained the genuine sense of Scripture far more happily than others among the Fathers, who were not inferior to him in learning or talent.

units.la: 14. Hebraicum itaque textum V.T. tanquam versionum omnium fundamentum in opere hoc Biblico subjiciernimus, cui adjuncta est versio interlinearis Pagnini & B. Ariæ Montani, magno, ni fallor, discentium commodo, nullo verò veteranorum incommodo qui hac non egent: qui enim Hebraicè callent, omittere hanc versionem possunt. Pagnini verò ubi ab interlineari differt versionem margini non adscripsimus, ut nec verborum radices (quarum investigatio pueris è trivio nota) ne margini satis angusto essent oneri: ipsos tamen Pagnini variantes locos, ne lector integrà Pagnini versione (optimâ sanè) fraudaretur, in ultimum tomum rejecimus. Cùm enim Vulgata Latina in omnibus Hebræo non respondeat, hoc merito in Parisiensibus culpat Valerianus Flavigny nuper Regius professor Hebraicꝰ Lutetiæ, in Epistolis quas de Heptaplis Parisiensibus (stylo licèt nimis acerbo) edidit, quòd nullam translationem habeant, quæ Hebræo ad amussim respondeat.
units.tr: 14. Accordingly, we have placed the Hebrew text of the Old Testament under this biblical work as the foundation of all the versions. To it is added the interlinear version of Pagninus and of Benedictus Arias Montanus. This will be, unless I am mistaken, of great convenience to learners and of no inconvenience to veterans, who do not need it, for those skilled in Hebrew may omit this version. Where Pagninus differs from the interlinear version, we have not added his version to the margin, so that the roots of the words (whose investigation is familiar to schoolboys) would not burden the rather narrow margin. Nevertheless, so that the reader would not be deprived of Pagninus's complete version (which is certainly excellent), we have relegated his variant passages themselves to the last volume. For the Vulgate Latin does not correspond to the Hebrew in all places, and Valerianus Flavigny, recently royal professor of Hebrew at Paris, rightly blames the Parisian (Polyglot) for this. In the letters on the Parisian Heptaplus which he published (although in a rather harsh style), he complains that they have no translation that corresponds exactly to the Hebrew.

units.la: Exemplar verò secuti sumus Antuerpiense, collatis insuper vetustis quibusdam MSS. Bibliis, & aliis melioris notæ impressis, Venetis, Basileensibus aliisque, etiam Manassis Ben Israel, nuper Amstelodami ab ipso magnâ diligentiâ editis. Distinctionem verò capitum & versuum ab Ecclesiâ hodiè receptam secuti sumus, omissis Iudæorum Parashis & Sidris, de quibus tamen in Apparatu. Varias verò lectiones, seu Keri, & Ketib, cum jetir, & Chaser, &c. de quarum origine, usu, numero, &c. magnâ hodiè inter doctos agitantur controversiæ (de quibus cū aliis ad Majoram spectantibus in Apparatu) circello, notisque pro more usitatis, additiones singulas notamus. Literas etiam majusculas, & minusculas, suspensas, inversas, &c. cum vocibus non punctatis, & quæ punctas vocales habent sine literis, in quibus mysteria magna inesse credunt nonnulli cum Rabbinis, licet magni haud æstimanda, ne aliquid deesse quisquam suspicaretur, retinuimus. Punctationem etiam usitatam, licet à Maforethis textui appositam, adhibuimus; non quòd ipsorum authoritate nitatur, sed quòd ab Ecclesiâ Christiana, cui tam Hebraicorum V. Testamenti quàm Græcorum Novi fœderis voluminum cura à Deo mandata est, queque semper etiam in densissimis ignorantiæ tenebris, exemplaria Hebr. MSS. in Bibliothecis habuit, virôsque quosdam tam hujus quàm aliarum linguarum peritos, recepta est. Non enim ad Iudæos ex quo populus Dei esse desierunt, sed ad Ecclesiam Christianam pertinuit codicum Hebraorum custodiam; nec enim est punctatio vera quia à Maforethis, sed quia concordat cum vero vocalium sono, quem Spiritus tus S. dictavit: aliud enim non fecerunt Masorethæ quàm vocales punctis exprimere secundum veram lectionem, quam à majoribus per traditionem acceperant, hanc verò, quia veram, etiam suo consensu firmavit Ecclesia Christiana.
units.tr: We have followed the Antwerp edition, having also collated some old manuscript Bibles and other printed editions of better repute, from Venice, Basel and elsewhere, and also that of Manasseh ben Israel, recently edited with great diligence by him at Amsterdam. We have followed the division into chapters and verses now received by the Church, omitting the Jewish parashiyot and sidrim, though these are discussed in the Appendix. We have marked each addition with a small circle and the usual notes, the various readings, that is, the Keri and Ketib, with the jetir and chaser, and so on, concerning whose origin, use, number and so forth there are today great controversies among the learned (these, together with others relating to the Masora, are treated in the Appendix). We have also retained the capital and small letters, the suspended and inverted letters, and so on, together with the words that are not pointed and those that have vowel points without letters, in which some, with the Rabbis, believe great mysteries lie hidden. Though these are not to be valued highly, we have retained them lest anyone suspect that something is lacking. We have also used the customary pointing, though it was added to the text by the Masoretes. Not that it rests on their authority, but because it was accepted by the Christian Church, to which God entrusted the care of the books both of the Hebrew Old Testament and of the Greek New Testament, and which, even in the thickest darkness of ignorance, always kept copies of the Hebrew manuscripts in its libraries and some men skilled in this language and in others. For the custody of the Hebrew codices has belonged not to the Jews, since they ceased to be the people of God, but to the Christian Church. The pointing is not true because it is from the Masoretes, but because it agrees with the true sound of the vowels, which the Holy Spirit dictated. For the Masoretes did nothing more than express the vowels by points according to the true reading which they had received from their forebears by tradition; and this reading, because it is true, the Christian Church has also confirmed by its consent.

units.la: 15. Post Hebraicum proximum sibi locum vendicat textus Hebræo-Samaritanus; ut qui de antiquitate characterum cum hodierno Hebraico contendat. Dicuntur verò Samaritani, à Samaria regni Metropoli, sicut & Cuthæi à regione Cutha in Perside, ut Ioseph.antiq.l.9.c.1. unde novas colonias introduxit Salmanassar. Character verò Samaritanus idem est cum antiquo Hebraico, quo lex primò à Mose tradita, & Decalogus digito Dei descriptus, qui apud Judæos in usu erat, donec post reditum è captivitate Babylonica Esras, qui Legem et Prophetas cum viris magnæ Synagogæ pristino nitori restituit, charactere Assyriaco, qui tunc Judæis exulibus magis notus erat, sacra volumina conscripserit; veterem Samaritanis relinquens, inter quos & Judæos, capitale semper erat dissidium. Hanc communem doctorum sententiam, à Christianis & Judæis, antiquis & recentioribus receptam, Hieronymo, scil. Theodoreto, Scaligero in Eusebium, Drusio, Fullero, Grotio, Lud. Capello, Mayero, Erpenio, Bellarmino, Villalpando, Morino, aliisque viris longè doctissimis & Hebraicæ linguæ peritissimis, præter utrumque Talmud, & plerosq; Rabbinos quos videre licet apud Morinum & alios, reperti sunt quidam neoterici qui in quæstionem vocant, infirmis quibusdam ratiunculis nixi ex præjudicatis suis opinionib'[?] haustis, à quibus potiùs quàm vel tantillùm recedere videri vellent, ipsum Solem meridie lucere negarent. Si verò Scaliger omnes contra-sentientes, pro more suo, semi-doctos, semi-theologos, vel semi-homines, nec pro aliis quàm asinis habendos, Drusius verò quasi alteros Carneades esse, qui de rebus omnib⁹ dubitare solent, censebant, cùm tamen neuter eorum vel Pentateuchum Samaritanum viderit, (cujus varia jam extant inter nos Exemplaria MSS.) alio sve doctorùm tractat⁹ de hoc argumento; quànâ censura eos notarent qui adhuc contra clarissima rationum momenta contrariam sententiam afferunt, si hodie viverent?
units.tr: 15. After the Hebrew, the Hebrew-Samaritan text claims the next place, since it contests with the present Hebrew the antiquity of its characters. The Samaritans are so called from Samaria, the metropolis of the kingdom, just as the Cutheans are called from the region of Cuthah in Persia, as Josephus says (Antiquities, book 9, ch. 1), whence Shalmaneser introduced new colonies. The Samaritan character is the same as the ancient Hebrew, in which the law was first delivered by Moses and the Decalogue written with the finger of God, and which was in use among the Jews until, after their return from the Babylonian captivity, Ezra restored the Law and the Prophets to their former splendour with the men of the Great Synagogue, and wrote the sacred books in the Assyrian character, which was then better known to the Jews in exile, leaving the old character to the Samaritans, between whom and the Jews there was always a deadly enmity. This common opinion of the learned, received by Christians and Jews, ancient and recent, is held by Jerome, Theodoret, Scaliger on Eusebius, Drusius, Fuller, Grotius, Louis Cappel, Mayer, Erpenius, Bellarmine, Villalpando, Morinus, and other very learned men most skilled in the Hebrew language, as well as by both Talmuds and most of the Rabbis, as may be seen in Morinus and others. Yet some modern writers have been found who call it into question, relying on some weak little arguments drawn from their own prejudiced opinions, and who would rather seem not to depart from those opinions even a little, and would deny that the sun shines at midday. If Scaliger, in his manner, thought that all who disagreed were half-learned, half-theologians, or half-men, to be regarded as nothing but asses, and Drusius thought them to be like a second Carneades, who are wont to doubt everything, though neither of them ever saw the Samaritan Pentateuch (several manuscript copies of which now exist among us), and though there is another treatise by learned men on this subject, with what censure would they mark those who still advance the opposite opinion against the clearest weight of reasons, if they were alive today?

units.la: 16. Hoc quidem ex Historia sacra constat, post defectionem à Rehoboamo, decem tribus Jeroboamo & Regibus Israelis adhæsisse, quorum regia sedes tandem facta est Samaria, sicut Hierosolyma Regum Judæ; unde Schisma in Religione factum, quo, alio loco & tempore ab aliisque sacerdotibus quàm lex postulabat colebatur Deus: lex tamen Mosis mansisse videtur, ejusque doctrina etiam inter 10. Tribus vigebat, quod sine exemplaribus Pentateuchi fieri non potuit. Cùm verò à Salmanassare abducti erant 10. Tribus, & alienigena in eorum locum introducti, qui Deum verum ignorantes à leonibus infestabantur, misit Rex unum è sacerdotibus captivis, qui legem Dei ipsos doceret; unde licèt cum Idolorum suorum cultu mixta, legem tamen Mosis & cultu ab ipso præscriptu gentes ista profitebantur: adeo ut de se testarentur Samaritani. Esr. 4.
units.tr: 16. It is certain from sacred history that after the defection from Rehoboam, the ten tribes adhered to Jeroboam and to the kings of Israel, whose royal seat at last became Samaria, just as Jerusalem was that of the kings of Judah. Hence a schism arose in religion, by which God was worshipped at another place and time, and by priests other than the law required. Yet the law of Moses seems to have remained, and its teaching flourished even among the ten tribes, which could not have happened without copies of the Pentateuch. When the ten tribes had been carried away by Shalmaneser and foreigners introduced in their place, who, not knowing the true God, were attacked by lions, the king sent one of the captive priests to teach them the law of God. Hence, although these peoples were mixed with the worship of their idols, they nevertheless professed the law of Moses and the worship prescribed by him, so that the Samaritans bore witness to themselves. Ezra 4.

units.la: 1. Zorobabeli & populi primoribus, se Deum eorum quærere, & ipsi sacrificasse à diebus Esarhaddon, qui illos istuc transtulit. Dubitare etiam nemo potest sacerdotem illum legem attulisse, non aliis characteribus descriptam, quam quibus Israelitæ à Mose ad illum usque diem usi fuerant: ab eo autem tempore Samaritanos antiquis literis Hebraicis, saltem in lege describenda, usos fuisse nulla est ratio cur dubitemus. Postea constat, ex Neh.13.4.28. Et Josephi Antiq.l.11.c.7,8. Manasse Jaddi Pontificis fratrem eo quod repudiare nollet uxore quâ duxerat filiâ Sanballati Samariæ præfecti, sacerdotio exutu ad socerū confugisse, qui templum alterum in monte Gerizim construxit, Hierosolymitano simile, in quo Manasses sacerdotio functus est apud Samaritanos, & quidem ritibus Mosaicis secundum legem (quâ habuisse eos & servâsse vero consentaneum est) et ad ipsum multi ex Judæis confugerunt qui reformationi ab Esrafastæ se submittere nollent. Hinc schisma & dissidium magis invaluit, utrisque legem Mosis profitentibus & se mutuo anathemate ferientibus, hocque non tantum stante utroque templo, sed & post utrumq; vastatum, & utri-usq; partis sequaces cum tota gente dissipatos: adeo ut non liceret Judæo cum Cuthæo seu Samaritano panem comedere, juxta adagium, Qui comedit panem Samariticum, æque est ac si comederet carnem suillam. Refertque Drusius de 3. Sectis Judæorum. lib.3.c. 11. ex Tanchuma, solennem excommunicationem Samaritanorum jactam ab Ezra & Nehemia.
units.tr: 1. To Zerubbabel and the leaders of the people, that they sought their God and had sacrificed to him since the days of Esarhaddon, who had transported them there. No one can doubt that this priest brought the law written in no other characters than those which the Israelites had used from Moses down to that day. From that time there is no reason for us to doubt that the Samaritans used the ancient Hebrew letters, at least in writing the law. Afterwards it is established, from Nehemiah 13:4, 28, and from Josephus, Antiquities, book 11, chs. 7, 8, that Manasseh, brother of the high priest Jaddua, because he would not put away the wife he had married, a daughter of Sanballat, governor of Samaria, was deprived of the priesthood and fled to his father-in-law, who built a second temple on Mount Gerizim, similar to that at Jerusalem, in which Manasseh served as priest among the Samaritans, and indeed in accordance with the Mosaic rites under the law, which it is consistent with the truth to suppose they had and kept. Many of the Jews also fled to him who were unwilling to submit to the reformation of Ezra. Hence the schism and division grew stronger, both parties professing the law of Moses and pronouncing anathema upon each other, and this not only while both temples stood, but also after both were destroyed and the followers of each side were scattered along with the whole nation. So much so that a Jew might not eat bread with a Cuthean or Samaritan, according to the proverb: Whoever eats Samaritan bread is just as if he ate swine's flesh. Drusius, in his work on the three sects of the Jews, book 3, ch. 11, reports from the Tanchuma that the solemn excommunication of the Samaritans was pronounced by Ezra and Nehemiah.

units.la: 17.Habent itaq; Samaritani Mosis Pentateuchum, quem ad hunc usque diem in Sichem, Damasco, aliisque locis ubi habitant ipsorum reliquiæ, publicè legunt, antiquis characteribus descriptum, quique non multum differt ab hodi-erno. erno Judaico, nisi vel ubi scribarum negligentia, vel exemplarium varietas diversitatem quandam intulit: vix enim alicubi corruptio spontanea invenitur, nisi ubi ad astruendam templi sui authoritatem mons Gerizim in textu positus sit pro monte Ebal. Deut.s.21. & 27.4. & Exod.20.17. & versus quaedam transpositi ex Deut.11.29,30. & 27.4. Nam licet Dositheus quidam Samaritanorum princeps, qui pro Messia se venditabat, loca aliqua dicatur corrupisse, ut se Messiam esse probaret; istas tamen corruptelas, omnia exemplaria non invasisse, vel exemplaria postea emendata suisse, liquido constat ex hodiernis exemplaribus, quae cum hodierno Masorethico collata, nullas istiusmodi corruptelas exhibent, praesertim ubi de Messia agitur, sed (minutis quibusdam exceptis) prorsus cum eodem conveniunt, ut in iis etiam locis qui ex Samaritano codice citantur ab Hieronymo, Scholiaste Graeco & aliis e veteribus: adeo ut Samaritanicum codicem eundem esse qualem supra 1000 annos, & quem citant patres, concedat Flavig. licet authenticum esse vel eandem cum Hebraico authoritatem habere merito neget. Imo in locis quibusdam dubiis & perplexis Hebraeo lucem adferre & facilem dubiorum solutionem, ex quibus sine codice Samaritano se vix quisquam extricare possit, vident & agnoscunt multi, & nos posthac plenius docebimus.
units.tr: 17. The Samaritans therefore have the Pentateuch of Moses, which to this day they publicly read in Shechem, Damascus, and the other places where their remnants live, written in ancient characters, and it does not differ much from the present-day Jewish text, except where the carelessness of scribes or variant copies have introduced some difference. Scarcely anywhere is there spontaneous corruption, except where Mount Gerizim has been put into the text in place of Mount Ebal, to support the authority of their temple (Deut. 5.21, 27.4; Exod. 20.17), and some verses have been transposed (Deut. 11.29-30, 27.4). For although a certain Dositheus, a prince of the Samaritans who passed himself off as the Messiah, is said to have corrupted some passages in order to prove that he was the Messiah, it is clear from present-day copies that these corruptions did not infect all copies, or that the copies were corrected afterwards. When these copies are compared with the present Masoretic text, they show no such corruptions, especially where the Messiah is concerned, but agree entirely with it, apart from a few minor exceptions. The same is true of the passages which Jerome, the Greek scholiast, and others among the ancients cite from the Samaritan codex. So Flavius concedes that the Samaritan codex is the same as it was more than a thousand years ago, and as the Fathers cite it, though he rightly denies that it is authentic or has the same authority as the Hebrew. Indeed, many see and acknowledge that in certain doubtful and perplexing passages it sheds light on the Hebrew and offers an easy solution to difficulties from which hardly anyone could extricate himself without the Samaritan codex; we shall teach this more fully hereafter.

units.la: 18. Eo vero quod asserit quidam, Samaritanum Pentateuchum ex Graeca 70. Seniorum versione descriptum fuisse, quod in multis locis cum hac congruat, ubi utrumq; ab Hebraico variat, probabilius multo est exemplaria illa vetera Hebraica, unde suam transtulerunt 70. versionem, eadem fuisse cum Samaritano, & a codice hodierno Maforethico in quibusdam variasse, ut alibi dicemus.
units.tr: 18. As for the claim of some that the Samaritan Pentateuch was copied from the Greek version of the Seventy Elders, because it agrees with that version in many places where both differ from the Hebrew, it is far more probable that those ancient Hebrew copies from which the Seventy made their translation were the same as the Samaritan, and differed in some respects from the present Masoretic codex, as we shall say elsewhere.

units.la: 19. Quódq; affirmat doctiss.Grotius, Samaritanos a Justiniano coactos fuisse suos codices ad verfionem 70, emendare, hoc ex conjectura sua, & (pace tanti viri dixerim) sine certo fundamento dictum: Edictum quidem edidit Imperator pro Judæis, qui 70. versionem in Synagogis legebant, contra aliorum Judæorum tyrannidem, qui post libros Hebraicos a Maforethis correctos, alios omnes abolebant, & anathemate percutere vellent omnes qui Græcam versionem publice legebant; liberúmq; fecit omnibus Græcam translationem usurpare fi vellent, ut ex Novella constat 146. at nullos compulit nec Judæos, nec Samaritanos, huic versioni suos codices conformes reddere; imò contrarium liquido constat ex innumeris locis, in quibus exemplaria Samaritana a versione Græca differunt.
units.tr: 19. As for the assertion of the most learned Grotius that Justinian compelled the Samaritans to correct their codices to agree with the Septuagint, this was said on his conjecture and, with respect to so great a man, without sure foundation. The Emperor indeed issued an edict in favour of the Jews who read the Septuagint in their synagogues, against the tyranny of other Jews who, after the Hebrew books had been corrected by the Masorites, wished to abolish all others and to strike with anathema all who publicly read the Greek version; and he allowed everyone to use the Greek translation if they wished, as appears from Novella 146. But he compelled neither Jews nor Samaritans to make their codices conform to this version; on the contrary, it is clear from countless passages that the Samaritan copies differ from the Greek version.

units.la: 20. Recipiunt vero Samaritani tantum Mosis quinque libros: reliquos Historicos, Propheticos, &c. non habent, nec traditiones, quas Judæi cum verbo scripto æquant, agnoscunt: cujus causa hæc mihi videtur, quod Pentateuchus fœdus inter Deum & populum, cultumque cum promissis & minis quæ ad omnes pertinebant, quorumque cognitio Judæis omnibus necessaria erat, in se continebat, ideóque Exemplaria quæ inter populum dispersa erant, ex quibus sacerdotes & Levitæ plebem instruebant, non erant nisi quinq; libri Mosis, reliqui vero libri Prophetici & Historici, licet in Templo asservarentur, & a sacerdotibus, & doctis legerentur, omnibus tamen non ita noti erant: propterea cum primum Schisma inter 12 Tribus factum est, Canon Scripturæ V.Test. nondum constitutus erat: nec enim omnes libri Historici, et ex Propheticis vix ulli extabant, cumque Prophetæ sub Regibus Judææ ut plurimum prophetarent, eorumque prophetiæ in Templo tantum servatæ essent; reliquæ tribus, quæ sub alio erant regimine, istiusmodi libros parum curabant, cum propter dissidium quod indies augebatur, tum quod Prophetæ multa contra 10. Tribus et reges Israel ob cultum corruptum vaticinabantur. Imo cum non ante Esræ [?] tempora, à viris Magnæ Synagogæ post multas disceptationes Canon in formam hodiernam redactus esset (imo ut quibusdam placet post Antiochi tempora) non mirum est Samaritanos, qui tum præsertim capitales inimicitias cum Judæis exercebant, omnes libros præter Pentateuchum, quem antiquitus semper habebant, rejecisse. Afferunt quidam, Mosen 12.legis exemplaria descripsisse quæ inter 12. Tribus dispersa erant, præter unum quod in arca fœderis servatum est; Jactántque Samaritani se unum habere ex Autographo descriptum in diebus Phinehas filii Eleazar, quod adhuc in Sichem ad montem Gerizim servatur; quod quidem, si verum esset, magnam apud omnes authoritatem haberet: sed donec exemplar istud producant et genuinum esse demonstrent, haud aliam authoritatem ipsorum exemplaribus deferendam judico, quam aliis Apographis antiquis quæ quæ lapsus aliquot injuria temporum, & scribarum inscitiâ, negligentiâ vel audaciâ habere possunt.
units.tr: 20. The Samaritans, however, accept only the five books of Moses; they do not have the remaining historical and prophetic books, nor do they recognise the traditions which the Jews place on a level with the written word. The cause of this seems to me to be that the Pentateuch contained the covenant between God and the people, with the worship, and the promises and threats which applied to everyone, and whose knowledge was necessary for all Jews. Therefore the copies dispersed among the people, from which the priests and Levites instructed the common folk, were only the five books of Moses. The remaining prophetic and historical books, although they were kept in the Temple and read by priests and learned men, were not so well known to everyone: therefore, when the first schism among the twelve tribes occurred, the canon of the Old Testament had not yet been fixed. For not all the historical books existed, and scarcely any of the prophetic books did; and since the prophets mostly prophesied under the kings of Judah, and their prophecies were kept only in the Temple, the other tribes, which lived under a different government, cared little for such books, both because of the division which grew daily and because the prophets often prophesied against the ten tribes and the kings of Israel on account of their corrupt worship. Moreover, since the canon was not reduced to its present form until after the time of Ezra (indeed, as some think, not until after the time of Antiochus), by the men of the Great Synagogue after many disputes, it is no wonder that the Samaritans, who especially at that time waged mortal enmity against the Jews, rejected all the books except the Pentateuch, which they had always possessed from ancient times. Some assert that Moses wrote twelve copies of the law, which were dispersed among the twelve tribes, apart from the one kept in the ark of the covenant; and the Samaritans boast that they have one copy written from the autograph in the days of Phinehas the son of Eleazar, which is still preserved at Shechem on Mount Gerizim. If this were true, it would have great authority with everyone. But until they produce that copy and demonstrate that it is genuine, I judge that their copies deserve no greater authority than other ancient transcripts which may contain some errors through the wrongs of time and the ignorance, negligence or boldness of scribes.

units.la: 21. Verum quidem est quod afferunt Jofeph. l.9. & l.12,c 1. Et Epiphanius Hæref. 9. Samaritanos, licèt cùm primùm legem receperunt, etiam Idola et cultus Idololatricos retinuerunt, postea tamen cùm Templum habuerunt in monte Gerizim, Deum verum diligenter coluisse, et hoc unicum studuisse, ut Idolorum repudiatâ superstitione verum Deum agnoscerent, patriarumque institutionum tenacissimos fuisse. Licèt enim eorum Templum à Joh. Hircano eversum fit 200. annis post jactá ejus fundamenta, & postea Herodes Samariam à fundamentis extruxerit, ejusque in medio templum ingenti sumptu condiderit, Samaritani tamen spreto Herodis templo,in monte Gerizim sacrificia et preces semper obtulerunt, ut ex Evangelio constat Joh. 4. & ex hodierna consuetudine, quâ eorum Pontifex Sichimis ad montem Gerizim sedet, Samaritanis reliquis imperat, iisque Paschatis & festorum tempora quotannis literis circularibus definit, ut de iis post Scaligerum testatur dictus Morinus.
units.tr: 21. It is true, as Josephus (books 9 and 12, chapter 1) and Epiphanius (Heresy 9) state, that the Samaritans, when they first received the law, also retained idols and idolatrous worship; but afterwards, when they had their temple on Mount Gerizim, they diligently worshipped the true God and made this their one aim, namely, that, having rejected the superstition of idols, they might acknowledge the true God, and they were most tenacious of the institutions of their fathers. For although their temple was overthrown by John Hyrcanus about two hundred years after its foundations were laid, and Herod afterwards built Samaria from the foundations and erected a temple in its midst at great expense, the Samaritans nevertheless, scorning Herod's temple, always offered sacrifices and prayers on Mount Gerizim, as is clear from the Gospel (John 4), and from the present custom by which their High Priest sits at Shechem on Mount Gerizim, commands the rest of the Samaritans, and each year fixes for them the times of the Passover and the festivals by circular letters, as the said Morinus testifies after Scaliger.

units.la: 22. Quod autem παραδόσεως[?] seu traditiones quæ in Mifehna à R. Jehuda collectæ sunt, et corpus utriusque Talmudis constituunt, rejiciunt, mirandum non est; cùm traditiones ipsæ (licèt omnes ad Mosem, et traditionem è Monte Sinai, impudenter referant Judæi) à Pharisæis primùm introductæ sint, quorum ortu[?] fuit circa tempora Maccabæorum, multò pos[?] Schisma Samaritanum, & nisi à R. Jehuda[?] quem Hakkadosch, ob eximiam, scil. sanctitatem vocant, in unum corpus digestæ essent, & in Talmud relatæ, fortasse inter tot Judæorum exilia & dispersiones tam Judæis ignotæ essent quàm Samaritanis.
units.tr: 22. It is no wonder that they reject the traditions which R. Judah collected in the Mishnah and which make up the body of both Talmuds, since the traditions themselves (although the Jews shamelessly trace them all to Moses and to the tradition from Mount Sinai) were first introduced by the Pharisees, whose origin was around the time of the Maccabees, long after the Samaritan schism; and unless they had been digested into one body by R. Judah, whom they call Hakkadosch, that is, for his remarkable holiness, and set down in the Talmud, perhaps among so many exiles and dispersions of the Jews they would have been as unknown to the Jews as to the Samaritans.

units.la: 23. Exemplaria verò MSS. Samaritana Pentateuchi, licèt ab Hieronymi tempore Christiani fere ignota & tenebris quasi sepulta jacuerint, multa tamen huj' ævi diligentia in lucem protulit, Johannes Morinus vir doctiss. cui multum o[?] labores in Samaritano Pentateucho docti omnes debent, 4 habuit exemplaria, quibus usus est in editione Parisiensi; unum quidem integrum, reliqua verò manca & lacerata: de quibus ut & de duobus codicibus versionis Samaritanæ ipse in præfatione ad Biblia, & in exercitationibus in Pentat. Samaritanum, & in præf. ad Biblia Græca 70 editionis Parisiensis.
units.tr: 23. The manuscript copies of the Samaritan Pentateuch, although from the time of Jerome they lay almost unknown to Christians and buried as it were in darkness, have been brought to light by the great diligence of this age. The most learned Johannes Morinus, to whom all scholars owe much for his labours on the Samaritan Pentateuch, had four copies, of which he used one complete copy and the rest incomplete and torn, for the Paris edition. He speaks of these, and of two codices of the Samaritan version, in his preface to the Bible, in his exercitations on the Samaritan Pentateuch, and in his preface to the Paris edition of the Greek Septuagint.

units.la: 24. Reverendiss. verò Doctissimúsque noster Armachanus, vir ad bonum reipublicæ literariæ natus, qui(que) primùs erat, vel inter primos qui Samaritanum Pentat. in Europam intulerunt, varia exemplaria ex partibus Orientalibus magnis sumptibus comparavit, quorum tria nobis communicavit, quæ magno nobis adjumento fuerunt. Duo habent Pentateuchum Hebraeo-Samaritanum, tertium imperfectum cum Textu Samaritano Arabicam versionem, at literis Samaritanis exaratam, exhibet, accuratam, scil. & cum judicio fallam: à quo verò, vel quo tempore Arabica hæc versio facta fit, conjicere non possum, exemplar verò descriptum erat à quodam Ab Helion circa annum Christi, 1514. Hæc autem cum Parisiensi contulit, & multa quæ Parisiense ubi deficiebat, supplere, lectionem veram restituere, & dubia quædam elucidare possint, collegit vir doctus, quæ in ultimum tomum relegantur : interpretationem etiam Latinam versionis Samaritanæ, ubi à textu Hebraeo-Samaritano differebat, ad singulas columnas idem adjecit. Licet enim unâ eandemque versionem Latinam utrique Samaritano inservire posse, afferat Morinus, in multis tamen differre, ex adjectis ad finem columnarum quilibet facile perspiciet, ut nil dicam de versione Morini Latina, quæ multis in locis nec Textui Samaritano, nec ejus versioni sed potius Vulgatæ Latinæ congruit, neutriusque ferfu apte exprimit, ut in Annotationibus ad calcem operis postea patebit : utque differentias Samaritani Textus ab Hebraeo Lectior-simul intueri poterit, hasce omnes collectas ex variis Exemplaribus habebit, una cum locis omnibus in quibus Samaritani & LXX. conveniunt, utrique vero ab Hebraeo dissentiunt, quæ omnia sacræ criticæ studiosis haud ingrata futura arbitror.
units.tr: 24. Our most reverend and most learned Archbishop of Armagh, a man born for the good of the republic of letters, who was the first, or among the first, to bring the Samaritan Pentateuch into Europe, at great expense procured various copies from the Eastern lands, and three of them he gave to us, which were of great help to us. Two contain the Hebrew-Samaritan Pentateuch; the third, which is imperfect, presents the Samaritan text with an Arabic version, written in Samaritan letters, accurate and, indeed, with judgement. I cannot conjecture by whom or when this Arabic version was made, but the copy was written out by a certain Abu Hilyon around the year of Christ 1514. He collated this with the Paris edition, and gathered together, in a learned collection which is relegated to the last volume, many things which can supply what the Paris edition lacked, restore the true reading, and clarify certain doubtful points. He also added to each column the Latin interpretation of the Samaritan version, wherever it differed from the Hebrew-Samaritan text. For although Morinus asserts that one and the same Latin version can serve for both Samaritan texts, it differs in many places, as anyone can easily see from the additions at the foot of the columns. To say nothing of Morinus's Latin version, which in many places agrees neither with the Samaritan text nor with its version, but rather with the Latin Vulgate, and does not aptly express either's meaning, as will later become clear in the notes at the end of the work. And so that the differences of the Samaritan text from the Hebrew may be seen together more readily, he will have all these gathered from the various copies, together with all the places in which the Samaritan and the Septuagint agree but both differ from the Hebrew. I think all of these will not be unwelcome to students of sacred criticism.

units.la: 25. Versionis vero Samaritanæ Dialectum quod attinet, ejusdem est cum lingua Chaldaica cognationis; voces tamen non paucas habet sibi proprias & peculiares: Arabicis etiâ nonnunquam utitur. In formatione tam Nominum, quàm Verborum modo Hebraicæ, modo Chaldaicæ regulis conformatur. Hoc insuper (erroris identidem ut vitetur suspicio) prænonere visum est, nempe, quod literarum homoorganicarum commutatione abundat ista versio quàm sæpissime ; nec non aliarum etiam , quæ vel iis propiores sunt, vel figurâ similes : adeò ut intra unam vel alteram lineam eadem vox aliquando variè exprimatur.
units.tr: 25. As for the dialect of the Samaritan Version, it is related to the Chaldee language, but it has not a few words of its own and peculiar to it, and sometimes it uses Arabic words too. Its formation of both nouns and verbs follows now Hebrew and now Chaldee rules. Moreover, so that the suspicion of error may be avoided, I have thought it right to warn in advance that this version very often interchanges letters with the same organ of speech, and also others that are either closer to them or similar in shape, so that within a line or two the same word is sometimes rendered in different ways.

units.la: 26. Post Hebraicâ, & Samaritanâ, Chaldaicâ (quæ Hebraicæ dialectus) nobis maximè commendant, antiquitas, utilitas, et addiscendi facilitas. In scriptura sæpius vocatur Aramæa seu Syra, & Dan. 1.4. לשון כשדים [?] lingua Chaldæorum.
units.tr: 26. After Hebrew and Samaritan, Chaldee (which is a dialect of Hebrew) most commends itself to us for its antiquity, its usefulness, and the ease of learning it. In Scripture it is often called Aramaic or Syriac, and in Dan. 1.4 "the language of the Chaldeans" [לשון כשדים].

units.la: 27. Antiquitas tanta est ut à nonnullis prima, omnium linguarum mater habeatur, multáq; profert argumenta ad hoc probandum Georg. Amyra in præf. Grammaticæ suæ Syriacæ. Doctissimus etiam Erpenius, adhuc sub judice litem esse affirmat, utrùm Hebraica, an Chaldaica sit antiquior. Dignitatis verò multum huic linguæ adfert, quòd post confusionem Babylonicam, hominumque dispersionem, in primo maximóq; regno post Diluvium vernacula fuerit, Chaldæorum, (scil. quorum rex, Rex Regum appellatur, Dan. 2.37. & per aureum caput ejus Regnum ut omnium nobilissimum & amplissimum repræsentatur. Vestigium hujus vetustissimum extat, Gen. 31. 47. ubi tumulus testimonii à Labane Syro vocatur יגר סהדותא [?] jegar sahadutha, à Jacobo verò lingua Hebraicâ גלעד Galed, vel Galaad. Hæc lingua etsi Hebraicæ vicina fuit, Judæorum tamen vulgus ante captivitatem eam non intellexisse constat, ex Jer. 5.15. Quàm verò necessaria & utilis sit ejus cognitio, ex hoc colligitur, quòd multa capitula in Scripturis Spiritus S. hac lingua consignari voluit, In Daniele, (scil. à Cap. 2. v. 4. ad Cap. 8. In Esra. à Cap. 4. v. 8. ad v. 27. Cap. 7. In Jeremia verò unicum comma, Cap. 10. v. 11.
units.tr: 27. Its antiquity is so great that by some it is regarded as the first and mother of all languages, and George Amyra in the preface to his Syriac grammar brings forward many arguments to prove this. The most learned Erpenius also affirms that the question is still undecided, whether Hebrew or Chaldee is the older. It adds much to the dignity of this language that after the confusion of Babel and the dispersion of men, it was the vernacular in the first and greatest kingdom after the Flood, that of the Chaldeans (whose king is called "King of kings," Dan. 2.37, and through whose golden head the kingdom is represented as the most noble and most extensive of all). The most ancient trace of this survives in Gen. 31.47, where the heap of testimony is called by Laban the Syrian [יגר סהדותא] jegar sahadutha, but by Jacob in the Hebrew language [גלעד] Galed or Galaad. Although this language was close to Hebrew, it is established that the common people of the Jews did not understand it before the captivity, from Jer. 5.15. How necessary and useful its knowledge is can be gathered from this: that the Holy Spirit wished many chapters of Scripture to be written in this language: in Daniel (namely from chap. 2 v. 4 to chap. 8), in Ezra from chap. 4 v. 8 to v. 27, and chap. 7; in Jeremiah only a single verse, chap. 10 v. 11.

units.la: 28. Præter hæc multa sunt loquendi formulæ, ver[?]ique non pauca in Canonicis Hebræorum bris, quæ sine hujus linguæ cognitione explicari vix possunt. Maxime vero hujus linguæ utilitatem nobis commendant Antiquissimæ paraphrases, circa Christi tempora scriptæ, quæque parem fere authoritatem apud Judæos habent cum ipso Textu Hebraico. Onkelosi, scil. in Legem, qui Συνάγωγον[?] erat Rabban Gamaliel S. Pauli præceptoris, quem perperam aliqui cum Aquila confundunt, qui longo tempore post Templi excidium vixit. Jonathanis, in Prophetas, quos vocant, priores; scil. libros Judic. Sam. & Regum, & posteriores, majores [scil. & minores (excepto Daniele:)] De hoc referunt Rabbini, cùm Targum suum scriberet, si forte vel musca in chartam insideret, igne cœlesti statim consumptam fuisse.
units.tr: 28. Besides these, there are many forms of speech and not a few verses in the canonical books of the Hebrews which can hardly be explained without knowledge of this language. But the most ancient paraphrases, written around the time of Christ, especially commend the usefulness of this language to us, and they have almost the same authority among the Jews as the Hebrew Text itself. Onkelos, namely on the Law, who was the synagogue leader [Συνάγωγος] of Rabban Gamaliel, the teacher of St Paul, whom some wrongly confuse with Aquila, who lived a long time after the destruction of the Temple. Jonathan, on the so-called former Prophets, namely the books of Judges, Samuel and Kings, and on the latter, the greater and the lesser (except Daniel). The rabbis report about him that when he was writing his Targum, if a fly perchance settled on the paper, it was immediately consumed by heavenly fire.

units.la: 29. Cùm enim lingua Hebraica post Captivitate, ut diximus, vulgo ignota fuerit, in subsidium popularium suorum quasdam Paraphrases conscribere cœperunt, quæ, ut quibusdam videtur, in Synagogis post Textum publicè prælecta erant: quod probabile magis fit ex antiquis quibusdam MSS. Chaldaicis Paraphrasibus, quarum unam se vidisse testatur Buxtorfius, aliam vero ipse habeo ex Bibliotheca Westmoniast. complectentem Pentateuchum, pulchrè & in magno folio exaratam, quàm in excidio Hormi in sinu Persico inter spolia à militibus emit & in Angliam intulit Mercator quidam Londinensis: aliúdque Volumen eodem modo scriptum doctissimo viro Tho. Gatakero donatum erat, complectens Psalmos & Isaiam. In hisce MSS. scriptus est Textus Hebraicus cum Paraphrasi Chaldaica, non per distinctas columnas, nec per lineas a se invicem separatas: sed post unum versiculum Hebraicum continuo sine ulla lineæ abruptione repetitur idem Chaldaice, adeo ut linguarum ignaris pro uno eodemque continuo orationis contextu in una eademque lingua videri possint. Hoc vero morem antiquum apud Judæos referre volunt, ab Esra temporibus usitatum, quo post Textum Hebraicè prælectum, explicatio vel verbo tenus, ut a Levitis Nehem. 8. 7. vel ex scripto, ut ævo posteriori, in lingua populo nota, fieret.
units.tr: 29. For since the Hebrew language after the Captivity, as we have said, was generally unknown, to help their people they began to write certain paraphrases, which, as some think, were read publicly in the synagogues after the Text. This is more probable from certain ancient manuscript Chaldee paraphrases, one of which Buxtorf testifies he saw, and another of which I myself have from the library of Westminster, containing the Pentateuch, beautifully written in a large folio, which a certain London merchant bought from soldiers during the sack of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf and brought into England.
