Another volume written in the same way was given to the most learned Thomas Gataker, containing the Psalms and Isaiah. In these manuscripts the Hebrew Text is written together with the Chaldee paraphrase, not in separate columns nor divided by lines; but after each Hebrew verse the same is repeated continuously in Chaldee without any break in the line, so that to those ignorant of languages it may appear to be one continuous discourse in one and the same language. They wish this to refer to an ancient custom among the Jews, in use from the time of Ezra, by which, after the Hebrew Text had been read aloud, an explanation was given, either word for word by the Levites (Neh. 8.7) or, in later times, in writing, in the language known to the people.

units.la: 30. Paraphrases verò ista quantum ad textus intelligentiam conferant, quantúmque ad Judæos convincendos, maximè in Articulo illo fundamentali de Messia, in quo explicando nobiscum prorsus consentiunt, contra ineptas & impias posteriorum Rabbinorum corruptelas, doctis notum, ita ut hic immorari supervacaneum esset. Buxtorfii p. verba tantum referam in præf. Gram. Syriacæ et Chald. Infinitæ sunt Linguæ Hebrææ voces obscuræ, locutiones irregulares, schemata ambigua, quæ ex Chaldæa lucem & explanationem accipiunt; sensum etiam Hebræi textus Chaldæa Paraphrasis sæpe concordiâ suâ corroborat, contractum dilatat, et explicatione illustrat.
units.tr: 30. How much these paraphrases contribute to understanding the texts, and how much to convincing the Jews, especially on that fundamental article concerning the Messiah, in explaining which they agree entirely with us, against the foolish and impious corruptions of the later rabbis, is known to scholars, so it would be superfluous to dwell on it here. I shall quote only the words of Buxtorf in the preface to his Syriac and Chaldee grammar: "The obscure words of the Hebrew language are innumerable, and so are its irregular expressions and ambiguous constructions, which receive light and explanation from the Chaldee. The Chaldee paraphrase often confirms by its agreement the sense of the Hebrew text, contracts it, widens it, and illustrates it by explanation.

units.la: 31.De singulis vero Paraphrasibus audiamus Buxtorfium f. præfatione ad Lexicon Chaldaico-Syriacum. Onkelos Pentateuchum transtulit, qui ut stylum simpliciorem & ad Danielis & Esræ puritatem magis accedentem habet, sic maximè literalis est, verbum fere de verbo reddens. Jonathan Prophetarum Paraphrastes in prioribus tum in sermone tum in re simplex est: In posterioribus qui obscuriores, paulò liberior, & allegoriis nimis indulgens. De Targum Hagiographorum (quod Josepho Caco ascribitur circa 600. post natum Christum annos) ex historia Hebraica nil certi habetur, authores varios fuisse ex stylo apparet, et præcedentibus longè recentiores. Targum Megilloth seu 5. librorum scil. Cantic. Thren. Ruth. Ecclesiastes et Esther, post Talmud consarcinatum est (quod 500. ad minimum post Christum annis obsignatum est) cujus expressa fit in illo mentio. Cant. 1. 2. Thren 2. 19. Linguæ etiam dialectus impurior ad Syro-Hierofolymitanum accedens, et ut prolixius esse solet, sic pluribus allegoriis refertum, idemque judicium est de Targum Hierofolymitano, altero Jonathanis in Legem, et de secundo Targum in Esther. Hactenus Buxtorfius. (Quum vero Paraphrases illæ præsertim antiquiores ante punctorum inventionem scriptæ fuerint, literaque [illegible, ~3 letters] matres lectionibus pro omnibus vocalibus inservirent, quae post appositā punctā saepe anomaliam inserebant, hinc imperfecta extitit punctatio, variaque absurda in Targumim relicta, quorum quaedam à Complutensibus reformata, in Bibliis Regiis plura, quamplurima verò fatente Ariā Montano sine emendatione relicta, tandem immensis Buxtorfii P. laboribus plerâque[?], quae in prioribus medelam postulabant, curata & integritati restituta erant, omnibus ad analogiam Esrae & Danielis reductis, ut ex Bibliis magnis Basileensibus. liquet. Commentarium quoque inscriptum Babel paravit, in quo, teste ipsius doctiss. filio, omnis differentia ratio redditur, & ex locorum collatione illustratur, omniaque quae ulterius animadversa & magnum medicam requirebant ad integritatem revocata sunt, adeò ut cum hoc evulgatum fuerit (sub prelo verò esse brevi proditurum nuper accepimus) pristinum Babyloniā nitorem hac lingua recuperasse videri possit. Chaldaicam itaque Paraphrasim Onkelosi in Pentateuchum, Ionathanis in Prophetas, et Iosephi Caeci in Hagiographa cum reliquis secundum editionem Basileensem, quae omnium quae hodie extant maximè emendata, in Bibliis nostris exhibemus. Latinam verò sequimur versionem quae in Regiis, nisi ubi à Basileensibus differt, quae differentia alio charactere notata est Parisienses enim (consilio an casu nescio) Chaldaicam, licèt ex Regiis & Basileensibus mixtam fecerint, Latinam tamen non Chaldaica respondentem, sed eandem quæ in Regiis ubique retinent. Collatio item facta est cum reliquis editionibus & MSS. quibusdam, & cum doctissimi P. Fagii versione Onkelosi Latina, variaque lectiones cum observationibus & notis (quæ à viro docto qui huic operis parti incumbit collecta sunt) ad appendicem referuntur.
units.tr: 31. Let us hear about the individual paraphrases from Buxtorf the son, in the preface to his Chaldee-Syriac lexicon. Onkelos translated the Pentateuch; since he has a plainer style, and comes closer to the purity of Daniel and Ezra, he is most literal, rendering almost word for word. Jonathan, the paraphraser of the Prophets, is simple in the earlier books, both in style and in matter; in the later books, which are more obscure, he is somewhat freer and too indulgent in allegories. Nothing certain is known about the Targum of the Hagiographa (which is ascribed to Joseph the Blind, around 600 years after the birth of Christ) from Hebrew history; it is clear from the style that there were various authors, and they were much more recent than the earlier ones. The Targum of the Megilloth, that is, of the five books, namely Canticles, Lamentations, Ruth, Ecclesiastes and Esther, was compiled after the Talmud (which was sealed at least 500 years after Christ), and explicit mention of it is made in that work: Cant. 1.2; Lam. 2.19. The dialect of the language is also more impure, approaching Syro-Jerusalemite, and, as is usual with longer works, it is filled with many allegories; the same judgment applies to the Jerusalem Targum, the second Targum of Jonathan on the Law, and the second Targum on Esther. So far Buxtorf. (Since indeed those paraphrases, especially the earlier ones, were written before the invention of the points, and since the letters [illegible] served as vowel-letters for all the vowels, which after the points were added often introduced irregularity, the pointing was therefore imperfect and many absurdities were left in the Targumim. Some of these were corrected by the Complutensians, many more in the Royal Bible, but very many, as Arias Montanus admits, were left without correction. At last, by the immense labours of Buxtorf the father, most of those things which needed a remedy in the earlier editions were cured and restored to integrity, all being brought back to the analogy of Ezra and Daniel, as is clear from the large Basel Bible. He also prepared a commentary entitled Babel, in which, as his most learned son testifies, the reason for every difference is given and illustrated by comparison of passages, and everything that was further noticed and needed great remedy has been restored to integrity; so that, now that this has been published (we have recently heard that it will shortly appear from the press), the ancient splendour of Babylon may seem to have been recovered in this language.) We therefore exhibit in our Bibles the Chaldee paraphrase of Onkelos on the Pentateuch, of Jonathan on the Prophets, and of Joseph the Blind on the Hagiographa, along with the rest, according to the Basel edition, which is the most emended of all that survive today. We follow the Latin version in the Royal Bible, except where it differs from the Basel edition; this difference is marked with another type. For the Parisians (by design or by chance, I do not know) made the Chaldee text a mixture of the Royal and Basel editions, yet retained for the Latin not the Chaldee-corresponding version but the same one that the Royal Bible keeps everywhere. A collation has also been made with the other editions and some manuscripts, and with the Latin version of Onkelos by the most learned Paul Fagius; the various readings, together with the observations and notes (which were collected by the learned man who has taken charge of this part of the work), are referred to the appendix.

units.la: 32. Hisce verò quæ maxima authoritatis sunt, Paraphrases duas alias, minoris licèt pretii, utiles tamen, adjungemus, scil. 1. Targum Jonathanis (ut dicitur) in Legem cum versione Latina. Jonatha ascribunt ex Judæis multi, et ex Christianis Galatinus, Paulus Fagius, Helvicus & alii; negant tamen plerique ejus esse, Buxtorfius scil. Drusius, &c. Schickardus in medio relinquit & concludit. Bechin. Hap. p. 35. Cujuscunque sit authoris vel antiquitatis plurimum nobis profuturum contra Judaicos commentatores, cum vaticinia quæ illi ad Davidem et alios referunt, de unico et solo Messia recte et prorsus Christiane exponat.
units.tr: 32. To these most authoritative works we will add two other paraphrases, of lesser value but still useful, namely: 1. The Targum of Jonathan (as it is called) on the Law, with a Latin version. Many Jews, and among Christians Galatinus, Paulus Fagius, Helvicus and others, ascribe it to Jonathan; but most deny that it is his, namely Buxtorf, Drusius, etc. Schickard leaves the question open and concludes. Bechin. Hap. p. 35. Whoever its author or however old it is, it will be of great use to us against the Jewish commentators, since it expounds, rightly and wholly in a Christian sense, the prophecies which they refer to David and others as concerning the one and only Messiah.

units.la: 2. Targum Hierosolymitanum in Pentateuchum, quod non totum Textum continuâ serie, ut reliqua, sed quædam potiora prosequitur; sic dictum vero vel à loco ubi prodiit, vel à dialecto Hierosolymitana, quæ Babylonica, quâ scripta sunt Onkelosi commentaria, impurior. De authore dubitatur, licèt plerique cum Elia referant ad R. Jochanan circa annum Christi 230. vel ad tempora Talmudis Hierosolymitani. Cujuscunque sit, utilitatem suam habet, ideoque cum versione Latina reliquis annectemus.
units.tr: 2. The Targum of Jerusalem on the Pentateuch, which does not follow the whole text in continuous sequence as the others do, but pursues certain more important passages. It is so called either from the place where it appeared or from the Jerusalem dialect, which is less pure than the Babylonian in which the commentaries of Onkelos are written. Its author is doubted, although most, with Elias, refer it to R. Jochanan around the year of Christ 230, or to the times of the Jerusalem Talmud. Whoever its author, it has its usefulness, and so we will append it, with a Latin version, to the others.

units.la: 33. Chaldaica lingua ita affinis est Syriaca, ut a plerisque pro una eademque habeantur, sola enim dialecto differunt: In Scripturis dicitur Aramæa ab Aram, ut Syriaca a Syria; in N. Test. sæpe vocatur Hebræa, quia ejus scil. dialectus erat, alias antiqua Hebraica tantum apud Sacerdotes, et doctos nota erat. Cum vero Judæi reduces, postquam 7o. annos in Captivitate Babylonica transfegissent, propriam linguam obliti[?] essent, scil. Hebraicam puram; mixtam quandam ex Hebræa et Chaldaica in patriam introduxerunt, quæ postea Syriaca dicebatur: unde erat quod cum Esra legem populo publicè prælegi curaret ex textu Hebraico, quem vulgus ignorabat, necessarium erat ut Levitæ exponerent, et intelligentiam legis darent, ut videre licet, Neh. 8. 7, 8. et hæc origo erat, ut plerique statunt, explanationum in Synagogis diebus Sabbati post legem prælectam, quarum mentio frequens in Evangelio et Actis. Contrà verò contendit Geor. Amyra præludio 1. in Gram Syr. nequaquam ortam esse Syram ex mixtura Hebraica et Chaldaica, sed Syriacam cum Chaldaica unam esse eandemque linguam: Cum vero agnoscat ipse accidentaliter differre, licet essentialiter eadem sint, idem dicit quod illi a quibus differre videri velit. Eandem enim esse linguam et solâ dialecto differre agnoscunt fere omnes; unde Lud. de Dieu licet ipse Chaldaicam a Syriaca distinguat, quia sic ab aliis fieri solet, & quod non raro phrasibus & flexione differant, unam tamen & eandem esse linguam fatetur, minoremque inter ipsas differentiam esse potuisse si punctatoribus placuisset: hinc Dan. 2. 4. Chaldaei dicuntur Regem ארמית id est, Syriace allocuti esse, nec quicquam inter se differrent nisi Judæi, inter quos Daniel & Esra, quædam de sua lingua admiscuissent. Inde dialectus linguæ Syriacæ nata est, quæ Chaldaica dicta, quia in Chaldæa nata, & inde a Judæis in Palæstinam transvecta fuit.
units.tr: 33. The Chaldee language is so closely related to Syriac that many regard them as one and the same, for they differ only in dialect. In the Scriptures it is called Aramaic from Aram, as Syriac is from Syria; in the New Testament it is often called Hebrew, because, namely, it was the dialect of that people, whereas the ancient Hebrew was known only to the priests and the learned. But when the Jews returned, having spent seventy years in Babylonian captivity and having lost their own language, namely pure Hebrew, they brought into their homeland a mixed language made from Hebrew and Chaldee, which was afterwards called Syriac. Hence it was that when Ezra took care to have the law read publicly to the people from the Hebrew text, which the common people did not understand, it was necessary for the Levites to explain it and give the sense of the law, as can be seen in Neh. 8. 7, 8. This, as most maintain, was the origin of the explanations in the synagogues on the Sabbath days after the reading of the law, of which there is frequent mention in the Gospels and Acts. On the contrary, Georg Amyra, in the Prelude 1 to his Syriac Grammar, contends that Syriac did not arise at all from a mixture of Hebrew and Chaldee, but that Syriac and Chaldee are one and the same language. Yet while he himself admits that they differ accidentally, although they are essentially the same, he says the very thing that those from whom he wishes to appear different say. For almost everyone agrees that it is the same language, differing only in dialect. Hence Ludovicus de Dieu, although he himself distinguishes Chaldee from Syriac, as others customarily do, and because they often differ in phrasing and inflection, nevertheless confesses that it is one and the same language, and that the difference between them could have been smaller had the punctuators wished it. Hence in Dan. 2. 4 the Chaldeans are said to have addressed the king in Aramaic [ארמית], that is, in Syriac, and nothing would have differed between them except that the Jews, among whom were Daniel and Ezra, had mixed in some things from their own language. From this arose the dialect of the Syriac language, which is called Chaldee because it was born in Chaldea and from there was carried by the Jews into Palestine.

units.la: 34. Hanc vero Christo Salvatori ejusque discipulis vernaculam fuisse, post Widmanstadii, communis est doctorum opinio, unde magna exsurgit hujus linguæ prærogativa, quam una cum virginali matris lacte Dominus suxit, quæ Redemptoris nostri ortu, educatione, doctrinâ, miraculis, ac patris voce e cœlo ad ipsum emissâ, consecrata est. Hanc æternus Dei filius sacro ore suo nobilitavit, cum legem evangelicam vitaque æterna aperta promissa, quibus omnis spes nostra nititur, in hac lingua primus orbi promulgavit. Observat quidem doctissimus noster Breerwoodus, Syriaca vocabula quæ ab Evangelistis citantur, ab iisdem quæ in N. Test. Syriaco leguntur aliquantum differre : unde infert non ita antiquam esse N. T. Syriaci versionem ut vulgo putatur, sed plus temporis post Christum interfuisse, ante quam facta effet ista versio, quod mutationem illam in linguam Syriacam intulit ; sed notandum, Syriacae linguae varias fuisse dialectos, ut idem Breerwoodus, Buxtorfius & alii observant : dialectus enim Galilaea, ab Hierofolymitana differebat adeo, ut ex Petri sermone colligerent ipsum esse Galilaeum Marc. 14. 70. magis enim rudis & agrestis erat sermo Galilaeus, ut existimat Buxtorf in Lexic. Talm.Rabb. voce [?].
units.tr: 34. That this was the vernacular of Christ the Saviour and his disciples is, after Widmanstadt, the common opinion of scholars, whence arises the great prerogative of this language, which the Lord sucked in with his mother's virginal milk, and which was consecrated by the birth, upbringing, teaching and miracles of our Redeemer, and by the voice of the Father sent down to him from heaven. The eternal Son of God ennobled it with his holy mouth, when he first proclaimed to the world in this language the gospel law and the promise of eternal life, on which all our hope rests. Our most learned Breerwood indeed observes that the Syriac words cited by the Evangelists differ somewhat from those read in the Syriac New Testament; whence he infers that the Syriac version of the New Testament is not as ancient as is commonly thought, but that more time passed after Christ before that version was made, and that this brought about the change in the Syriac language. It should be noted, however, that there were various dialects of Syriac, as Breerwood himself, Buxtorf and others observe. For the Galilean dialect differed so much from the Jerusalem one that from Peter's speech they gathered he was a Galilean (Mark 14. 70); the Galilean speech was rougher and more rustic, as Buxtorf thinks in his Talmudic-Rabbinic Lexicon under the word [?].

units.la: 35. Præcipuæ verò ejus Dialecti erant. 1. Babylonica omnium purissima, in qua scripta sunt capitula quædam Danielis & Efræ, & postea licet stylo non ita puro Onkelofi & Jonathæ Paraphrases, & Talmud Babylonicum. 2. Hierofolymitana, quæ à genuina Chaldaica plus distabat per mixturam verborum peregrinorum, fcil. Arabicorum, Græcorum & Latinorum quam longo tempore contraxit : & in hac scripta sunt Talmud & Targum Hierofolymitanum, Targum in Hagiographa, & Jonathanis in Legem, liber Zohar, & quædam Medrashim seu expositiones allegoricæ. 3. Antiochena Comagena & Maronitica, quæ Antiochena dicebatur, quia circa Antiochenum tractum in usu fuit, & in Ecclesia Antiochena & per totum Patriarchatum in Sacris usurpata ; Comagena verò à Comagene ultimâ Syriæ regione, & Maronitica, à Maronitis qui habitant in pagis montis Libani, et in minoribus Syriæ oppidis: et hæc καὶ ἐξοχὴν Syriaca dicitur, quam Christiani per Orientem sibi fere propriam fecerunt, dum utriusque Testamenti versiones in hac dialecto habuerint, et Sacra in eadem celebrârint, reliquis Paraphrasibus Chaldaicis, de quibus supra, Judæis relictis. Litera quoque Syriacæ seu Maronitica à Christianis Antiochenis, nascente Ecclesiâ, introductæ erant, ne quid cum Nazaræis et Ebionitis Judæis commune haberent, ut inter alios Fabric. Boderianus. In hac dialecto scriptum est N. Test. Syriacum, ideóque facile evenire potuit, ut quædam verba essent à sermone Hierosolymitano paululùm variantia, cùm tamen una eademque sit utrisque lingua: Ideóque verè dici poterit linguam Syriacam fuisse Christo vernaculam, licèt dialectus Hierosolymitana, quâ Christus usus est, et Antiochena, in qua habemus utriusque Testamenti libros, aliquam admittant inter se varietatem. In hac nostra insula, quantùm varient pronuntiatio et dialectus pro singulis 40. vel 50. milliaribus, omnes novimus, adeò ut si plures eandem historiam idiomate Cantiano, Devoniensi, et Eboracensi conscriberent, majorem, ni fallor, discrepantiam quis inveniret, quàm in istis dialectis Syriacis: nemo tamen eandem esse apud omnes linguam Anglicanam negaret. Imò unam eandémque fuisse dialectum Hierosolymitanam et Antiochenam (eò quòd parùm differebant) videtur affirmare Gregorius apud Claris. Pocockium, in Histor. Arab. p.360. تنقسم الي ثلاث لغات افصحها الارمايية وهي لغة اهل الرها وحران والشام الكارجة وبعدها الفلسطينية وهي لغة اهل دمسق[?] وجبل لبنان وباقي الشام الداخلة * واسمحيها[?] الكلدانية النبطية وهي لغة اهل جبال أدور وسواد العراق *
units.tr: 35. The principal dialects of it were these. 1. The Babylonian, the purest of all, in which are written certain chapters of Daniel and Ezra, and afterwards, though in a less pure style, the paraphrases of Onkelos and Jonathan, and the Babylonian Talmud. 2. The Jerusalem dialect, which differed more from genuine Chaldee because of the admixture of foreign words, namely Arabic, Greek and Latin, which it picked up over a long period; in this are written the Jerusalem Talmud and Targum, the Targum on the Hagiographa, the Jonathan on the Law, the book Zohar, and certain Midrashim, or allegorical expositions. 3. The Antiochene, Commagenian and Maronite, which was called Antiochene because it was in use around the district of Antioch, and was employed in the Antiochene Church and throughout the whole patriarchate in sacred services; Commagenian, however, from Commagene, the furthest region of Syria, and Maronite from the Maronites who live in the villages of Mount Lebanon and the smaller towns of Syria. This is called Syriac by way of eminence [καὶ ἐξοχήν], and the Christians of the East made it almost their own, since they had both Testaments translated into this dialect and celebrated the sacred rites in it, leaving the other Chaldee paraphrases to the Jews. The Syriac or Maronite script was also introduced by the Christians of Antioch when the Church was first emerging, so that they might have nothing in common with the Nazarene and Ebionite Jews, as Fabricius and Boderianus, among others, observe. The Syriac New Testament is written in this dialect, and so it could easily happen that some words differed slightly from the Jerusalem speech, although the language of both is one and the same. Hence it may rightly be said that Syriac was Christ's vernacular, although the Jerusalem dialect which Christ used and the Antiochene, in which we have the books of both Testaments, admit some variety between them. In our own island we all know how much pronunciation and dialect vary from one district to another every forty or fifty miles; so that if several men wrote the same history in the Kentish, Devonshire and Yorkshire idioms, one would find, unless I am mistaken, a greater discrepancy than among these Syriac dialects, yet no one would deny that the English language is one and the same among them all. Indeed Gregory, in Pococke's Historia Arabum p. 360, seems to affirm that the Jerusalem and Antiochene dialects were one and the same, because they differed little. [tanqasimu ila thalath lughat, afsahuha al-aramaiyya, wa-hiya lughat ahl al-Ruha wa-Harran wa-al-Sham al-kharija, wa-ba'daha al-Filastiniyya, wa-hiya lughat ahl Dimashq wa-Jabal Lubnan wa-baqi al-Sham al-dakhila, wa-asmahiyya al-Kaldaniyya al-Nabatiyya, wa-hiya lughat ahl jibal Adur wa-sawad al-'Iraq]

units.la: hoc est (Lingua Syriaca) distinguitur in tres dialectos,quarum elegantissima est Aramæa, quæ est lingua incolarum Rohæ, & Harran, et Syriæ exterioris ; proxima illi est Palæstina, quæ est ea quâ utuntur Damasci et montis Libani, et reliquæ Syriæ interioris incolæ : at omnium impurissima Nabatæa , quæ est dialectus populi montium Assyriæ; et pagorum Eraci. Ubi sub Palæstina comprehendit Hierosolymitanam & Antiochenam dialectum, quæ parum inter se differebant.
units.tr: That is, (the Syriac language) is divided into three dialects. The most elegant of these is Aramaic, which is the language of the inhabitants of Edessa, Harran and outer Syria; next to it is Palestinian, which is used by the people of Damascus and Mount Lebanon and the other inhabitants of inner Syria; but the most impure of all is Nabataean, which is the dialect of the people of the mountains of Assyria and the villages of Eraci. Here under Palestinian he includes the Jerusalem and Antiochene dialects, which differed little from each other.

units.la: 36. Utque magna huius linguæ nobilitas ex dictis apparet, sic etiam utilitas maxima, ad tum Vet. tum Nov. Testamentum intelligendum: cum enim Christi & Apostolorum effet vernacula, non nisi ex ea vocum quæ in N. Test. extant Syriacarum interpretatio peti potest; et quod magis est, ut observat L. de Dieu, Ipsarum Phrasium quæ passim in N. Test. usurpantur verus sensus, vix aliunde quam ex Syriaco petendus est. Phrasim enim Evangeliarum et Apostolorum Græcam esse nemo dixerit: et facilius Europæis foret, Platonis et Aristotelis elegantiam imitari, quâ Platoni vel Aristoteli N. Testamentum nobis interpretari; quia scil. Sancti viri Syriacè conceperunt quæ Græcè scripserunt, et linguæ vernaculæ emphasim peregrinis verbis indiderunt.
units.tr: 36. And just as the great nobility of this language appears from what has been said, so too is its usefulness very great for understanding both the Old and New Testaments. Since it was the vernacular of Christ and the Apostles, the meaning of the words found in the New Testament can be drawn only from the Syriac translation of them. What is more, as L. de Dieu observes, the true sense of the very phrases used throughout the New Testament is hardly to be sought from anywhere but the Syriac. No one would call the phrasing of the Evangelists and Apostles Greek. It would be easier for Europeans to imitate the elegance of Plato or Aristotle than to render the New Testament into our language as Plato or Aristotle would have written it, because the holy men conceived in Syriac what they wrote in Greek, and put the emphasis of their vernacular into foreign words.

units.la: 37. Veteris etiam Testamenti in Syrum-sermonem ex Hebræo traduEti, prope Apostolorum tempora, exemplaria varia MSS. hodie sunt in multorum manibus: mentionem quidem fecit Arias Mont. versionis Syriacæ ex Græca 70. ut et doctissimus Mafius præf. in Iofuam, qui MSS. Syriaca multorum V. T. librorum ante mille annos conscripta habuit, sed ex versione 70. omnia; at ex Heb. factam versionem Syriacam omnium antiquissimam non viderunt Arias Montanus, vel Mafius, quam tamen nemo hodie in dubium vocat. Hanc etiam per omnes fere Orientales Ecclesias in usu esse certissimum est: licet enim aliam habeant ex Græca versionem, illam tamen ex Hebraeo quam antiquam & simplicem vocant, in usu Ecclesiarum publico esse testatur Gregorius Scholiastes Syrus apud Bootium in Indice animadversionum Sacrarum. Imo non tantum Scripturas sed & liturgias & ritualia apud plerasque Christianorum sectas in Oriente, in Syriaca lingua esse, licet doctis inter eos solum nota, clare ostendit doctissimus Breerwoodus. Sic etiam, ut hoc obiter addamus, Judæi in precibus publicis Hebraica lingua utuntur quam vulgus ignorat: & Ecclesia Græca, antiquâ Græcâ, quæ ab hodierna vulgari tantum differt quantum Italica à Latina. Etiam apud Muhammedanos ubique in lingua Arabica tum preces publicæ fiunt, tum Alcoranum legitur (quod prophanari existimant si in aliam linguam transferatur) etiam ubi Arabica non est vulgaris.
units.tr: 37. Also, various manuscript copies of the Old Testament translated from Hebrew into Syriac, dating from near the time of the Apostles, are today in the hands of many. Arias Montanus did mention a Syriac version made from the Greek of the Seventy, as did the most learned Masius in his preface to Joshua, who had Syriac manuscripts of many books of the Old Testament written a thousand years ago, but all of them from the version of the Seventy. Yet neither Arias Montanus nor Masius saw the most ancient Syriac version, made from the Hebrew, which no one today calls into doubt. It is quite certain that this version is in use in nearly all the Eastern Churches. For although they have another version made from the Greek, they attest that the one from the Hebrew, which they call ancient and simple, is the one used in the public services of the Churches, as Gregory the Syrian scholiast testifies, cited by Bootius in his Index of Sacred Observations. Indeed, the most learned Breerwood has clearly shown that not only the Scriptures but also the liturgies and rituals among most Christian sects in the East are in the Syriac language, though known only to the learned among them. So also, to add this in passing, the Jews use the Hebrew language in their public prayers, though the common people do not understand it; and the Greek Church uses ancient Greek, which differs from the modern vernacular as much as Italian differs from Latin. Among the Muhammadans, too, public prayers are everywhere said in Arabic, and the Koran is read in Arabic (which they think would be profaned if translated into another language), even where Arabic is not the vernacular.

units.la: 38. Duplicis vero versionis Syriacæ etiam mentionem facit Gregorius, apud D. Pocockium in prædicta Historia Arabica, pag. 184, cujus verba ex Arab. ita sonant: Versio 70. illa est quam sequuntur apud nos doctí, et quæ Græcorum manibus teritur, aliarumque apud Christianos sectarum, exceptis Syris, et præcipuè Orientalibus. Siquidem exemplar ipsorum quod simplex appellatur, quia qui illud elaborárunt, de ornatu verborum soliciti non fuerunt, convenit cum exemplari Judæorum: at Syri Occidentaliores duas habent versiones, simplicem illam, quæ e lingua Hebraica in Syriacam translata est post adventum Domini Christi, tempore Addæi Apostoli, vel juxta alios ante eum, tempore Salomonis filii David, et Hirami; et alteram figuratam juxta 70. Seniorum interpretationem, e lingua Græca in Syriacam traductam, longo post Salvatoris incarnationem intervallo.
units.tr: 38. Gregory also mentions a twofold Syriac version, in the work of Dr Pocock cited above, the Arabic History, p. 184, whose words in Arabic run thus: The version of the Seventy is the one which our learned men follow, and which is handled by the Greeks and by the other Christian sects, except the Syrians, and especially the Easterners. For their copy, which is called the simple one, because those who prepared it were not concerned with ornate wording, agrees with the copy of the Jews. But the Western Syrians have two versions: that simple one, which was translated from the Hebrew language into Syriac after the coming of the Lord Christ, in the time of the Apostle Addaeus, or, according to others, before him, in the time of Solomon the son of David and of Hiram; and another, figurative one, made according to the interpretation of the seventy Elders, translated from the Greek language into Syriac a long interval after the incarnation of the Saviour.

units.la: 39. Quod vero affirmant Maronitæ, versionem Syram ex Hebræo factam esse circa tempora Salomonis, & Hirami regis, nullo negotio refutatur; cum certum sit ante Christi tempora, nullas versiones inter Judæos notas fuisse, præter Onkelosi & Jonathanis paraphrases, & Græcam 70. Nec necessarium erat ex textu Hebraico versionem ullam in Judæorum usum instituere, cum lingua Hebraica pura Judæis longo post Salomonem tempore erat vernacula: vetustam tamen esse versionem Syram tam V. quam N. Testamenti, & vel ipsis Apostolorum temporibus vel non multo post factam, facile agnoscimus; nam præter constantem Ecclesiarum Orientalium traditionem, ex antiquis multi ejus meminerunt, ut Jacobus Syrus qui concilio Nicæno interfuit anno 325. & post ipsum Magnus Ephrem Syrus, qui etiam versionis simplicis ex Hebræo mentionem facit. Interpretem Syrum etiam citant Chrysost. in Psal. 94. & Heb. 11. Scholiastes Græc. in Pentat. frequenter, Theodoret. in Psal. 104. 113. 116. in Ionam cap. 3. & alibi, Chronicon Alexandrinum, &c. Nec mirū est apud Hieronymum altum esse de hac versione silentium, cùm linguam non intellexerit. Cùm enim catalogum Scriptorum illustrium Eccles. scripsit, linguæ Syrę ignarum fuisse inde probat Gennadius, quòd Iacobum Nisibenæ Persarum civitatis Episcopum, Syrum Scriptorem, in lingua Græca mondū conversu, silentio prætermiserit, ac Ephremi & Archelai Bardesanisq; opera Syriaca, non prius, quā Græca essent facta, potuerit evolvere. Lingua igitur Syriaca, quæ rullibi[?] hodiè vernacula, nisi in paucis vicis circa Libanum cùm ubiq; fere per Asiam & Africam inter Christianos pro eruditoru lingua habeatur, in qua Scripturas legunt & Sacra peragunt, multaq; sint veterum monumenta, quæ nondum edita[?] sunt, ut magni Ephrem, & Iacobi Syri, qui universam scripturam commentariis Syriacis illustrárunt, de quibus Greg. Nyssen. in vita Ephrem, & Sozom. lib. 3. Hist. cap. 15. quis dubitabit de magna ejus utilitate, præsertim ad Textus sacri intelligentiam? majorem enim cum Hebraica affinitatem habet quàm quælibet alia, unde est quòd pluribus vocibus & phrasibus inter se conveniant, ut ex Magno Ephrem observavit Basil. Magnus in Hexam. in Gen. 1. Magnum itaq; hunc & antiquissimum Ecclesiarum Orien. alium Thesaurum, versionem Syriacam Vet. et N. Testamenti, una cum interpretatione Lati a, Biblia nostra etiam exhibent. N. quidem T. primus edidit Widmanstadius s.C. Imperatoris Ferdinandi per Germaniam Cancellarius, ius,idque Syriacè tantum, quod postea per Faricium Boderianū,Tremelinm,Troftium & aios Latinitate donatum variis formis impressum rat. Epistolas vero Catholicas quasdam,scil. ecundam Petri,secundam & tertiam Iohannis, uda, cum Apocalypsi quæ in antiquioribus colicibus Syriacis desiderantur,magnumque suppeditant argumentum pro antiquitate istius versionis,factamscil.fuisse antequam publico Ecclesiarum consensu hæ partes N.T.receptæ erant,(nam nitio nascentis Ecclesiæ de iis dubitatum esse ex Ecclesiastica historia constat.) Hasce,inquam, um Apocalypsi quæ opera Clariff. Pocockii & Lud. de Dieu in lucem prodierunt, cum reliquis N.T. libris conjungemus,unà cum variis lectionibus ex libris MSS. aliisque à viris doctis collectis & observationibus inde factis. Interim præer exemplar Parisiense V.Test.quod non ex omni arte perfectum,licet magnam Gabrielis Syonitæ diligentiam, qui primus V.T.punctavit & Latinum reddidit, agnoscamus; alia etiam MSS. Syriaca vetustissima, optimaque fidei adhibe-nus.
units.tr: 39. But the Maronites' claim that the Syriac version was made from the Hebrew about the time of Solomon and King Hiram is refuted without difficulty. For it is certain that before Christ's time no versions were known among the Jews, except the paraphrases of Onkelos and Jonathan and the Greek of the Seventy. Nor was there any need to make a version of the Hebrew text for the Jews' use, since pure Hebrew was the vernacular of the Jews for a long time after Solomon. Yet we readily acknowledge that the Syriac version, both of the Old and of the New Testament, is ancient, and was made either in the very times of the Apostles or not long after. For apart from the constant tradition of the Eastern Churches, many ancient writers mention it: James the Syrian, who was present at the Council of Nicaea in 325, and after him Ephrem the Great the Syrian, who also mentions the simple version from the Hebrew. Chrysostom too cites the Syrian interpreter on Psalm 94 and Hebrews 11; the Greek scholiast on the Pentateuch frequently; Theodoret on Psalms 104, 113 and 116, on Jonah chapter 3 and elsewhere; the Alexandrian Chronicle, and others. Nor is it surprising that Jerome keeps a deep silence about this version, since he did not understand the language. For when he wrote his catalogue of illustrious ecclesiastical writers, Gennadius proves from this that he was ignorant of Syriac, because he passed over in silence James of Nisibis, bishop of the Persian city, a Syriac writer who had been translated into Greek, and could not unroll the Syriac works of Ephrem, Archelaus and Bardesanes until they had been made into Greek. The Syriac language, therefore, which is nowhere vernacular today except in a few villages around Lebanon, is almost everywhere in Asia and Africa regarded among Christians as the language of the learned, the language in which they read the Scriptures and perform the sacred rites. There are also many monuments of the ancients not yet published, such as those of the great Ephrem and of James the Syrian, who illustrated the whole of Scripture with Syriac commentaries (on whom see Gregory of Nyssa in the Life of Ephrem, and Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 15). Who will doubt its great usefulness, especially for understanding the sacred text? For it has a greater affinity with Hebrew than any other language, which is why in many words and phrases they agree with one another, as Basil the Great observed from Ephrem the Great in his Hexaemeron on Genesis 1. Therefore our Bibles also present this great and most ancient other treasure of the Eastern Churches, the Syriac version of the Old and New Testaments, together with a Latin translation. The New Testament was first published by Widmanstadt, Chancellor of the Emperor Ferdinand in Germany, but only in Syriac; it was afterwards given a Latin dress by Faricius Boderianus, Tremellius, Trostius and others, and printed in various formats. The Catholic Epistles that are lacking in the older Syriac copies, namely 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John and Jude, together with Apocalypse, supply a great argument for the antiquity of this version, since they were made before these parts of the New Testament were received by the common consent of the Churches (for it is known from Church history that doubts about them arose at the beginning of the nascent Church). These, I say, together with Apocalypse, which have come to light through the work of the distinguished Pocock and Ludovicus de Dieu, we shall join to the other books of the New Testament, along with variant readings gathered from manuscript books and other sources by learned men, and the observations made from them. Meanwhile, besides the Parisian copy of the Old Testament, which we acknowledge is not perfect in every respect, despite the great diligence of Gabriel Sionita, who first pointed the Old Testament and rendered it into Latin, we also make use of other very ancient and most trustworthy Syriac manuscripts.

units.la: 4o. Duo suppeditavit Reverendissimus Archiepiscopus Armachanus[?]. Unum totius V.Test.quod multo uro describendum curavit ex exemplari Patriarchæ Antiocheni (excepto Psalmorum libro qui intea evulgatus erat.) Hoc comparavit vir doctus[?] cum MS. Syriaco altero, quod cùm Parisiis agebat, à viro antiquitatis studiosissimo mutatus erat, & quædam in margine utilia notavit. 2. Alterum, ejusdem Reverendiss. Patris,Pentateuchum solum completitur, priori tamen multò antiquius,& maxima cum diligen-tia tia defcriptu. Tertiu est Clarissimi D.Pocockii, quod etiam accurate descriptum ipse ex Oriente attulit :-Hæc tria exemplaria fe mutuo confirmant, cum minima fit inter ipsa differentia; cum Parisianis vero collata sunt et ipsorum opera integri versiculi, imo libri qui in Parifienfi deficiebat vel exemplaris vel Typographi vitio, reftituuntur, præter innumera alia minoris momenti errata emendata, virorum doctorum opera & cura, qui ex collatione exemplarium, aliisque MSS. Syriacis, librisque impressis, quæ sigillatim hic enumerare instituti nostri brevitas non permittit, notas et observationes quæ ad textum elucidandum multum, ni fallor, conferent, elaborarunt.
units.tr: 40. The Most Reverend Archbishop of Armagh supplied two. One is of the whole Old Testament, which he had copied at great expense from the copy of the Patriarch of Antioch (except the Psalter, which had already been published). A learned man compared this with another Syriac manuscript, which had been acquired from a man devoted to the study of antiquity when he was at Paris, and noted some useful things in the margin. The second, from the same Reverend Father, contains only the Pentateuch; it is much older than the former, and was copied with the greatest diligence. The third is that of the most distinguished Dr Pocock, which he himself brought from the East and also had carefully copied. These three copies confirm one another, since the difference between them is very small. When they were collated with the Parisian copy, whole verses and even whole books that were missing from the Parisian copy, through the fault of the scribe or the printer, were restored; countless other errors of lesser importance were also corrected, through the work and care of learned men who, from the collation of copies and of other Syriac manuscripts and printed books (which the brevity of our plan does not allow us to list here one by one), have prepared notes and observations which, unless I am mistaken, will contribute much to elucidating the text.

units.la: 41. De Arabica lingua antiquitate, amplitudine et usu inter alios scripserunt Erpenius Orat. de ling. Arab.-Breerwoodus noster in libro doctissimo de Religionum et linguarum diversitate, Brochartus in Geographia sacra, ex quibus aliisque hæc nobis annotasse satis erit. Post linguarum confusionem, in Saba, vel Sabæa (quæ postea Arabia dicta est) à Seba Chusi filio, Chami nepote, ita nominata, fuit hæc lingua per 3000. annos sine aliarum mixtione conclusa: cum vero Arabia deserta per Ismaelem habitata erat, lingua hæc etiam inter ejus posteros propagata est, qui ab Hagar Hagareni vocantur, & hi quidem quia peregrini [illegible, ~8 letters] Arabes
units.tr: 41. On the antiquity, extent and use of the Arabic language among other peoples, Erpenius wrote in his Oration on the Arabic language, our Breerwood in his most learned book on the diversity of religions and languages, and Bochart in his Sacred Geography. From these and other writers it will be enough for us to note the following. After the confusion of tongues, this language was kept unmixed with others for 3000 years in Saba, or Sabaea (later called Arabia), so named from Seba, son of Cush and grandson of Ham. When the desert of Arabia was inhabited by Ishmael, this language also spread among his descendants, who are called Hagarenes after Hagar; and these, because they became foreigners, were called Arabs, just as the Sabaeans were called Arabs by birth.

units.la: facti; ut Sabæi [illegible, ~8 letters] Arabes nati appellati sunt.
units.tr: [They were called] Arabs by birth.

units.la: 42. Post annum vero Christi 610[?] ortus est impo-stor stor ille Muhamedes, qui cum Arabs effet, doctrina suam, quæ in Alcorano est consignata, Arabico sermone conscripsit: quæ quidem superstitio, cum ob Muhamedanorum victorias, tum ob alias causas, longe lateque per orbem diffusa esset, etiam & lingua Arabica una propagata fuit, ita ut universam fere Asiam et Africam, & bonam Europæ partem occupárit, nulla post linguarum divisionem tantum terrarum tractum possidente: & licet barbara ante Muhamedem erat, postea tamen culta. Turca etiam plerique barbari, Arabes vero literis dant operam. Cum enim Muhamedani preces suas publicas ubiq; in lingua Arabica celebrent, etiam ubi Arabica non est vernacula, & Alcoranum in hac lingua tantum legi permittant, ut supra innuimus, hinc factum est, ut ubicunque valet Muhamedana impietas, hac lingua (nisi ubi vernacula est) in scholis ut Latina & Græca apud nos, pro eruditorum lingua, a pueris addiscatur. Ipsique Christiani qui per imperium Turcicum, Persicum, aliorumque Muhamedanorum terras dispersi vivunt per magnam Asiæ & Africæ partem, ut & Judæi, Samaritani, & pagani vicini, hac lingua utantur: imo Sacros Codices in hanc transtulerunt tum Judæi, tum Christiani, ut postea dicem*[?]. Elegantiam ejus positâ volunt in vocum copia quâ Græcam & Latinam multo superat, licet compositionem vocum non agnoscat; significationis vi & suavitate, præ qua Græcorum χαλεῖς ἀχαλεῖς[?] sunt; linguæ gravitate ipsiusque facilitate, quæ tanta est ut inter omnes linguas nobiles facillima fit: adeo ut si quis paucis mensibus quotidie quasdam horas huic linguæ impendat, progressus laudabiles fa-
units.tr: 42. Some time after the year of Christ 610[?], that impostor Muhammad arose, who, being an Arab, wrote his doctrine, which is set down in the Quran, in the Arabic tongue. This superstition, spread far and wide over the world both because of the victories of the Muslims and for other reasons, carried the Arabic language along with it, so that it occupied almost all of Asia and Africa and a good part of Europe, no language since the division of tongues having possessed so large a tract of land. Although it was barbarous before Muhammad, it was afterwards cultivated. Most Turks are barbarians, but the Arabs devote themselves to letters. For Muslims everywhere perform their public prayers in the Arabic tongue, even where Arabic is not the vernacular, and they permit the Quran to be read only in this language, as we have hinted above. Hence it has come about that wherever Muhammadan impiety prevails, this language (except where it is the vernacular) is learned from boyhood in schools, as Latin and Greek are among us, as the language of the learned. Moreover, Christians who live dispersed through the Turkish and Persian empires and the lands of other Muslims, over a large part of Asia and Africa, use this language, as do Jews, Samaritans and neighbouring pagans; indeed, both Jews and Christians have translated the sacred books into it, as I shall say later. Its elegance is said to lie in the abundance of its vocabulary, which far surpasses Greek and Latin, although it does not admit the compounding of words; in the force and sweetness of its meaning, before which the Greek [words] are ...; in the dignity of the language and its ease, which is so great that among all noble languages it is the easiest. So that if anyone devotes some hours each day for a few months to this language, he will make praiseworthy progress and can lay the foundations of the language within four or five weeks. For it is not necessary to learn Hebrew in order to master it; although it is descended from Hebrew and has letters in common with it, the Arabic language is free of the difficulties of Hebrew, and it is so regular that most of its rules lack exceptions, and more anomalous and difficult words can be found in one book of the Bible, or in Homer, than in the whole of Arabic.

units.la: turus[?] sturus[?] fit, et inter 4. vel 5. septimanas fundamenta lingua edificere possit. Non enim necesse est Hebraica discere ut hanc calleas; licèt vero ab Hebraea prognata sit, communésque cum ea habeat literas, difficultates tamen Hebraea lingua ignorat, éstque adeo regularis ut pleraque praecepta exceptionibus careant, pluráque anomala & difficilia verba in uno Bibliorum libro, vel in Homero, quā in toto Arabismo reperire liceat.
units.tr: [Continuation of the preceding sentence, rendering the fragmentary words:] ...will make progress and can lay the foundations of the language within four or five weeks. For it is not necessary to learn Hebrew in order to master it; although it is descended from Hebrew and shares letters with it, Arabic has none of the difficulties of Hebrew, and it is so regular that most of its rules lack exceptions, and more irregular and difficult words can be found in a single book of the Bible, or in Homer, than in the whole of Arabic.

units.la: 43. Utilitas vero longe maxima, non tantum ad peregrinationes per totam Asiam, Africam, & Europae partem, sed & ad scientias edificendas, cum infinitos fere libros habeant Medicos, Geographicos, Mathematicos, Historicos, Politicos, Chymicos, &c. praeter plurimos Gracorum Latinorumque authores antiquos, etiam aliquos quos in Europa desideramus in sermonem Arabicum traductos, ita ut infinitum habeant librorum supellectilem & Academias multas. In Africa fuisse 30. Academias, testatur Joh. Leo. In Bibliotheca Fessana[?] libros 32000. fuisse testantur alii: et in Bibliotheca Regis Maroccani, quae in Bibliothecam Regis Hispaniarum avecta erat circa annum Christi 16 10. erant libri 7800.
units.tr: 43. The greatest usefulness of the language, not only for travel through the whole of Asia, Africa and part of Europe, but also for building up the sciences, lies in the fact that they have almost endless books on medicine, geography, mathematics, history, politics, chemistry and so on, besides many ancient Greek and Latin authors, and even some that we lack in Europe, translated into Arabic; so that they have an unlimited stock of books and many academies. John Leo testifies that there were thirty academies in Africa. Others testify that the library at Fez held 32,000 books; and the library of the King of Morocco, which was carried off to the library of the King of Spain around the year of Christ 1610, contained 7,800 books.

units.la: 44. Maxima tamen ejus utilitas & necessitas est ad linguam Hebraeam & sacra Biblia intelligenda, cum Hebraea lingua, quae mutila & exigua ex parte in veteri Testamento reliqua est, ex Arabica quae adhuc integra est, suppleri & disci possit: multa enim vocum Hebraicarum radices Arabicae sunt, unde Hebraica vocabula quae semel tantum in V. T. occurrunt, ex consuetudine Arabici sermonis exponenda esse statuit Aben Esra. Comment. in Cant. Salom. ob linquarum[?] affinitatem. Arabismis plurimis refertos esse libros Scriptura Poeticos observarunt docti, maxime librū Job (unde et linguæ antiquitas elucet) ut dudum observavit Hieronymus, qui in præfatione in Job affirmat translationem suam nullum ex veteribus sequi interpretem, sed ex ipso Hebraico Arabicoque sermone, & interdum Syro, nunc verba, nunc sensus, nunc simul utrumq; resonare: & in præf. in Danielem asserit Job cum Arabica lingua plurimam habere societatem. Idcirco ad Hebræa lingua perfectam cognitionem multo plus confert quam hactenus creditum fuit, ut verissime asserit Brochartus: hocque ex Hebraeorum commentariis videre licet, qui tum illis aqua hæret ad hanc linguam ut ad sacram anchoram confugiunt, & longe plura observassent ex Arabismo, ad Sacri textus intelligentiam, si illius linguæ fuissent peritiores.
units.tr: 44. Its greatest usefulness and necessity, however, is for understanding the Hebrew language and the Holy Bible, since the Hebrew language, which survives in the Old Testament maimed and only in small part, can be supplemented and learned from Arabic, which is still complete; for many Hebrew words have Arabic roots, and so Aben Ezra decided that Hebrew words which occur only once in the Old Testament must be explained from the usage of the Arabic tongue, on account of the affinity of the languages. Learned men have observed that the poetic books of Scripture are full of Arabisms, especially the book of Job (whence the antiquity of the language also appears), as Jerome long ago observed; he affirms in his preface to Job that his translation follows no earlier interpreter but the Hebrew itself and the Arabic speech, and sometimes the Syriac, so that now words, now sense, now both together resound; and in his preface to Daniel he asserts that Job has very much in common with the Arabic language. Therefore Arabic contributes much more to a perfect knowledge of Hebrew than has hitherto been believed, as Bochart rightly asserts; and this can be seen from the Hebrew commentaries, whose writers, when they stick fast, flee to this language as to a sacred anchor; and they would have observed far more from Arabism for understanding the sacred text, had they been more skilled in that language.

units.la: 45. Licet itaque versiones Biblicæ quas habemus Arabicæ, antiquitate reliquis cedant, utilitate tamen ad verum textus sensum eruendum multum conferre possunt.
units.tr: 45. Although, therefore, the Arabic Bible versions we have are inferior to the others in antiquity, they can nevertheless contribute much to bringing out the true sense of the text.

units.la: 46. Translationes vero Arabicæ quæ hodie tum in Bibliis Parisiensibus tum in nostris exhibentur, partim a Judæis, partim a Christianis factæ sunt.
units.tr: 46. The Arabic translations which are now presented, both in the Paris Bible and in ours, were made partly by Jews and partly by Christians.

units.la: 47. R. Saadias, quem Gaon, ob doctrinæ excellentiam vocant, tum Pentateuchum, tum reliquos V. Test. libros in Arabicam transtulit circa annum 900. in usum Judæorum popularium suorum per imperium Saracenicum longe lateque dispersorum, licet verso ejus in Pentateuchum tantum hactenus lucem viderit. De authore quem sequitur in Pentateucho tacet quidem D. de Say, in præfatione sua ad Biblia Parisiensia, etsi de translatione quadam libri Job Arabica, qua Hieronymus usus est, quadam habeat, quasi hanc suam versionem ejusdem esse antiquitatis lectori insinuare velset: certum tamen est, ut ex collatione patet, versionem hanc Pentateuchi Arabicam, non esse aliam quam illam R. Saadiæ, licet in paucis mutatam, contra Hottingerum & Erpenium qui aliter sentire videntur, ut ex viri doctissimi & linguarum Orientalium peritissimi notis patebit, qui Pentateuchum hunc Parisiensem cum Saadiæ exemplari duplici, uno MS. altero a Judæis Constantinopoli centum abhinc annis una cum Hebraico textu, & Onkelosi Paraphrasi Chaldaica impressó, contulit, variasque lectiones collegit; quas, cum observationibus suis, inter alia ejusdem generis imprimenda curabimus. Reliqui V. Testamenti libri a Christianis versi sunt, ut & N. Testamentum : sed licet elegantem & satis antiquam translationem illam esse afferat Erpenius, nec tamen ipse nec qui opus Parisiense ediderunt, a quibus authoribus vel quo tempore facta sit nobis indicant, sed hoc aliorum indagini reliquerunt.
units.tr: 47. R. Saadia, whom they call Gaon on account of his excellence in learning, translated both the Pentateuch and the other books of the Old Testament into Arabic around the year 900, for the use of his fellow Jews, who were widely dispersed through the Saracen empire, although only his version of the Pentateuch has so far seen the light. Concerning the author whom he follows in the Pentateuch, Mr. de Say is silent in his preface to the Paris Bibles, although he has something to say about a certain Arabic translation of Job which Jerome used, as if he wished to suggest to the reader that his own version is of the same antiquity. It is certain, however, as comparison shows, that this Arabic version of the Pentateuch is none other than that of R. Saadia, though changed in a few places; this is against Hottinger and Erpenius, who seem to think otherwise, as will be clear from the notes of a most learned man and most expert in Oriental languages, who collated this Paris Pentateuch with two copies of Saadia's version, one manuscript and the other printed by Jews at Constantinople a hundred years ago together with the Hebrew text and the Chaldee paraphrase of Onkelos, and gathered the various readings; these we will take care to print, along with his observations and other matters of the same kind. The remaining books of the Old Testament were translated by Christians, as was the New Testament; but although Erpenius asserts that this translation is elegant and fairly ancient, neither he nor those who published the Paris work tell us by whom or at what time it was made, but they left this to the investigation of others.

units.la: 48. Datur et alia Pentat. Arabica translatio in Bibliotheca Laurentiana, ab Harit-Ibn-Sina facta, quæ teste Hottingero ex magna parte respondet editioni Græcæ, ubi vero ab ea recedit, Syriacam vel Chaldaicam sequitur.
units.tr: 48. There is also another Arabic translation of the Pentateuch in the Laurentian Library, made by Harit ibn Sina, which, according to Hottinger's testimony, for the most part agrees with the Greek edition, but where it departs from it, follows the Syriac or Chaldee.

units.la: 49. Pentat. etiam Arabicum edidit Erpenius, Judæorum Mauritanorum, quem R. Saadiæ versioni præfert eo quod textui Hebræo magis adhæreat, adeo ut versio Interlinearis Ariæ Montani tam huic Arabicæ quam Hebræo textui ad amussim quadret. Exemplari tamen in quibusdam ab Hebraico hodierno diverso authorem usum fuisse ex locis quibusdam probat idem Hottingerus, quos una cum iis quæ majoris momenti sunt lectionibus à Saadia codice differentibus, inter alia Lector in ultimo Bibliorum tomo inveniet.
units.tr: 49. Erpenius also published an Arabic Pentateuch of the Moorish Jews, which he prefers to Saadia's version because it adheres more closely to the Hebrew text, so much so that the interlinear version of Arias Montanus fits this Arabic and the Hebrew text exactly. Hottinger shows from certain passages, however, that the author used a copy which in some places differed from the Hebrew of today; the reader will find these passages in the last volume of the Bibles, together with those readings of greater importance which differ from Saadia's manuscript, among other things.

units.la: 5o: Extant & alia duo Pent. Arabici exemplaria in Bibliotheca Oxoniensi secundum versionem 70. quæ multis abhinc annis contulit vir doctus cum celebri nostro MS. Alexandrino 70. Seniorū, cujus annotationes cū Nobilii aliisq; ad 70. verfionem spectantibus, adjicere decrevimus. Dantur & variæ editiones N.Test. Arab. variæque exemplaria MSS. & impressa quibus usi sumus, de quibus etiam suo loco, Lectori rationem reddemus.
units.tr: 5o: Two other copies of the Arabic Pentateuch, following the Septuagint version, are extant in the Bodleian Library at Oxford. A learned man collated them some years ago with our famous manuscript of the Septuagint Alexandrinus. We have decided to add his notes, together with those of Nobilius and others relating to the Septuagint version. There are also various printed editions of the Arabic New Testament, and various manuscripts and printed copies, which we have used. We will give the reader an account of these in their proper place.

units.la: 51. Ante Cyri tempora sub Hebræis nominibus כּוּשׁ [?] Cuth, & עֵילָם [?] Elam nota erat Persia; sic Josephus antiq. l. 1. c. 7. Ἔλυμον & Ἐλυμαῖς, ait fuisse Πέρσων ἀρχηγέτας [?], Persarum generis authores. Postea cum a Cyro, qui equorum usum in Persiam introduxerat, ex peditibus equites facti essent, & nemo Persarum vir bonus haberetur, si ultro pedes iret (hæc tria enim ab anno 5. ad vicesimum liberos docuisse asserit Herodotus, ἱππεύειν, τοξεύειν, ἀληθίζεσθαι [?], equitare, sagittare, & vera loqui,) Arabice vero فرس pharas est equus & فارس pharis equus Hebraice פָּרָס [?] paras, hinc ex hac subita mutatione regio dicta est פָּרַס Paras & incolæ פָּרְסָא [?] Persæ, quasi dicas equites: unde, ut observat doctiss. Brochartus, nec in libris Mosis, Regum, Esaiæ, vel Jeremiæ, Persarum fit mentio, quia ante Cyrum scripti sunt, qui occasionem mutati nominis dedit: at in Daniele et Ezechiele, et in libris Chronic. Esr. & Esther, quorum authores vel Cyro coævi, vel post eum vixerunt, Persarum frequens est mentio, multaq; vocabula occurrunt Persica, ut Dan.3. 2.Neh.2.8. Esth.3. &c. quæ sine hujus linguæ cognitione perfectè explicari vix possunt.
units.tr: 51. Before the time of Cyrus, under the Hebrew names Cuth [?] and Elam [?], Persia was known; so Josephus, Antiquities book 1, chapter 7, says that Elymus and Elymaeans were the originators of the Persians, the founders of the Persian race [?]. Afterwards, when Cyrus, who had introduced the use of horses into Persia, made horsemen out of foot soldiers, and no Persian was regarded as a worthy man if he went on foot (for Herodotus asserts that these three things were taught to their sons from the age of five to twenty: to ride horses, to shoot with the bow, and to speak the truth), the Arabic word for horse is pharas, and the word for horseman is pharis; in Hebrew, paras [?]. Hence from this sudden change the region was called Paras [?] and its inhabitants Persae [?], as if you should say horsemen. Whence, as the learned Bochart observes, the Persians are not mentioned in the books of Moses, Kings, Isaiah or Jeremiah, because these were written before Cyrus, who gave the occasion for the changed name; but in Daniel and Ezekiel, and in the books of Chronicles, Ezra and Esther, whose authors either were contemporaries of Cyrus or lived after him, the Persians are frequently mentioned, and many Persian words occur, such as Dan. 3:2, Neh. 2:8, Esth. 3, etc., which can scarcely be fully explained without knowledge of this language.

units.la: §2. Licet autem ex multis mutationibus quæ in Persia acciderunt per gentium variarum irruptionem, et mixturam, quæ eam subjugarunt, Romanorum &c. Arabum, Turcarum, &c. lingua eorum multum mutata fit; ex multis tamen antiquis Persarum vocabulis, in Scripturis & antiquis authoribus repertis, quæq; adhuc apud Persas manent, (ut videre licet apud eundem Brochartum) constat, veterem Persarum linguam non periisse funditus, sed manere adhuc ejus reliquias. Ex quo tamen Muhamedana impietas in Persia receptafuit, ut Religionem sic literas seu characteres Arabes Persis dedere, adeo ut quis sit proprius & antiquus Persarum character, hodie ignoretur.
units.tr: §2. Although, through many changes that took place in Persia because of the invasion and mixing of various peoples who subjugated it, Romans, etc., Arabs, Turks, etc., its language has changed greatly, nevertheless, from many ancient Persian words found in the Scriptures and ancient authors, and which still survive among the Persians (as the same Bochart may be consulted to see), it is evident that the old Persian language has not perished utterly, but that its remnants still remain. Yet since the Muhammadan impiety was received in Persia, and with that religion they also adopted Arabic letters or characters, it is now unknown what the proper and ancient character of the Persians was.

units.la: §3. Quod ad versiones Biblicas attinet, certum est ex Theodoreto, Chrysostomo, Hieronymo, & aliis qui circa annum 400. floruerunt, ut in alias sic in Persicam linguam, Scripturam antiquitus fuisse versam; an vero antiquæ ejus versionis aliquæ adhuc supersint reliquiæ post eversam illic Religionem Christianam & introductam Muhamedanam, nullibi, quod sciam, constat.
units.tr: §3. As for the Biblical versions, it is certain from Theodoret, Chrysostom, Jerome, and others who flourished around the year 400, that Scripture was anciently translated into the Persian language, as into others. But whether any remains of that ancient version survive after the Christian religion was overthrown there and the Muhammadan introduced, is nowhere established, so far as I know.

units.la: §4. Hæc tantum habemus Persica, quæ, ob rationes quas quas alibi (Deo dante) reddemus, editioni nostræ inferere, non inutile judicamus.
units.tr: §4. We have only these Persian materials, which, for reasons that we will give elsewhere (God willing), we judge not unworthy of inserting in our edition.

units.la: 1. Pentateuchum Persicum, quem ex Hebræa in linguam Persicam transtulit Jacobus Thawasius, vel Tusius (ab urbe Tus, propter Academiam celebri, denominatus) in usum Judæorum, in Persia degentium. Hunc typis mandarunt Judæi literis Hebraicis, Constantinopoli, anno 1551, una cum textu Hebraico, Arabicâ Saadiæ, & Chaldaicâ Onkelosi versionibus, de quibus suprà: voces vero obscuras & difficiles Persicè non reddidit, ut nec multa bestiarum & avium peregrina nomina, præsertim Levit. 11. quorum significatio genuina tum Rabbinos, tum nos latet. Hanc vero versionem ex Hebræis in Persicos characteres transcriptam, cum Latina interpretatione, Jonathanis etiam (quæ dicitur) & Hierosolymitana paraphrasi, appendicis loco ad vetus Testamentum adjicienda remittimus: ita tamen ut si quis hæc in uno volumine cum reliquis Pentateuchi versionibus compingere velit, commodè id liceat.-
units.tr: 1. The Persian Pentateuch, which Jacob Thawasius, or Tusius (named from the city of Tus, famous for its academy), translated from the Hebrew into Persian for the use of the Jews living in Persia. The Jews printed it at Constantinople in 1551, in Hebrew letters, together with the Hebrew text and the Arabic version of Saadia and the Chaldee version of Onkelos, mentioned above. He did not, however, render into Persian the obscure and difficult words, nor the many foreign names of beasts and birds, especially in Lev. 11, whose genuine meaning is unknown both to the rabbis and to us. We refer this version, transcribed from Hebrew into Persian characters, together with a Latin translation, and also the so-called Targum of Jonathan and the Jerusalem paraphrase, to be added to the Old Testament as an appendix. Nevertheless, if anyone wishes to bind these together in one volume with the other versions of the Pentateuch, that may conveniently be done.

units.la: 2. Psalmorum versionem Persicam quam ex Oriente attulit vir doctus & linguarum Orientalium callentissimus: quam pro propenso suo in hanc editionem Biblicam animo, communicare paratus est.
units.tr: 2. A Persian version of the Psalms, which a learned man and very skilled in the Oriental languages brought from the East. In keeping with his favourable disposition towards this Biblical edition, he is ready to share it.

units.la: 3. Evangelia Quatuor Persicè reddita, quæ cum versione Latina evulgare decreverat Abrahamus Wheelocus nuper linguæ Arabicæ professor Cantabrigiensis, sed præmatura morte ereptus, opus incœptum perficere non potuit. Hanc tamen versionem ex MSS. variis invicem collatis, una cum versione Latina cum ad N. Testamentum accedemus publici juris faciemus.
units.tr: 3. The Four Gospels rendered into Persian, which Abraham Wheelock, recently professor of Arabic at Cambridge, had decided to publish with a Latin version, but, snatched away by an untimely death, he could not complete the work he had begun. Nevertheless, we will make this version, collated from various manuscripts, public, together with the Latin version, when we come to the N. Testament.

units.la: 55. Æthiopiam olim Hebraice לוּד[?] Lud vocatam, & Æthiopes Ludim, seu Ludæos, contra veteres qui Chus Æthiopiam esse crediderunt, valide probat doctissimus Brochartus Geograph. Sacra. l. 4. c. 2.3[?]. & 26. De his vaticinatus est Esaias cap. 66.19. ubi de conversione gentium per prædicationem Evangelii loquens, eos qui evasuri erant cladem quam genti Judæorum interminatus erat Deus, &c. Apostolos eorumque discipulos, in Tarshish, Pul, & Lud qui arcum trahunt, gloriam suam inter gentes celebraturos prædicit, quod impletum erat cum ex illa gente Eunuchus à Philippo baptizatus Evangelium Æthiopibus tanto successu prædicavit, ut in hodiernum diem per tot secula, fides & Ecclesiasticum regimen sub Abuna suo, qui Patriarcham Alexandrinum agnoscit perdurârint. Eunuchus ille erat Dynasta Candaces Reginæ Æthiopum, Candaces enim nomen Æthiopum Reginis commune erat, ut ex Plinio, l. 6. c. 29. Strabone lib. 17.1. Dione in Augusto aliisque videre licet. Rex vero Æthiopiæ qui longè lateque multis populis per Africam imperat, à multis vocatur Presbyter Johannes seu Pretegianus, quem, contra Scaligerum, Regem Abyssinorum esse volunt, errore manifesto, cum certum sit in ultimis Asiæ finibus non in Africa ante 400. annos regnâsse regem Christianum qui sermone Persico [illegible, ~5 letters] (line break) [illegible, ~6 letters] Padesha Prestigiani, id est, Rex Apostolicus vocabatur, unde Presbyteri Johannis nomen ortum.
units.tr: 55. Ethiopia was formerly called in Hebrew Lud [לוּד] and the Ethiopians Ludim, or Ludites, contrary to the ancients who believed that Cush was Ethiopia; the most learned Bochart strongly proves this in Geographia Sacra, book 4, chapters 2, 3 and 26. Isaiah prophesied about these people in chapter 66:19, where, speaking of the conversion of the nations through the preaching of the Gospel, he describes those who would escape the destruction that God had threatened upon the Jewish nation, etc. He predicts that the apostles and their disciples, in Tarshish, Pul and Lud who draw the bow, would proclaim their glory among the nations. This was fulfilled when the eunuch baptized by Philip from that nation preached the Gospel to the Ethiopians with such success that, to this day, through so many centuries, faith and ecclesiastical government have endured under their Abuna, who acknowledges the Patriarch of Alexandria. That eunuch was a minister of Candace, Queen of the Ethiopians, for Candace was a name common to the Ethiopian queens, as may be seen from Pliny, book 6, chapter 29, Strabo book 17, Dio in Augustus, and others. The king of Ethiopia, who rules over many peoples far and wide throughout Africa, is called by many Presbyter John or Prester John. Against Scaliger, they maintain that he is king of the Abyssinians, a manifest error, since it is certain that, for 400 years, a Christian king who spoke Persian reigned not in Africa but at the farthest limits of Asia, and was called [illegible] Padesha Prestigiani, that is, the Apostolic King, whence the name Prester John arose.

units.la: 56. Æthiopes autem in ritibus sacris, Coptitis seu Ægyptiis maxime similes esse, testantur ritualia, & liturgiæ utriq; genti communes, de quibus videatur Kircherus de Coptitarū moribus, lib.1. c.9. Æram etiam martyrum usurpant, cum in dira illa persecutione Diocletiana, non Ægyptii tantum sed & Æthiopes martyrii gratia adepti sint, unde erat, quod Annus Gratiæ ab iis dicebatur, licet perspicax Scaliger unde sic dictus esset se ignorare profiteatur. Causam hujus affinitatis præcipuam esse liquet quod Ecclesia Æthiopica una cum Ægyptiaca uni episcopo Patriarchæ Alexandrino subjecta erat, hodie enim licet Abunam seu Primatem quendam inter se habeant, tamen consecrationem ejus a Patriarcha Alexandrino (cujus sedes est Cairi) petunt, uti refert Damianus à Goes: ritus enim & consuetudines Ecclesiam & ejus Antistites comitari, passim testantur historiæ, unde est, quod, ut eosdem ritus Idololatricos olim coluisse Ægyptios & Æthiopes testatur Diodorus, sic unam eandemq; Ecclesiam fuisse testantur præter Nicephorum, Zonaram, Cedrenum, Chron. Alexand. [?] inum, etiam ritualia Æthiopica quæ in Bibliotheca patrum extant.
units.tr: 56. The Ethiopians, moreover, are attested by their ritual books and liturgies, which they hold in common with the Copts or Egyptians, to be most similar to them in sacred rites. On this see Kircher, On the Customs of the Copts, book 1, chapter 9. They also use the era of the martyrs, since in that terrible persecution under Diocletian, not only Egyptians but also Ethiopians obtained the crown of martyrdom; hence the Year of Grace was called by them thus, although the perceptive Scaliger professes that he does not know why it was so called. The principal cause of this affinity is clear: the Ethiopian Church, together with the Egyptian, was subject to one bishop, the Patriarch of Alexandria. Even today, although they have among themselves a certain Abuna or Primate, they nevertheless seek his consecration from the Patriarch of Alexandria, whose see is at Cairo, as Damian à Goes reports. For customs and usages accompany the Church and its bishops, as histories attest everywhere; hence it is that, just as Diodorus testifies that the Egyptians and Ethiopians once practised the same idolatrous rites, so they testify that there was one and the same Church, besides Nicephorus, Zonaras, Cedrenus, the Chronicon Alexandrinum, and also the Ethiopian ritual books which are extant in the Bibliotheca Patrum.

units.la: 57. Ex relatione sacerdotum quorundam Abyssinorum refert idem Kircherus duplicem apud ipsos fuisse characterem, unum antiquum, Surianum dictum (quem & Sanctum vocant) quo libri sacri quondam conscripti erant; quo soli sacerdotes & viri docti utebantur: alterum vulgarem & communem, qui adhuc manet, quo etiam libri sacri, olim & hodie scribuntur, hoc verò hodie promiscuè utuntur omnes: & hunc characterem volunt esse Æthiopicæ linguæ proprium quem Geets, seu Liberum vocant, eò quòd à nullo alio origine duxerit, ut ipsi gloriantur, illum verò Surianum vel Chaldaicum, unde à quibusdam lingua Æthiopica, Chaldaica vocatur, Potkenio sc. Baronio & aliis.
units.tr: 57. From the account of certain Abyssinian priests, Kircher reports that among them there were two characters: one ancient, called Surian (which they also call Holy), in which the sacred books were once written, and which only priests and learned men used; and the other common and ordinary, which still remains, and in which the sacred books, both formerly and today, are written, and which everyone now uses indiscriminately. They maintain that this character is proper to the Ethiopic language and call it Geez, or Free, because it has derived its origin from no other, as they boast; but the Surian or Chaldean character, whence some call the Ethiopic language Chaldean, is, according to Pothenius, that is, Baronius and others.

units.la: §8. Utilitate verò hujus linguæ qd. attinet, antiqua habet Æthiopes totiⁱ scripturæ versione, quæ ipsis credendum sit, ipsis Apostolorum temporibus facta est, nec enim alia à primo recepta fide Christiana habuisse probari potuit, Alvarez Hist. Æthiop. c. 159. qui multis annis apud Æthiopes vixit, affirmat ipsos scripturas legere linguâ Tegianâ quæ Abassinorum est dialectus: est enim Tegia pars Habassiæ quæ primò Christianismum recepit, in quam linguam tam Vetus quàm Novum Testamentum translata fuisse ex Chaldaica vel Syriaca affirmat Sabellicus in supplemento Hist. lib. 8.
units.tr: §8. As for the usefulness of this language, the Ethiopians have an ancient version of the whole of Scripture, which must be believed to have been made in the very times of the Apostles, since it could not be shown that they had any other after first receiving the Christian faith. Alvarez, Hist. Aethiop. c. 159, who lived among the Ethiopians for many years, affirms that they read the Scriptures themselves in the Tigrean language, which is a dialect of the Abyssinians. For Tigre is the part of Abyssinia that first received Christianity. Sabellicus, in the supplement to his History, book 8, affirms that both the Old and New Testaments were translated into that language from Chaldee or Syriac.

units.la: Liturgiam etiam celebrant linguâ propriâ, li et Chaldæa inter ipsos pro divinorum[?] lingua habeatur, ut Alvarez, Postellus & alii tradunt.
units.tr: They also celebrate the liturgy in their own language. Chaldee is regarded among them as the language of sacred things, as Alvarez, Postellus and others report.

units.la: Quod verò suspicatur vir doctus Evangelia Æthiopica versa fuisse non ante 300. annos, & fidem à Maronitis è monte Libano Æthiopes habuisse cum Pontifici Romano se subjicerent, alibi expendemus.
units.tr: As for the learned man's suspicion that the Ethiopic Gospels were translated not earlier than 300 years ago, and that the Ethiopians received their faith from the Maronites of Mount Lebanon when they submitted to the Roman Pontiff, we shall weigh that elsewhere.

units.la: §9. Qui hodie impressi sunt libri Æthiopici, sūt Psalmi Davidis, qui tum Romæ tum Coloniæ editi, Canticum Canticorum, & Testamentum Novum Romæ impressum, sed multis mendis scatens. Hos, et si quos alios scripturæ libros comparare possumus ex optimis exemplaribus emendatos, licet in nullis Bibliorum editionibus hactenus extantes, Bibliis nostris non sine Ecclesiæ commodo adjiciendos duximus.
units.tr: §9. The Ethiopic books printed today are the Psalms of David, published both at Rome and at Cologne, the Song of Songs, and the New Testament printed at Rome, though it teems with many errors. These, and whatever other books of Scripture we can obtain corrected from the best copies, although they have hitherto not appeared in any edition of the Bible, we have thought should be added to our Bible, not without benefit to the Church.

units.la: 60. Jam ut ad Græcam & Latina versione accedamus: Celebris est 70. interpretum versio ut quæ prima erat omnium veteris Test. quod singulari Dei providentia in linguam latissime propagata versum erat, ut viam gentibus pararet, ad Evangelium, per adventum filii sui, recipiendum. Hac usi sunt Judæi in Synagogis ab ultima antiquitate, hac usa etiam Ecclesia primitiva & veteres scripturæ interpretes, a quibus omnis Theologiæ & librorum sacrorum intelligentia nobis derivatur, adeo ut omnia fere quæ habemus in Theologia, & in Bibliorum cognitione, huic verfioni debeamus, imo exigua esset absque hac linguæ Hebrææ cognitio, ut ostendit Capell. Crit. lib. 6. c. 10. Nobilissimum itaque hoc Ecclesiæ & Synagogæ monumentum, quoad fieri poterit integritati suæ restituere operæ pretium esse nemo dubitat, quod in editionibus Complut. Regia, Parif. hactenus vix tentatum est, in Bibliis nostris quid præstitum sit judicet lector æquus.
units.tr: 60. Now let us come to the Greek and Latin versions. The version of the Seventy translators is famous. It was the first of all versions of the Old Testament, and by the singular providence of God it was rendered into a language widely spread, to prepare the way for the Gentiles to receive the Gospel at the coming of his Son. The Jews have used it in their synagogues from the most ancient times, the primitive Church and the early interpreters of Scripture have also used it, and from them all our understanding of theology and of the sacred books is derived. So almost everything we have in theology and in knowledge of the Bible we owe to this version; indeed, without it the knowledge of the Hebrew language would be scanty, as Capellus shows, Crit. book 6, ch. 10. No one doubts, then, that it is worth the effort to restore this most noble monument of Church and Synagogue to its integrity as far as possible. This was hardly attempted in the Complutensian, Regian and Paris editions; let the fair reader judge what has been achieved in our Bible.

units.la: 61. Autographum ipsum quod Ptolomæo obtulerunt 70. Seniores, in Bibliotheca sua celebri Alexandrina Rex collocavit, quæ postea tempore Julii Cæsaris, magno & nunquam satis dolendo reipub. literaria damno, incendio conflagravit, exemplaria vero plurima inter Judæos fuisse certum est, cum publice ab ipsis lecta esset hæc versio, & cum magna veneratione ubique recepta, sic enim Azar. p. 16. Meor enajim. קיום הפתרון[?] : מאת כל עדת היהודים[?] confirmatio interpretationis (Græcæ) fuit ab universo Israelitarum coetu. Apud Christianos vero in tanto honore fuit, at referente Augustin.[?]de Civ. Dei. l. 18. c. 43. tanquam sola esset sic receperit Ecclesia, eâque utantur Græci Christiani, quorum plerique, utrum sit alia aliqua ignorant.
units.tr: 61. The autograph itself, which the Seventy elders offered to Ptolemy, the King placed in his famous library at Alexandria. That library was afterwards burned in the time of Julius Caesar, to the great and never sufficiently lamented loss of the literary commonwealth. But there were certainly many copies among the Jews, since this version was read publicly by them and received everywhere with great veneration. Thus Azariah, p. 16, Meor Enayim: the confirmation of the interpretation (Greek) [קיום הפתרון] was by the whole assembly of the Jews [מאת כל עדת היהודים]. Among Christians it was held in such honour that, as Augustine reports, De Civ. Dei book 18, ch. 43, the Church received it as if it alone existed, and Greek Christians use it, most of whom do not know whether there is any other.

units.la: 62.[?] Origenes vero, (quem Hieronym. praef. in lib. nom.
