Hebraicorum, post Apostolos Ecclesiarum magistrum, neminem nisi imperitum negare asserit) Primo, Aquila, Theodotionis & Symmachi versiones ex Hebraeo Græcas una cum 70 translatione per columnas varias disposuit, quibus sibi mutuo omnes respondebat; hæc autem volumina appellavit Tetrapla, quæ cum magno applausu recepta essent, duas alias columnas addidit prioribus parallelas, in quarum una textus Hebraeus literis Hebraicis inscriptus erat, in altera, idem Græcis literis, unde Hexapla dicta sunt: Postea vero duabus aliis versionibus etiam Græcis ex Hebraeo factis, in doliis quibusdam repertis Hiericunte et Nicopoli, sex prioribus columnis adjunxit, unde Octopla dicebantur. Hoc vero & opus perfectum erat, tantaque etiam æstimationis, ut opus Ecclesiæ vocatum sit; quod postea quia carius veniret, Eusebius et Paphilus publici juris fecerunt, collocando in Bibliotheca Cæsariensi: Cumque magna ista volumina pauci parare possent, aliud opus aggressus est idem Origenes, versionem sc. 70 edidit a reliquis separata quâ cum Hebraeo textu contulit, positis asteriscis ubi aliquid ex Hebraeo addidit, quod ex Theodotionis versione mutuavit (quæ ad reliquis propius accedebat) & obelis ubi aliqua habebant 70 quæ non erant in Hebraeo. Hujus vero exemplaria ut facile parabilia, Bibliothecas omnes etiam privatas implerunt: Quumq;[?] plures exemplaria transcriberent, asteriscos vero & obelos (quos possit Origenes ut vera 70 lectio servaretur, & a Theodotionis additamentis distinguueretur) five negligentia, five alia de causa saepe omiserint, inde mixta facta est versio, adeo ut difficile effet nisi in Origenis Hexaplis, vel in exemplaribus quibus publicè usa est Ecclesia Graeca, vel ex aliis vetustis exemplaribus quorum multa post Origenem per multa secula servata esse veri simile est, veram & genuinam 70. lectionem habere, & haec potissima causa est cur multi genuinam 70. versionem extare hodie negent.
units.tr: 62. Origen, however (whom Jerome, in his preface to the book of Hebrew names, says that after the Apostles, the teacher of the churches, no one but an ignorant man would deny), first arranged in parallel columns the Greek versions of Aquila, Theodotion and Symmachus, made from the Hebrew, together with the translation of the Seventy, so that each answered to the others. He called these volumes the Tetrapla. Since they were received with great applause, he added two more columns parallel to the former: in one the Hebrew text was written in Hebrew letters, in the other the same in Greek letters, and so they were called the Hexapla. Afterwards, with two other Greek versions also made from the Hebrew, found in certain jars at Jericho and Nicopolis, he added to the six former columns, and they were called the Octapla. This work too was finished, and was held in such esteem that it was called the work of the Church. Because it would have been too dear, Eusebius and Pamphilus later made it public property by placing it in the Caesarean library. And since few could procure such large volumes, Origen undertook another work: he published the version of the Seventy separately from the others, and compared it with the Hebrew text. Where he added something from the Hebrew, borrowed from the version of Theodotion (which came closer to the Hebrew than the others), he placed asterisks; where the Seventy had things not found in the Hebrew, he placed obelisks. Copies of this, being easily obtained, filled all libraries, even private ones. But since many people made copies, they often omitted the asterisks and obelisks (which Origen had used so that the true reading of the Seventy would be kept and distinguished from Theodotion's additions), either through carelessness or for some other reason. So the version became mixed, and it was difficult to find the true and genuine reading of the Seventy except in Origen's Hexapla, or in the copies which the Greek Church used publicly, or in other old copies, many of which it is likely were preserved through many centuries after Origen. This is the chief reason why many today deny that the genuine version of the Seventy exists.

units.la: 63. Omissis vero quæstionibus variis quæ de hac editione inter doctos agitantur: An alia aliqua versio facta sit ante hanc à Judæis Alexandrinis tempore Alex. Magni? An tempore Ptolomæi Philadelphi, an Philometoris hæc facta sit? An tantum 5 libros Mosis an totum vetus Testamentum transtulerint? Quibus exemplaribus usi sint, & quibus characteribus descripta essent, vulgaribus sc. seu Chuthæis an sacris? An sp. Sancto afflati essent, an nudi interpretes? An vera sint quæ de separatis cellulis, miraculoso omnium consensu, & de 72[?] diebus quibus factam esse hanc versionem volunt, narrantur? De Aristea qui historiam hanc primo conscripsit authoritate: De Josephi, Philonis, &c. testimoniis: An ad verbum transtulerint an pro libitu, addiderint, ademerint, mutârint? De 13. locis quos tradunt Rabbini à 70, mutatos & in eis à textu Hebraico ipsos discessisse[?]: De jejunio quod fingunt Judæi propter legis translationem celebrari: De vero Origenis asterisco-rum, obeliscorum, lemnisco-rum & hypolemnisco-rum usu: An varia lectiones ex hac versione colligi possint? An ubiq; cum ab Hebræo hodierno differt juxta illum corrigi debeat? De computo Græcorum secundum versionem 70, &c. His inquam & aliis hujusmodi omissis, de quibus alibi in tractatu peculiari, hæc in præsentiarum æquis lectoribus consideranda proponimus.
units.tr: 63. Setting aside the various questions that learned men debate about this edition: Was some other version made before this one by Alexandrian Jews in the time of Alexander the Great? Was it made in the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus or of Philometor? Did they translate only the five books of Moses or the whole Old Testament? Which copies did they use, and in what characters were they written, the common ones, that is the Chuthaean, or the sacred ones? Were they inspired by the Holy Spirit, or were they plain interpreters? Are the things told about separate cells, the miraculous agreement of all of them, and the seventy-two days in which they want this version to have been made, true? About Aristeas, who first wrote this history, and his authority; about the testimonies of Josephus, Philo and others; did they translate word for word or as they pleased, adding, removing and changing? About the thirteen places where the rabbis say the Seventy changed the text and departed from the Hebrew; about the fast which the Jews invent to be kept on account of the translation of the Law; about Origen's true use of asterisks, obelisks, lemnisci and hypolemnisci; can variant readings be gathered from this version; and wherever it differs from the present Hebrew, ought it to be corrected by that text? About the Greek reckoning according to the Seventy, and so on. These and other such matters, I say, being set aside (we shall treat them elsewhere in a separate treatise), we propose that the following be considered by fair readers for the present.

units.la: 1. Versionem quandam Græcam celebrem fuisse, veteris Testamenti per 300. fere annos ante natũ Christum, ab Ecclesia Judaica magno applausu receptam, & 70. interpretibus adscriptam, quæ à Judæis per totam Asiam, Syriam, & Ægyptum publicè in Synagogis prælecta erat, & expositä, cum Hebraicum textum vix unus è centum intelligeret.
units.tr: 1. That there was a certain famous Greek version of the Old Testament about 300 years before the birth of Christ, received with great applause by the Jewish Church and ascribed to the Seventy translators. It was read publicly and expounded by the Jews in their synagogues throughout Asia, Syria and Egypt, at a time when hardly one in a hundred understood the Hebrew text.

units.la: 2. Pleraque testimonia quæ à Christo & Apostolis ex V. Testam. citantur, secundum Græcam versione proferri, etiam iis in locis ubi quadam discrepantia verborum inter Hebr. et Græc. esse videatur. Quod enim Hieronymus, & post ipsum alii, asserunt Apostolos nunquam testimonia ex 70. protulisse nisi cum Hebraeo codice convenirent, & Epistolæ ad Hebræos à veteribus contradictum fuisse, eò quòd testimoniis utebatur ex 70. depromptis, ex locorum inspectione apertissime deceptos fuisse demonstratum est à pluribus; imò vix unum aut alterum locum cum Hebraeo convenire, quosdam nec cum Hebraeo codice nec Græco, verbis sc. licet in sensu cum utrisque concordant. Hæc enim, & alia ex zelo in Hebræum, cujus linguæ ante plerosque sui temporis peritus erat, in præjudicium omnium versionum isum scripsisse constat. Miserum vero effugium est viri cujufdam docti, sc. loca parallela qua ab Apoftolis & Evangelistis adducuntur non ex Græca versione citata fuisse, sed ab Apostolis de novo reddita, prout ipsis visum fuerit, ac postea in omnia Græca exemplaria τῶν[?] 70 à scribis vel interpretibus post Apostolorum tempora verbatim transcripta & infulta esse; Hoc ab omni veri specie ita alienum est, ut nominasse apud cordatos omnes est confutasse, feriam enim confutationem non meretur. Quantum vero authoritatis huic versioni vel inde accedat, quod ipsi primi fidei doctores qui infallibilem Sp. S. assistentiam habuerunt, tum in disputationibus cum Judæis teftimonia inde peterent, cum in Oraculis sacro sanctis N. Testamenti ex hac versione testimonia Spiritus sancti authoritate sacrata reliquerint, cum in promptu ipsis effet, si necessarium ipsi judicaffent versiones alias in usum Ecclesiæ ex fontibus Hebraicis conficere, si tam despicatim de hac translatione judicassent ac neoterici quidam, qui pleno ore convitia in ipsos 70 eorumque versionem etiam cum in maxima extabat puritate conjiciunt, pio & prudenti leetori judicandum relinquo.
units.tr: 2. Most of the testimonies that Christ and the Apostles cite from the Old Testament are brought forward according to the Greek version, even in those places where some discrepancy of words between the Hebrew and the Greek seems to exist. For Jerome, and others after him, assert that the Apostles never brought forward testimonies from the Seventy except when they agreed with the Hebrew codex, and that the Epistle to the Hebrews was contradicted by the ancients because it used testimonies taken from the Seventy. Many have clearly shown, by inspecting the passages, that this is mistaken: scarcely one or two passages agree with the Hebrew, and some agree neither with the Hebrew codex nor with the Greek in words, though they agree with both in sense. It is known that Jerome wrote this, and other things, out of zeal for the Hebrew, whose language he knew better than most of his time, and to the prejudice of all versions. A miserable escape is the one a certain learned man takes, namely that the parallel passages which the Apostles and Evangelists adduce were not cited from the Greek version, but were rendered anew by the Apostles as they saw fit, and were afterwards copied word for word into all the Greek copies of the Seventy and inserted there by scribes or interpreters after the time of the Apostles. This is so far from any appearance of truth that to name it before sensible men is to refute it; it does not deserve a formal refutation. How much authority this version gains even from this, that the very first teachers of the faith, who had the infallible assistance of the Holy Spirit, sought testimonies from it when disputing with the Jews, and left testimonies from this version in the sacred oracles of the New Testament with the sacred authority of the Holy Spirit, although other versions made from the Hebrew sources for the use of the Church lay ready to hand if they had judged it necessary; and whether they would have judged this translation as contemptuously as some modern men, who with full mouth heap abuse on the Seventy and their version even though it was then in its greatest purity, I leave to the pious and prudent reader to judge.

units.la: 3. Ecclesiam Græcam & Latinam per 400. annos usque ad Hieronymi tempora hanc versionem solam recepisse, hanc unicam & quæ ex ipsa facta sunt translationes tum publice tum privatim usurpasse, hanc patres & scriptores commentariis illustrasse, & ex iis plures ut summæ authoritatis prædicasse, nam ut ex Augusti. supra di-ximus; Hanc tanquam sola esset recepit Ecclesia, et inter Græcos plerique an alia effet ignorabant. Philastrius vero Hærei. 39. 40. ait, quòd Ecclesia Catholica hanc colit, legit, & prædicat, alias autem (sc. Aquilæ, Theodotionis, & Symmachi) supervacaneas & contrarias tantæ editioni contemnit. Quæ enim ab Aquila, Theodotione & Symmacho, Hæreticis & apostatis Judæis facta erant nunquam Ecclesia publicè approbavit, sola exceptâ Theodotionis versione Danielis, quam certis de causis in Ecclesiis legi permisit, adeo ut tres istæ versiones, una cum 5 & 6 anonymis quas Origenes Hexaplis addidit, jam penitùs extinctæ sint, nullaque illarum reliquiæ nisi in quibusdam veterum scriptis hodiè inveniantur. Lucianus vero Martyr, & Hesychius, novas nunquam attentârunt versiones, sed tantùm veterem 70 versionem a mendis quibusdam purgatam ediderunt. Quod enim asserit Hieronymus praef. in Paralip. de tribus editionibus quæ in variis Ecclesiis singula obtinebant, quod Ægyptus sc. & Alexandria, Hesychii editionem sequebantur, Constantinopolis usque ad Antiochiam, Luciani Martyris, media vero inter hasce provincias Palestinos codices ab Origene elaboratos & ab Eusebio & Pamphilo evulgatos, quasi insignis aliquis esset inter hasce editiones differentia. Hoc pro more suo (ut observat vir doctus) hyperbolicè scripsit, nec enim aliquis ex patribus de varietatibus istarum editionum alicujus momenti conqueritur, & ut omnes perspicere possint, patrum qui in variis regionibus scripserunt magnus est ubique in 70. textus relatione consensus.
units.tr: 3. That the Greek and Latin Church, for 400 years down to the time of Jerome, received this version alone, used this one and the translations made from it exclusively, both publicly and privately, that the Fathers and writers illustrated it with commentaries, and that many of them proclaimed it of the highest authority; for as we said above from Augustine; the Church received it as though it were the only version, and most of the Greeks did not even know whether there was another. Philastrius, however, in Heresies 39 and 40, says that the Catholic Church honours, reads and preaches this one, but scorns the others (namely those of Aquila, Theodotion and Symmachus) as superfluous and contrary to so great an edition. What was made by Aquila, Theodotion and Symmachus, heretics and apostate Jews, the Church never publicly approved, except Theodotion's version of Daniel, which for certain reasons it allowed to be read in the churches. So these three versions, together with the fifth and sixth anonymous ones which Origen added in the Hexapla, are now wholly extinct, and no remains of them survive except in some ancient writings. Lucian the Martyr and Hesychius never attempted new versions, but only published the old Septuagint cleansed of certain errors. As for what Jerome says in his preface to Chronicles, about the three editions which held sway in different churches (that Egypt, namely Alexandria, followed Hesychius' edition, Constantinople as far as Antioch that of Lucian the Martyr, and the middle provinces of Palestine the manuscripts worked over by Origen and published by Eusebius and Pamphilus, as if there were some notable difference between these editions), he wrote this hyperbolically, as is his way (as a learned man observes). For none of the Fathers complains of any variation of real importance among these editions, and so that all may see it, there is everywhere a great agreement in the reports of the Fathers who wrote in various regions about the text of the Seventy.

units.la: Aliud enim est de vulgaribus loqui exemplaribus quæ plerumque ex scribarum festinatione & lucri desiderio vitiosè scripta erant, aliud de exemplaribus quæ erant in publico Ecclesiarum usu, quæ diligenter & accuratè scripta erant & per optimorum exemplarium textum emendata.
units.tr: For it is one thing to speak of common copies, which were mostly written carelessly through the haste and greed of scribes, and another to speak of the copies in public use in the churches, which were written diligently and accurately and corrected against the text of the best exemplars.

units.la: Quum autem Hieronymus versionem suam ex Hebræo instituisset, non statim ab Ecclesia Latina recepta fuit, sed à multis Episcopis contradictum est, & inter alios S. Augustinus per diœcesin suam publicè legi non permisit, tam altas radices fixerat in omnium animis veneranda Græca versionis æstimatio, imò Apologias sæpe Hieronymus scribere coactus est, & profiteri sibi nunquam in mentem venisse Græcæ versioni vel tantillum derogare, quam sacrosanctam agnoscit, eamque in Hexaplis puram & incorruptam asservari fatetur, & à se in Latinam versam suisse antequam Hebraica aggressus est, ut non uno in loco videre licet, sc. Apol. 2. cont. Ruffin. Proœm. quæst. in Genef. Epist. ad Suniam & Fretelam, præf. 2. ad lib. Paralip. &c. Imo licet Hieronymi versio à pluribus avidè legeretur, utpote nova, tamen antiquam Vulgatam Latinam ex 70. factam statim abolere non potuit, nam Greg. Mag. tempore utraque in usu erat, ut ex ejus scriptis constat, donec tandem ex utraque coaluerit hodierna Vulgata, ut non tantum Protestantium plerique, sed & inter Romanæ Ecclesiæ doctiores, multi statuunt, ut statim videbimus.
units.tr: When Jerome had made his version from the Hebrew, it was not received at once by the Latin Church; many bishops objected to it, and among others St Augustine did not permit it to be read publicly in his diocese. So deep had the veneration for the Greek version taken root in everyone's minds. Indeed Jerome was often compelled to write apologies, and to profess that it had never entered his mind to detract even slightly from the Greek version, which he acknowledges as most sacred, and he confesses that it is preserved pure and uncorrupted in the Hexapla, and that he himself had translated it into Latin before he undertook the Hebrew, as may be seen in more than one place: see Apology 2 against Rufinus, the Preface to the Questions on Genesis, the Letter to Sunia and Fretela, the second preface to the book of Chronicles, etc. Moreover, although Jerome's version was eagerly read by many because it was new, it could not at once abolish the old Latin Vulgate made from the Seventy; for in the time of Gregory the Great both were in use, as his writings show, until at last the present Vulgate coalesced out of both, as not only most Protestants but also many of the more learned Roman Church writers hold, as we shall shortly see.

units.la: Non tamen affirmo versionem Græcam unquam divinam habuisse authoritatem, licet ex antiquis multi ita loqui videantur : Interpretes enim, non Propheras [?] 70 seniores fuisse ut olim Hieronymus verissimum existimo, ideoque mirum est Joh. Morinum virum alias doctissimum statuere tam Græcam 70 quam Vulgatam Latinam divinæ authoritatis esse, cum inter se disrepent, & contraria affirment, ut in Chronologicis, qua nullo modo reconciliari possunt, quod & ipse tandem fateri cogitur : nec enim necessarium est ad fidem in populis ingenerandam versionem omnino infallibilem habere, cum de facto constet nullam inter innumeras quæ hodie in Europa extant versiones, esse divinæ & infallibilis authoritatis ; fides enim nititur authoritate seu veracitate Dei quæ semper certa & infallibilis, licet media omnia infallibilia non sint, ut loquuntur Scholæ : versiones enim eatenus tantum authoritatem habent, quatenus cum primis Autographis concordant ; sufficientia vero sunt fidei media, cum omnia ad salutem necessaria contineant, sine ullo errore contra fidem & mores. Talem itaque authoritatem in Ecclesia Græca & Latina habuit hæc versio, ut inter omnes primas haberet, quodque nihil fidei vel bonis moribus contrarium, sed omnia salutaria dogmata in se complecteretur ; varietates enim tales sunt, ut quæ necessario credenda sunt non evertant, vel quæ credenda non sunt, non docent, ut optime Heins. proleg. in exercit.
units.tr: I do not, however, affirm that the Greek version ever had divine authority, although many of the ancients seem to speak so. That the translators were Seventy elders and not prophets, as Jerome once said, I think most true. Hence it is strange that John Morinus, otherwise a most learned man, should maintain that both the Greek Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate are of divine authority, since they disagree with each other and affirm contrary things, as in the chronologies, which can in no way be reconciled, as he himself is at last compelled to admit. For it is not necessary, in order to engender faith among the people, that a version be wholly infallible, since it is in fact established that none of the innumerable versions now extant in Europe has divine and infallible authority. For faith rests on the authority or truthfulness of God, which is always certain and infallible, although the means are not all infallible, as the Schools say. Versions have authority only so far as they agree with the original autographs; but they are sufficient means of faith, since they contain all things necessary to salvation, without any error against faith and morals. Such authority did this version have in the Greek and Latin Church, that it held first place among all, and that it contained nothing contrary to faith or good morals, but embraced all the saving doctrines. For the variations are such that they do not overturn what must necessarily be believed, nor teach what is not to be believed, as Heinsius rightly says in his Prolegomena to the Exercitations.

units.la: 4. Veram & genuinam 70. versionem Origenis Hexaplis conservatam fuisse. Hoc præter Ecclesiæ testimonium quæ iisdem exemplaribus publice in Ecclesiis usa est, quibus Origenes, etiam fatetur ipse Hieronymus, qui maxime inter veteres huic versioni minus æquus erat, ut propriam in ejus locum surrogaret in Ecclesia Latina : Inter multa quæ ex ipso afferri poterunt, hoc unicum initio Epist. ad Suniam et Fretellam, satis erit. Hoc interest (inquit) inter utramque, (Vulgatam scil. editionem, & eam quæ in Hexaplis) quod κοινὴ [?] pro locis et temporibus et pro voluntate scriptorum veterum corrupta editio est, ea autem quæ habetur in ἑξαπλοῖς [?] et quam nos vertimus, ipsa est quæ in eruditorum libris incorrupta et immaculata 70 Interpretum translatio reservatur; Quicquid vero ab hac discrepat nulli dubium est quin ita et ab Hebræorum authoritate discordet. Non dico cum Morino, versionem 70 Apostolorum tempore cum Hebræo per omnia concordasse, et quod differentiæ quæ jam conspiciuntur corruptelæ sunt quæ ante Origine Hebræos codices invaserant; hoc enim facillime refutatur ex Onkelosi et Jonath. paraphrasibus quæ omnium consensu circa Christi tempora scripta erant, & in omnibus fere cum hodierno codice Hebræo ubi a 70. variat, conveniunt. Nec etiam 70 viralem per omnia cum hodierno Hebræo unquam convenisse existimo ; Loca enim multa variantia semper fuerunt ab antiquis notata, uti ex Origenis Epist.ad Julium Africanum, tum ex omnibus fere veterum monumentis constat, quæ ex triplicifonte emanarunt 1. Exscribarum incuria & negligentia, vel temeritate & audacia. 2. Ex ipsorum interpretum hallucinatione circa literas similes, vel voces homonymas, vel forte quod quadam pauca consulto aliter ob certas causas transtulerint ut quidam arbitrantur, de quo tamen dubitatur.
units.tr: 4. That the true and genuine Septuagint version preserved in Origen's Hexapla. This is shown, besides by the testimony of the Church, which publicly used in its churches the very copies that Origen used, as Jerome himself admits, though he was the most unfair of the ancients to this version, so that he might put his own in its place in the Latin Church: "Among the many things that could be brought forward from him, this one at the beginning of the letter to Sunia and Fretela will suffice." "This is the difference" (he says) "between the two" (namely the Vulgate edition and that in the Hexapla): "the common edition is corrupted according to places, times and the will of the ancient writers; but that which is found in the Hexapla, and which we have translated, is the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, preserved uncorrupted and unblemished in the books of the learned. Whatever differs from it is beyond doubt equally at odds with the authority of the Hebrews." I do not say with Morinus that the Seventy agreed in every respect with the Hebrew in the time of the Apostles, and that the differences now seen are corruptions which had crept into the Hebrew manuscripts before Origen. For this is most easily refuted from the paraphrases of Onkelos and Jonathan, which were written by common consent about the time of Christ, and which in almost every place where the Seventy vary from the present Hebrew codex, agree with it. Nor do I think that the Seventy ever agreed in every respect with the present Hebrew, for many variant passages have always been noted by the ancients, as is clear from Origen's letter to Julius Africanus, and from almost all the monuments of antiquity. These variations sprang from a threefold source: 1. From the carelessness and negligence of scribes, or their rashness and boldness. 2. From the mistakes of the interpreters themselves, concerning similar letters or homonymous words, or perhaps because they deliberately translated a few things differently for certain reasons, as some think, though this is doubted.

units.la: 3. Ex exemplarium Hebraicorum varietate, quæ licet in omnibus quæ ad fidem & mores spectant convenirent, in quibusdam tamen levioribus discrepasse tempore 70. seniorum, sicut postea Hieronymi tempore, & tam ante Masoretharum criticam (cùm multo rigidiores essent Judæi, adsuperstitionem usque, in codicum suorum conservatione, quàm ante Antiochi tempora) quæ postea, variasse, ut et hodie variare Babylonica ab Europæis notum est, nullus dubito. Nullū enim privilegium Judæis pro veteri, præ Christianis pro Novo Testamento concessum novimus, vel providentiam divinam eorum codicibus magis invigilasse quàm Christianorum, ut cùm multæ variantes lectiones in Græcis Codicibus etiam antiquissimis occurrant, codices Hebræos immunes esse credendæ sit: Quod enim quidam superstitiosè verentur, ne hoc modo vacillet fides, & de salutis doctrina actum sit nisi eandem scribis [?]ἀναμαρτησίαν quam ipsis scriptoribus sacris tribuamus, vanum & frivolum est: Cùm enim de facto constet lectiones varias inveniri in antiquissimis & probatissimis codicibus, quod negari à nemi-ns ne possit nisi oculos occludat, quam absurdum est ob consequentias fictitias quas quidam sibi imaginantur, negare quod palam & omnibus notum est? hoc enim est, ac si quis quum solis Eclipsim oculis conspiciat, negaret tamen hoc fieri posse, quia tabula Prutenica nulla tali hora futuram praedixerat. Licet vero tā ipsorū[?] qui tales consequentias metuunt interfit quam nostra, ad eas respondere, quam dilutum tamen sit argumentum quivis facile perspicere potest. Quis enim ita argumentante non rideret? In Livii scriptis errata quaedam irrepserunt librariorum incuria, ergo vacillat tota Romanae historiae fides, vel nihil certi habemus de Caesare, Pompeio & aliis, vel in Aristotelis & Platonis libris, exemplaria in quibusdam variant minutis, ergo nihil certum est in eorum Philosophia. Hoc profecto effet omnem historiarum fidem de mundo tollere, & libros omnes antiquos ut corruptos abjiciendos statuere. Praeterea multo magis invigilavit Divina providentia uti supra diximus in hisce codicibus conservandis, ita ut immunes sint in omnibus quae ad fidem & salutem necessaria sunt, & in articulis omnibus fundamentalibus, inter codices ab Ecclesia receptos Hebraeos, Græcos, Syriacos, Latinos, &c. summa sit consensio. Serio itaque responso indignos esse vult Heinsius, qui aut variasse olim in quibusdam libros, aut ex iis minus emendatos codices cum cura restitutos negent, prolog. in exerc.
units.tr: 3. From the variety of Hebrew copies, which, although they agreed in all matters touching faith and morals, nevertheless differed in some minor points at the time of the Seventy elders, and again in Jerome's time. This was so both before the critical work of the Masoretes (when the Jews were far stricter in preserving their codices, even to superstition, than they were before the time of Antiochus) and afterwards, when they varied, as the Babylonian copies known to Europeans vary today, I do not doubt. For we know of no privilege granted to the Jews for the Old Testament, as Christians have for the New, nor that divine providence watched over their codices more than over those of the Christians, so that, although many variant readings occur even in the most ancient Greek codices, the Hebrew codices should be believed to be free of them. What some superstitiously fear, that in this way faith would waver and the doctrine of salvation would be undone unless we ascribed to the copyists the same inerrancy that we ascribe to the sacred writers themselves, is vain and frivolous. For since it is established in fact that varied readings are found in the most ancient and most approved codices, which no one can deny unless he shuts his eyes, how absurd it is to deny what is plain and known to all, because of fictitious consequences which some imagine for themselves! This is as if someone, seeing a solar eclipse with his own eyes, should nevertheless deny that it can happen, because the Prussian Tables had predicted none at that hour. Although it is as much in the interest of those who fear such consequences as it is in ours to answer them, how weak the argument is anyone can easily see. For who would not laugh at one arguing thus? Some errors have crept into the writings of Livy through the carelessness of copyists; therefore the whole credibility of Roman history wavers, and we have nothing certain about Caesar, Pompey and others? Or, in the books of Aristotle and Plato the copies vary in minor points; therefore nothing is certain in their philosophy? This would indeed be to abolish all trust in the histories of the world and to decree that all ancient books be cast aside as corrupt. Moreover, divine providence has watched far more over the preservation of these codices, as we said above, so that they are free in all matters necessary to faith and salvation, and there is complete agreement in all the fundamental articles among the Hebrew, Greek, Syriac, Latin and other codices received by the Church. Heinsius therefore holds that those are unworthy of a serious answer who either deny that some books were once varied, or deny that codices restored with care from less emended ones.

units.la: 5. Veram 70. versionem quæ in Hexaplis olim extabat, hodiè extare, & non periisse, licet in multis scribarum incuria vel injuria temporum vitiatam, quod omnium librorum fors & conditio est, ita tamen ut eadem translatio dici possit & debeat. 1. Enim verso hac in Ecclesia Graeca publice semper usurpata erat & ad hunc usque diem retinetur, nec aliam ab ipso nascentis Ecclesiae primordio unquam habuit; cumque in quotidiano usu semper fuerit, in Ecclesiis publice praelecta, a patribus Graecis commentariis illustrata, in concionibus populo expositia, & ut Sacrosancta in magna semper erat veneratione, cur non hanc aeque puram conservare possit Ecclesia Graeca, ac Judaei Hebraicum textum, Romana Ecclesia Vulgatam Latinam, Antiochena Syriacam, plane non video, praesertim cum Ecclesia Graeca, nec amplitudine, nec viris sanctitate & eruditione claris, nec Episcoporum zelo in ritibus moribusque antiquis conservandis Romana, vel aliis cesserit, & 70. versionem quae in publico usu fuit accurate semper distinxerit ab Aqu.Theod.[?] & Symm.[?] versionibus, quae quia in publico usu nunquam erant penitus evanuerunt. 2. Praeterea si conferatur haec versio cum Hebraeo, infinita invenientur loca in quibus desunt quae in Hebraeo habentur, unde constat hanc non eandem esse editione quam Origenes suppleverat ex aliis versionibus. 3. Qui Scholia & commentarios ediderunt, ubique fere notant, ubi Aq. Theod. et Symm. &c. aliter ac 70. reddiderint, imo ipsius Hieronymi Prophetarum versio ubique fere cum hodierna consentit. Criteria quaedam annotarant quidam viri antiquitatis studiosi, ex quibus veram 70. versionem quae Origenis tempore extabat, etiam in quibusdam exemplaribus adhuc haberi demonstratur; si enim exemplar aliquod careat supplementis quæ sub asterisco addebat Origenes ex Hebraeo, habeat vero sententias quas testantur veteres obelo notatas ab Origene, quia non erant in Hebraeo, transpositiones etiam habeat versuum & capitum quorundam quæ testantur ve-teres aliter in 7o. quam in Hebraeo collocari, si denique concordet cum iis Scripturæ partibus quæ apud veteres reperiuntur, vel in Latinam versa vel commentariis expositæ, vel inscriptis suis citata, hoc exemplar verum & genuinum esse quis negare poterit? jam si quis hæc applicaverit quibusdam editionibus quæ hodie extant, &c. Aldinæ quæ Venetiis prodiit An. 1518. aliisque quæ Aldinam sequuntur, &c. Argentoratensi 1526. Basileensi anno 1545 (nam alteri 1526 Latina est pura puta Complutensis) & Francofurtensi, Anno 1597. quæ editiones fere cum Aldina consentiunt, nisi quod capita & versus in quibusdam ad normam Hebræam repositæ sint, & quædam in aliquibus ex Complutensi interpolata, per nimiam eorum audaciam qui editiones procurarunt, maxime vero cum Romana, quæ secundum exemplar Vaticanum MS. nobilissimum, ante Hieronymi tempora scriptum, aliaque, elaborata erat, expertus comperiet hæc ipsa esse Hexaplorum apographa, et verissima τῶν 70 versionis quæ ab antiquis celebrata fuit antitypa, paucis ut antea dictum exceptis quæ substantiam religionis nullo modo spestant.
units.tr: 5. That the true Septuagint version, which once existed in the Hexapla, still exists today and has not perished, though in many places corrupted by the carelessness of scribes or the injuries of time (which is the lot and condition of all books), can and must be held to be the same translation. First, this version has always been publicly used in the Greek Church and is retained to this day. From the very beginning of the nascent Church it has been the only one it has had. Since it has always been in daily use, read publicly in the churches, illustrated by the Greek Fathers in their commentaries, expounded to the people in sermons, and held in great reverence as sacred, I cannot see why the Greek Church should not be able to preserve this version as pure as the Jews preserved the Hebrew text, the Roman Church the Latin Vulgate, and the Antiochene Church the Syriac. The Greek Church has not yielded to the Roman Church, or to others, in extent, in men of holiness and learning, or in the zeal of its bishops for preserving ancient rites and customs. It has also always carefully distinguished the Septuagint version, which was in public use, from the versions of Aquila, Theodotion and Symmachus, which, because they were never in public use, have utterly vanished. 2. Moreover, if this version is compared with the Hebrew, countless passages will be found where things are lacking that are in the Hebrew. From this it is clear that it is not the same edition that Origen had supplemented from the other versions. 3. Those who have published scholia and commentaries almost everywhere note where Aquila, Theodotion, Symmachus and others rendered differently from the Seventy. Indeed, Jerome's own version of the Prophets agrees almost everywhere with the present text. Certain criteria have been noted by some men devoted to antiquity, by which it is shown that the true Septuagint version that existed in Origen's time is still found in some copies. For if a copy lacks the supplements that Origen added from the Hebrew under the asterisk, but has the sentences which the ancients testify Origen marked with the obelus because they were not in the Hebrew; if it also has transpositions of certain verses and chapters, which the ancients testify were placed differently in the Seventy than in the Hebrew; and finally if it agrees with those parts of Scripture which are found among the ancients, either translated into Latin, expounded in commentaries, or cited under their own headings, who could deny that this copy is true and genuine? Now if someone applies these criteria to certain editions which exist today, such as the Aldine, published at Venice in 1518, and others that follow the Aldine, the Strasbourg edition of 1526, the Basel edition of 1545 (for the other edition of 1526 is pure Latin, namely the Complutensian), and the Frankfurt edition of 1597, which almost agree with the Aldine except that some chapters and verses have been rearranged to the Hebrew norm, and some things have been interpolated from the Complutensian by the excessive boldness of those who prepared the editions; and above all with the Roman edition, which was prepared according to the most noble Vatican manuscript, written before the time of Jerome, and others: he will find, as I said before, that these are copies of the Hexapla and the most faithful antitypes of the version of the Seventy celebrated by the ancients [τῶν 70], with only a few exceptions, as stated above, which in no way touch the substance of religion.

units.la: 64 Quod vero ad editionem Græcam quæ in Complutensi primum, postea in Regiis, & nuper in Parisianis Bibliis extat, attinet, hanc in multis ad Hebraeum hodiernum adaptarunt, refectis, appositis, transpositis variis, ut Hebræo textui respon-deret, adeo ut mixtam & interpolatâ versionem confecerint, quam quidem pro moderni Hebraei Codicis translatione Græca haberi posse concedo, nec non rationes suas fortasse habuisse viros doctos cur hoc fecerint, at pro vera 70 versione quæ à patribus tantopere celebrata fuit nequaquam esse habendam aperte constat, cum omnium maxime inter editiones quæ hodie extant, ab ea distare ex dictis patet: unde Doctiss. Masius in 21. Ios. affirmat, meram esse inscitiam si quis dicat Complutenses purâ 70. interpretum translationem dedisse; nec minori inscitiâ laborant, qui de 70 sinceritate ex omnimoda cum Hebræo hodierno vel Vulgata Latina aliâve versione conformitate pronunciant. Scripsère ex patribus multi commentaria in magnam Bibliorum partem, Chrysostomus, Augustinus & alii, Hieronymus Prophetas ex Hexaplis transtulit, scripsit Procopius in Esaiâ, ipsumq; exemplar cum Procopio typis editum descriptum est ex Abbatis Apollinarii exemplari, in quo testatur Apollinarius se illud diligenter cum ipsius Origenis Hexaplis in Bibliotheca Cæsariensi, et etiam cum Tetraplis contulisse, et obelos et asteriscos in margine notâsse. MSS. vetustissima quadâ habuit Doctiss. Masius Syriaca, ante mille annos scripta, quæ ex Græco exemplari quod in Hexaplis in eadem Cæsariensi Bibliotheca repositis exscriptum erat Syriacè versa, de quibus ipse præf. in Josuam, quibusque in Josuæ editione usus est; citantur quædam ex 70. per Clementem in celeberrima illa Epistola quam edidit Patricius Junius. Jam si quis editiones prædictas, maxime Romanam cum istis contulerit, omnia sibi invicem respondere pene ad amussim reperiet. Dolendum itaque viros doctos ita affectibus & partium studiis abreptos inveniri, alios quidem sub prætextu afferendæ Vulgatæ Latinæ, alios ex opposito sub specie defendendi Hebraicam veritatem, ut in antiquissimam & ipsa canicie venerandam hanc 70 versionem, sacrum depositum ab Apostolis Ecclesiæ traditum, quo obstetricante nata, quo lactante nutrita erat, quo dirigente orbem occupavit, & Christo subjecit, ita iniqui sint, ut omni authoritate spoliatam tantūm non pedibus conculcent; qui nec Judaorum ante Christum, nec ipsius Domini ac Apostolorum, qui ipsam sæpius usurparunt, nec primævæ puraque Ecclesiæ rationem ullam habeant. Habeat sane Textus Hebraeus, prærogativam fontis, habeat etiam Vulgata Latina locum suum, Græca tamen apud omnes cordatos & moderatos viros, qui de istiusmodi rebus optime judicare nôrunt, semper in honore erit.
units.tr: 64 As for the Greek edition which appears first in the Complutensian Bible, then in the Royal Bible, and lately in the Paris Bible, I grant that in many places they have adapted it to the Hebrew text of today, by revising, adding and transposing various things so that it would correspond to the Hebrew. So they have produced a mixed and interpolated version, which I concede may be regarded as a Greek translation of the present Hebrew text. I also grant that learned men may have had their reasons for doing this. But it is clearly evident that it must by no means be held to be the true version of the Seventy, which has been so greatly celebrated by the Fathers, since it is shown above that it differs most of all from the editions that exist today. Hence the most learned Masius, on Joshua 21, affirms that it is pure ignorance to say that the Complutensians gave the pure translation of the Seventy interpreters. Those who pronounce on the sincerity of the Seventy from its complete conformity with the present Hebrew, or with the Latin Vulgate or some other version, labour under no less ignorance. Among the Fathers, many wrote commentaries on a large part of the Bible: Chrysostom, Augustine and others. Jerome translated the Prophets from the Hexapla. Procopius wrote on Isaiah, and the copy itself, printed together with Procopius, was transcribed from the copy of the Abbot Apollinarius, in which Apollinarius testifies that he had carefully compared it with Origen's own Hexapla in the Caesarean library, and also with the Tetrapla, and had noted the obeli and asterisks in the margin. The most learned Masius had a very ancient Syriac manuscript, written a thousand years ago, which was translated into Syriac from a Greek copy transcribed from the Hexapla kept in the same Caesarean library. He speaks of it in his preface to Joshua, and used it in his edition of Joshua. Certain passages of the Seventy are cited by Clement in that famous Epistle which Patricius Junius published. Now if someone compares the aforesaid editions, especially the Roman, with these, he will find that they almost exactly correspond to one another. It is therefore to be lamented that learned men are found so carried away by passions and partisan zeal: some under the pretext of defending the Latin Vulgate, others on the contrary under the appearance of defending the Hebrew truth, are so unjust toward this most ancient version, venerable for its very grey hairs, the sacred deposit handed down to the Church by the Apostles, by whose midwifery it was born, by whose nursing it was raised, under whose guidance it occupied the world and subjected it to Christ, that they would tread it underfoot, stripped of all authority. They have no regard either for the Jews before Christ, or for the Lord himself and the Apostles, who used it very often, or for the reasoning of the primitive and pure Church. Let the Hebrew text certainly have the prerogative of the source, and let the Latin Vulgate have its place. Yet the Greek version will always be held in honour by all sensible and moderate men, who know how to judge such matters well.

units.la: 65 Licet autem editio Romana omnium quæ hactenus extant maxime pura sit & genuina, in cujus editione per 9. annos à multis viris doctis do-ctis[?] his desudatum est, non tamen ex omni parte absolutam esse obfervarunt viri doctissimi, ita ut fortasse adhuc pumice critico indigeat: Cumque MS. habeamus versionis 70 quod Alexandrinum vocamus, ex Bibliotheca Regia desumptum, ipsi Vaticano nec antiquitate, nec sinceritate cedens, de cujus editione vir doctus Patricius Junius multis abhinc annis cogitavit, ejusque librum unicum Iobi fcil. Londini, speciminis ergo, promulgavit, unde magnam per orbem Christianum inter viros doctos expectationem de ejus editione excitavit: De hoc nobilissimo & antiquissimo monumento, quod Bibliis nostris adjiciendum duximus, aliquid breviter praefari libet. MS. hoc ex Alexandria secum attulit Cyrillus Lucaris nuper Patriarcha Alexandrinus, cum ad sedem Patriarchalem Conftantinopolitanam promotus effet, tanquam magnum Orientis Thesaurum, illudque Regi nostro qui magnum librorum impressórum fuppellectilem eidem Cyrillo misit, per D. Thomam Roe equitem auratum Regis apud Turcarum Imperatorem legatum, dono dedit, quod ut pretiosissimum κειμήλιον[?] in Bibliotheca sua Regia asservari jussit. Scriptum vero erat (ut testatur idem Cyrillus propria manu ad initium libri,) per S. Theclam prout fama erat apud Alexandrinos, ejufq; Theclæ nomen libro inscriptum erat, quod jam obliteratum non conspicitur: licet vero quod de Thecla asserit incertum sit, liber vero, eò quòd fortassè ad Theclæ Monasterium aliquod pertinebat, ejus nomen inscriptum habuit, & fama fallaci parum tribuendum: summæ tamen antiquitatis esse multa sunt quæ arguunt, scriptionis &c. modus, magnis enim seu uncialibus literis antiquis in pergameno descriptus est, sine ulla versuum, capitum, vel verborum distinctione, sine ullis accentibus vel aspirationis notis, quæ à Grammaticis forte tunc nondum inventa erant, adeo ut unum quasi verbum continuatim videri posset, quale de antiquis Bibliorum codicibus Hebraicis, longè ante Masorethas testantur quidam ex Rabbinis, & de Pindari aliorumque poëtarum Græcorum poëmatis affirmant alii, sectiones tamen quasdam habet, & in 5. libris &c. Job. Psalm. Eccles. Proverb. & Cantic. ut apud antiquos, in στίχος[?] quosdam partitus est, ut ex libro Job à D. Junio evulgato videre liceet.
units.tr: 65 Although the Roman edition is the purest and most genuine of all those that have appeared so far, and although in its preparation many learned men toiled for nine years, the most learned men have observed that it is not absolutely complete in every part, so that perhaps it still needs the critical pumice. And since we have a manuscript of the version of the Seventy, which we call the Alexandrian, taken from the Royal Library, which yields to the Vatican itself neither in antiquity nor in soundness, the learned Patricius Junius thought for many years about its edition, and published, as a specimen, its single book of Job at London. This aroused great expectation among learned men throughout the Christian world about its edition. Concerning this most noble and most ancient monument, which we have thought fit to add to our Bibles, it is pleasing to say a few things briefly by way of preface. This manuscript was brought with him from Alexandria by Cyril Lucaris, lately Patriarch of Alexandria, when he was promoted to the patriarchal see of Constantinople. He gave it, as a great treasure of the East, to our King, who sent Cyril a great supply of printed books. It was given as a gift through Sir Thomas Roe, a knight and the King's ambassador to the Emperor of the Turks. The King ordered it to be kept in his Royal Library as a most precious heirloom. It was written, as Cyril himself testifies in his own hand at the beginning of the book, by St Thecla, according to the report among the Alexandrians, and the name of Thecla was inscribed in the book, though it can no longer be seen because it has been erased. Although what is said about Thecla is uncertain, and the report is not to be given much weight since it is deceptive, the book, perhaps because it belonged to some monastery of Thecla, had her name inscribed on it. Still, there are many things that argue for the highest antiquity: the manner of writing, for it is written on parchment in large or uncial letters of the ancient kind, without any division into verses, chapters or words, without any accents or marks of breathing, which grammarians perhaps had not yet invented. So it could seem like one continuous word, as some of the rabbis testify about the ancient Hebrew Bible manuscripts, long before the Masorites, and as others affirm about the poems of Pindar and other Greek poets. Yet it has certain divisions, and in the five books, namely Job, Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Proverbs and Canticles, it has divided the text into lines (stichoi) as the ancients did, as may be seen from the book of Job which Junius has published.

units.la: In N.T. præter dicta, alia sunt quæ summam antiquitatem spirant, de quibus alibi, ad finem vero libri, annexæ sunt Epistolæ duæ, una integra & genuina sine dubio, &c. celeberrima illa apud antiquos Clementis Romani S. Pauli discipuli ad Corinthios, quæ post sacras literas maximæ erat authoritatis, & in Ecclesiis quibusdam publicè legebatur, quam cùm supra mille annos intermortua jacuisset, magno Ecclesiæ commodo Typis evulgavit idem D. Junius cum versione Latina, & notis ad calcem doctissimis: altera verò lacera & imperfecta, ab eodem tamen publici juris facta, quæ licet D. Grotio primi seculi esse videatur & ante constitutum Ecclesiarum consensu Canonem fcripta, Clementisque nomen præfe ferat, alterius tamen Clementis esse antiqui judicárunt.
units.tr: In the New Testament, besides the passages already mentioned, there are other works that breathe great antiquity, which I deal with elsewhere. At the end of the book, however, two Epistles are appended. The first is whole and undoubtedly genuine, etc.: the most famous letter of Clement of Rome, the disciple of St Paul, to the Corinthians. Among the ancients it was of the greatest authority after the sacred writings, and it was publicly read in some churches. After lying dead for more than a thousand years, it was brought to light by the same Junius, with a Latin version and most learned notes at the foot of the page, to the great benefit of the Church. The second, however, is mangled and imperfect, though Junius also published it. Although it seems to Grotius to belong to the first century and to have been written before the churches agreed on the canon, and although it bears Clement's name, the ancients judged that it belonged to another, older Clement.

units.la: 67. Hujus vero M S. licet magnus fit cum Vaticano consensus, adeo ut fe mutuo confirment, omniaque argumenta quæ à Morino proferuntur ad probandam Vaticani sin-ceritatem, etiam huic nostro quadrent; cum tamen illud ex Luciani Martyris, hoc ve-ro ex Hefychii editione multis esse videatur: Hefychii enim exemplaria Alexandriæ in usu publico erant teste Hieronymo, unde in minutis quibusdam, varietates quædam occurrunt, præsertim in propriis nominibus, in quibus frequentior inter exemplaria diffensus reperitur; cumque textum codicis noftri Alexandrini imprimere effet fere actum agere. idem enim fere est cum Vaticano, præter dignitatem tamen tanti & tam celebris MS. effet, inter varias aliorum codicum lectiones ad finem cujuslibet Tomi, vel ad calcem totius operis detrudi, ideo ut uno intuitu ista duo nobiliff: & antiquissima exemplaria lectori repræsentarentur, Romanum primo in columna peculiari posuimus, Alexandrinum vero ad finem cujuflibet columnæ, ubi fcil. à Romano differt, ut hoc modo lector collationem inter u-trumque facere posset. Lectiones etiam istas ex MS. ne possit nisi oculos occludat, quam absurdum est ob consequentias fictitias quas quidam sibi imaginantur, negare quod palam & omnibus notum est? hoc enim est, ac si quis quum solis Eclipsim oculis conspiciat, negaret tamen hoc fieri posse, quia tabulæ Prutenicæ nullâ tali horâ futuram prædixerat. Licet vero tâ ipsorū qui tales consequentias metuunt interesse quam nostra, ad eas respondere, quam dilutum tamen sit argumentum quivis facile perspicere potest. Quis enim ita argumentante non rideret? In Livii scriptis errata quædam irrepserunt librariorum incuriâ, ergo vacillat tota Romanæ historiæ fides, vel nihil certi habemus de Cæsare, Pompeio & aliis, vel in Aristotelis & Platonis libris, exemplaria in quibusdam variant minutis, ergo nihil certum est in eorum Philosophia. Hoc professo[?] effet omnem historiarum fidem de mundo tollere, & libros omnes antiquos ut corruptos abjiciendo statuere. Præterea multo magis invigilavit Divina providentia uti supra diximus in hisce codicibus confervandis, ita ut immunes sint in omnib⁹ quæ ad fidem & salutem necessaria sunt, & in articulis omnibus fundamentalibus, inter codices ab Ecclesia receptos Hebræos, Græcos, Syriacos, Latinos, &c. summa sit consensio. Serio itaque responso indignos esse vult Heinsius, qui aut variasse olim in quibusdam libros, aut ex iis minus emendatos codices cum cura restitutos negent, proleg. in exerc.
units.tr: 67. The agreement of this manuscript of ours with the Vatican one is indeed great, so that the two confirm each other, and all the arguments that Morinus brings forward to prove the sincerity of the Vatican codex also suit ours. Yet the Vatican text seems to come from the edition of Lucian the Martyr, and ours from that of Hesychius. For the Hesychian copies were in public use at Alexandria, as Jerome testifies, and so in minor details certain variants occur, especially in proper names, where disagreement among the copies is most frequent. Since printing the text of our Alexandrian codex would amount to almost the same thing as printing the Vatican (the two are nearly identical), yet the dignity of so great and famous a manuscript would not allow it to be thrust among the various readings of other codices at the end of a volume or at the foot of the whole work, we have placed the Roman text first in a separate column so that both these noble and most ancient copies can be seen at a single glance. The Alexandrian text we have put at the foot of each column, wherever it differs from the Roman, so that the reader can compare the two. As for these readings from the manuscript, who can deny what is plain and known to all, unless he shuts his eyes? How absurd it is to deny what is publicly known because of fictitious consequences that some imagine for themselves! It is as if someone who sees a solar eclipse with his own eyes were nonetheless to deny that it is happening, because the Prussian Tables had predicted none at that hour. Although those who fear such consequences have more reason than we to answer them, anyone can easily see how weak the argument is. For who would not laugh at someone who argued thus? Some errors crept into the writings of Livy through the carelessness of copyists; therefore the whole credibility of Roman history totters, and we have nothing certain about Caesar, Pompey and others. Or again, the copies of Aristotle and Plato vary in small details; therefore nothing is certain in their philosophy. To profess this would be to remove all trust in history, and to settle the matter by rejecting all ancient books as corrupt. Moreover, divine providence has watched over the preservation of these codices much more closely, as we said above, so that they are free from error in all matters necessary to faith and salvation. Among the Hebrew, Greek, Syriac, Latin and other codices received by the Church there is complete agreement on all the fundamental articles. Heinsius therefore deserves no serious reply, he who denies either that books were once altered in some places, or that less well emended codices were carefully restored. Prolegomena to the Exercitationes.

units.la: §. Veram 70. versionem quæ in Hexaplis olim extabat, hodie extare, & non periisse, licet in multis scribarum incuriâ vel injuriâ temporum vitiatam, quod omnium librorum fors & conditio est, ita tamen ut eadem translatio dici possit & debeat. 1. Enim versio hæc in Ecclesia Græca publice semper usurpata erat & ad hunc usque diem retinetur, nec aliam ab ipso nascentis Ecclesiæ primordio unquam habuit; cumque in quotidiano usu semper fuerit, in Ecclesiis publice præleƈta, à patribus Græcis commentariis illustrata, in concionibus populo exposita, & ut Sacrofanƈta in magna semper erat veneratione, cur non hanc æque puram conservare posset Ecclesia Græca, ac Judæi Hebræicum textum, Romana Ecclesia Vulgatam Latinam, Antiochena Syriacam, plane non video, præsertim cum Ecclesia Græca, nec amplitudine, nec viris sanƈtitate & eruditione claris, nec Episcoporum zelo in ritibus moribusque antiquis confervandis Romanæ, vel aliis cesserit, & 70. versionem quæ in publico usu fuit accurate semper distinxerit ab Aqu. Theod. & Symmachi versionibus, quæ quia in publico usu nunquam erant penitus evanuerunt. 2. Praterea si conferatur hæc versio cum Hebræo, infinita invenientur loca in quib² desunt quæ in Hebræo habentur, unde constat hanc non eandem esse editione quam Origenes asteriscis suppleverat ex aliis versionibus. 3. Qui Scholia & commentarios ediderunt, ubique fere notant, ubi Aq. Theod. et Sym. &c. aliter ac 70. reddiderint, imo ipsius Hieronymi Prophetarum versio ubique fere cum hodierna consentit. Criteria quædam annotârant quidam viri antiquitatis studiosi, ex quibus veram 70. versionem quæ Origenis tempore extabat, etiam in quibusdam exemplaribus adhuc haberi demonstratur; si enim exemplar aliquod careat fupplementu qua sub asterisco addebat Origenes ex Hebraeo, habeat vero sententias quas testantur veteres obelo notatas ab Origene, quia non erant in Hebraeo, tranfpofitiones etia habeat versuum & capitum quorundam qua testantur veteres aliter in 7o. quam in Hebraeo collocari, fi denique concordet cum iis Scripturae partibus quae apud veteres reperiuntur, vel in Latinam versa vel commentariis exposita, vel inscriptis suis citata, hoc exemplar verum & genuinum esse quis negare poterit? Iam fi quis hac applicaverit quibufdam editionibus quae hodie extant, fc. Aldina quae Venetiis prodiit An. 1518. aliisque quae Aldinam sequuntur, fc. Argentoratenfi 1526. Bafileenfi anno 1545 (nam alteri 1526 Latina est pura puta Complutenfis) & Francofurtenfi, Anno 1597. quae editiones fere cum Aldina consentiunt, nisi quod capita & versus in quibusdam ad normam Hebraeam reposita sint, & quaedam in aliquibus ex Complutenfi interpolata, per nimiam eorum audaciam qui editiones procurarunt, maxime vero cum Romana, quae fecundum exemplar Vaticanum MS. nobilissimum, ante Hieronymi tempora scriptum, aliaque, elaborata erat, expertus comperiet haec ipsa esse Hexaplorum apographa, et verissima τῶν 70 versionis quae ab antiquis celebrata fuit antitypa, paucis ut antea diftum exceptis quae substantiam religionis nullo modo spestant.
units.tr: §. That the true version of the Seventy, which once stood in the Hexapla, is extant today and has not perished, although in many places corrupted by the carelessness of scribes or the injuries of time, is the fate of all books; yet the same translation can and should be called by that name. First, this version was always used publicly in the Greek Church and is retained to this day. From the very beginning of the nascent Church it never had any other. Since it has always been in daily use, read publicly in the churches, illustrated by Greek Fathers in commentaries, expounded to the people in sermons, and always held in great veneration as most sacred, I do not see why the Greek Church could not preserve it as purely as the Jews preserved the Hebrew text, the Roman Church the Latin Vulgate, or the Antiochene Church the Syriac. The Greek Church has yielded to the Roman or any other church neither in extent, nor in men distinguished for holiness and learning, nor in the zeal of its bishops for preserving ancient rites and customs. And it has always carefully distinguished the Seventy's version, which was in public use, from the versions of Aquila, Theodotion and Symmachus, which, because they were never in public use, have entirely vanished. 2. Moreover, if this version is compared with the Hebrew, countless passages will be found that lack what is in the Hebrew. This shows that it is not the same edition that Origen had supplemented with asterisks from the other versions. 3. Those who have published scholia and commentaries almost everywhere note where Aquila, Theodotion, Symmachus and others translated differently from the Seventy. Indeed, Jerome's own version of the Prophets agrees with the present text almost everywhere. Certain tests have been noted by some men devoted to antiquity, by which it is shown that the true Seventy version which existed in Origen's time is still to be found in some copies. For if a copy lacks the additions which Origen supplied from the Hebrew under the asterisk, but has the sentences which the ancients testify Origen marked with an obelus because they were not in the Hebrew; if it also has transpositions of verses and chapters which the ancients testify were placed differently in the Seventy than in the Hebrew; and if, finally, it agrees with those parts of Scripture which are found among the ancients, whether translated into Latin, expounded in commentaries, or cited in their own writings, who could deny that this copy is true and genuine? Now if anyone applies these tests to some editions that exist today, namely the Aldine, published at Venice in 1518, and the others that follow the Aldine, namely the Strasbourg of 1526, the Basel of 1545 (for the other of 1526 is purely Latin, namely the Complutensian), and the Frankfurt of 1597, which editions mostly agree with the Aldine, except that in some the chapters and verses have been rearranged to the Hebrew norm, and in some a few things have been interpolated from the Complutensian through the excessive boldness of those who prepared them; and especially if he tests them against the Roman edition, which was prepared from the most noble Vatican manuscript, written before Jerome's time, and other sources, he will find that these are copies of the Hexapla and the truest images of the Seventy's version celebrated by the ancients, with a few exceptions, as said before, which in no way concern the substance of religion.

units.la: 64 Quod vero ad editionem Graecam quae in Complutenfi primum, postea in Regiis, & nuper in Parisianis Bibliis extat, attinet, hanc in multis ad Hebraeum hodiernum adaptarunt, refestis, appositis, transpositis variis, ut Hebraeo textui responderet, adeo ut mixtam & interpolatam verfionem confecerint, quam quidem pro moderni Hebraei Codicis translatione Graeca haberi posse concedo, nec non rationes suas fortasse habuisse viros doctos cur hoc fecerint, at pro vera 70 versione quae a patribus tantopere celebrata fuit nequaquam esse habendam aperte constat, cum omnium maxime inter editiones quae hodie extant, ab ea distare ex dictis patet: unde Doctiss. Masius in 21. Ios. affirmat, meram esse inscitiam si quis dicat Complutenses puram 70. interpretum translationem dedisse; nec minori inscitia laborant, qui de 70 sinceritate ex omnimoda cum Hebraeo hodierno vel Vulgata Latina aliave versione conformitate pronunciant. Scripsere ex patribus multi commentaria in magnam Bibliorum partem, Chrysostomus, Augustinus & alii, Hieronymus Prophetas ex Hexaplis transtulit, scripsit Procopius in Esaia, ipsumq; exemplar cum Procopio typis editum descriptum est ex Abbatis Apollinarii exemplari, in quo testatur Apollinarius se illud diligenter cum ipsius Origenis Hexaplis in Bibliotheca Casariensi, et etiam cum Tetraplis contulisse, et obelos et asteriscos in margine notasse[?]. MSS. vetustissima quadā habuit Doctiss. Masius Syriaca, ante mille annos scripta, quae ex Graeco exemplari quod in Hexaplis in eadem Casariensi Bibliotheca repositis exscriptum erat Syriacè versa, de quibus ipse præf. in Iosuam, quibusque in Iosuæ editione usus est; citantur quædam ex 70. per Clementem in celeberrima illa Epistola quam edidit Patricius Junius. Jam si quis editiones prædictas, maximè Romanam cum istis contulerit, omnia sibi invicem respondere pene ad amussim reperiet. Dolendum itaque viros doctos ita affectibus & partium studiis abreptos inveniri, alios quidem sub prætextu afferendæ Vulgatæ Latinæ, alios ex opposito sub specie defendendi Hebraicam veritatem, ut in antiquissimam & ipsa canicie venerandam hanc 70 versionem, sacrum depositum ab Apostolis Ecclesiæ traditum, quo obstetricante nata, quo lactante nutrita erat, quo dirigente orbem occupavit, & Christo subjecit, ita iniqui sint, ut omni authoritate spoliatam tantum non pedibus conculcent; qui nec Judæorum ante Christum, nec ipsius Domini ac Apostolorum, quipsam sæpius usurpárunt, nec primævæ puraque Ecclesiæ rationem ullam habeant. Habeat sanè Textus Hebræus, prærogativam fontis, habeat etiam Vulgata Latina locum suum, Græca tamen apud omnes cordatos & moderatos viros, qui de istiusmodi rebus optimè judicare nôrunt, semper in honore erit.
units.tr: 64. As for the Greek edition that first appears in the Complutensian, afterwards in the Royal Bibles, and lately in the Paris Bibles, they adapted it in many places to the present Hebrew, by cutting, adding and transposing various things so that it would correspond to the Hebrew text. The result is a mixed and interpolated version. I grant that it may be regarded as a Greek translation of the modern Hebrew codex, and that learned men perhaps had their reasons for doing this. But it is plainly clear that it is not to be held as the true version of the Seventy that the Fathers celebrated so greatly, since it differs from it most of all among the editions that exist today, as has been shown. Hence the most learned Masius, on Joshua 21, affirms that it is sheer ignorance to say that the Complutensians gave the pure translation of the Seventy interpreters. Those who pronounce on the Seventy's sincerity from complete conformity with the present Hebrew, or with the Latin Vulgate or any other version, labour under no less ignorance. Among the Fathers, many wrote commentaries on a large part of the Bible: Chrysostom, Augustine and others. Jerome translated the Prophets from the Hexapla. Procopius wrote on Isaiah, and the very copy printed together with Procopius was transcribed from the copy of Abbot Apollinarius, in which Apollinarius testifies that he had carefully collated it with Origen's own Hexapla in the Caesarean library, and also with the Tetrapla, and had noted the obeli and asterisks in the margin. The learned Masius had a very ancient Syriac manuscript, written a thousand years ago, which was translated into Syriac from a Greek copy that had been transcribed from the Hexapla kept in the same Caesarean library. Of this he himself speaks in his preface to Joshua, and he used it in his edition of Joshua. Some passages of the Seventy are cited by Clement in the celebrated Epistle that Patricius Junius published. Now if anyone compares the editions mentioned, especially the Roman, with these, he will find that they correspond to one another almost exactly. It is to be lamented, therefore, that learned men are found so carried away by passions and party spirit: some, under the pretext of upholding the Latin Vulgate, and others, on the contrary, under the appearance of defending the Hebrew truth, are so unjust to this Seventy version, venerable for its very age, the sacred deposit handed down to the Church by the Apostles, by whose midwifery it was born, by whose milk it was nourished, and by whose guidance it occupied the world and subjected it to Christ, that they strip it of all authority and scarcely tread it underfoot. They have no regard either for the Jews before Christ, or for the Lord himself and the Apostles, who used it very often, nor for the principles of the primitive and pure Church. Let the Hebrew text indeed have the prerogative of the source, and let the Latin Vulgate keep its place. Yet the Greek will always be held in honour by all sensible and moderate men who know how to judge such matters well.

units.la: 65 Licèt autem editio Romana omnium quæ hactenus extant maximè pura sit & genuina, in cujus editione per 9. annos à multis viris doIstis[?] desudatum est, non tamen ex omni parte absolutam esse observarunt viri doctissimi, ita ut fortasse adhuc pumice critico indigeat: Cumque MS. habeamus versionis 70 quod Alexandrinum vocamus, ex Bibliotheca Regia desumptum, ipsi Vaticano nec antiquitate, nec sinceritate cedens, de cujus editione vir doctus Patricius Junius multis abhinc annis cogitavit, ejusque librum unicum Iobi scil. Londini, specimînis ergo, promulgavit, unde magnam per orbem Christianum inter viros doctos expectationem de ejus editione excitavit: De hoc nobilissimo & antiquissimo monumento, quod Bibliis nostris adjiciendum duximus, aliquid breviter praefari libet. MS. hoc ex Alexandria secum attulit Cyrillus Lucaris nuper Patriarcha Alexandrinus, cum ad sedem Patriarchalem Constantinopolitanam promotus esset, tanquam magnum Orientis Thesaurum, illudque Regi nostro qui magnum librorum impressorum suppellectilem eidem Cyrillo misit, per D. Thomam Roe equitem auratum Regis apud Turcarum Imperatorem legatum, dono dedit, quod ut pretiosissimum κειμήλιον in Bibliotheca sua Regia asservari jussit. Scriptum vero erat (ut testatur idem Cyrillus propria manu ad initium libri,) per S. Theclam prout fama erat apud Alexandrinos, ejusq; Thecla nomen libro inscriptum erat, quod jam obliteratum non conspicitur: licet vero quod de Thecla asserit incertum sit, liber vero, eo quod fortasse ad Theclæ[?] Monasterium aliquod pertinebat, ejus nomen inscriptum habuit, & fama fallaci parum tribuendum: summæ tamen antiquitatis esse multa sunt quæ arguunt, scriptionis sc. modus, magnis enim seu uncialibus literis antiquis in pergameno descriptus est, sine ulla versuum, capitum, vel verborum distinctione, sine ullis accentibus vel aspirationis notis, quæ a Grammaticis forte tunc nondum inventa erant, adeo ut unum quasi verbum continuatu videri posset, quale de antiquis Bibliorū codicibus Hebraicis, longe ante Masorethas testantur quidam ex Rabbinis, & de Pindari aliorumque poëtarum Græcorum poëmatis affirmant alii, sectiones tamen quasdam habet, & in 5. libris sc. Job. Psalm. Eccles. Proverb. & Cantic. ut apud antiquos, in στίχως[?] quosdam partitus est, ut ex libro Job a D. Junio evulgato videre licet.
units.tr: Although the Roman edition is the purest and most genuine of all those that have appeared hitherto, and though many learned men have toiled over its production for nine years, learned men have observed that it is not in every respect perfect, so that perhaps it still needs the critical pumice. We have a manuscript of the Septuagint version, which we call the Alexandrian, taken from the Royal Library, which yields neither in antiquity nor in soundness to the Vatican itself. Long ago the learned Patricius Junius considered its edition, and as a specimen he published at London its single book, that of Job, whence he aroused great expectation among learned men throughout the Christian world about its full edition. I should like to say briefly beforehand something about this most noble and most ancient monument, which we have thought should be added to our Bibles. Cyril Lucaris, lately Patriarch of Alexandria, brought this manuscript with him from Alexandria when he was promoted to the patriarchal see of Constantinople, as a great treasure of the East. He gave it as a gift to our King, who had sent a large store of printed books to the same Cyril through Sir Thomas Roe, knight, the King's ambassador to the Emperor of the Turks. The King ordered it kept in his Royal Library as a most precious treasure [κειμήλιον]. It was written, however, as Cyril himself attests in his own hand at the beginning of the book, by St Thecla, as was the report among the Alexandrians, and the name of Thecla was inscribed in the book, though that name, now effaced, is no longer visible. What he asserts about Thecla is uncertain, and the book, perhaps because it belonged to some monastery of Thecla, had her name written in it, and little should be attributed to a deceptive report. Nevertheless, many things argue that it is of the highest antiquity. The manner of writing is one: it is written on parchment in large or uncial letters of old, without any division into verses, chapters or words, without accents or marks of breathing, which the grammarians perhaps had not yet invented, so that it could seem to be one continuous word. Some of the rabbis testify that the ancient Hebrew Bible manuscripts, long before the Masoretes, were like this, and others affirm the same of the poems of Pindar and other Greek poets. Yet it has certain divisions: in the five books, namely Job, Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Proverbs and Canticles, it is divided into certain lines [στίχοι], as among the ancients, as may be seen from the book of Job published by Dr Junius.

units.la: In N.T. præter dicta, alia sunt quæ summam antiquitatem spirant, de quibus alibi, ad finem vero libri, annexæ sunt Epistolæ duæ, una integra & genuina sine dubio, sc. celeberrima illa apud antiquos Clementis Romani S. Pauli discipuli ad Corinthios, quæ post sacras literas maxima erat authoritatis, & in Ecclesiis quibusdam publicè legebatur, quam cum supra mille annos intermortua jacuisset, magno Ecclesiæ commodo Typis evulgavit idem D. Junius cum versione Latina, & notis ad calcem doctissimis: altera vero lacera & imperfecta, ab eodem tamen publici juris facta, quæ licet D. Grotio primi seculi esse videatur & ante constitutum Ecclesiarum consensu Canonem scripta, Clementisque nomen prafe ferat, alterius tamen Clementis esse antiqui judicarunt.
units.tr: In the New Testament, besides what has been mentioned, there are other things which breathe the greatest antiquity, of which I shall speak elsewhere. At the end of the book two Epistles are appended. One is whole and undoubtedly genuine: that most celebrated letter of Clement of Rome, disciple of St Paul, to the Corinthians, which among the ancients was of the greatest authority after the sacred writings, and was publicly read in certain churches. After lying dead for more than a thousand years, Dr Junius brought it to light in print, with a Latin version and most learned notes at the foot, to the great benefit of the Church. The other is mutilated and imperfect, and was likewise made public by the same man. Although it seems to Dr Grotius to belong to the first century and to have been written before the consensus of the churches established the canon, and although it bears the name of Clement, they judged it to be the work of another ancient Clement.

units.la: 67. Hujus vero MS. licet magnus sit cum Vaticano consensus, adeo ut se mutuo confirment, omniaque argumenta quæ à Morino proferuntur ad probandam Vaticani sinceritatem, etiam huic nostro quadrent; cum tamen illud ex Luciani Martyris, hoc vero ex Hesychii editione multis esse videatur: Hesychii enim exemplaria Alexandriæ in usu publico erant teste Hieronymo, unde in minutis quibusdam, varietates quædam occurrunt, præsertim in propriis nominibus, in quibus frequentior inter exemplaria differens reperitur; cumque textum codicis nostri Alexandrini imprimere esset fere actum agere, idem enim fere est cum Vaticano, præter dignitatem tamen tanti & tam celebris MS. esset, inter varias aliorum codicum lectiones ad finem cujuslibet Tomi, vel ad calcem totius operis detrudi, ideo ut uno intuitu ista duo nobiliss[?]: & antiquissima exemplaria lectori representarentur, Romanum primo in columna peculiari posuimus, Alexandrinum vero ad finem cujuslibet columnæ, ubi scil. à Romano differt, ut hoc modo lector collationem inter utrumque facere posset. Lectiones etiam istas ex MS. Alexand. posuimus, sine ulla mutatione præter accentuum appositionem (nisi manifestus erat librarii error) ut in ipso MS. reperiuntur, licet quædam sint illius sæculi propria, quæ a Grammaticorum nostrorum regulis discrepant, & a nasutulis quibusdam fortasse inter errata Typogr. reponentur: ut cum αι scribunt pro (ε) ut παιδίον pro πεδίον [?], ἀρεστὸν pro ἀρεσὸν [?]: et e contra (ε) pro αι, ut φύλαξε pro φύλαξαι; sic (ε) simplex pro ει diphthongo ponitur, ut λέιψει pro λείψει [?], μ pro ν, ut ἐμμένω pro ἐν μένω [?], μ sæpe interponitur præsertim in descendentibus a λαμβάνω, ut λέμψομαι pro λείψομαι [?], υ duplex pro simplici, in verbis a βαίνω, ut διαζευγνύεις pro διαζευγνύεις [?], aliaque ejusmodi, quæ quia summæ antiquitatis indicia sunt, et non ex Scribæ errore fortuito orta, sed constanter per totum librum reperta et sæculi illius in pronunciando et scribendo modum indicant, religio nobis erat mutare.
units.tr: 67. The agreement of this manuscript with the Vatican is great, so that the two confirm each other, and all the arguments which Morinus brings forward to prove the soundness of the Vatican fit this our manuscript as well. Yet while the Vatican text seems to come from the edition of Lucian the Martyr, this one seems, as many think, to come from the edition of Hesychius. For copies of Hesychius were in public use at Alexandria, as Jerome testifies, and so in minor points certain variants occur, especially in proper names, where the more frequent differences among copies are found. Since to print the text of our Alexandrian codex would be almost to do the same thing as printing the Vatican, for the two are nearly identical, yet on account of the dignity of so great and so celebrated a manuscript, it ought not to be thrust among the various readings of other codices at the end of each volume or at the foot of the whole work. Therefore, so that these two most noble and most ancient copies might be presented to the reader at a single glance, we have placed the Roman text first in a separate column, and the Alexandrian at the foot of each column, wherever it differs from the Roman, so that in this way the reader can make a comparison between the two. We have also set down these readings from the Alexandrian manuscript without any change except the addition of accents (unless it was a manifest scribal error), just as they are found in the manuscript itself. Some of them are peculiar to that age and depart from the rules of our grammarians, and perhaps some nit-pickers will put them down as printer's errors: for instance, a diphthong is written for a simple vowel, as [παιδίον] for [πεδίον] and [ἀρεστὸν] for [ἀρεσὸν]; conversely a simple vowel is written for a diphthong, as [φύλαξε] for [φύλαξαι]; a simple vowel stands for the diphthong, as [λέιψει] for [λείψει]; μ stands for ν, as [ἐμμένω] for [ἐν μένω]; μ is often inserted, especially in derivatives of λαμβάνω, as [λέμψομαι] for [λείψομαι]; a double υ stands for a single one in verbs from βαίνω, as [διαζευγνύεις] for [διαζεύγνυς]; and other things of this kind. Since these are signs of the highest antiquity, not chance errors of a scribe, but are constantly found throughout the whole book and indicate the manner of pronouncing and writing of that age, we felt bound not to change them.

units.la: 68. Quod ad Latinas.
units.tr: 68. Concerning the Latin versions.

units.la: 70 Versiones attinet, licet multæ essent ut testatur Augustinus, nec earum ulla parem cum Græca authoritatem unquam habuerit, una tamen erat cæteris celebrior quæ ab Augustino Itala, à Hieronymo Vulgata, à Greg. Vetus dicebatur, quamque Hieronym. ipse ad Græcam quæ in Hexaplis sincera erat castigavit, quæ post evulgatam Hieronym. novam versionem ex Hebræo, vel cum eadem coaluit, vel fere periit, adeo ut nullæ ejus reliquiæ (exceptis Psalmorum libro aliisque paucis) ullibi reperta sint, nisi quæ in patrum Latinorum aliorumque commentariis & scriptis hic illic dispersa essent. Ut igitur una cum Græco Textu etiam ipsa antiqua Versio Latina a mortuis resuscitaretur, rem magnam & laude dignissimam aggressus est Flaminius Nobilius, vir doctiss. & in antiquis patrum ac Ecclesiæ monumentis multum versatus, ut hanc veterem Latinam translationem redivivam sisteret. Primo enim versionem Latinam non ex ingenio suo composuit, sed ex omnibus patrum aliorumque Latinorum veterum monumentis, collectis quæ ab iisdem translata vel citata erant scripturæ particulis, & in unum corpus digestis, Herculeo plane labore contexuit.
units.tr: 70 Although there were many Latin versions, as Augustine testifies, none of them ever had authority equal to the Greek. One was more famous than the rest, however.
