Augustine called it the Italic, Jerome the Vulgate, and Gregory the Old. Jerome himself corrected it against the Greek text that was sound in the Hexapla. After Jerome published his new version from the Hebrew, the old one either merged with it or nearly perished, so that no remains of it have been found anywhere (except the Psalter and a few other books), apart from scattered fragments in the commentaries and writings of the Latin Fathers and others. So that the old Latin version might be brought back to life along with the Greek text, Flaminius Nobilius, a very learned man well versed in the ancient monuments of the Fathers and the Church, undertook a great task, deserving of the highest praise, to present this old Latin translation restored to life. First, he did not compose the Latin version from his own ability but, with truly Herculean labour, put it together from all the monuments of the Fathers and other ancient Latin writers, gathering the scriptural passages that they had translated or cited and arranging them into a single body.

units.la: Quæ vero ex Patrum scriptis supplere non poterat (quæ pauca erant) proprio marte addidit, ita tamen ut antiquæ versionis stylum & simplicitatem exprimeret: nec solum Latinam versionem redintegravit, sed etiam thesaurum instructissimum, notarum & variarum lectionum ex patribus tam Græcis quam Latinis aliisque MSS. modernisque 70. editionibus, etiam Complutensi, quibus tam Græca quam Latina versio confirmata est, immensis studiis & vigiliis compilavit, adeo ut tam Græca quam Latina versio, quæ per mille annos in Occidentali Ecclesia fere intermortuæ jacuerant, non quidem ausim cum Morino dicere, ab omnibus erroribus & & mendis pura & perfecta, maxima tamen exparte nitori et pristina integritati restituta exhibeantur.
units.tr: What he could not supply from the writings of the Fathers (and there were few such passages), he added on his own, yet in such a way as to express the style and simplicity of the old version. He not only restored the Latin version but also compiled, with immense study and many sleepless nights, a very well-furnished storehouse of notes and variant readings drawn from the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, from other manuscripts, and from modern editions of the Seventy, including the Complutensian, by which both the Greek and the Latin version were confirmed. As a result, both the Greek and the Latin version, which for a thousand years had lain almost dead in the Western Church, are presented, though I would not dare to say with Morinus that they are free from all errors and faults, pure and perfect, but restored in great part to their former splendour and original integrity.

units.la: 69. Cumq; uti diximꝰ Graeca illa quae in Complut. Regiis, & Parisiensibus Bibliis extat versio, omnium maxime a primaeva distet, ut quae pro arbitrio propalantium mutata & interpolata sit, Latina etiam eidem apposita, sit plane nova, nec veterem Latinam ullo modo referat, nobis autem propositum sit non novas versiones cudere, sed antiquas quantum fieri poterit nativa sua forma exprimere, iudicium de singulis lectori pio & docto relinquentes, rejecta plane mixta illa Complutensium, quam tamen ubi a reliquis differt, inter varias lectiones lector inveniet; rem gratam omnibus antiquitatis studiosis totique Ecclesiae futuram existimavimus, Graecam illam Romanae editionis versionem & antiquam Latinam, una cum exemplari nostro Alexandrino, quae omnium quae hodie extant ad veram & genuinam τῶν 70 versionem proximè accedit, cum reliquis antiquis versionibus in hisce Bibliis imprimere. In variis lectionibus quae per literas Alphab. in versione Latina indicantur, a Nobilio collectis, lectori exhibentur multa ex codicibus MSS. antiquissimis, commentariis, scholiis, aliisque Graecorum scriptis, et fragmentis aliarum translationum collecta, una cum asterisciS et obelis qui ab antiquis notati erant, quibus textus tum Vaticanus, tum Alexandrinus in multis illustrantur. Annotata vero quæ in Græca editione Romana erant, negleximus, quia omnia fere in Nobilii notis repetuntur: quæ vero deerant, vel Latine tantùm à Nobilio citata erant, appositis Græcorum patrum verbis supplevimus. Præter has etiam, annotationes alias ex variis MSS. antiquissimis, & veterum monumentis, quarum quædam ex duobus MSS. in Bibliotheca Oxoniensi Arabicis, alia ex MS. quodam Vaticano excerpta, una cum observationibus in multa loca à Nobilio prætermissa, virorum doctorum summa industria collectas lectori non invidemus; versuum etiam distinctionem ut in editione τῶν 70 Parisiana sequuti sumus, ubi in versuum transpositionibus, numerus uncis inclusus juxta Vulgatam Latinam retinetur, nisi in ultimis quibusdam Exodi capitibus aliisve locis, ubi ita transpositæ sunt omnia, ut versuum distinctio juxta Hebraici textus, vel Vulg. Lat. verionis formam fieri non potuerit sine Græci textus dilaceratione. Quas quidem transpositiones cum in Græcis codicibus semper fuisse, tum ex veteris scriptis tum ex antiquis MSS. constet, idcirco loco movere vel transponere, ut cum Hebræo vel Vulg. Lat. congruerent, sicut in quibusdam aliis editionibus post Aldinam, temere, ne dicam sacrilegè factum est, mihi piaculum videtur, & contra dictum Sapientis, de non mutando tando terminos quos posuêre majores nostri; in quo etiam alicubi præeuntes habemus Parisienses, in Arab. versione Jeremiæ, ubi cùm magna fit capitulorum transpositio à cap.25.[?] ad finem libri, juxta 70. ex quibus facta est ista Jeremiæ versio, ordinem tamen non mutârunt, licèt cum aliis versionibus per columnas non congruat, sed Lectore monent de hac transpositione quam juxta exemplar suum Arabicum sequuntur, ad finem istius Prophetiæ. Monendus etiam est Lector, ubi inter varias lectiones ex MS. Alexandrino collectas, asterisco conspicitur, aliquid inter annotationes ad finem libri observari; quod ad finem columnæ inter varias easdem lectiones rejici commodè non poterat.
units.tr: 69. And since, as I have said, the Greek version that appears in the Complutensian and Parisian Bibles is, of all versions, the furthest removed from the original, having been altered and interpolated at the whim of its publishers, and since the Latin set beside it is entirely new and does not reflect the old Latin in any way, our purpose is not to coin new versions but, as far as possible, to express the ancient ones in their native form, leaving the judgement on each point to the pious and learned reader. We have thought it would be a welcome thing for all lovers of antiquity and for the whole Church to print in these Bibles, alongside the other ancient versions, that Greek version of the Roman edition and the ancient Latin version, together with our Alexandrian manuscript, which of all the texts available today comes closest to the true and genuine version of the Seventy. The Complutensian mixed version, which is plainly rejected, will be found by the reader among the variant readings wherever it differs from the others. In the variant readings, marked by the alphabetical letters in the Latin version and collected by Nobilius, the reader will be shown much taken from very ancient manuscripts, commentaries, scholia, and other Greek writings, and from fragments of other translations, together with the asterisks and obeli that the ancients had marked, by which the text of both the Vatican and the Alexandrian is illustrated in many places. We have omitted the annotations that were in the Roman Greek edition, because nearly all of them are repeated in the notes of Nobilius; where they were lacking, or where Nobilius had cited them only in Latin, we have supplied them with the words of the Greek Fathers. Besides these, we do not grudge the reader the other annotations, gathered with the greatest diligence of learned men from various very ancient manuscripts and ancient monuments, some excerpted from two manuscripts in the Oxford Bibliotheca Arabica, others from a certain Vatican manuscript, together with observations on many passages that Nobilius had passed over. We have followed the division into verses of the Parisian edition of the Seventy, where, in verse transpositions, the number enclosed in brackets is retained according to the Latin Vulgate; except in certain final chapters of Exodus or other places where everything has been so transposed that the division into verses according to the form of the Hebrew text or the Latin Vulgate could not be made without tearing the Greek text apart. Since it is established both from the ancient writings and from the old manuscripts that these transpositions have always existed in the Greek codices, it seems to me a sin to move or transpose passages in order to make them agree with the Hebrew or the Latin Vulgate, as has been done rashly (I might even say sacrilegiously) in certain editions after the Aldine, and against the saying of the Wise Man, not to move the boundaries which our forefathers set. In this matter we have as precedent the Parisians, in the Arabic version of Jeremiah, where, although there is a great transposition of chapters from chapter 25 to the end of the book, following the Seventy from whom that Arabic version was made, they nonetheless did not change the order, although it does not agree column by column with other versions, but they warn the reader about this transposition, which they follow according to their Arabic copy, at the end of that prophecy. The reader must also be warned that where an asterisk appears among the variant readings collected from the Alexandrian manuscript, something must be noted among the annotations at the end of the book, since it could not conveniently be put at the foot of the column among those same variant readings.

units.la: 70. De N.Testamenti textu Græco, hæc pauca annectam; Cùm summopere laborârint multi de genuina ejus editione, idcircò juxta emendatissimas editiones illum dabimus, una cum versione Latina interlineari Ariæ Montani, ut sic tyrones tota Biblia interlinearia habere possint. Varias verò lectiones adjiciemus cum annotatis tam ex præstantissimis illorum qui in hisce laborârunt notis & commentariis, Erasmi, Stephani, Bezæ, Lucæ Brugensis, Casauboni, H. Grotii & aliorum; quam ex antiquiss. & optimis MSS.sc. Alexandr.nostro, Lugdunensi & Claremontano quibus usus est Beza (qui postea Lugdunense Acad.Cantabrig. donavit) aliisque quæ Oxonii in Novi Collegii, Magdalenensis & Lincolniensis Bibliothecis servantur, quæ ut etiâ Bezæ Lugdunensi, aliáque antiqua MSS. Cantabrig. multis abhinc annis cum exemplari impresso conferri curavit Reverendiss. Armachanus, omnésque variantes lectiones excerpsit. Hæc nominâsse hoc loco sufficiet, de quibus alibi plura.
units.tr: 70. Concerning the Greek text of the New Testament, let me add a few words. Since many have laboured greatly over its genuine edition, we shall give it according to the most carefully corrected editions, together with the interlinear Latin version of Arias Montanus, so that beginners may have the whole Bible interlinear. We shall add the variant readings, with the annotations taken from the most distinguished notes and commentaries of those who have worked on it, namely Erasmus, Stephanus, Beza, Lucas of Bruges, Casaubon, H. Grotius, and others; and from the most ancient and best manuscripts, namely our Alexandrian one, the Lyons one, and the Claremont one used by Beza (who afterwards gave the Lyons manuscript to the Cambridge Academy), and others kept in the libraries of New College, Magdalen, and Lincoln at Oxford. These, together with the Lyons manuscript of Beza and other ancient Cambridge manuscripts, the Most Reverend Archbishop of Armagh took care many years ago to collate with the printed copy, and he excerpted all the variant readings. It will be enough to have named these here; of them we shall say more elsewhere.

units.la: 71. Restat ut quædam de Latina Vulgata, breviter dicamus, quam, inter antiquas versiones referendam, ut quæ à Greg. Magni tempore per mille annos ferè sola in Ecclesia Latina in usu erat, non est quod dubitemus, licet de ejus authore, & de tempore quo in Ecclesiam introducta fuit, déque ejus authoritate, & sinceritate, præsertim ex quo per Tridentinum stabilita est, inter doctos acriter decertatum sit.
units.tr: 71. It remains that I say a few words briefly about the Latin Vulgate. It must be counted among the ancient versions, since from the time of Gregory the Great it was almost alone in use in the Latin Church for a thousand years; there is no reason to doubt this, although concerning its author, the time when it was introduced into the Church, and its authority and purity, especially since it was established by the Council of Trent, learned men have disputed sharply.

units.la: 72. De versione Latina nomen ante Hieronymi tempora obtinuerat, quædam supra diximus. Hanc se emendâsse fatetur Hieronymus lib. 2. contra Ruff. postea versionem novam ex Hebræo fecisse, hortatu Damasi Papæ, est extra controversiam; Psalmi verò, quia in templis assiduè decantati, sine populi offensione mutari non poterant, ut antea relicti sunt; licet enim Psalmos etiam ex Hebræo verterat, nunquam tamen erant in publico usu Ecclesia. Huic versioni licet Episcoporum multi antiquam prætulerint, authoritate tamen Damasi quâ suffultus erat in hac controversia Hieronymus, à multis in Ecclesiis publicè usurpata fuit, unde utramque publicè in Ecclesia lestam fuisse usque ad Greg. Mag. tempora ex scriptis ejus clarissimè constat, ex Epist.sc. ad Leandrum præfixa libro Moralium, & lib.20. Moral.cap. 13, ubi ita loquitur; Quia sedes Apostolica cui authore Deo præsideo utrâque utitur, mei quoque labor studii ex utraque fulcietur. Licet autem utrâque usus sit, Hieronymi tamen versionem præferebat, ut alibi ipse declarat. Et post Gregorii, licet quo anno incertum sit, ea quæ nunc Vulgata dicitur, ex utrisque conflata ut videtur, paulatim tacitóque consensu invaluit. Nam quodacriter contendunt quidam hanc esse ipsius Hieronymi, duplici argumento, ut mihi videtur, refutari possunt; tum quod Hieronymi versio Hebræo exacte conformis erat, ut fatentur Sixtus Senensis & alii, quod de Vulgata hodierna dici non potest: tum quod Hieronymum aliter ex Hebræo transtulisse quàm nunc in Vulgata Latina legitur, ex locis innumeris inter ejus opera constet, ut observarunt multi inter ipsos Romanenses viri docti; ut Villalpandus, Pradus, Bonfrerius et alii, & fatetur ipse Morinus exercitat.3.lib.1.cap.1. Unde non tantum Protestantium plerique, sed & Ecclesiæ Romanæ multi, puram Hieronymi versionem esse negant, sed ex antiqua Vulgata & Hieronymi nova mixtam: sic enim Driedo, Sixt.Senensis, Pagninus, Erasmus, Lindanus, Azorius, Simeon de Muis, Theologi Duacenses praef.in V. Test. Cardinalis Baronius, & praefatio Bibliorum Clem.8.aliique multi. Verba Baronii referam, ad annum Christi 231. Sect.47.
units.tr: 72. That the Latin version had its name before the time of Jerome, we have said above. That Jerome, in book 2 against Rufinus, confesses that he had corrected this version, and afterwards made a new version from the Hebrew at the urging of Pope Damasus, is beyond dispute. But the Psalms, because they were sung constantly in the churches and could not be changed without offence to the people, were left as they had been before; for although Jerome had also translated the Psalms from the Hebrew, they were never in public use in the Church. Although many bishops preferred the old version to this one, Jerome, supported by the authority of Damasus in this controversy, was used publicly in many churches. Hence it is clear from his writings that both were publicly read in the Church until the time of Gregory the Great, as is evident from his letter to Leander prefixed to the book of Morals, and from book 20 of the Morals, chapter 13, where he speaks thus: "Because the Apostolic See, over which by God's authority I preside, uses both, the labour of my study too shall be supported by both." Although he used both, Gregory nevertheless preferred the version of Jerome, as he himself declares elsewhere. And after Gregory, although the year is uncertain, that which is now called the Vulgate, apparently compounded from both, gradually prevailed by silent consent. For those who vehemently contend that this is Jerome's own work can, as it seems to me, be refuted by two arguments: first, because Jerome's version agreed exactly with the Hebrew, as Sixtus of Siena and others admit, which cannot be said of the Vulgate today; and second, because it is clear from innumerable passages in Jerome's works that he translated from the Hebrew differently from what is now read in the Latin Vulgate, as many learned men among the Roman Catholics themselves have observed, such as Villalpando, Prado, Bonfrère, and others, and Morinus himself admits it in Exercitation 3, book 1, chapter 1. Hence not only most Protestants but also many of the Roman Church deny that the Vulgate is Jerome's pure version, holding instead that it is a mixture of the old Vulgate and Jerome's new one. So think Driedo, Sixtus of Siena, Pagninus, Erasmus, Lindanus, Azorius, Simon de Muis, the Theologians of Douai in their preface to the Old Testament, Cardinal Baronius, the preface of the Bible of Clement VIII, and many others. I shall cite Baronius's words, at the year of Christ 231, section 47.

units.la: 73. Accidit Gregorii tempore (quo vero potissimum anno quóve auctore incertum remanet) ut quoniam duæ Vulgatæ versiones Vetus et Nova, dissensionum et contentionum ministrarent occasionem, in diversa studia fideles ea in re distraherentur, cùm alii Veterem, Novam alii sequerentur, effetque ea diversitas veluti seminarium jurgiorum ac turpem redderet Ecclesiæ faciem, dum in Divinis laudibus cæterisque sacris officiis alii aliam legendo, psallendo, concionando, tractando, consectarentur; ne ex hac parte pene divisa schismate Ecclesia videretur, divino afflante Numine provisum est, optimeque consultum, ut ad Ecclesiasticum communem usum una ex duabus, quæ usui omnibus esset Ecclesiis, conflaretur, quæ Communis omnibus atq; Vulgata uno nomine à cunctis dicebatur, explosa Veteris & Novæ nomenclatura. Résque evenit ex sententia, ut eam unam Occidentali Ecclesiâ recipiente, omnis mox cessaverit controversia, &c. Licet alicui Ecclesiæ, venerandæ antiquitatis ergo, permissum fuerit veteri illâ 70. in psallendo uti editione, cum alioqui eâdem, sed ab Hieronymo emendatâ reliquæ omnes utantur Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 73. In Gregory's time (though the exact year and the author remain uncertain), the two Vulgate versions, the Old and the New, gave occasion for disputes and quarrels. The faithful were divided in this matter: some followed the Old, others the New. This difference became a seedbed of wrangling and made the face of the Church shameful, since in the divine praises and other sacred offices some read, sang, preached and handled one version and others another. So that the Church should not appear almost divided by schism on this account, the divine Power, breathing upon it, provided and most wisely decided that one of the two should be shaped into the version used by all churches for common ecclesiastical use. This was called by everyone by one name, the Common or Vulgate, and the names Old and New were discarded. The outcome matched the decision: once the Western Church adopted it, every controversy soon ceased. It was permitted to one church, out of respect for its venerable antiquity, to use the old version of the Seventy in chanting, though all the other churches otherwise use the same version, emended by Jerome.

units.la: Sic Baronius : cui subjungere libet verba præsationis Bibliorum quæ edidit (Clem. 8. Textus Latinus ex Hieronymi translatione vel emendatione susceptus, partim retentus ex antiqua versione Latina, quâ S.Hieron. Communem & Vulgatam, S. Augustinus Italam, S.Gregorius Veterem translationé appellat.
units.tr: Thus Baronius. To his words I wish to add those of the preface to the Bibles which he published under Clement VIII: the Latin text, taken from Jerome's translation or emendation, partly retained from the old Latin version, which St Jerome calls the Common and Vulgate translation, St Augustine the Italian, and St Gregory the Old translation.

units.la: Ex hisce testimoniis clarissime constat, Vulgatâ Latinam non esse puram Hieronymi, sed mixtam.
units.tr: From these testimonies it is most clearly established that the Latin Vulgate is not purely Jerome's, but mixed.

units.la: 47. Quod ad N.Testamentum attinet, illud tantum emendavit Hieronymus, non de novo transtulit: sic enim ipse libro de scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis slicis[?] : Vetus sc. Testamentum juxta Hebraicum transtuli, Novum Græcæ fidei reddidi, & Præf. ad Evangelistas ; Hæc præfatiuncula pollicetur Evangelia, codicum Græcorum emendatâ collatione, sed veterum, quæ ne multùm à lectionis Latinæ consuetudine discrepárent ita calamum temperavimus, ut his tantùm quæ sensum videbantur mutare correctis reliqua manere pateremur ut fuerant.
units.tr: 47. As for the New Testament, Jerome emended it only and did not translate it anew. For he himself says in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers: "I translated the Old Testament according to the Hebrew; the New I rendered faithfully to the Greek." And in the Preface to the Gospels: "This little preface promises the Gospels with a collation of Greek manuscripts, emended but ancient. So that they might not differ much from the custom of Latin reading, I have tempered my pen so that only those things which seemed to change the sense were corrected, and the rest we allowed to remain as they were."

units.la: 75. Antiquissima itaq; esse hanc N.T. versione dubitari vix potest; nam cum plures erat versiones Latinæ, hanc tamen, quæ reliquis ita eminebat, ut Hieronymi tempore Vulgatæ & Veteris nomen adepta sit, primam omnium Latinarum fuisse, veri simile est; & cùm Ecclesia Latina sine Latina translatione esse non potuerit, ante hanc verò nulla extet alicujus apud antiquos memoria, ab initio nascentis Ecclesiæ factam fuisse valdè probabile est, ne dicam cum Baronio, Bonfrerio, Serrario & aliis, ab aliquo Apostolorum Discipulo factam, & ab ipsis Apostolis visam & approbatam. Quod autem alicubi barbarismum sapere videatur, non mirandum si auribus delicatulis non semper arrideat; cùm, ut optimè loquitur S. August. Verba cœlestis oraculi non sint restringenda ad regulas Donati, meliùsque est ut nos reprehendant Grammatici, quàm ut non intelligant populi.
units.tr: 75. It can hardly be doubted that this version of the New Testament is very ancient. For although there were several Latin versions, this one stood out above the rest, so that in Jerome's time it gained the name of the Vulgate and Old version; it is likely to have been the first of all the Latin versions. And since the Latin Church could not exist without a Latin translation, and no record of any earlier one survives among the ancients, it is very probable that it was made at the beginning of the nascent Church, not to say, with Baronius, Bonfrère, Serarius and others, that it was made by some disciple of the Apostles and seen and approved by the Apostles themselves. As for the fact that it may seem somewhere to smack of barbarism, it is no wonder if it does not always please delicate ears; for, as St Augustine says very well, the words of the heavenly oracle are not to be confined to the rules of Donatus, and it is better that the grammarians should rebuke us than that the people should not understand.

units.la: 76. Authoritatem quod attinet, à quibusdam summa esse authoritatis statuitur, imo asslatu Sp. Sancti factam, ut in exercitationibus Morinus, (qui tamen Diatr. part. 2. Sect. 2. contrarium videtur afferere) & post sanctionem Concilii Tridentini, in omnibus puram, nullaque mendæ vel erroris obnoxiam esse; unde Congregatio Cardinalium sub Greg.13. omnia ad syllabam quæ in Vulgata sunt probat, & recipienda declarat.
units.tr: 76. As for its authority, some hold it to be of the highest authority, indeed made by the breath of the Holy Spirit, as Morinus holds in his Exercitations (though in Diatribe part 2, section 2, he seems to assert the contrary). And after the sanction of the Council of Trent, it is held to be pure in all things and liable to no fault or error; whence the Congregation of Cardinals under Gregory XIII approved everything in the Vulgate down to the syllable and declared it to be received.

units.la: Hoc tamen à doctioribus inter ipsos Romanenses merito in quæstionem vocatur, qui declarationem istam suspectam habent, (vide, D'Espeires disp.3. de Vulg.Lat. dub.4.) statuuntque tam ante Concilium, quàm postea errores irrepsisse, & in quibusdam casibus per Hebræos & Græcos codices, Vulgatam Vet.& N.Testam. corrigi deberi, hocque tantum tenendum esse, In Vulgata non esse errores contra fidem & mores, sic enim Concilii mentem explicant qui eidem interfuerunt, Andr. Vega Cardinalis S. crucis qui postea Marcellus secundus, & Johannes Mariana cum aliis; imo errores quosdam adhuc esse tum Typographi tum Interpretis affirmant iidem, quibus Sixtum Senens.[?] Canum, Salmeronem, Dominicum Bannes, Card. Bellarminum, Simeonem de Muis, aliosque adjungere licet. Idemque patet ex variarum lectionum catalogo quæ in Vulgata reperta, quarum aliquot millia collegit Lucas Brugensis, plurésque superesse constat ex epistola Bellarm. ad eundem, ubi inter alia, hæc habet: De libello ad me misso gratias ago, sed scias velim Biblia Vulgata non esse à nobis accuratissimè castigata, multa enim de industria justis de causis pertransivimus quæ correctione indigere videntur. Unde infert L. Brugensis & Bellarminum unum fuisse ex correctoribus, & posse aliquando fieri ut accuratior castigatio exhibeatur. Imo in ipsa præf. Bibl. Vulg. dicunt, quod in hac Vulgata editione : Sicut nonnulla consulto mutata, ita alia quæ mutanda videbantur, immutata relicta sunt, quod ita faciendu esse tu ad offensionem populorum vitandu S.Hieronymus non semel admonuit, tum quod facile credendu sit ut majores nostri, qui ex Hebræis & Græcis Latina fecerunt, copiam meliorum & emendationum librorum habuerint quàm ii qui post illorum ætatem ad nos pervenerunt, &c.
units.tr: Yet this is rightly called into question even among the more learned Romanists themselves, who regard that declaration with suspicion (see D'Espeisses, Disputation 3 on the Latin Vulgate, doubt 4). They hold that errors crept in both before and after the Council, and that in certain cases the Vulgate of the Old and New Testaments ought to be corrected by the Hebrew and Greek codices; and that this alone must be held: that there are no errors against faith and morals in the Vulgate. For thus explain the mind of the Council those who were present at it: Andreas Vega, cardinal of Holy Cross, who afterwards became Marcellus II, and Juan de Mariana, with others. Indeed, the same men affirm that certain errors still exist, both of the printer and of the translator, to whom one may add Sixtus of Siena, Cano, Salmerón, Domingo Báñez, Cardinal Bellarmine, Simon de Muis and several others. The same is evident from the catalogue of variant readings found in the Vulgate, of which Lucas of Bruges collected some thousands, and it is established that more remain, from a letter of Bellarmine to the same man, where among other things he says: "I thank you for the little book sent to me, but you should know, I would have you know, that the Vulgate Bible has not been most accurately corrected by us; for we have passed over many things on purpose, for just reasons, which seem to need correction." Whence Lucas of Bruges infers that Bellarmine was one of the correctors, and that it can sometimes happen that a more accurate correction is put forward. Indeed, in the preface of the Vulgate Bible itself they say, regarding this Vulgate edition: "Just as some things have been deliberately changed, so others which seemed to need changing have been left unchanged," which St Jerome more than once admonished should be done to avoid offending the people; and also because it is easily believed that our forefathers, who made the Latin from the Hebrew and Greek, had a supply of better and more correct books than those who came after their time, etc.

units.la: Biblia etiam edidit correcta Sixtus 5. post Concilium, quæ ab omnibus recipi per Bullam imperavit, omnemq; alteratione prohibuit, & in præf. testatur se, quo magis incorrupte res perficeretur, sua ipsius manu correxisse si quæ prelo vitia obrepserant. Vide Aug. de Roccha Biblioth. Vatic. p. 129 [?]. vix tamen exacto biennio Clem. 8. correctiora Biblia edidit, nova Bulla præfixa, ubi non modo errata Typog. emendata, ut volunt Tirinus et alii, sed multa alia reperiuntur differentia in locis de industria mutatis, ut notarunt Sixt. Amama Antibarb. Bibl. p. 221 [?]. aliique plures.
units.tr: Sixtus V also published a corrected Bible after the Council, which he ordered by bull to be received by all, forbidding any alteration; and in the preface he testifies that, so that the work might be more free from corruption, he corrected with his own hand whatever faults had crept in at the press. See Augustino de Roccha, Bibliotheca Vaticana, p. 129 [?]. Yet scarcely two years had passed before Clement VIII published more correct Bibles, with a new bull prefixed, in which not only typographical errors are emended, as Tirinus and others claim, but many other differences are found in places deliberately changed, as Sixtus Amama noted in Antibarbarus Biblicus, p. 221 [?], and several others.

units.la: 77. [?] Vulgata itaq; non esse ex omni parte perfecta ex ipsis Romanæ Ecclesiæ Doctoribus constat, magni tamen faciendam nec temere rejiciendam, imo si fortasse cum Hebræo vel Græco non conveniat, non statim erroris damnandam, sed antiqua exemplaria consulenda quibus cum sæpe convenit, statuunt viri inter Protestantes doctissimi. Theod. Beza omnibus cæteris Latinis versionibus praeferendam fatetur, praef. in N. T. anni 1559. ubi Erasmum reprehendit, eò quòd veterem interpretem rejicit, quia à Græcis dissentiebat, cūm emendatius exemplar secutus esse videatur. Videatur idem in Luc. 2.33. Mar. 3.5. & 14.36. & alibi. Doctissimè[?] P. Fagius in Chald. Paraph. Gen. 4. de iis qui ubi vulgatā non ad literam per omnia Textui Hebræo respondere vident, illa exibilant, damnant, &c. ita loquitur: Non attendunt, quid vel quem secutus fuerit Vulgatus author; cūm enim à veritate Heb. differre videtur, vel Sept. vel Paraph. Chald. vel aliquem ex Rabbinis sequutum fuisse fere semper deprehendo. Non est ergo temerè nata Vulgata editio, ut quidam scioli stultè et impudenter clamitant. Lud. de Dieu praef. Animadv. in 4. Evang. authorem Vulgatæ doctissimum esse judicat, ejúsque fidem et judicium admiratur. If.[?] Casaubonus differentias Vulgatæ à Græco non semper in Vulgatæ depravationem vel Interpretis errorem referunt; sed in Græcos codices quibus usus est interpres Latinus, à quibus variant hodierni, quòque sæpè hodiernis præfert. Vide Matth. 11. 21, 22. & 15. 39. & 21. 7. Joh. 12. 40. & 18. 1. Act. 3. 24. & 12. 8. &c. Et quidem de MS. nostro Alexandr. observatum est, quòd ubi à Vaticano Codice differt, sæpissimè cum Vulgata Latina congruat. Agmen claudat doctiss. H. Grotius praef. in annot. in Bibl. qui fatetur se Vulgatum Latinum interpretem semper plurimi fe- cisse, cilfe, non modò quòd nulla dogmata infalubria contineat, sed etiam quòd multum in se habeat eruditionis, quanquam in dicendi genere satis horridus. Testes plures adferre supervacaneum erit, ex hijce enim ratio reddi poteft cur Vulgatam Latinam inter reliquas antiquas versiones retineamus in Bibliis nostris, cateris hujus ævi Latinis omissis, quæ ut Augustinus de Latinis fui temporis, numerari vix possunt: Omnes enim ex uno exemplari, Hebraeo fc. hodierno Teft. Vet. & Græco impresso N. Teft. factæ sunt, id oque unum tantum exemplar referunt, quod cum hic exhibeatur, superfluum plane erit pluribus versionibus recentibus pagina onerare.
units.tr: 77. [?] It is therefore established, even by the very doctors of the Roman Church, that the Vulgate is not perfect in every part. Yet it is to be greatly esteemed and not rashly rejected; indeed, if perhaps it does not agree with the Hebrew or Greek, it is not to be condemned at once as erroneous, but the ancient copies are to be consulted, with which it often agrees, as the most learned men among the Protestants maintain. Theodore Beza confesses that it is to be preferred to all the other Latin versions, Preface to the New Testament, 1559, where he rebukes Erasmus because he rejects the old translator on the ground that he differed from the Greek, whereas he seems to have followed a more accurate exemplar. See the same at Luke 2.33, Mark 3.5 and 14.36, and elsewhere. Most learned P. Fagius, in the Chaldee Paraphrase on Genesis 4, speaks thus about those who, when they see the Vulgate not answering word for word to the Hebrew text in all things, hiss at it and condemn it: They do not consider what, or whom, the Vulgate author followed; for when he seems to differ from the Hebrew truth, I almost always find that he followed either the Septuagint, or the Chaldee Paraphrase, or some one of the rabbis. The Vulgate edition was therefore not rashly produced, as certain half-learned men foolishly and shamelessly clamour. Ludovicus de Dieu, in the preface to his Animadversions on the four Gospels, judges the author of the Vulgate most learned, and admires his faith and judgment. Isaac Casaubon does not always refer the differences of the Vulgate from the Greek to corruption of the Vulgate or error of the translator, but to the Greek codices which the Latin translator used, from which today's copies differ, and which he often prefers to today's copies. See Matthew 11.21, 22, 15.39, 21.7, John 12.40, 18.1, Acts 3.24, 12.8, etc. And indeed, concerning our Alexandrian manuscript it has been observed that where it differs from the Vatican Codex, it very often agrees with the Latin Vulgate. The most learned H. Grotius closes the line, in the preface to his notes on the Bible, where he confesses that he has always thought very highly of the Latin Vulgate translator, not only because it contains no unwholesome doctrines, but also because it has much learning in it, though it is rather rough in its manner of speaking. It would be superfluous to adduce more witnesses; for from these the reason can be given why we retain the Vulgate Latin among the other ancient versions in our Bibles, the other Latin versions of this age being omitted, which, as Augustine said of the Latin versions of his own time, can scarcely be counted: For all were made from one exemplar, namely the present Hebrew of the Old Testament and the printed Greek of the New, and they refer only to that one exemplar. Since this one is exhibited here, it would be plainly superfluous to burden the page with several recent versions.

units.la: 78. Latinam itaq; versione fecundum exemplaria à Sixto. 5. & Clem. 8. recognita & emendata exhibem̃ una cū correctionib̃ Romanis Lucæ Brug. nam in hoc excusari non possunt Parifienses, quòd versionem Vulgatam non emendatum, sed innumeris mendis scatentem secuti sint, contra Concilii Tridentini & Pontificum duorum (quorum authoritatem ipsi agnoscunt, quibúsque ipsis parere æquum erat) decreta.
units.tr: So I present the Latin version according to the exemplars revised and corrected by Sixtus V and Clement VIII, together with the Roman corrections of Lucas Brugensis. The Parisians cannot be excused in this, that they followed the Vulgate not as corrected but as teeming with countless errors, contrary to the decrees of the Council of Trent and of the two Popes, whose authority they themselves acknowledge and to whom it was right for them to submit.

units.la: 79. Præter hasce versiones, & variantes fingularū lectiones cum annotationibus, alia multa non inutilia adjicere proponimus, ex libro valde docto Lucæ Brugenfis de variantibus scripturæ locis, Scholiaste Syro, Lud. de Dieu de versionibus Syriaca, Arabica, Vulgata, & Æthiopica, inter fe & cum Bezæ & Erafmi versionibus col- latis, D. Pocockio, Capello, Buxtorfio, aliisque viris doctis, una cum quibusdam de Mafora, ejus Clave, & Castigatione per eundem Buxtorfium, Chronologia brevi, indicibus necessariis, aliisque, de quibus plura dicere chartarum angustia non permittit.
units.tr: Besides these versions, and the individual variant readings with notes, we propose to add many other useful things: from the very learned book of Lucas Brugensis on the variant places of Scripture; the Syrian scholiast; Ludovicus de Dieu on the Syriac, Arabic, Vulgate and Ethiopic versions, collated with one another and with the versions of Beza and Erasmus; Dr Pococke, Cappellus, Buxtorf and other learned men; together with certain things about the Masora, its Key and its Castigation by the same Buxtorf; a brief chronology; necessary indexes; and others, about which the narrowness of the pages does not permit me to say more.

units.la: 80. Ante omnia etiam, post Præfationem generalem, in qua totius instituti operis, & omnium quæ in ipso occurrunt, Lectori ratio reddenda est, gratáque eorum memoria recolenda, quorum sumptibus & auxiliis opus aggressi sumus, particulares etiam quasdam præfationes ad versiones quasdam spectantes, Prolegomena & Apparatum, Tabulas etiam quasdam Geographicas, cum figuris eorum quæ ad Tabernaculi Templique structuram & cultum, & ad Aaronicum vestitum spectant, aliáque hujusmodi, exprimenda curabimus.
units.tr: 80. Above all, after the General Preface, in which the reader must be given an account of the whole plan of the work and of everything that occurs in it, and in which the grateful memory of those by whose expense and help we undertook the work must be recalled, we will also take care to print certain particular prefaces relating to particular versions, Prolegomena and an Apparatus, some geographical tables, with figures of those things which pertain to the structure and worship of the Tabernacle and the Temple and to the Aaronic vestments, and other things of this kind.

units.la: 81. Hæcque sit brevis totius operis adumbratio, quod ad Dei O.M. gloriam, Ecclesiæ bonum, omniumq; studiosorum, præsertim Theologiæ & Linguarum, commodum, favente clementiâ divinâ, quantâ fieri poterit diligentiâ, promulgabimus. Armenorum & Coptorum versiones uti supra diximus, promittere non audemus: quia tamen ad linguarum istarum lectionem quædam in hoc opusculo exhibentur, de ipsis linguis, et versionibus scripturæ quæ in eis habentur, pauca adjicere non inutile judicamus.
units.tr: 81. This is to be a brief outline of the whole work, which, by the favour of divine clemency, we will publish with as much diligence as we can, to the glory of God, most good and great, the good of the Church, and the advantage of all students, especially of Theology and the languages. As we said above, we do not dare to promise the Armenian and Coptic versions. Yet because some things for reading those languages are presented in this little work, we judge it not useless to add a few words about the languages themselves and the versions of Scripture that are found in them.

units.la: 82. Armeniam ab Hebræorum [?]מני[?] Meni vel Minni derivari, regione sc. quam cum Ararat, ubi arca Noæ requieviť, conjungit Jeremias, cap. 51. 27. ubi de Babylone loquens, Convocate (inquit) contra eum Regna Ararat, Minni & Ascenaz, probabile facit Chaldæus interpres, qui pro [?]מנ[?] habet [?]מנני[?] Armeniam, tum hoc lo-go, co,tum Mich.7.11. Armeniæ vero,quæ jam sub Turcarum imperio est, duæ sunt partes; Major, trâs Euphrate, quæ hodie Turcomannia, & Minor quæ cis Euphrate cui Cilicia contermina, quæ etiam Armenis abundat,et Carmania à Turcis vocatur.
units.tr: 82. That Armenia is derived from the Hebrew מני [Meni] or Minni is made probable by Jeremiah, chapter 51, verse 27, who joins the region with Ararat, where the ark of Noah rested. Speaking of Babylon, he says: "Call against her the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni and Ashkenaz." The Chaldee interpreter, who for the Hebrew reads Armenia, supports this, both in this place and at Micah 7.11. Of Armenia, which is now under Turkish rule, there are two parts: the Greater, beyond the Euphrates, which today is Turcomannia, and the Lesser, on this side of the Euphrates, bordering on Cilicia, which also abounds in Armenians and is called Carmania by the Turks.

units.la: 83. Stephanus vult Armenos esse Phryges genere, eorumque linguam in multis imitari; Strabo vero probabilius: τὸ τῶν Ἀρμενίων ἔθνος[?], καὶ τὸ τῆς Συρῶν, καὶ τῶν Ἀραβῶν, πολλὴν ὁμοφυλίαν ἐμφαίνειν, κατά τε τὴν διάλεκτον, καὶ τὰς βίας, καὶ τὰς τῆς σωμάτων χρόας[?], καὶ μάλιστα καθὸ πλησιόχωροι εἰσι. Armenorum gentem, ut & Syrorum & Arabum multum præ se ferre cognationis, dialecto, vita, & corporum formâ, maximè cùm vicini sint. Arabes enim Mesopotamiam penetrârunt & Armeniæ vicina loca, & partim ex Syris, & partim ex Phrygibus Armenos coaluisse verisimile est, & ex gentium istarum lingua tertiam conflatam esse. Syriacè olim scripsisse Armenos videtur colligi posse ex Polyæni lib. 4. ubi de Eumene dicitur, quod Ἐπιστολὴν προσ-ηνεγκεν[?]. παρὰ Ὀρόντου[?] σατράπου τῆς Ἀρμενίας γεγραμμένην Συρίοις γράμμασι. Epistolam protulit quasi ab Oronte Armeniæ satrapa Syriacis literis conscriptam. Unde colligere est Syris & Armenis propter viciniam linguæ communes literas fuisse.
units.tr: 83. Stephanus holds that the Armenians are Phrygians by race and that in many things they imitate the Phrygian language. Strabo judges more probably: "the nation of the Armenians, like those of the Syrians and the Arabs, shows much kinship, both in dialect and in way of life and in the colour of their bodies, and especially in being neighbours" [τὸ τῶν Ἀρμενίων ἔθνος, καὶ τὸ τῆς Συρῶν, καὶ τῶν Ἀραβῶν, πολλὴν ὁμοφυλίαν ἐμφαίνειν, κατά τε τὴν διάλεκτον, καὶ τὰς βίας, καὶ τὰς τῶν σωμάτων χρόας, καὶ μάλιστα καθὸ πλησιόχωροι εἰσι]. The Arabs penetrated Mesopotamia and the regions near Armenia, and it is likely that the Armenians coalesced partly from the Syrians and partly from the Phrygians, and that their language was compounded from the languages of those peoples. That the Armenians once wrote in Syriac seems to be gathered from Polyaenus, book 4, where it is said of Eumenes that he produced a letter "written in Syriac letters, from Orontes, satrap of Armenia" [Ἐπιστολὴν προσηνεγκεν παρὰ Ὀρόντου σατράπου τῆς Ἀρμενίας γεγραμμένην Συρίοις γράμμασι]. Hence it may be inferred that, because of their proximity, the Syrians and Armenians had common letters.

units.la: 84. Armeni postquam fidè Christi recepissent, Patriarchæ Constantinopolitano subditi erat: cùm verò Muhammedana impietas Orientem invasi-set, & Saracenorum victoria Ecclesiarum ordine & subordinationem Episcoporu[?],quâ sibi invicem connexierant, dirupissent, Armenia ab ejus jurisdiction̄e subduxerunt, & Patriarchas duos sibi erexerunt, quos Catholicos vocant, unum in Armenia Majori, alterum in Minori, qui sub se multos habent Episcopos, utriusque vero jurisdictionem terminat fluens intermedius Euphrates. Constantinopolitana etiam Ecclesia non tantum jurisdictionem sed & communionem abjecerunt, receptâ Eutychis hæresi cum Jacobitis in Syria, cui tamen hodie renunciâsse videntur, ut ex eorum Confessione Patriarchæ Constantinopolitano missa constat. In Liturgiis vero & cæremoniis præ omnibus Orientis sectis Ecclesiæ Latinæ propius accedunt, cui etiam reconciliati erant unà cum Græcis in Concilio Florentino, ut ex actis Concilii patet. Ex omnibus etiam Christianis sub imperio Turcico, indultis & privilegiis maximis fruuntur, vi diplomatis sub ipsa Muhammedis manu ipsis olim concessi, ut ipsi asserunt.
units.tr: 84. After the Armenians had received the faith of Christ, they were subject to the Patriarch of Constantinople. But when Muhammadan impiety invaded the East, and the victory of the Saracens broke the order of the Churches and the subordination of the bishops by which they had been bound to one another, the Armenians withdrew from his jurisdiction and set up for themselves two patriarchs, whom they call Catholicoi, one in Greater Armenia and the other in Lesser Armenia, who have many bishops under them; the middle course of the Euphrates, flowing between them, marks the boundary of each one's jurisdiction. They also cast off not only the jurisdiction but also the communion of the Church of Constantinople, having embraced the heresy of Eutyches together with the Jacobites in Syria, though today they seem to have renounced it, as is clear from their Confession sent to the Patriarch of Constantinople. In their liturgies and ceremonies they come closer to the Latin Church than any other sect of the East, and they were also reconciled to it, together with the Greeks, at the Council of Florence, as the acts of the Council show. Among all the Christians under Turkish rule they enjoy the greatest indulgences and privileges, by virtue of a charter once granted to them, as they assert, under the very hand of Muhammad himself.

units.la: §5. Ut vero ad ipsorum Linguam revertamur, quicquid de characteribus antiquis disputant, certum est hodiernos multum à Syriacis differre, quos à Chrysostomo inventos fuisse ex monumentis Bibliothecæ Vaticanæ affirmat Angelus de Roccha. p. 157. Eundemque Scripturam totam in Linguam Armenam transtulisse, eámque versionem hodie apud ipsos in usu esse, quam post exilium ejus à Constantinopoli confecit, cum in Armeniam Imperatoris decreto, teste Sozomeno Hist. l. 8. c. 11. relegatus esset, ubi etiam vitam finivit, ut ex Historia Georgii Patriarchæ Alexandriæ, quam scripsit de vita Chrysostomi, probat Sixtus Senensis in Bibliotheca sancta.lib.4. Certè Theodoretus qui prope Chrysostomi tempus vixit, (floruit enim circa annum 440) affirmat S. Scripturas suo tempore in linguam Armenam versas fuisse licèt de versionis authore sileat, lib. de curandis Græc. affect. post med. Totam etiam scripturam Armeniacè versam hodie in Bibliotheca Vaticana extare testatur Kircherus Prodr. Copt.cap. 5 p.129. &c. Quatuor Evangelia ipse habeo ex Oriente allata, & in aliis Bibliothecis privatis quorundam virorum doctorum eadem versio tota habetur, qui, ut spero, exemplaria sua communicare non gravabuntur. In Bibliotheca Oxoniensi asservantur Psalterii Armenorum exemplaria tria antiqua, tribus voluminibus descripta, à se invicem discrepantia, quæ à viro docto collata fuerunt, sed inter bellicos nostros tumultus nota ejus perierunt.
units.tr: §5. But to return to their language: whatever they dispute about the ancient characters, it is certain that the present ones differ much from the Syriac. Angelus de Rocha, p. 157, affirms that these were invented by Chrysostom, from the monuments of the Vatican Library. The same man is said to have translated the whole of Scripture into the Armenian language, and that version is in use among them today, which he made after his exile from Constantinople, when he had been banished by decree of the Emperor to Armenia, as Sozomen witnesses, Hist. book 8, ch. 11, and where he also ended his life, as Sixtus of Siena proves in his Bibliotheca sancta, book 4, from the History of George, Patriarch of Alexandria, which he wrote on the life of Chrysostom. Certainly Theodoret, who lived near the time of Chrysostom (for he flourished about the year 440), affirms that in his time the Holy Scriptures had been translated into the Armenian language, although he is silent about the author of the version, in his book on curing Greek maladies, after the middle. Kircher, Prodromus Coptus, ch. 5, p. 129 etc., attests that the whole of Scripture translated into Armenian is still extant in the Vatican Library. I myself have the four Gospels, brought from the East, and the same version is found entire in other private libraries of certain learned men, who, as I hope, will not hesitate to share their copies. In the Bodleian Library at Oxford are kept three ancient copies of the Armenian Psalter, written in three volumes, which differ from one another; these were collated by a learned man, but during our wartime disturbances their notes were lost.

units.la: 86. Linguam Coptam hodiernam ex antiqua Ægyptiaca et Græca mixtam esse, & à Copto olim in Ægypto urbe celeberrimâ & Thebaidos Metropoli sic dictam, inter doctos constat. Quod enim Kircherus in Prodromo Copto linguâ Græcam ab Ægyptiaca seu Copta fluxisse asserit, non eget refutatione, cum ipse à viris doctis monitus, & rei evidentiâ convictus errorem hunc retraxerit. Linguæ Ægyptiacæ restituta, pag. 507. Quanquam verò Ægyptiacam linguam unam esse ex matribus αὐτογενέσι apleris[?]que statutum sit, & cum nulla alia affinitatem habere, quantum ex idiotismo, conjugatione, et inflexione verborum colligere liceat:
units.tr: 86. It is established among the learned that the present Coptic language is mixed from the ancient Egyptian and Greek, and that it is so called from Coptos, once a most celebrated city in Egypt and metropolis of the Thebaid. As for Kircher, who in his Coptic Prodromus asserts that the Greek language flowed from the Egyptian or Coptic, that needs no refutation, since he himself, warned by learned men and convinced by the evidence of the thing, retracted this error (Lingua Aegyptiaca restituta, p. 507). Although it is agreed that the Egyptian language is one of the original, self-generated mother tongues, and that, so far as one can gather from its idiom, conjugation and inflection of verbs, it has no affinity with any other:

units.la: Literas tamen hodiernas (optas à Græcis derivatas esse (ut et Græcas à Phœnicibus per Cadmum omnibus notum est) à singularum figuris & nominibus in Alphabeto videre licet. Cùm enim multa Græcorum colonie in Ægyptum migrâssent, præsertim post Alexandr. Magnum, & temporibus Ptolemæorum Græcorum qui per 300 annos in Ægypto regnârunt, dubitari non potest linguam Græcam per Ægyptum multum propagatam fuisse. Imò ante Alexandrum, Psammetichum Ægypti Regem memorat Herodotus in Euterpe, Græcorum millia, Ionesc. & Cares in Ægyptum admisisse, & pueros Ægyptiacos ipsis instituendos tradidisse. Ἀπὸ [?]ῆ τῶν ἐκμαθόντων τὴν Ἑλλάδα γλῶσσαν, οἱ νῦν ἑρμηνεῖς ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ γεγόνασι. Et ab his linguam Græcam edoctis, ortos qui nunc in Ægpto interpretes, ut idem Herodotus. Post Ptolemæos etiam altas radices egit in Ægypto Græca lingua, adeo ut Coptorum dialectus hodie multò plura habeat Græca vocabula quam Ægyptiaca.
units.tr: Yet one can see from the individual figures and names in the alphabet that the present letters were derived from the Greeks (just as it is known to all that the Greek letters were derived from the Phoenicians through Cadmus). For when many Greek colonies had migrated into Egypt, especially after Alexander the Great, and under the Ptolemies, Greeks who reigned in Egypt for 300 years, there can be no doubt that the Greek language was greatly spread through Egypt. Indeed, even before Alexander, Herodotus in Euterpe records that Psammetichus, king of Egypt, admitted thousands of Greeks, Ionians and Carians, into Egypt, and handed over Egyptian boys to be taught by them: "And from those who had learned the Greek language, the interpreters who are now in Egypt have arisen" [Ἀπὸ τῶν ἐκμαθόντων τὴν Ἑλλάδα γλῶσσαν, οἱ νῦν ἑρμηνέες ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ γεγόνασι], as the same Herodotus says. After the Ptolemies too, the Greek language struck deep roots in Egypt, so that the Coptic dialect today has many more Greek words than Egyptian ones.

units.la: 87 Causa statuunt duplicem mutationis antiquæ linguæ Coptæ seu Ægyptiacæ; prima fuit Cambysis tyrannis, qui Ægyptum subjugavit & omnia literarum monumenta delere conatus est, est ; altera Græcorum imperium, qui tum ipsorum tum aliorum linguas in Ægyptum (more victorum) introduxerunt: quibus & tertia additum est, celeberrima totius orbis Bibliotheca Alexandrina, tempore Julii Cæsaris incendium, quo ut omnium nationum monumenta antiqua, & totius sapientiæ veterum scrinia sacra, (omnes enim qui tum extabant libri per totum orbem terrarum, à Ptolemæo Philadelpho, qui nullis sumptibus parcebat, in unum colleƈti & ibi repositi erant, & inter reliquos famosissimæ illius omniumque primæ versionis Græcæ 70 [?] Seniorum (ἀντιγραφον) ita innumera exemplaria Coptica, priscæ sapientiæ Ægyptiorum, & linguæ ipsorum certissima monumenta, damno rei literariæ maximo, conflagratione perierunt. Libros tamen habent Copti in omni facultate hac lingua scriptos, ut ex Coptorum Onomastico apud Kircherum patet, quorum ope multa obscurissima antiquitatis mysteria, præsertim in Hieroglyphicis obeliscorum notis abdita, explicantur. Imo in lingua Ægyptiaca magni illius & vetustissimi scriptoris Trifmegisti famosa volumina supra tria millia, vel potius totidem versus (non enim supra 42 libros numerat Clem. [?] Alexandr. qui catalogum horum librorum accuratè instituit, Stromatum lib. 6.) scripta erant.
units.tr: 87 They give two causes for the change in the ancient Coptic or Egyptian language. The first was the tyranny of Cambyses, who conquered Egypt and tried to destroy all its literary monuments. The second was the rule of the Greeks, who, as conquerors, brought their own language and that of others into Egypt. To these a third was added: the very famous Library of Alexandria, destroyed by fire in the time of Julius Caesar. In that fire perished the ancient records of all nations and the sacred repositories of the wisdom of the ancients, for all the books then existing throughout the world had been gathered together and deposited there by Ptolemy Philadelphus, who spared no expense. Among the rest was that most famous first Greek version, the Septuagint [copy, ἀντιγραφον]. In the same way, countless Coptic copies, the most certain records of the ancient wisdom of the Egyptians and of their language, perished in the fire, to the very great loss of learning. Yet the Copts have books on every subject written in this language, as is clear from the Coptic Onomasticon in Kircher, and by their aid many most obscure mysteries of antiquity, especially those hidden in the hieroglyphic signs of the obelisks, are explained. Indeed, the famous volumes of that great and most ancient writer Trismegistus were written in the Egyptian language, more than three thousand, or rather as many verses (for Clement of Alexandria, who drew up an exact catalogue of these books, numbers them at no more than forty-two, in Stromata book 6).

units.la: §8. Utilitas etiam hujus linguæ vel inde patet, quod hanc antiquiss. Ægypt. Ecclesia, non Græcam,
units.tr: §8. The usefulness of this language is also clear from the fact that the most ancient Egyptian Church used it, not Greek,

units.la: Græcam, nec quæ jam cum Alcorano invaluit Arabicam, in Liturgiis & sacris usurpaverit; partim ob summum erga propriam linguam afsectum, partim ut hoc modo ab Orientalibus cæteris discriminaretur, & ut fidei mysteria ab infidelibus abscondita essent, ut Syri Maronitæ charactere suo fecerunt. In hac etiam scriptos habent omnes Scripturæ libros, cum quatuor primis Conciliis, aliisque multis; quibus constat, quod in sacris peragendis, & librorum sacrorum numero ab Ecclesia Latina parum differant.
units.tr: not Greek, nor the Arabic which has now prevailed with the Koran, in its liturgies and sacred services; partly from its great attachment to its own language, and partly so that in this way it might be distinguished from the other Orientals, and so that the mysteries of the faith might be hidden from unbelievers, as the Maronite Syrians did with their own script. In this language they also have all the books of Scripture written out, together with the first four Councils and many others; from which it is evident that in performing the sacred rites and in the number of the sacred books they differ little from the Latin Church.

units.la: Quantum vero ad Vet. Test. intelligentia conserat hujus Linguæ cognitio, vel inde liquet, quod licet multum differant Ægyptiaca & Hebræa, unde illud, Psal. 81. 6. Cùm exiret contra terram Ægypti, ubi sermonem ignotum audiebam. Et Josephus Ægyptium se simulans fratres per interpretem alloquebatur. Gen 42. 23. cùm tamen Judæis vicini essent Ægyptii, & per multos annos vixerint in Ægypto Jacobi posteri, fieri vix potuit quin Hebræorum & Ægyptiorum sermo multa haberet communia, & ut voces invicem commutarent, quæ sine utriusque cognitione explicari vix possunt.
units.tr: How much knowledge of this language contributes to the understanding of the Old Testament is clear from this: although Egyptian and Hebrew differ greatly, there is that passage in Psalm 81:6, "When he went out against the land of Egypt, where I heard a language I did not know." And Joseph, pretending to be an Egyptian, addressed his brothers through an interpreter (Gen. 42:23). Since the Egyptians were neighbours of the Jews, and the posterity of Jacob lived in Egypt for many years, it could hardly fail that the speech of the Hebrews and the Egyptians had much in common, and that they exchanged words, which can scarcely be explained without knowledge of both.

units.la: §9. Exempla multa habemus in Scripturis, ut celebre illud Josephi nomen צָפְנַת פַּעְנֵחַ Tsaphnath Paaneach. Gen. 41. 45. Ψαφνὰν aut Ψεμφανὴχ. Act. 7. 43. חָנָּה Channa. Psal. 80. 16. aliáque multa à viris doctis annotata mere Ægyptiaca, in quorum explicatione hactenus frustrà sudárunt interpretes, ex linguâ verò Ægyptiacâ quæ hactenus servantur ruderibus multum lucis emersit. Bibliorum verò MSS. exemplaria quæ hodiè in Bibliotheca Vaticana reperiuntur, hæc recensèt Kircherus qui singula lustravit. Prodr. Copt. cap.8. p. 187. &c.
units.tr: §9. We have many examples in Scripture, such as the famous name of Joseph, צָפְנַת פַּעְנֵחַ [Tsaphnath Paaneach] (Gen. 41:45), Ψαφνὰν or Ψεμφανὴχ [Psaphnan or Psemphanech] (Acts 7:43), חָנָּה [Channa] (Psalm 80:16), and many other words noted by learned men as purely Egyptian, in whose explanation the interpreters have so far laboured in vain. From the Egyptian language, however, which survives so far in its remnants, much light has come forth. Kircher, who examined each item, lists the manuscript copies of the Bible that are found today in the Vatican Library. See Prodromus Copticus, chap. 8, p. 187, etc.

units.la: 1. Pentateuchus in 4. Tomis in folio magno, descriptus anno Copto, SS. scilicet Martyrum 1115. operâ Gabrielis filii Phanus. Distinguitur in lectiones, quas versus appellant Copti, Judaicis Parashim & Sedarim multò breviores, cujusmodi numerant in Genesi. 630. In Exod. 603. in Levit. 702. in Numer 835. in Deuter: numerus vetustate exesus est.
units.tr: 1. Pentateuch in 4 volumes, in large folio, written in the Coptic year of the Holy Martyrs 1115, by the work of Gabriel son of Phanus. It is divided into lessons, which the Copts call "verses," much shorter than the Jewish parashiyot and sedarim; of these they count 630 in Genesis, 603 in Exodus, 702 in Leviticus, 835 in Numbers; the number in Deuteronomy has been eaten away by age.

units.la: 2. Evangelia 4. scripta in Ægypto in conventu S. Mercurii à quodam Gabriele, anno SS. Martyrum 986. & anno Arab. 918.
units.tr: 2. The four Gospels, written in Egypt in the convent of St. Mercurius by a certain Gabriel, in the year of the Holy Martyrs 986, and in the Arabic year 918.

units.la: 3. Epistolæ 14. S. Pauli, cum tribus Canonicis, & Act. Apostolorum, scripta anno SS. Martyrum 1220.
units.tr: 3. The fourteen Epistles of St. Paul, with the three Catholic Epistles and the Acts of the Apostles, written in the year of the Holy Martyrs 1220.

units.la: 4. Apocalypsis scripta an. SS. Martyr 1061.
units.tr: 4. The Apocalypse, written in the year of the Holy Martyrs 1061.

units.la: 5. Psalterium Davidis descriptum jussu Gabrielis Patriarchæ, anno (Copt. 1082.
units.tr: 5. The Psalter of David, copied by order of the Patriarch Gabriel, in the Coptic year 1082.

units.la: 90. Memorat etiam codicem alium Evangeliorum una cum variis Liturgiis SS. Marci, Greg. Basilii, et Cyrilli, Missali Copto, aliisque missalibus, ritualibus, manualibus variarum precum, Grammaticis & Lexicis quæ tum in Vaticano,tum in aliis Romæ Bibliothecis præfertim Colleg. Maronit. habentur, ex quibus cum MS S. Coptis quæ ab eodem enumerantur in supplemento, cap. 1. p. 511. &c. quæque in celebrioribus Ægypti Bibliothecis, maximè Cairi supersunt, maximam utilitatem, præfertim ex Thesauro Copt. Arab. Latino, quem typis mandavit, non tantùm SS. literarum & Theologiæ studiosis, sed & omnibus Literatis, Medicis scilicet, Astronomis, Philosophis, Mathematicis, maximè antiquitatum studiosis oriturum fuse idem ostendit. Catalogúmque Patriarcharum Alexandrinorum qui Ægypti, Æthiopum, omniúmque per Africam Ecclesiarum gubernaculum tenebant, à S. Marco primo Patriarcha, ad hunc usque diem ex eorum monumentis recenset.
units.tr: 90. He also mentions another manuscript of the Gospels, together with various liturgies of St. Mark, Gregory, Basil and Cyril, a Coptic missal, and other missals, rituals, and manuals of various prayers, as well as grammars and lexicons, which are held in the Vatican and other Roman libraries, especially that of the Maronite College. Together with the Coptic manuscripts that the same author lists in the supplement, chap. 1, p. 511, etc., and those that survive in the more famous libraries of Egypt, above all at Cairo, he shows at length that these will be of the greatest use, especially from the Latin-Arabic Coptic Thesaurus, which he has committed to print, not only to students of the Holy Scriptures and of theology but to all scholars, namely physicians, astronomers, philosophers, mathematicians, and above all those devoted to antiquities. He also recounts, from their records, the catalogue of the Patriarchs of Alexandria, who held the helm of the churches of Egypt, Ethiopia and all Africa, from St. Mark the first Patriarch down to the present day.

units.la: 91. MS. etiam Copticum vetustissimum in Bibliotheca Oratoriana Parisiis extare, complectens 4. Evangelia Linguâ Coptâ scriptum sine ulla versuum vel dictionum distinctione (quod magnum est antiquitatis argumentum) testatur Joh. Morinus, exercit. Bibl.lib 1.exercit. 6.cap 22 p.197.
units.tr: 91. Johannes Morinus testifies that there is also a very ancient Coptic manuscript in the Oratorian Library at Paris, containing the four Gospels written in the Coptic language without any division into verses or words (which is a great argument for its antiquity). Exercitationes Bibliacae, book 1, exercise 6, chap. 22, p. 197.

units.la: 92 Quo vero tempore factæ sint istæ scripturæ translationes, ex Martyrologio Copt. Arabico in Collegio Maronitarum, conjicit Kircherus, fuisse sc.annis abhinc mille circiter & trecentis, circa tempora concilii Niceni, quo tempore ut testantur Historici studium jacrarum literarum in Thebaïde et per totam Ægyptum florebat maximè: præcipue enim Monachi horum temporum occupabantur in SS.Scripturis è Græcis, Chaldaicis et Hebr. codicibus in suam, Coptam sc.transferendis, ut idem Martyrologium testatur in I. Prolusione Mensis Thoth, quæ translationes ab aliis postea descriptæ, ad hunc usque diem perdurârunt.
units.tr: 92. As to when these translations of the Scriptures were made, Kircher conjectures, from the Coptic-Arabic Martyrology in the Maronite College, that it was about 1300 years ago, around the time of the Council of Nicaea, when, as the historians testify, the study of the sacred letters flourished most of all in the Thebaid and throughout Egypt. For the monks of that age were especially occupied in translating the Holy Scriptures from the Greek, Chaldee and Hebrew manuscripts into their own, Coptic, language, as the same Martyrology attests in the first prelude of the month Thoth. These translations, copied later by others, have endured down to the present day.

units.la: 93. Ut finem huic dissertationi imponam, etsi invidorum latratus non moramur, quibus nihil gloriosum magis, quā quæ alii sciunt ignorare, et quæ ipsi ignorant vituperare, et dum alii studiis et vigiliis se macerant, ad promovendum bonum publicum, ipsi turpi otio consenescunt, vel vino madidi cutem curant, et inter pocula virus ex impuro pectore in omnium scripta evomunt; inter quos sunt qui jactant, nihil novi in hac editione haberi, quod non in Parisiensi, quæ calumnia ex ipsa editionum collatione in fumos evanescit: ad ora tamen hujusmodi obstruenda libet paucis Catalogum eorum quæ in hac editione supra Parisiensem, vel jam præstita, vel auxilio divino præstanda, expectari possunt, hic contexere.
units.tr: 93. To bring this discourse to an end: although we do not heed the barking of envious men, to whom nothing is more glorious than to disparage what others know and what they themselves do not know, and who, while others wear themselves out with study and vigils to advance the public good, grow old in shameful idleness, or, soaked in wine, look after their skin, and between their cups vomit forth poison from impure breasts into the writings of all: among them are those who boast that there is nothing new in this edition that is not in the Parisian. This calumny vanishes like smoke upon a comparison of the editions themselves. Nevertheless, in order to stop such mouths, it is worth setting out here briefly a catalogue of the things which, in this edition beyond the Parisian, either have already been provided or can be expected with divine help.

units.la: I. Textus & versiones quæ in diversis voluminibus habentur in Parisiana editione, hic simul per varias columnas in singulis paginis Lectori objiciuntur, ita ut omnes uno intuitu aspicere, collationémq; instituere possit sine aliorum librorum evolutione.
units.tr: I. The texts and versions which in the Parisian edition are found in different volumes are here set before the reader together, in various columns on each page, so that he can view them all at one glance and compare them without turning through other books.

units.la: 2. Editio nostra quamquam studiosorum usibus magis accomodata, vix quarta parte pretii Parisiana constabit.
units.tr: 2. Our edition, though better suited to the use of students, will cost scarcely a quarter of the price of the Parisian.

units.la: 3. Multa etiam exhibebit quæ in Parisiana non habentur, qualia sunt quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: 3. It will also present much that is not found in the Parisian, such as the following.

units.la: 1. Versio interlinearis Hebraei textus, Pagnini & Ariæ Montani.
units.tr: 1. An interlinear version of the Hebrew text, by Pagninus and Arias Montanus.

units.la: 2. Versio 70. editionis Romanæ, juxta exemplar Vaticanum omnium quæ hodie extant maximè genuinū, rejectā Complutensi mixtā, & pro arbitrio interpolatā, quam tamen quatenus à Romana differt inter varias lectiones Lector inve-niet.
units.tr: 2. The Septuagint of the Roman edition, according to the Vatican manuscript, which of all those extant today is the most genuine; the mixed and arbitrarily interpolated Complutensian is rejected. Nevertheless, the reader will find the variant readings between it and the Roman edition, so far as they differ.

units.la: 3. Vetus etiam vulgata Latina ✠ 70, quā sola usa est Ecclesia Latina per 400. circiter annos post Apostolos, jam supra mille annos intermortua, rediviva sistitur, ex Patribus Latinis per Nobilium compilata.
units.tr: 3. Also the old Latin Vulgate of the Seventy, which alone the Latin Church used for about 400 years after the Apostles, and which has lain dead for more than a thousand years, is presented restored to life, compiled by Nobili from the Latin Fathers.

units.la: 4. MS. Alexandrinum 70. versionis, è Bibliotheca Regia desumptum, nobilissimum & antiquissimum, non multò post Concilium Nicenum descriptum, dīn & avidè à doctis expectatū, quod quatenus à Romano differt ad sinem cujusque columna annexum: adeo ut duo totius orbis Antiquissima & maximè sincera exemplaria versionis Græcæ, Vaticanum sc. & Alexandrinum, hïc simul Lectori repræsententur.
units.tr: 4. The Alexandrian manuscript of the Septuagint, taken from the Royal Library, very noble and very ancient, copied not long after the Council of Nicaea, which scholars have long and eagerly awaited. It is annexed at the foot of each column, showing where it differs from the Roman text. Thus the two most ancient and most genuine copies of the Greek version in the world, the Vatican and the Alexandrian, are presented to the reader here side by side.

units.la: 5. Versionis Samaritanæ ubi à textu Samaritano differt translatio Latina.
units.tr: 5. The Samaritan Version, where the Latin translation differs from the Samaritan text.

units.la: 6. Pentateuchus Persicus Jacobi Tusii, Charaktere Persico descriptus cum versione Latina.
units.tr: 6. The Persian Pentateuch of James Tusius, written in Persian characters, with a Latin version.

units.la: 7. Chaldaica Jonathanis (quæ dicitur) Paraphrasis in Legem, cum versione Latina.
units.tr: 7. The so-called Chaldee Paraphrase of Jonathan on the Law, with a Latin version.

units.la: 8. Targum,seu Paraphrasis Hierosolymit.cum versione Latina.
units.tr: 8. The Targum, or Paraphrase of Jerusalem, with a Latin version.

units.la: 9. Psalmi Æthiopici,Canticum Canticorum, & N.Test. Æthiopicum cum versione Latina.
units.tr: 9. The Ethiopic Psalms, the Song of Songs, and the New Testament in Ethiopic, with a Latin version.

units.la: 10. Evangelia 4. Persico-Latina.
units.tr: 10. The four Gospels in Persian-Latin.

units.la: 11. Liber Esther Canonicus, cum Tobit, Judith, Maccab. uno, qui nec Syriace nec Arabice in Parisiensi habentur, ut ex MSS. quibusdam typis mandentur, operam dabimus.
units.tr: 11. The canonical Book of Esther, with Tobit, Judith, and the First Book of the Maccabees, which are not found in Syriac or Arabic in the Paris edition, we will take care to have printed from certain manuscripts.

units.la: 12. Prolegomena seu Apparatus,in quibus quæstiones quæ de Textu Hebr.& Græco, de versionum singularum antiquitate,authoritate & usu, & de variis lectionibus inter doctos agitantur ; cum Chronologia sacra ab orbe condito, Tabulis Geographicis terræ Sanctæ,&c. descriptione Templi, Tabernaculi, eorumque utensilium, vestitus Aaronici,&c.
units.tr: 12. Prolegomena, or Apparatus, in which the questions debated among scholars concerning the Hebrew and Greek text, the antiquity, authority and use of each version, and the various readings are treated; with sacred chronology from the creation of the world, geographical tables of the Holy Land, etc., a description of the Temple, the Tabernacle and its furnishings, the garments of Aaron, etc.

units.la: 13. Varia lectiones Textûs Hebr. ubi de Keri, Ketib,&c. de variis lectionibus exemplarium Ben Ascher & Ben Nephthali, de literis deficientibus,redundantibus,&c. aliisque quæ ad textum illustrandum & confirmandum conferunt; Buxtorfii Clavis Masoreth.& Castigationes Masoræ,&c.
units.tr: 13. Various readings of the Hebrew text, where concerning the Keri and Ketib, etc., and the various readings of the Ben Asher and Ben Naphtali manuscripts, concerning deficient and redundant letters, etc., and other matters that help to illustrate and confirm the text; Buxtorf's Key to the Masorah and Corrections of the Masorah, etc.

units.la: 14. Differentia Textûs Hebr. à Textu Samaritano, cum variis lectionibus ex codicum Samaritanorum collatione, notis & observationibus, viri doctissimi operâ collectis.
units.tr: 14. The difference between the Hebrew text and the Samaritan text, with various readings collected from a comparison of Samaritan manuscripts, with notes and observations gathered by the work of a most learned man.

units.la: 15. Flaminii Nobilii in Rom. 70. nota & lectiones varia longè doctissima, cum fragmentis veterum Translationum, Aquila, Sym. & Theodot. 5. & 6. Anonym. per Drufium & alios collectis.
units.tr: 15. Flaminius Nobilius's notes and various readings on the Roman Septuagint, far the most learned, together with fragments of the ancient translations, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the fifth and sixth anonymous versions, collected by Drusius and others.

units.la: 16. Patricii Junii annotationes ad MS. Alexandr. cum aliis aliorum virorum doctorum ex MSS. & antiquis scriptoribus, à Nobilio & Junio praetermissis.
units.tr: 16. Patricius Junius's annotations on the Alexandrian manuscript, together with those of other learned men from manuscripts and ancient writers, which Nobilius and Junius passed over.

units.la: 17. Syriacæ versionis & Arabicæ cum MSS. variis Syriacis & Arab. collatæ variantes lectiones, cum notis et observationibus operâ virorum doctorum collectæ.
units.tr: 17. The variant readings of the Syriac and Arabic versions, collated with various Syriac and Arabic manuscripts, with notes and observations gathered by the work of learned men.

units.la: 18. Variæ lectiones Chaldaicæ Paraphraseos ex variis exemplaribus cum notis & observationibus studio viri doctissimi collectis.
units.tr: 18. Various readings of the Chaldee Paraphrase from various copies, with notes and observations collected by the diligence of a most learned man.

units.la: 19. Indices varii, rerum & verborum.
units.tr: 19. Various indexes of things and words.

units.la: 4. Præter prædicta omnia, quæ in Parisiensibus non habentur, versiones etiam quas habent Parisienses, ex melioribus exemplaribus & MSS. exhibemus, sc. 1. Samaritanam, Syriacam, & Arabicam, collatione variorum MSS. antiquissimorum, in plurimis locis obscuris, vel male redditis, Typographi vel exemplarium vitio, emendatas.
units.tr: 4. Besides all the above, which are not found in the Paris edition, we also present the versions which the Parisian edition does contain, drawn from better copies and manuscripts: (1) the Samaritan, Syriac and Arabic, emended by comparison with various very ancient manuscripts in many obscure or badly rendered passages, where the fault lay with the printer or the copies.

units.la: 2. Chaldaicam Paraphrasim exhibemus editionis Basil. ab infinitis in punctatione erroribus quæ erant in Veneta, Complut. Reg. & Parif. ad analogiam Esræ & Danielis immensis Buxtorsii laboribus restitutam.
units.tr: 2. We present the Chaldee Paraphrase from the Basel edition, restored from the countless errors in pointing that were in the Venice, Complutensian and Paris editions, to the analogy of Ezra and Daniel, by the immense labours of Buxtorf.

units.la: 3. Vulgatam Latinam juxta exemplaria emendata & recognita, & à diversis mendarum millibus repurgatam, cum correctionibus Romanis Lucæ Brugensis.
units.tr: 3. The Latin Vulgate according to emended and revised copies, purged of many thousands of errors, with the Roman corrections of Lucas of Bruges.

units.la: 94. Hæc sunt inter alia, per quæ judicium ferat æquus lector quid inter hanc aliasque editiones intersit, quæ ut secundum methodum à nobis propositam perficiantur totis viribus conabimur, votisque ardentibus numen veneramur, ne ab incepto pto tramite, donec ad metā perventum sit, malevolorum artibus avellamur. Omnibus placere impossibile est; nam ut optime Iul. Cæs. Scal. Epi-
units.tr: 94. These are among the things by which a fair reader may judge what difference there is between this edition and others. We shall strive with all our strength to complete them according to the method we have proposed, and with ardent prayers we worship the divine will, that we may not be drawn away from the path we have begun, until we reach the goal, by the tricks of ill-wishers. It is impossible to please everyone; for, as Julius Caesar Scaliger very well put it,

units.la: Non sæpè Deus placet, & tu placere credis? Nobis igitur satis est, doctis & probis placuisse, cum aliis serram reciprocare non vacat. Semotis affectibus judicabit sera posteritas, nam Pascitur in vivis livor, post fata quiescit.
units.tr: Does God not often please, and do you think you please? It is enough for us, therefore, to have pleased the learned and the upright, since we have no time to saw back and forth with others. Let the late posterity judge with the passions set aside; for envy feeds on the living and rests after death.

units.la: Londini Oct.1.1654.
units.tr: London, 1 October 1654.

units.la: Errata quædam inter alia leviora in Intro- ductione sequenti emendanda.
units.tr: Certain errata, among other minor ones, to be corrected in the following Introduction.
