units.la: Literæ sunt 22, quarum Nomina, Figuræ, & Potestas apud Hebræos & Chaldæos prorsus conveniunt. Leguntur vero à dextra versus sinistram, ut apud plerosque Orientales. At Armeni, Æthiopes & Copti seu Ægyptii legunt à sinistra, ut nos Europæi.
units.tr: There are 22 letters, and their names, forms and values are entirely the same among the Hebrews and the Chaldeans. They are read from right to left, as among most Orientals. The Armenians, Ethiopians and Copts, or Egyptians, however, read from left to right, as we Europeans do.

units.la: Literarum Rabinicarum figuras quæ à quadratis hisce Biblicis differunt, quibusque ob celeritatem scriptionis utuntur Iudæi Itali & Hispani, item Hebræo-Germanicarum quæ in libris MSS: tum Germanicis tum Hebraïcis à Iudæis usurpantur, vide apud Buxtorf. in Thesauro Grammat. lib. 1. cap. 1. & ad finem libri, & Schickhardum in Horologio.
units.tr: For the forms of the rabbinic letters, which differ from these square Biblical letters and which Italian and Spanish Jews use for the sake of speed in writing, and likewise for the Hebrew-German forms that Jews use in manuscripts, both German and Hebrew, see Buxtorf, Thesaurus Grammaticus, book 1, chapter 1, and the end of that book, and Schickhard, Horologium.

units.la: Literæ ח & ע difficillimæ sunt pronunciationis. ח est spiritus asperior in medio gutture coarctatus, & ad palati summum illisus.
units.tr: The letters ח and ע are the most difficult to pronounce. ח is a rougher breath, constricted in the middle of the throat and pressed against the top of the palate.

units.la: 70 Interpretes sæpe expresserunt per Græcum χ, ut in ῥαχάβ. y spiritus asperrimus ope summi gutturis & narium efferendus. Graeci saepe omiserunt, ut in ἔ[?]ς, ἠ[?]αιδ &c. interdum per (γ) expresserunt, Judaei per א efferunt, quidam per (gn) vitiose.
units.tr: The Seventy often rendered it by the Greek χ, as in Rachab [ῥαχάβ]. ע is a very harsh breathing, to be uttered with the help of the top of the throat and the nostrils. The Greeks often left it out, as in the words given as ἔ[?]ς and ἠ[?]αιδ, and sometimes rendered it by γ. Jews pronounce it with א, and some wrongly with gn.

units.la: SECT. 2.
units.tr: SECT. 2.

units.la: De numerandi ratione.
units.tr: On the manner of numbering.

units.la: Numerant Hebraei per literas Alphabeti, ut in schemate praecedente, quibus addunt pro aliis centuriis literas finales, sic ; ץ ף ן ם ך 900 800 700 600 500
units.tr: The Hebrews number by the letters of the alphabet, as in the preceding table, and for the other hundreds they add the final forms of the letters [ץ ף ן ם ך], thus: 900, 800, 700, 600, 500.

units.la: Vel in quinque centuriis posterioribus priores repetunt, ut [illegible, ~2 letters] 500, [illegible, ~2 letters] 600, [illegible, ~2 letters] 700, [illegible, ~2 letters] 800, [illegible, ~3 letters] 900. Post denarios addunt minores, ut יא 11. יב 12. יג 13. יד 14. at טו 15 pro יה, ne Nomen Dei prophanetur.
units.tr: Or, for the last five hundreds, they repeat the earlier letters: [illegible] 500, [illegible] 600, [illegible] 700, [illegible] 800, [illegible] 900. After the tens they add the units, e.g. 11 [יא], 12 [יב], 13 [יג], 14 [יד]; but 15 is written [טו] rather than [יה], lest the Name of God be profaned.

units.la: Millenarios sic exprimunt א 1000. בא 2000. גא 3000. דא 4000. &c. at cum centenariis compositos solummodo per אבגדה &c. ut אג ter mille, [?] 3500. saepius vero Mille voce integra per אלף exprimunt, 2000 per אלפים plura per אלפים, praemittendo literam numeralem, quot scil. millia significare volunt.
units.tr: They express thousands thus: [א] 1000, [בא] 2000, [גא] 3000, [דא] 4000, and so on. But when thousands are combined with hundreds, they use only the letters [אבגדה] and so on, e.g. [אג] (three thousand) with [?] 3500. More often, however, they write the word for thousand in full, [אלף], and express 2000 by the dual [אלפים] and several thousands by the plural [אלפים], prefixing the numeral letter for the number of thousands they mean.

units.la: SECT. 3. De Literarum divisionibus.
units.tr: SECT. 3. On the divisions of the letters.

units.la: Literas distinguunt Hebræi ut omnes Orientales in 5 classes, secundum 5 organa pronunciandi. Gutturales אהחע Linguales תנלטד Palati ק ג י כ [?] Dentales ש ם צ ר ו [?] Labiales פ ו מ ב
units.tr: Like all Orientals, the Hebrews divide the letters into five classes according to the five organs of pronunciation: gutturals [אהחע]; linguals [תנלטד]; palatals [ק ג י כ]; dentals [ש ם צ ר ו]; labials [פ ו מ ב].

units.la: De hisce est regula generalis, quod literæ ejusdem organi facilè inter se permutantur, quod frequentissimè fit in vocibus ex una lingua in alteram traductis.
units.tr: The general rule about these classes is that letters of the same organ are easily interchanged with one another. This happens most often in words carried over from one language into another.

units.la: Distinguuntur etiam in Radicales, & serviles:
units.tr: They are also distinguished into radical and servile letters.

units.la: Radicales Thema, seu Radicem constituunt, quæ plærumque ex tribus literis constat, raro ex pluribus, quomodo omnes literæ possunt esse radicales; sed hic peculiariter intelliguntur ea quæ semper sunt de radice, nunquam serviles: sunt q; ꝗ 1, his dictionibus cōprehensæ, חש ספר נועצק [?]
units.tr: The radicals make up the theme or root, which usually consists of three letters and rarely of more. All letters can be radicals, but here the term is used specifically for those that always belong to the root and are never servile. There are seven of these, comprised in the words [ח ש ספר נועצק].

units.la: Servites sunt quæ flexione vel formatione radici inserviunt; aliquando tamen sunt de radice, ut reliquæ 11, in has voces memoriales collectæ, משׁה וכלב איתן [?]
units.tr: The servile letters serve for inflection or formation of the root, though sometimes they belong to the root itself. The remaining eleven are collected in these memorial words: [משׁה וכלב איתן], that is, Moses, Caleb, Ethan.

units.la: Serviunt à capite 4. אלבש[?]
units.tr: Servile letters at the beginning, four of them: [אלבש].

units.la: à capite & fine 4. כן[?]
units.tr: At the beginning and end, four: [כן].

units.la: à capite medio & fine 3. יו[?]
units.tr: At the middle and end, three: [יו].

units.la: Huic literarum divisioni non inepte subjungi possunt.
units.tr: To this division of the letters the following may fittingly be added.

units.la: Regulæ de investiganda radice;
units.tr: Rules for investigating the root.

units.la: 1. Si abjectis servilibus remanserint tres, ipsæ sunt radix.
units.tr: 1. If three letters remain after the servile letters are removed, these three are the root.

units.la: 2. Si duæ, quarum prior habet Daghes, tunc plerunque præponitur ו raro, ut ויגד[?] à ויגן[?] & ויצב[?] à יצב[?]. At in duobus, ut אקף[?] à קף[?] & לחע[?] à נחעו[?]. Sed in Chaldaicis posterior sæpe geminari debet, cum prior habet Daghes, ut infra patebit.
units.tr: 2. If two remain, and the first has a dagesh, then generally a vav is prefixed, though rarely. Thus [ויגד] comes from [ויגן] and [ויצב] from [יצב]. But in the case of two letters such as [אקף] from [קף] and [לחע] from [נחעו]. In Chaldee, however, the second letter must often be doubled when the first has a dagesh, as will appear below.

units.la: 3. Si posterior fit Dagessata geminanda est, ut סבב[?] à סבב[?]. Sin verò Daghes fit characteristica Conjugationis Piel (quod ex forma vocis sciendum) tum postponendum ה, ut ילד[?] à ילד[?]. Excipiuntur etiam hæc nomina quæ cum affixis dagessantur, ira, ab אנף[?] filia, à בנה[?] & חטה[?] triticum, ab חנט[?].
units.tr: 3. If the second letter takes a dagesh, it must be doubled, as [סבב] from [סבב]. But if the dagesh becomes the characteristic of the Piel conjugation (which is to be known from the form of the word), then a he must be postponed, as [ילד] from [ילד]. Excepted are also the nouns which are doubled with their suffixes: ira (anger), from [אנף]; filia (daughter), from [בנה]; and triticum (wheat), from [חטה] and [חנט].

units.la: 4. Si duarum remanentium neutra fit dagessata, tum præponendum ꞏ vel ꞏ rarius א, vel interponendum[?], vel postponendum ה rarissimè א, aut ultima geminanda.
units.tr: 4. If neither of the two remaining letters takes a dagesh, then a yod or a vav is prefixed, or more rarely an aleph; or a letter is inserted; or a he is postponed, and very rarely an aleph; or the last letter is doubled.

units.la: 5. Si unica tantum remanserit, præpone ꞏvel ꞏ, & postpone ה: exceptis חיה[?] à ח[?]; & vocibus quibusdam præteriti à מות[?] mori, & שוה[?] ponere, quæ ה amittunt ante aliud ה: ut, שוה[?] posuisti, מת[?] mortuus es. Chaldæis litera ה est servilis, & ף etiam apud Talmudicos, ו vero radicalis, quibus & hoc peculiare est quod deficientem fecundam compensent per Daghes forte in prima, non in tertia, quotiescunque præfigitur characteristica litera temporis, ut הִוְיִקְ[?] comminnerant. Dan.6.24. à פִּפְּ[?].
units.tr: 5. If only one letter remains, prefix yod or vav and postpone he, except [חיה] from [ח], and certain forms of the past tense from mori (to die) [מות] and ponere (to place) [שוה], which drop the he before another he: for example, [שוה] "you placed", [מת] "you died". For the Chaldeans the letter he is servile, and among the Talmudists the letter [ף] is too, but vav is radical. They also have this peculiarity: where the second radical is missing, they compensate with a dagesh forte in the first letter, not the third, whenever the characteristic letter of time is prefixed. Thus [הִוְיִקְ] "they had crushed" (Dan. 6.24) from [פִּפְּ]; comminuerant.

units.la: Schickhardi Regulæ de investigando Themate.
units.tr: Schickhardt's Rules for investigating the Theme.

units.la: Abjice
units.tr: Remove:

units.la: I. Initio. 1. Formativas Derivatorum, septem, הַאָמְנָתִי[?], quæ literæ Heemanticæ dicuntur.
units.tr: I. At the beginning: (1) the formative letters of derivatives, seven in number, [הַאָמְנָתִי], which are called the Heemantic letters.

units.la: 2. Præfixa מֹשֶׁה וּכְלָב.
units.tr: (2) Prefixed letters: [מֹשֶׁה וּכְלָב], Moses and Caleb.

units.la: 3. Verborum augmenta, Conjugationis הָנָחִית[?]
units.tr: (3) The augments of verbs of the conjugation [הָנָחִית].

units.la: Futurorum אֵיתָן
units.tr: Of the futures: [אֵיתָן].

units.la: Participiorum מ מָם[?]
units.tr: Of the participles: [מ מָם].

units.la: II. In medio expletivas Vocalium ו[?]
units.tr: II. In the middle: the expletive vowel letters [ו].

units.la: III. In fine,
units.tr: III. At the end:

units.la: 1. Nominum, [illegible, ~8 letters]
units.tr: 1. Of nouns: [illegible].

units.la: 2. Verborum, [illegible, ~8 letters]
units.tr: 2. Of verbs: [illegible].

units.la: 3. Suffixa, [illegible, ~12 letters]
units.tr: 3. Suffixes: [illegible].

units.la: Adde
units.tr: Add:

units.la: 1. Initio Verborum imperfectorum, [illegible, ~4 letters]
units.tr: 1. At the beginning of imperfect verbs: [illegible].

units.la: 2. Medio quiescentium, [illegible, ~3 letters]
units.tr: 2. In the middle of quiescent verbs: [illegible].

units.la: geminatorum, alteram similem
units.tr: of geminated verbs, the second letter being similar.

units.la: 3. Fini anomalorum, [illegible, ~4 letters]
units.tr: 3. At the end of anomalous verbs: [illegible].

units.la: Da principio, vel ⅃, medioque, vel indas ⅃, vel conduplices mediam, seu ה dato fini:
units.tr: Take from the beginning, or [?], and from the middle, or [?], or double the middle, or [?] with he given at the end:

units.la: SECT. 4.
units.tr: SECT. 4.

units.la: De literis quiescentibus:
units.tr: On the quiescent letters:

units.la: Literæ אהוי[?] interdum quiescunt; id est non pronunciantur, quia vocalibus destitutæ (vulgo Ehevi vel Jehu memoriæ causa dicuntur). Hoc accidit literis אהו in medio & fine vocis, literæ ה in fine tantum.
units.tr: The letters aleph, he, vav and yod sometimes become quiescent, that is, they are not pronounced, because they are deprived of vowels (commonly they are said as Ehevi or Jehu, for the sake of memory). This happens to the letters aleph, he and vav in the middle and at the end of a word, but to he only at the end.

units.la: א quiescit post vocalem longam, aliquando post Pathach & Segol:
units.tr: Aleph is quiescent after a long vowel, and sometimes after Pathach and Segol.

units.la: י[?] quiescit, initio in Schurec sequente Scheva, aut unâ ex literis בגדכפת[?]. In medio in Schurec & Cholem, & similiter in fine.
units.tr: Yod is quiescent at the beginning, when Schureq follows a Sheva, or one of the letters BGDKPT. In the middle it is quiescent with Schureq and Cholem, and likewise at the end.

units.la: י[?] quiescit in medio & fine in Chirec, sæpe in Tsere & Segol.
units.tr: Yod is quiescent in the middle and at the end with Chireq, and often with Tsere and Segol.

units.la: ה in fine tantum quiescit, idque in Camets, Tsere, Cholem, & Segol
units.tr: He is quiescent only at the end, and this with Qamets, Tsere, Cholem and Segol.

units.la: Apud Chaldæos, א quiescit in Camets, Tseri, & Patach, ut לא non, ראש caput. בלשצר Belschazar. ו in Chirec & Tsere, ut מלכי Rex meus. מלכי Reges. ה In Camets & Tsere, ut גלה revelabit, גלה revelat, utrumque tamen rarius, quia ה finale Hebræorum plerunque hic mutatur in Aleph, nisi aliud Aleph præcedat.
units.tr: Among the Chaldeans, aleph is quiescent with Qamets, Tseri and Patach, as in lo (not), rosh (head), Belshazar (Belshazzar). Vav is quiescent with Chireq and Tsere, as in malki (my king), malkei (kings). He is quiescent with Qamets and Tsere, as in gelah (he will reveal) and gelah (he reveals); both occur, though the latter more rarely, because the final he of the Hebrews is mostly changed here into aleph, unless another aleph precedes.

units.la: De his quatuor literis verum etiam est (quod supra de literis ejusdem organi dictum) quod facile inter se permutentur.
units.tr: Of these four letters it is also true, as said above of the letters of the same organ, that they are easily interchanged with one another.

units.la: SECT. 5.
units.tr: SECT. 5.

units.la: De Vocalibus, & Diphthongis.
units.tr: On the Vowels and Diphthongs.

units.la: Vocales sunt 5 longæ, totidemque breves, quibus addunt quidam Scheva simplex & compositum.
units.tr: There are five long vowels and as many short ones, to which some add a simple and a compound Sheva.

units.la: Vocales longæ.
units.tr: Long vowels.

units.la: Camets | אָ | valet a longum, obscurū. Tsere | אֵ | e longum, ut η Græc. Chirec longum, seu magnum | אִ | i longum. Cholem | אֹ | o longum. Schurec | אֻ | u longum, vel υ Græcorum.
units.tr: Qamets (אָ) has the value of a long, obscure a. Tsere (אֵ) is a long e, like the Greek η. Hireq, the long or great one (אִ), is a long i. Holem (אֹ) is a long o. Shureq (אֻ) is a long u, or the Greek υ.

units.la: Breves:
units.tr: Short vowels:

units.la: Pathach | אַ | a clarum. Segol | אֶ | e breve. Chirec breve, seu parvum | אִ | i breve. Camets-catuph | אֹ | o breve. Kibbuts | אֻ | u breve.
units.tr: Patah (אַ) is a clear a. Segol (אֶ) is a short e. Hireq, the short or small one (אִ), is a short i. Qamets-hatuph (אֹ) is a short o. Qibbuts (אֻ) is a short u.

units.la: Scheva duplex est:
units.tr: Sheva is of two kinds:

units.la: 1. Simplex. אְ valet e brevissimum.
units.tr: 1. Simple: אְ has the value of a very short e.

units.la: 2. Compositum triplex:
units.tr: 2. Compound, and this is threefold:

units.la: 1. Chateph-patach אֲ a raptum.
units.tr: 1. Hateph-patah (אֲ), a snatched a.

units.la: 2. Chateph-segol אֱ e raptum.
units.tr: 2. Hateph-segol (אֱ), a snatched e.

units.la: 3. Chateph-camets אֳ o raptum.
units.tr: 3. Hateph-qamets (אֳ), a snatched o.

units.la: Antequam vocalium puncta à Maforethis inventa sunt, tres quiescentes ו א omnium vocalium vices supplebant, unde matres lectionis dicebantur: א indicabat Pathach & Camets. ו o & u; scil. cholem, camets chatuph, schurec, & kibbuts. erat pro e & i; scil. pro tfere, segol, & utroque chirec. Jod etiam chateph-segol vocalem brevissimam annotabat & aliquando simplex fcheva.
units.tr: Before the vowel points were invented by the Masoretes, the three quiescent letters ו, א and י took the place of all the vowels, and so were called mothers of reading (matres lectionis). א indicated Patah and Qamets; ו indicated o and u, that is, holem, qamets-hatuph, shureq and qibbuts; י stood for e and i, that is, for tsere, segol, and either hireq. Yod also marked the very short vowel hateph-segol, and sometimes the simple sheva.

units.la: Hinc fit, ut post inventa & superaddita vocalium puncta, relictis illis consonis quae vocalium erant indices confusa extiterit punctatio, tum in Targumim seu paraphrasibus Chaldaicis (quae confusio quum in Venetis, tum in Regiis Bibliis passim invenitur, & summo labore Buxtorfii in Bibliis Basilienf. sublata est) tum in variis scripturae locis, ut Pfalm. 77.10. ubi in [illegible, ~4 letters] Jod post Lamed, quod non pluralem numerum sed scheva denotabat, post additam vocalem relictu est; sic etiam Pfalm. 120. 5. [illegible, ~3 letters] pro [illegible, ~3 letters], ubi ו non Shurec sed Kibbuts sequente daghes secundum analogiam denotaret: vide Lud. de Dieu. Gram. l. 1. c. 7. Sixtinum Amam. & alios, praecipue librum eruditissimum Lud. Capelli ab Erpenio editum, Punctationis arcanum revelatum inscriptum, cujus lectio cordatos omnes (paucis quibusdam pervicacibus exceptis) in suam sententiam de punctorum & accentuum novitate adduxit; quae vero nuper edidit vir quidam doctus contra Capelli Arcanum, ita jejuna & frigida sunt, ut paucos (nisi fallor) sibi confentientes habeat.
units.tr: Hence, after the vowel points were invented and added, and the consonants that had indicated the vowels were left in place, the pointing became confused. This confusion is found both in the Targumim, or Chaldee paraphrases, and in various places of Scripture. It occurs everywhere in the Venice and the Royal Bibles, and was removed by the great labour of Buxtorf in the Basel Bible. In Ps. 77.10, in [illegible], the yod after lamed, which denoted not the plural but a sheva, was left in place after the vowel had been added. So too in Ps. 120.5, [illegible] for [illegible], where the vav, following a dagesh, would by analogy denote not shureq but qibbuts. See Lud. de Dieu, Grammar, book 1, chapter 7; Sixtinus Amama; and others, especially the most learned book of Louis Cappel, published by Erpenius, entitled The Secret of Punctuation Revealed. Its reading has brought all sensible men (apart from a few obstinate ones) round to its view on the novelty of the points and accents. But what a certain learned man lately published against Cappel's Arcanum is so dull and cold that it has, unless I am mistaken, few who agree with it.

units.la: Cholem cum supra ו notatur sic [illegible, ~1 letter], dicitur Vau Cholem,& tunc vocalis semper ad præcedentem literam spectat. si vero ו habeat etiam sub se vocalem, pronunciatur; aliàs quiescit.
units.tr: When holem is marked above a vav, it is written thus [illegible], and is called vav holem. The vowel then always belongs to the preceding letter. If the vav also has a vowel beneath it, it is pronounced; otherwise it is quiescent.

units.la: Cum ו[?] habet ante se vocalem brevem non alia mediante litera, punctum in medio non est cholem, sed Daghes forte quæ literam geminat.
units.tr: When a vav has a short vowel before it, with no other letter intervening, the point in the middle is not holem but perhaps a dagesh, which doubles the letter.

units.la: Sæpe etiam Cholem per puncta literæ וֹ[?] & וּ[?] denotatur, ita ut idem punctum & literam & vocalem notet, tum vero litera præcedens וּ[?] vocali caret & וּ[?] aliud punctum vocale adjunctum non habet.
units.tr: Holem is also often denoted by the points of the letters וֹ and וּ, so that the same point marks both the letter and the vowel. In that case the preceding letter has no vowel, and the וּ has no other vowel point attached.

units.la: Sæpe eadem litera utrumque punctum habet, ut וֹ[?], ubi alterum pro Cholem ponitur, utrum vero ex litera præcedente vel subsequente vocali destituta dignoscendum.
units.tr: Often the same letter carries both points, as וֹ, where one of them is put for holem. Which of the two it is must be discerned from whether the preceding or following letter lacks a vowel.

units.la: Camets-chatuph sæpè figura nihil differt à simplici Camets, distinguuntur autem sic.
units.tr: Qamets-hatuph is often no different in form from simple qamets, but they are distinguished as follows.

units.la: Est Camets-chatuph, seu o breve
units.tr: It is qamets-hatuph, or short o:

units.la: 1 Ante Scheva absque accentu Metheg, ut חָכְמָה :chochma.
units.tr: 1. before a sheva without the metheg accent, as חָכְמָה: chochma.

units.la: 2 Ante Daghes forte absque accentu tonico, ut רָנּוּ[?] ronnu.
units.tr: 2. before a dagesh forte without the tonic accent, as רָנּוּ: ronnu.

units.la: 3 Ante consonam mobilem in fine, fine accentu, ut יַעֲקֹב[?] Jakom. Sunt tamen qui contendunt semp ita scribi oportere fine duobus punctis, v. Buxt. thesaur. pag. 26. 27.
units.tr: 3. before a movable consonant at the end of a word, with the accent on the final syllable, as יַעֲקֹב: Jakom. Yet some contend that it ought always to be written this way, with two points at the end; see Buxtorf, Thesaurus, pp. 26, 27.

units.la: Camets-chatuph, vero à Chateph-camets distinguitur sic, quòd Chateph-camets nunquam scribatur simplici forma ut Camets, nec locum habeat ante Scheva aut Daghes, nec proprie inveniatur nisi sub gutturalibus.
units.tr: Qamets-hatuph is distinguished from hateph-qamets in this way: hateph-qamets is never written in the simple form, as qamets is; nor does it stand before sheva or dagesh; nor is it properly found except under gutturals.

units.la: Scheva simplex non semper pronunciatur (imò natura sua mutum est) quiescit autem .
units.tr: Simple sheva is not always pronounced (indeed by its nature it is mute), but it is quiescent:

units.la: 1 In medio dictionis post vocalem brevem nisi sit sub litera daghessata.
units.tr: 1. in the middle of a word after a short vowel, unless it stands under a letter with dagesh.

units.la: 2. Post vocalem longam accentu notatam.
units.tr: 2. after a long vowel that carries the accent.

units.la: 3 In fine dictionis etiam geminum.
units.tr: 3. at the end of a word, even when it is doubled.

units.la: Apud Chaldæos Scheva simplex quiescit etiam post vocalem longam quamcunque, ut [illegible, ~6 letters] petitio Dan. 4. 14.
units.tr: Among the Chaldeans simple sheva is quiescent after any long vowel whatever, as [illegible] petitio (petition), Dan. 4.14.

units.la: Omnibus literis Scheva convenit, at cum א & ה rarissime reperitur.
units.tr: Sheva belongs to all letters, but it is found very rarely with א and ה.

units.la: Gutturales nunquam admittunt Scheva vocale, sed solum mutum, at Scheva compositum est ipsorum proprium.
units.tr: Gutturals never admit a vocal sheva, only a mute one; the compound sheva is proper to them.

units.la: De Dipthongis.
units.tr: On the Diphthongs.

units.la: ו & י post Camets, Tsere, Pathach & Chirec in sine dictionis, cum vocalibus hisce dipthongos constituunt, ו triplicem facit dipthongum, viz. 1. (au) per ּ, ut [illegible, ~3 letters] mansuetus, sæpe interveniente ו ut [illegible, ~3 letters] vel per , ut [illegible, ~3 letters] regula. 2. (eu) ut [illegible, ~4 letters] pacificus. 3. (iu) ut [illegible, ~3 letters] os ejus.
units.tr: Vav and yod, after qamets, tsere, patah and hireq at the end of a word, form diphthongs with these vowels. Vav makes three diphthongs: (1) au, by means of the dagesh-point, as in [...] mansuetus, often with an intervening vav, as in [...] or with the point, as in [...] regula; (2) eu, as in [...] pacificus; (3) iu, as in [...] os ejus.

units.la: ו etiam triplicem facit ai, oi, et ui, ut [illegible, ~3 letters] panai, [illegible, ~2 letters] goi, [illegible, ~3 letters] galui, Judæi vero dipthongum in ו non agnoscunt, sed ו ut consonam pronunciant, & de ו dubitatur à quibusdam. Irregulare est [illegible, ~5 letters] Jer 26. 18. quod legendum & pronunciandum [illegible, ~5 letters] Jerushalajim. Apud Chaldæos fit (eu) dipthongus ex ו tum in fine ut apud Hebræos, tum in medio, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] bestia, ubi & ו intervenit.
units.tr: Vav also makes three diphthongs: ai, oi and ui, as in [...] panai, [...] goi, [...] galui. The Jews, however, do not recognise a diphthong in vav, but pronounce vav as a consonant, and some doubt about vav. The form [...] in Jer. 26.18 is irregular, and must be read and pronounced Jerushalajim. Among the Chaldeans, the diphthong (eu) arises from vav both at the end, as among the Hebrews, and in the middle, as in bestia, where vav also intervenes.

units.la: Jod facit (ai) dipthongum apud Chaldæos, per ו ante ' in medio ut [illegible, ~4 letters] prima. Dan.7.4. Dipthongum (ui) per Vau Schurec ante Jod, Chaldæi non observant.
units.tr: Yod makes the diphthong (ai) among the Chaldeans, through vav before a yod-point in the middle of a word, as in prima. Dan. 7.4. The Chaldeans do not observe the diphthong (ui) formed by vav with shureq before yod.

units.la: SECT. VI.
units.tr: SECTION VI.

units.la: De Daghes & Mappic.
units.tr: On Daghesh and Mappiq.

units.la: Puncta duo sunt ventri literarum inscripta, & aliquid de sono ipsarum notantia apud Hebræos & Chaldæos, funtq; Daghes & Mappic.
units.tr: Two points are placed inside the bellies of letters, and they indicate something about their sound among the Hebrews and the Chaldeans. These are Daghesh and Mappiq.

units.la: Daghes est, duplex, lene & forte.
units.tr: Daghesh is of two kinds, lene and forte.

units.la: 1. Lene in sex literis בגדכפת begadkephat, asperationem tollit, adeo ut sonent b. g. d. k. p. t. Raphe, remissio, olim per virgulam supra hasce literas notata, indicabat eas manere aspiratas, bh, gh. dh. ch. ph th.
units.tr: 1. Lene occurs in the six letters בגדכפת [begadkephat]. It removes the aspiration, so that they sound b, g, d, k, p, t. Rafe, meaning relaxation, was formerly marked by a little stroke above these letters, and it showed that they remain aspirated: bh, gh, dh, ch, ph, th.

units.la: 2. Forte literam geminat & omnibus literis imprimitur nisi gutturalibus & ו ut בֻּגַּשׁ huggash קַבּוֹ kavvo. in [illegible, ~1 letters] tamen & ו quibusdam locis Bibliorum observarunt Masorethæ Daghes imprimi. Locos vide apud Buxtorf. Thesaur. Grammat. lib. 1. cap. 4. at non omnia exemplaria Biblica Daghes in omnibus illis locis exprimunt.
units.tr: 2. Forte doubles the letter and is impressed on all letters except the gutturals and ו, as in בֻּגַּשׁ [huggash] and קַבּוֹ [kavvo]. The Masoretes, however, observed that Daghesh is also placed in ו and in some other places in the Bibles. For the places, see Buxtorf, Thesaurus Grammaticus, book 1, chapter 4. But not all Biblical manuscripts mark Daghesh in all those places.

units.la: Distinguuntur sic, Post vocalem brevem in medio dictionis est daghes forte: lene est, 1. initio dictionis, quod fit semper cum vox præcedens consona mobili terminatur, vel accentu regio.
units.tr: It is distinguished thus: after a short vowel in the middle of a word there is forte Daghesh. Lene is at the beginning of a word, which always happens when the preceding word ends in a mobile consonant, or when the accent falls on it.

units.la: 2. post Scheva quiescens, ejusdem vel diversæ dictionis, quod tamen varias habet exceptiones.
units.tr: 2. Lene also comes after a quiescent Sheva, whether in the same word or a different one; this, however, has various exceptions.

units.la: Aliquando tamen in prima litera est forte, si vox præcedens cum sequenti in unam dictionem coalescat, sive per Maccaph; sive aliter. Mappic est punctum literæ ה & secundum quosdam ' inscriptum, quod indicat eas proprio sono efferendas esse, quæ alias quiescerent. Inscribitur ה tantum in fine vocis, ׀ in medio: olim scriptum erat sub litera, sic ׀ hodie vero inscribitur & monet ה illud esse mobile. Adhibent illud & Hebræi & Chaldæi ad affixum sing. num. 3. perf. fœm. designandum, ut רַגְלָהּ pes ejus, fœm. Ch. רַגְלָהּ
units.tr: Sometimes, however, there is forte in the first letter, if the preceding word coalesces with the following into one word, either by Maqqef or otherwise. Mappiq is a point placed inside the letter ה and, according to some, inside י. It indicates that those letters, which would otherwise be silent, are to be pronounced with their proper sound. ה receives it only at the end of a word, and in the middle of a word the mark is different: formerly it was written under the letter, but today it is placed inside, and the ה warns that it is consonantal and mobile. The Hebrews and the Chaldeans both use it to mark the third person feminine singular suffix, as in רַגְלָהּ [raglah], her foot, feminine; Chaldee רַגְלָהּ.

units.la: Chaldæi vero peculiariter Mappic utuntur in ה masculino, præcedente Tsere, ut רַגְלוֹ pes ejus, viri.
units.tr: The Chaldeans, however, use Mappiq in a special way in masculine ה, after Tsere, as in רַגְלוֹ [raglo], his foot, of a man.

units.la: SECT. VII.
units.tr: SECT. VII.

units.la: De syllaba & legendi ratione.
units.tr: On the syllable and the manner of reading.

units.la: Omnis syllaba incipit a consona, idque a dextra versus sinistram.
units.tr: Every syllable begins with a consonant, and this is read from right to left.

units.la: Syllaba simplex ex una consona & una vocali constat, quæ plerunque longa, ut הָיִיתִי ha-ji-thi, אֹתוֹ o-tho, קוֶךָ ko-ve-cha, ubi punctum superius ad ׀ pertinet, non ad ׀ quæ propriam vocalem habet, interdum fit ex vocali brevi, segol, chirec, & kibbuts.
units.tr: A simple syllable consists of one consonant and one vowel, which is usually long, as הָיִיתִי [ha-ji-thi], אֹתוֹ [o-tho], קוֶךָ [ko-ve-cha], where the upper point belongs to the letter and not to the letter that has its own vowel. Sometimes it arises from a short vowel: segol, chirec, and kibbuts.

units.la: Syllaba composita est cum plures consonæ in unam syllabam conjunguntur cum vocali, ut רֹאשִׁי בְרָא מֶלֶךְ [?]
units.tr: A compound syllable arises when several consonants are joined with a vowel in one syllable, as רֹאשִׁי, בְרָא, מֶלֶךְ [?].

units.la: Hoc sæpius fit per scheva simplex, at sub guturalibus plerunque per scheva compositum.
units.tr: This happens more often with a simple shewa, but under gutturals usually with a compound shewa.

units.la: Syllaba componitur vel ab initio vel a fine vel utrinque.
units.tr: A syllable is compounded either at the beginning, at the end, or at both.

units.la: Si syllabæ compositæ prior consona vocalem habeat [quæ plerunque brevis est] posterior ei adjungitur per Scheva quiescens vel expressum vel subintellectum per Daghefch forte vel absque eo in fine dictionis, ut in Hiph-kidu [?] Hig-gifch. nisi posterior sit litera quiescens, ut [?] atque hoc modo fit syllaba à fine composita.
units.tr: If the first consonant of a compound syllable has a vowel [which is usually short], the second is joined to it by a quiescent shewa, either expressed or understood, with or without dagesh forte, at the end of the word, as in Hiph-kidu and Hig-gifch. Unless the second letter is itself quiescent, as [?]; and in this way a syllable is compounded from the end.

units.la: Sin vero consona posterior vocalem possideat, [ut plurimum longam] prior adscisçit Scheva simplex vocale, vel compositum si fit gutturalis, quod suam consonam sono rapidissimo conjungit litteræ sequenti [nunquam enim per se syllabam constituit] ut in [?] be-rechu, quæ vox diffyllaba est ultimam habens ab initio compositum.
units.tr: But if the second consonant has the vowel [usually long], the first takes a simple shewa, or a compound one if it is a guttural. This shewa joins its consonant to the following letter with a very rapid sound, since it never forms a syllable by itself. So in be-rechu, which is a disyllabic word, the last syllable is compounded from the beginning.

units.la: Quando autem literam vocali insignitam præcedit Scheva vocale, sequitur Scheva mutatur fit syllaba utrinque compositæ ut in [?] pekad voce monosyllaba, [?] pekōd-nah duarum syllabarum, quarum prior utrinque composita quatuor consonis, tribus motis una quiescente, constat.
units.tr: When a vowel-marked letter is preceded by a vocal shewa, and the shewa changes, a syllable compounded on both sides arises. Thus pekad is a monosyllable, while pekōd-nah has two syllables, the first of which, compounded on both sides, consists of four consonants: three moved and one quiescent.

units.la: Apud Chaldæos usitatissimum est Syllabam compositam non tantùm vocali brevi, ut apud Hebræos feré, sed longa etiam inchoari, ut [?] schuv-hera gloriatio.
units.tr: Among the Chaldeans it is very common for a compound syllable to begin not only with a short vowel, as it nearly always does among the Hebrews, but also with a long one, as in schuv-hera, glorying.

units.la: Notandum, quod prima distinctio vocalium in longas & breves, non fuit ad notandā syllabarum quantitatem, seu prosodiam Hebraicam (sic enim eæ quæ breves vulgò vocantur, longæ potius dicendæ essent, utpote positione producte) sed ad faciliorem lectionem, docendo quænam syllabæ simplices sunt, quænam compositæ. Hoc enim perpetuum est, quod initio & medio distinctionis in diffyllabis et polyfyllabis, vocales longæ nunquam usurpentur nisi in syllabis simplicibus aut ab initio compositis ut in דְּבָרִים, דָּבָר [?], nec breves nisi in compositis, nisi penultima afficiatur accentu Grammatico.
units.tr: It should be noted that the first division of vowels into long and short was not made to mark the quantity of syllables or Hebrew prosody (for those called short would more properly be called long, since they are lengthened by position), but to make reading easier, by showing which syllables are simple and which compound. For this is a constant rule: at the beginning and in the middle of disyllables and polysyllables, long vowels are used only in simple syllables or in those compounded at the beginning, as in דְּבָרִים and דָּבָר, and short vowels only in compound syllables, unless the penultimate bears the grammatical accent.

units.la: Cum vero in monosyllabis, & in polysyllabarum fine interdum reperitur vocalis longa, fit hoc ex causa speciali. vide Capell. in Punct. Arcan. lib. 1. c. 13.
units.tr: But since a long vowel is sometimes found in monosyllables and at the end of polysyllables, this happens for a special reason. See Capellus, in Punctorum Arcanum, book 1, chapter 13.

units.la: ה & י in fine vocis, post Tsere Chirec longum, Cholem & Schurec, sæpe ad faciliorem pronunciationem assumunt Pathach, quod ante eas rapide & quasi furtim pronunciatur, unde vocatur Pathach genubha, seu furtim ascitum, ut מַשְׂכִּיחַ mafchiach. רוּחַ ruach יָדוּחַ [?] jaduah.
units.tr: ה and י at the end of a word, after Tsere, long Chirec, Cholem and Shureq, often take Pathach for easier pronunciation. This is pronounced rapidly and almost furtively before them, whence it is called Pathach genuba, that is, furtively added, as in מַשְׂכִּיחַ [mafchiach], רוּחַ [ruach], יָדוּחַ [jaduah].

units.la: ה cum Mappic, idem aliquando imitatur, ut גָּבוֹאָה [?] Gaboah. Chaldaeis eadem syllabæ ratio est quæ Hebraeis.
units.tr: ה with Mappic sometimes imitates the same, as גָּבוֹאָה [Gaboah]. The Chaldeans have the same rule of syllables as the Hebrews.

units.la: In Bibliis voces quæ circellum supra se habent, aliter leguntur quàm scribuntur, Cùm enim Masorethæ ex M.SS. antiquis varias lectiones annotarunt, lectionem unam in textu reliquerunt, alteram in margine posuerunt, quam ut plurimum meliorem judicabant, & hujus vocales textui addebant, unde legunt prout in margine notatur, ut Psal. 9. 13. in textu est עֲנוִים [?] at in margine עֲנָיִים [?] unde ratione punctorum legitur mansuetorum at ratione literarum esset afflictorum עֲנוּיִים [?] Hujusmodi varias lectiones vocant Keri & Kethib, lectio & scriptio.
units.tr: In the Bibles, words that have a small circle above them are read otherwise than they are written. For when the Masoretes noted variant readings from ancient manuscripts, they left one reading in the text and put the other in the margin, which they mostly judged better, and they added its vowels to the text. Hence they read as noted in the margin. So in Psal. 9. 13 the text has עֲנוִים, but the margin has עֲנָיִים; by the points it is read "of the meek", but by the letters it would be "of the afflicted", עֲנוּיִים. Such variant readings they call Keri and Kethib, that is, reading and writing.

units.la: Notandum etiam nomen Tetragrammaton יְהוָה [?] si punctetur hoc modo יְהֹוִה [?] legendum אֱלֹהִים Elohim secundum puncta; si vero sic legendum יְהוָה Adonai, אֲדֹנָי cujus puncta mutatur, nec ante avorum nostrorum memoriam aliter pronunciavit quisquam; primus qui Jehova legebat erat Galatinus. Septuag. interpretes semper legebant Adonai, unde transtulerunt semper Κύριος; nec aliter Christus vel Apostoli legerunt, ut in Nov. Test. liquet, nec ulli ex patribus Graecis vel Latinis: Judaei etiam fatentur veram pronunciationem se ignorare eamque ab everso templo amissam esse. Vide orationem Capelli de nomine יהוה ad calcem libri de arcano punctationis, & in appendice ad Criticam Sacram.
units.tr: Note also the name of the Tetragrammaton יְהוָה. If it is pointed thus, יְהֹוִה, it is to be read Elohim according to the points; but if it is read as יְהוָה, Adonai, אֲדֹנָי, its points are changed, and no one pronounced it otherwise within the memory of our grandfathers. The first who read it as Jehovah was Galatinus. The Septuagint always read Adonai, whence they always translated it Κύριος; nor did Christ or the Apostles read it otherwise, as is clear from the New Testament, nor did any of the Greek or Latin Fathers. The Jews also confess that they do not know the true pronunciation, and that it was lost after the temple was overthrown. See Capellus's oration on the name יהוה at the end of his book on the secret of punctuation, and in the appendix to the Critica Sacra.

units.la: SECT. VIII.
units.tr: SECT. VIII.

units.la: De Accentibus & Maccaph.
units.tr: On the Accents and the Maccaph.

units.la: Accentus duplex est Tonicus & Euphonicus.
units.tr: The accent is twofold: tonic and euphonic.

units.la: Euphonicus tonico praemittitur & suaviorem ejus pronunciationem efficit, vocalem enim suspendit: unde Metheg, id est frænum dicitur. Estque virgula recta sub litera, ut פָּקְדָה pakedha, quod sine metheg legendum esset pok-da.
units.tr: The euphonic accent is placed before the tonic one and makes its pronunciation smoother, since it holds back the vowel. Hence it is called Metheg, that is, bridle. It is a straight stroke under the letter, as in pakedha [פָּקְדָה], which without the metheg would have to be read pok-da.

units.la: Tonicus ultimam vel penultimam acuit: vox quae in ultima acuitur vocatur voce Chaldaica מִלְרַע milra, id est infra, seu in fine; quae in antepenultima מִלְעֵיל milhel, i. e. supra.
units.tr: The tonic accent sharpens either the last or the penultimate syllable. A word sharpened on the last syllable is called in Chaldee milra [מִלְרַע], that is, below, or at the end. One sharpened on the antepenult is milhel [מִלְעֵיל], that is, above.

units.la: Tonici sunt 15. quorum 14 notantur supra vocem; 11. infra.
units.tr: There are 15 tonic accents: 14 are marked above the word and 11 below.

units.la: Supra vocem.
units.tr: Above the word.

units.la: Infra vocem.
units.tr: Below the word.

units.la: De hifce notentur istæ regulæ. Pafchta & Kadma eandem figuram habent, at ille initio vel medio vocis inhæret, hic fini tantum, nisi in eadem voce geminetur.
units.tr: Let these rules be noted about these signs. Pashta and Kadma have the same shape, but the former attaches to the beginning or middle of a word, and the latter only to the end, unless it is doubled in the same word.

units.la: Jethif initio ante primam vocalem ponitur.
units.tr: Jethif is placed at the beginning, before the first vowel.

units.la: Mahpach extremæ vel mediæ literæ adhæret.
units.tr: Mahpach attaches to the last or the middle letter.

units.la: Rebbiah mediæ literæ incumbit: Sic differt à Cholem, quod ad latus.
units.tr: Rebbiah rests on the middle letter. It thus differs from Cholem, which stands at the side.

units.la: Triplicem accentuum usum faciunt Grammatici.
units.tr: Grammarians assign three uses to the accents.

units.la: 1. Musicam seu cantus rationem apud Judæos designare, qui textum Biblicum cantillant.
units.tr: 1. To indicate the musical or chanting pattern among the Jews, who chant the biblical text.

units.la: 2. Pronunciationem legitimam, in syllabæ elevatione designare.
units.tr: 2. To indicate the correct pronunciation, by the raising of a syllable.

units.la: 3. Sententiam in membra distinguere.
units.tr: 3. To divide a sentence into its members.

units.la: Usus primus Judæis relinquitur: secundus habet has regulas..
units.tr: The first use is left to the Jews; the second has these rules:

units.la: 1. Omnis dictio habet accentum tonicum, nisi habeat post se virgulam quæ Maccaph dicitur, [−]
units.tr: 1. Every word has a tonic accent, unless it has after it a stroke called Maccaph [−].

units.la: 2. Syllaba quæ habet accentum tonicum acuitur, exceptis Telisha majori, Jethis, Paschta & Telischa minori, Sægolta, & Sarka, quæ primæ vel ultimæ vocis literæ semper adhærent, sed eam non semper afficiunt.
units.tr: 2. The syllable which has the tonic accent is raised, except with Telisha gedola, Jethif, Paschta, Telischa ketana, Segolta and Sarka, which always adhere to the first or last letter of the word, but do not always affect it.

units.la: 3. Ejusdem accentus in eadem voce geminati, prior syllabam acuit, diversorum posterior, ut תֹהוּ tóhu. וְהָאֵצִים [?] vehaetzím.
units.tr: 3. Where the same accent is doubled in one word, the first raises the syllable; where the accents are different, the second does. Examples: tóhu [תֹהוּ], vehaetzím [וְהָאֵצִים].

units.la: 4. Accentus tonicus vocali longæ additus, Scheva sequens constituit quiescens, ut תַּגְלֶנָה [?] tagélna.
units.tr: 4. A tonic accent added to a long vowel, when a quiescent sheva follows, fixes the syllable: tagélna [תַּגְלֶנָה].

units.la: Tertius usus orationis membra spectat, & sic distinguuntur in Ministros & Reges.
units.tr: The third use concerns the members of the sentence, and so the accents are divided into Ministers and Kings.

units.la: Ministri orationem continuant, Reges distinguunt.
units.tr: Ministers continue the sentence; Kings divide it.

units.la: Ministri sunt 8. Munach, Mahpach, Merca simplex, & duplex, Darga, Jerach, Kadma, Telischa Ketanna, qui cùm nihil distinguant, ideo nullius fere usus sunt nec in aliis linguis usurpantur.
units.tr: There are eight Ministers: Munach, Mahpach, Merca simple and double, Darga, Jerach, Kadma, and Telischa Ketanna. Since they distinguish nothing, they are of almost no use, and they are not employed in other languages.

units.la: Reliqui 17. sunt Reges, quorum præcipui sunt, 1. Rebhia, 2. Sakeph gadol, 3. Sakeph-caton, qui omnes distinguunt in commata. 4. Athnach;
units.tr: The remaining seventeen are Kings, of whom the chief are: (1) Rebbia; (2) Sakeph gadol; (3) Sakeph katon, all of which divide into commas; (4) Athnach;

units.la: 5. Segolta, cujus vicem aliquando sustinet Schalscheleth, qui Colon designant. 6. Silluc, qui periodos distinguit, & in sine omnium versuum reperitur.
units.tr: (5) Segolta, whose place is sometimes taken by Schalscheleth, which mark a colon; (6) Silluk, which divides the periods and is found at the end of every verse.

units.la: Reliqui Reges curiosius distinguunt quàm in aliis linguis, sæpe nihil, unde cum ministris sine incommodo omitti possent, si Grammiticis placuisset, & Masorethæ textui non apposuissent. Vide Lud. de Dieu. Gram. lib. 1. c. 9. Capelli Critic. Sacr. lib. 6; cap. 11. Sed præ aliis Valentinum Schindlerum qui in tractatu suo de accentibus Hebræorum doctrinam hanc erudite & compendiose tractavit, ad cujus mentem, quantum fieri licuit, latinam Chaldaicæ paraphraseos versione Pentateuchi in hoc opere Biblico distinguere conati sumus, ut eo modo studiosi accentuum in distinguendo vim melius perciperent: hoc tantum notetur, nos ad exprimendum ejus comma hanc notam (;) plerunque adhibuisse, pro semicommate vero hanc (,).
units.tr: The other Kings divide more finely than in other languages, often to no purpose. The grammarians could have omitted them without inconvenience, had they wished, and the Masoretes had not added them to the text. See Ludovicus de Dieu, Grammar, book 1, chapter 9; Capellus, Critica Sacra, book 6, chapter 11. But above all others, Valentinus Schindler, who in his treatise on the Hebrew accents has handled this doctrine learnedly and concisely. Following his mind, as far as was possible, we have tried to distinguish the Latin version of the Chaldee paraphrase of the Pentateuch in this biblical work, so that students might better grasp the force of the accents in dividing. Let this only be noted: for his comma we have mostly used this mark (;), and for the semicomma this one (,).

units.la: Accentus Euphonicus seu Metheg vocalibus longis ante Scheva addi solet, unde Camets ante Scheva absque Metheg breve est, seu Cametschatuph, ut חָכְמָה[?] chóchma, non chachema: additur & semper vocalibus ante Scheva compositum, ut [illegible, ~4 letters].
units.tr: The euphonic accent or Metheg is usually added to long vowels before a sheva; hence a Qamets before a sheva without Metheg is short, or Qamets khatuph, as chóchma [חָכְמָה], not chachema. It is also always added to a vowel compounded before a sheva, as [example illegible].

units.la: Distinguitur Metheg à Silluc, quòd hic ultimæ versus voci semper, ille quibuscunque vocibus apponitur, si vero in ultima voce concurrunt, Silluk est figura ultima.
units.tr: Metheg is distinguished from Silluk in that the latter always stands on the last word of a verse, whereas the former is placed on whatever words. If they meet on the last word, Silluk is the final sign.

units.la: Maccaph [–] duas vel tres dictiones connectit, ut cum ultimæ dictionis accentu suavi pronunciatione coalescant.
units.tr: Maccaph [–] joins two or three words, so that with a smooth pronunciation they coalesce with the accent of the last word.

units.la: In Job, Psalmis, & Proverbiis alia est accentuum ratio quam in reliquis Bibliorum libris, ob metrum, musicam, &c. cujus ratio nondum ab aliquo sufficienter est explicata.
units.tr: In Job, the Psalms and Proverbs the system of accents differs from that in the remaining books of the Bible, on account of metre, music, and so on; the reason for this has not yet been sufficiently explained by anyone.

units.la: In Decalogo magna est anomalia accentuum, qui duplicati videntur, mysteria hic latere volunt Judæi, quæ non explicant, sed per Cabalam oralem discenda sunt, & superstitionem Rabbinicam olent.
units.tr: In the Decalogue there is a great anomaly of the accents, which seem to be doubled. The Jews wish mysteries to lie hidden here, which they do not explain, but which must be learned through oral Cabala, and which smell of Rabbinic superstition.

units.la: Accentus addunt vulgo sex alios: 1. Pefik, 2. Legarme, utrumque lineola recta inter duas dictiones, illud post Munach hoc alibi notatur, & musicæ inservit nec quidquam facit ad pronunciationem. 3. Sophpasuk, puncta duo quæ versum terminant. 4. Hillui, 5. Mecarbel, varia nomina accentus Munach pro situ vario. 6. Meajiela, idem cum Tiphca.
units.tr: Commonly six other accents are added: (1) Pesik and (2) Legarme, both a straight little line between two words, the former placed after Munach, the latter noted elsewhere; these serve music and contribute nothing to pronunciation. (3) Sophpasuk, two points which end a verse. (4) Hillui and (5) Mecarbel, various names of the accent Munach according to its varying position. (6) Meajiela, the same as Tiphcha.

units.la: Apud Chaldæos eadem est ratio accentuum, quæ apud Hebræos saltem in Dan. & Esra. Paraphrases vero omnes, Jonathani, Josephi Cæci, &c. præter Onkelos in Pentateuchum, accentibus destituuntur.
units.tr: Among the Chaldeans the system of accents is the same as among the Hebrews, at least in Daniel and Ezra. But all the paraphrases, those of Jonathan, Joseph the Blind, and others, except Onkelos on the Pentateuch, are without accents.

units.la: Notandum vero quod sicut magna erat Masoretharum diligentia in apiculis hisce excogitandis, sic non minor erat illorum incuria quod nulla excogitarent interrogationum, interjectionum, parenthesium, &c. signa, ut in aliis linguis, quæ magis necessaria erant quàm multi ex accentibus, & punctis, quæ sine ulla necessitate, & cum parva utilitate textui adscripserunt.
units.tr: It must be noted that, just as great was the diligence of the Masoretes in devising these little marks, so no less was their carelessness in devising no signs for questions, interjections, parentheses and the like, as in other languages. These were more necessary than many of the accents and points, which they added to the text without any necessity and with little usefulness.

units.la: Et hæc quidem ex Buxtorfio, de Dieu, aliisque collecta, ad lectionem hujus linguæ sufficiant; Qui vero plenam linguæ hujus cognitionem desiderat, Grammaticos consulat, qui præcepta Grammaticalia tradiderunt. Inter innumeros vero qui hodie extant, Buxtorfius videtur palmam aliis præripere, cujus Epitomen primum, vel Schickardi Horologium ediscat, postea evolvat Buxtorfii Thesaurum Grammaticum qui omnium accuratissime, & copiosissime hujus linguæ mysteria pandit. De ipso enim Judæi hoc Elogium reliquerunt in præf. Bibl. Rabbinicorum quæ præfixa est editioni Bafilienfi: "Sapiens præ sapientibus Nazaræorum, Doctor magnus in lingua sacra, & Chaldaica, & in Grammaticis earum, ita ut similis ei non inveniatur inter eos, vir Magnificus, dominus Johannes Buxtorfius."
units.tr: These things, gathered from Buxtorf, de Dieu and others, are enough for reading this language. But whoever desires full knowledge of the language should consult the grammarians who have handed down the grammatical rules. Among the countless ones now extant, Buxtorf seems to carry off the palm above others. Let one learn first his Epitome, or Schickard's Horologium, and afterwards work through Buxtorf's Grammatical Thesaurus, which unfolds the mysteries of this language most accurately and most copiously of all. For the Jews themselves left this praise of him in the preface to the Rabbinic Bibles prefixed to the Basel edition: "A sage above the sages of the Nazarenes, a great teacher in the sacred language, and in Chaldee, and in their grammars, so that none like him is found among them, the magnificent man, Lord John Buxtorf."

units.la: Hujus vero Lexicon Hebraicum & Chaldaicum una cum Lexico Chaldæo-Rabbinico-Talmudico (opere 30 annorum) & concordantiis ejus Hebraicis, quæ præter concordantias Biblicas etiam Lexicon Hebraicum absolutissimum exhibent, ut maximè utilia, ad perfectam hujus & aliarum Linguarum Orientalium cognitionem, omnium doctorum calculo approbantur.
units.tr: His Hebrew and Chaldee Lexicon, together with his Chaldee-Rabbinic-Talmudic Lexicon (a work of thirty years) and his Hebrew concordances, which besides the biblical concordances also present a most complete Hebrew lexicon, are approved by the judgement of all learned men as most useful for a perfect knowledge of this language and of the other oriental languages.

units.la: Chaldaicam vero Grammaticam inter alios, scripsit idem Buxtorf. cum Syriaca conjunctim; Idem etiam compendiose præstitit Andr. Sennertus, qui Syriaca proprio charactere describit, non Hebraico, ut Buxtorfius.
units.tr: The Chaldee grammar, among others, the same Buxtorf wrote jointly with the Syriac. Andreas Sennertus also did this concisely. He describes Syriac in its own character, not in Hebrew letters as Buxtorf did.

units.la: Unà cum Syriaco Chaldaicum etiam Lexicon edidit Buxtorf. Filius in 4° quod magno studiosis usui esse potest.
units.tr: Along with Syriac, Buxtorf the son also published a Chaldee lexicon in quarto, which can be of great use to students.

units.la: Buxtorfii vero P. Consilium de facili hujus linguæ cognitionem adipiscendi modo, quod Manuali ejus Lexici Heb. & Chald. præfixit Filius, adscribere placuit.
units.tr: I have thought fit to add the advice of Buxtorf the father on an easy way of attaining knowledge of this language, which his son prefixed to his Manual Hebrew and Chaldee Lexicon.

units.la: Compendiosa ratio discendi linguam Hebræam & Chaldaicam.
units.tr: A concise method of learning the Hebrew and Chaldee language.

units.la: Cognitis literis & vocalibus, observatis etiam generalibus ad legendum regulis, ipsa lectio statim tentanda erit.
units.tr: Once the letters and vowels are known, and the general rules for reading have also been observed, reading itself should be attempted at once.

units.la: Lectio instituatur quotidiana per horam minimam, nec dies ullus sine exercitio abeat.
units.tr: Reading should be practised daily for at least an hour, and no day should pass without exercise.

units.la: Primum lectionis tentamen sit in formis conjugationum, quæ ordine juxta septem verborum classes perlegendæ.
units.tr: The first trial of reading should be made on the forms of the conjugations, which are to be read through in order, according to the seven classes of verbs.

units.la: Ratio, 1. quia ibi legendi modus est facilior, quum eædem literæ & voces repetantur, unà duntaxat aut altera syllaba immutata. 2. quia facilitatem hanc statim sequitur aliquis profectus. 3. quia profectus ille amorem studii generat, & continuationem urget. 4. quia utilitatem aliquam simul affert, quod umbratilis quædam inde nascatur conjugationum, temporum, modorum, personarum, numerorum, &c. cognitio quæ paulo post faciliorem memoriæ laborem conciliat. Continuetur per dies circiter 15[?].
units.tr: The reasons are these: (1) because the method of reading there is easier, since the same letters and words recur with only one syllable, or at most two, changed; (2) because this ease is at once followed by some progress; (3) because that progress creates a love of study and urges one to continue; (4) because it also brings some further benefit, in that from it arises a shadowy knowledge of the conjugations, tenses, moods, persons, numbers, and so on, which a little later makes the work of memorising easier. This should be continued for about fifteen [?] days.

units.la: Secundum exercitium lectionis fit in Textu Biblico. Ratio, quia cum singulæ voces hic sint aliæ & novæ, ideoque lectio non nihil tardior & operosior, ad eam non est accedendum, nisi lingua & pronuntiatione in facilioribus non nihil prius assuefactâ & informatâ. Continuetur per dies 15 alios.
units.tr: The second exercise of reading is made in the Biblical text. The reason is that, since the individual words here are different and new, reading is somewhat slower and more laborious; one should not come to it unless the tongue and pronunciation have first been somewhat accustomed and trained on the easier material. This should be continued for another fifteen days.

units.la: Tota hæc exercitatio fiat præsente præceptore (si haberi posset; multi enim in hac & aliis linguis Orientalibus proprio Marte clari evaserunt ut Clenardus, Erpenius ipse in Arabica, & alii. Vide Capelli Arcanum Punctationis lib. 2. c. 27. n. 4, 5, 6, 7.) aut aliquo doctiore qui linguam errantem dirigat, & pronunciationem pravam corrigat. Discipulus autem privatim legens, clara voce legat, non per meditationem. Sic enim & lingua fiet promptior ac expeditior, & convenienti pronuntiationi rectius assuescet. Neque est, quod turbetur, si quandoq; in lectione erret: id enim postea præceptor, usus, & prosectus plenior mox emendabunt.
units.tr: The whole of this practice should be carried out with a teacher present (if one could be had; for many have become famous in this and the other Oriental languages by their own efforts, such as Clenardus, Erpenius himself in Arabic, and others. See Capellus, Arcanum Punctationis, book 2, chapter 27, numbers 4, 5, 6, 7), or with some more learned person who will guide the wandering tongue and correct faulty pronunciation. The pupil, however, should read alone aloud, not silently in meditation. For in this way the tongue will become more ready and quick, and will more correctly accustom itself to proper pronunciation. Nor need he be troubled if he sometimes makes mistakes in reading; for the teacher, with practice and fuller progress, will soon correct these afterwards.

units.la: Altero mense discipulus conjugationes verborum memoriæ mandare incipiet, & lectionem Textus Biblici per aliquam capitis partem continuabit. Præceptor interea, verborum & conjugationum formationem & differentiam breviter inculcabit. Quam primùm conjugationes persectas tenuerit, præceptor unum & alterum versum Latinè explicabit, quos discipulus sequente die reddet. Postea omnia perfecta ad paradigmata applicare docebit, quo ipso omnia accidentia & ipsam radicem uno momento persectissimè discipulus cognoscet. Idem faciet per verba imperfecta, ubi memoriæ bene commissa fuerint. Explicatio Textus ad versus duodecim & plures paulatim accrescet, ex quibus nuda & simplicia verba, primùm duntaxat considerabuntur, & modus applicandi ad paradigmata oftendetur. Si vero pronomen adjunctum in fine fuerit, id præceptor seqarabit, & nudam verbi formam discipulo examinandam proponet.
units.tr: In the second month the pupil will begin to commit the conjugations of the verbs to memory, and will continue reading a part of a chapter of the Biblical text. Meanwhile the teacher will briefly impress upon him the formation and difference of the verbs and conjugations. As soon as he has mastered the perfect conjugations, the teacher will explain one or two verses in Latin, which the pupil will render the following day. Afterwards he will teach him to apply all the perfect forms to the paradigms, by which means the pupil will know perfectly, in a single moment, all the inflections and the root itself. He will do the same with the imperfect verbs, once these have been well committed to memory. The explanation of the text will gradually grow to twelve verses and more, from which, at first, only the bare and simple verbs will be considered, and the method of applying them to the paradigms will be shown. If, however, a pronoun is attached at the end, the teacher will separate it and set the bare form of the verb before the pupil to examine.

units.la: Tertio mense pronominum rationem cum verbis præceptor explicabit. Nominum item doctrinam tractabit, ostensâ primum juxta præceptorum doctrinam nudâ ipsorum de numero in numerum declinatione prout varietas formæ singularis id admittet: deinde formam quoque illorum in constructione & cum pronominibus affixis secundum utrumq; numerû ostendet, reductis illis ad formam absolutâ & separatâ, mutatione, si quæ vel in literis, vel in vocalibus, vel utrobiq; occurrit, ejusque ratione ostensa. Voces indeclinabiles quia paucæ sunt, nudo tantum indicio indigent.
units.tr: In the third month the teacher will explain the treatment of pronouns along with the verbs. He will likewise deal with the doctrine of nouns, first showing, according to the rules of the grammarians, their bare declension from number to number, so far as the variety of the singular form allows; then he will also show their form in the construct state and with attached pronouns in each number, reducing these to the absolute and separate form, noting any change that occurs in the letters, the vowels, or both, and explaining the reason for it. Since indeclinable words are few, they need only a bare indication.

units.la: Quarto mense fyntaxis examinabitur, Hebraifmi explicabuntur, anomaliæ quælibet, accentuum distinguentium ratio, & quicquid ad Grammaticæ absolutam tractationem facit, exquisitè tractabitur. Continuetur repetitio singulis diebus per horam, unde fiet, ut anno absoluto tota quoque Biblia legendo, interpretando, Grammatice examinando absolvere, ac majori ex parte sponte & per se intelligere & interpretari possit.
units.tr: In the fourth month syntax will be examined, Hebraisms explained, any anomalies, the principle of the distinguishing accents, and whatever pertains to the full treatment of grammar will be thoroughly handled. Daily repetition should continue for an hour, so that at the end of the year the pupil will be able to have gone through the whole Bible by reading, interpreting and examining it grammatically, and for the most part to understand and interpret it of his own accord and unaided.

units.la: Quinto & sexto mense, addatur linguæ Chaldaicæ ex Daniele & Esra repetitio similis, primum in verbis, deinde in nominibus cognosoendis, quæ omnia tanto erunt faciliora quanto quis plus in Hæbraicis profecerit.
units.tr: In the fifth and sixth months, a similar repetition from Daniel and Ezra should be added in the Chaldee language, first learning the verbs and then the nouns; all of which will be the easier the more one has progressed in Hebrew.

units.la: Hic docendi & discendi modus Grammaticam,
units.tr: This method of teaching and learning grammar

units.la: in ufu ipfo linguæ, & ex ufu practico, pluribus exemplis ad unum præceptum Grammaticum revocatis, & eadem doctrina sæpius repetita, longè firmius memoriæ imprimet, & longè dilucidius explicabit, quam si in nuda præceptorum theoria primum quis infistat.
units.tr: from the actual use of the language and from practice, with many examples reduced to a single grammatical rule, and with the same doctrine often repeated, will impress it far more firmly on the memory and explain it far more clearly than if one first dwelt on the bare theory of the rules.
Basel, 20 December 1630.

units.la: Exercitatio lectionis Hebr: ex Zeph. 3. verf. 8. in quo omnes Alphabeti literæ etiam finales exhibentur.
units.tr: Exercise in reading Hebrew from Zephaniah 3, verse 8, in which all the letters of the alphabet, including the final ones, are presented.

units.la: furgam quo diem ad ,Dominus inquit ,me expectate Ideo קומי ליום נאם־יהוה לי־חכו לכן kumi lejom Adonai-neum li-chakku lachen

units.tr: that I may gather the nations, that I may assemble the kingdoms, my decree; for [לקבצי גוים לאסף משפטי כי]

units.tr: Another from 1 Reg. 1, verse 6, where nearly all the accents are gathered together,

units.tr: "A man came up to meet us and said to us: 'Go, return to the king who sent you, and speak to him: Thus says the LORD: Is it because there is no God in Israel that you send to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you shall not come down from the bed on which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'" [וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֵלָיו אִישׁ עָלָה לִקְרָאתֵנוּ; כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה הַמְבַלִּי אֵין אֱלֹהִים בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל; לָכֵן הַמִּטָּה אֲשֶׁר־עָלִיתָה שָּׁם לֹא־תֵרֵד כִּי־מוֹת תָּמוּת]

units.la: Alphabetum Samaritanum.
units.tr: Samaritan Alphabet.

units.la: Habent Samaritani literas tantùm 22, Vt Hebræi; quarum ordo, potestas, & nomina, cum Hebræis eadem sunt, figurâ tantùm discrepant; nullas verò literarum initialium, sinalium, vel mediarum discrepantes formas habent: ut ex Tabella sequenti liquet. 1 | Aleph | [?] | א | 80 | Pe | [?] | פ 2 | Beth | [?] | ב | 90 | Tsade | [?] | צ 3 | Gimel | [?] | ג | 100 | Koph | [?] | ק 4 | Daleth | [?] | ד | 200 | Resh | [?] | ר 5 | He | [?] | ה | 300 | Shin | [?] | ש 6 | Vau | [?] | ו | 400 | Tau | [?] | ת 7 | Zain | [?] | ז 8 | Hheth | [?] | ח 9 | Teth | [?] | ט 10 | Jod | [?] | י 20 | Caph | [?] | כ | 500 | [?] | [?] | [?] 30 | Lamed | [?] | ל | 600 | [?] | [?] | [?] 40 | Mem | [?] | מ | 700 | [?] | [?] | [?] 50 | Nun | [?] | נ | 800 | [?] | [?] | [?] 60 | Samech | [?] | ס | 900 | [?] | [?] | [?] 70 | Aain | [?] | ע | 1000 | [?] | [?]
units.tr: The Samaritans have only 22 letters, as the Hebrews do. Their order, value and names are the same as the Hebrew ones, and they differ only in shape. They have no distinct forms for initial, final or medial letters, as the following table makes clear: 1 Aleph, 80 Pe; 2 Beth, 90 Tsade; 3 Gimel, 100 Koph; 4 Daleth, 200 Resh; 5 He, 300 Shin; 6 Vau, 400 Tau; 7 Zain; 8 Heth; 9 Teth; 10 Jod, 20 Caph, 500 [final Kaph]; 30 Lamed, 600 [final Mem]; 40 Mem, 700 [final Nun]; 50 Nun, 800 [final Pe]; 60 Samech, 900 [final Tsade]; 70 Ayin, 1000 [final Kaph].

units.la: Reliquos numeros supplent ut apud Hebræos.
units.tr: They supply the remaining numerals as the Hebrews do.

units.la: Puncta vocalia habent nulla, sed literæ [?] [?] [?] quæ matres lectionis apud Hebræos vocantur, eorum locum supplent, uti apud Syros, Arabes, Chaldæos, ante punctorum inventionem.
units.tr: They have no vowel points. Instead, the letters that the Hebrews call matres lectionis take their place, as among the Syrians, Arabs and Chaldeans before the invention of the points.

units.la: Constans enim & antiquissima est Rabbinorum sententia legem à Mose scriptam esse sine punctis,sine accentibus, sine Parașchis, sine versuum,imo sine verborum distinctione; prout hodie in Synagogis Judæi legem sine puncťis, accentibus, et versuum distinctione, legunt, ut hoc modo antiquum morem conservarent, quem Masorethárum critica mutare non potuit. Habeo exemplar ejusmodi, constans ex membranis in rotulo convolutis, scriptum ad morem in synagogis visitatum, ubi nulla punćta, nulli accentus nec versuum distinctio conspiciuntur : imo in aliis linguis antiquitus ita scribere consueverunt, ut ex antiquiss: M SS. constat. Tale est MS. Vaticanum Græcum 70 interpretum, quod primò Romæ, postea Parisiis editum est. Tale etiam est antiquissimum nostrum, M S. Græcum supra 1000 abhinc annis scriptum, quod Theclæ ascribitur, sine accentibus, sine dictionum vel versuum distinctione, litteris uncialibus seu majoribus conscriptū : cujus collationem cum edit. Romanâ in Bibliis nostris exhibemus. Tale M S. quatuor Evangeliorum Coptum seu Ægyptiacum, in Bibliotheca oratoriana Parisiis memorat Morinus exercit. Bibl.lib. 1.exerc.6. cap.2.p.197. Dictiones verò à se invicem separâsse Esram veri simile est: at farraginem punćtorum & accentuum Talmude posteriorem esse luce claclarius à doctis demonstratum est. Inter alios vide Capelli Arcanum punctationis revelatum. Samaritani verò hodiè dictiones separant puncto unico,non solo spatio : periodos verò et membra puncto duplicato ; vel asterisco : Sectiones verò duobus lineis, vel tribus punctis cum lineis, ut ex hisce figuris patet, := vel -<: Distinguunt etiam singulos libros Moses in sectiones quas [illegible, ~6 letters] Katsin vocant, parafchis & fidris Judaicis longè breviores, quales in universa lege numerant 966. Judæi verò habent tantum 53 Parafchas, & lidras[?] seu sectiones minores tantùm 145.
units.tr: For the constant and most ancient opinion of the rabbis is that the Law was written by Moses without points, without accents, without parashahs, without verse divisions, and even without division of words. So today the Jews in their synagogues read the Law without points, accents or verse divisions, and in this way they keep the ancient custom, which the critical work of the Masoretes could not change. I have such a copy, made of parchment rolled up on a scroll and written in the manner used in synagogues, where no points, no accents and no verse division can be seen. Indeed, in other languages too they were accustomed to write in this way, as the most ancient manuscripts show. Such is the Vatican manuscript of the Greek Seventy, which was published first at Rome and afterwards at Paris. Such too is our most ancient Greek manuscript, written more than a thousand years ago, which is ascribed to Thecla, without accents and without division of words or verses, written in uncial or capital letters; we present a collation of it with the Roman edition in our Polyglot Bible. Such also is the Coptic or Egyptian manuscript of the four Gospels, which Morinus mentions in the Oratorian library at Paris, Exercitationes Biblicae, book 1, exercise 6, chapter 2, page 197. It is likely that Ezra separated the words from one another, but that the mass of points and accents is later than the Talmud has been shown more clearly than light by learned men. Among others, see Cappellus, Arcanum punctationis revelatum. The Samaritans, however, today separate words with a single point, not merely with a space; they separate sentences and clauses with a double point or an asterisk; and they mark sections with two lines, or with three points together with lines, as these figures show: := or -<. Moses also divides each of the books into sections which they call Katsin, far shorter than the Jewish parashahs and sidras; they count 966 of them in the whole Law, whereas the Jews have only 53 parashahs and 145 smaller lidras or sections.

units.la: Sæpe etiam habent virgulam supra literam, quâ notatur dictionem in usitatiore significatione non accipi, sed passivè legendam, vel homonymiâ laborare, vel præter consuetam formam scribi.
units.tr: They also often place a little stroke above a letter, which marks that a word is not to be taken in its more usual meaning but read passively, or that it is ambiguous, or that it is written in an unusual form.

units.la: Cùm verò punctis vocalibus & accentibus carent, patet ipsos ex traditione & usu[?] à majoribus derivatis vocum lectionem & pronunciationem hactenus confervâsse, ope tri-um literarum prædictarum, sicut & Judæi ipsi ad Maforetharum tempora quinque fere post Christum centuriis, fecerunt.
units.tr: Since they lack vowel points and accents, it is clear that they have hitherto preserved the reading and pronunciation of the words, by tradition and usage derived from their forefathers, with the help of the three letters mentioned above, just as the Jews themselves did until the time of the Masoretes, about five centuries after Christ.

units.la: Porrò Grammaticam Samaritanam, vel Lexicon aliquod verborum quæ huic dialecto propria sunt, nemo quod sciam hactenus edidit: Promisit quidem aliquid Joh.Morinus in praefatione ad Biblia Parisiana, sed promissis hactenus non stetit. In usum Bibliorum nostrorum fortasse aliquid opera viri doctissimi qui Samaritana nostra exemplaria diligenter contulit, & multa utilia congesit, posthac edi curabimus.
units.tr: Further, as far as I know, no one has hitherto published a Samaritan grammar or any lexicon of the words that are peculiar to this dialect. John Morinus did indeed promise something in his preface to the Paris Bible, but he has not kept his promise so far. For the use of our Bibles we shall take care to publish in future something perhaps from the work of that most learned man, who has carefully collated our Samaritan copies and gathered many useful things.

units.la: Antiquas literas Hebraicas easdem fuisse cum Samaritanis ex siclis seu numismatis constat, quae ex ruderibus Hierofolymitanis essossa, charactere Samaritano pleraque percussa sunt, ex quibus literam Tau crucis figuram olim repraesentasse, literasque hodiernas Samaritanas ab antiquis parum differre colligitur. A Samaritanis vero non cusa clarum est ex inscriptione quam habent, scil. Hierosolymæ sanctæ, quam Samaritani abominantur. Siclorum autem figuras quas ex Aria Montano, Wafero, Villalpando, aliisque collegit Morinus, hic visum est exprimere.
units.tr: That the ancient Hebrew letters were the same as the Samaritan ones is clear from the shekels or coins, dug out of the ruins of Jerusalem, most of which were struck in Samaritan characters. From these it is gathered that the letter Tau once represented the shape of a cross, and that the present Samaritan letters differ little from the ancient ones. That they were not struck by the Samaritans is clear from the inscription they bear, namely Jerusalem the Holy, which the Samaritans abominate. I have thought fit to set out here the figures of the shekels which Morinus collected from Arias Montanus, Wafer, Villalpando and others.
