units.la: In siclis hisce omnium literarum figuræ non habentur, sed tantum 13. scil. ࠀ[?] ࠉ[?] ࠒ[?] ࠕ[?] ࠊ[?] ࠌ[?] ࠐ[?] ࠀ[?] ࠓ[?] ࠊ[?] ࠍ[?] ࠏ[?] ࠎ[?] ex quarum tamen cum hodiernis Samaritanis convenientia de reliquis judicare licet.
units.tr: On these shekels the forms of all the letters are not found, but only 13, which are given here in the Samaritan script; from their agreement with the present Samaritan letters one may judge the rest.

units.la: Ex his ࠀ[?] et ࠌ[?] magis à nostris differre videntur, ࠕ[?] minus, reliquæ parum vel nihil. Conjiciunt alii præter has quatuor alias ex hisce siclis, scil. v ࠈ[?] ࠑ[?] ࠕ[?] In sexta enim figura v ex una parte, & ex altera Tau instar crucis repræsentatur; at ࠊ[?] & ࠑ[?] obscuriores.
units.tr: Of these, the first and the sixth seem to differ more from ours, the fourth less, and the rest little or not at all. Others conjecture that, besides these four, there are others on these shekels, namely a Vav, and the forms shown in the figures. For on the sixth shekel the Vav is represented on one side, and on the other side the Tau in the form of a cross; but the others are more obscure.

units.la: Literam vero Tau crucis figuram repræsentâsse, prout affirmantOrigines et Hieronym in Ezech.etiam ex hodierno Tau Samaritano sic colligit Morinus. Ut enim ex Aleph nostro Samaritano, si unam lineolam ex latere dextro tollas fit figura Tau, sic in siclis 2. & 5. si tollas lineolam quæ rectam lineam per medium tangit, quod reliquum est Tau repræsentabit: nam istius lineæ adjectio Aleph à Tau distinguit, & hoc modo exactam crucis figuram repræsentabit Tau. Azarias verò Judæus in Alphabeto suo duplicem ostendit figuram literæ Tau, unam nostræ similem, alteram verò instar Latinæ X decussatam, quam vocamus S. Andreæ crucem. In siclo primo, secundo, & tertio, eadem est Aleph figura supra urnam, à qua sitollas inferiorem lineam, quod reliquum est, crucem refert. In Alphabeto Samaritano quod ex Bibliotheca Vaticana produxit Schickardus in libro, cui titulus Bechinath Happeruschin, p.8.ultima litera figuram crucis habet. Observat etiam idem characterem unctionis sacerdotalis fuisse cruciculam quam faciebant intersupercilia Pontificis, ut ex Maymon.-& R. D. Kimchi probat in tract. de Jure Regio Hebræorum, hanc verò dicunt Rabbini, cum crucem non invenerunt in Alphabeto Hebraico, esse instar Græci χ quod idem plane cum Tau Samaritano, unde sacerdotem summum in hoc typum fuisse Christi arguit idem Schick. sed ad singulorum siclorum explicationem veniamus.
units.tr: That the letter Tau represented the figure of a cross, as Origen and Jerome affirm in their commentary on Ezekiel, Morinus also gathers from the present Samaritan Tau. For just as, if you remove one little line from the right side of our Samaritan Aleph, the figure of Tau results, so on the second and fifth shekels, if you remove the little line which touches the straight line through the middle, what remains will represent Tau; for the addition of that line distinguishes Aleph from Tau, and in this way Tau will represent the exact figure of a cross. But the Jew Azariah, in his alphabet, shows a double figure of the letter Tau: one like ours, and the other shaped like a Latin X crossed, which we call St Andrew's cross. On the first, second and third shekels the figure of Aleph is above the urn; if you remove its lower line, what remains represents a cross. In the Samaritan alphabet which Schickard produced from the Vatican Library, in the book entitled Bechinath Happeruschin, page 8, the last letter has the figure of a cross. The same writer observes that the mark of priestly anointing was a little cross which they made between the eyebrows of the high priest, as Maimonides and R. D. Kimchi prove in the treatise on the royal law of the Hebrews; but the rabbis say that this mark, since they did not find a cross in the Hebrew alphabet, is like the Greek [χ], which is exactly the same as the Samaritan Tau; hence Schickard argues that the high priest was a type of Christ in this respect. But let us come to the explanation of the individual shekels.

units.la: Primus omnium perfectissimè literas suas repræsentat, cujus inscriptio literis Hebraicis expressa ex una parte est ירושלימה קדושה Jerusalem sancta, ex altera verò שקל ישראל siclus Israelis, ex illa parte est virga Aaronis ex hac urna Mannæ cui imminent literæ Schin & Daleth,quæ ut conjicit Morinus,significa nt siclum Davidis, quia in urbe Davidis percussa , scil. Hierosolymis: quod & ex alia conjectura probant quidam,quia scil. scribitur Jerusalem cum Jod post Lamed, & He ad finem, ita ut legatur inscriptio Jerusalimah,quæ pronuntiatio erat peculiaris dialecto Hierosolymitanæ. In siclis vero quæ habent eandem inscriptionem sine Jod & He,literæ istæ Schin & Daleth supra urnam non videntur, sed Aleph, vel quod fortasse urbis nomen ab Aleph incipiebat ubi cusi erant, vel ad significandum ירושלם[?] seu urbem generaliter, quæ scil. diversa erat ab Hierosolyma:hoc enim frequens est numismatis, loci nomen ubi cuduntur, exprimere.
units.tr: The first, most perfectly of all, represents its letters. Its inscription, expressed in Hebrew letters, reads on one side ירושלימה קדושה [Yerushalima qedosha] Jerusalem sancta, and on the other שקל ישראל [shekel Yisrael], the shekel of Israel. On that side is Aaron's rod, and on this side the urn of manna, over which stand the letters Shin and Daleth. As Morinus conjectures, these signify the shekel of David, because it was struck in David's city, namely Jerusalem. Some also support this by another conjecture: Jerusalem is written with a Yod after the Lamed and a He at the end, so that the inscription is read Jerusalimah, a pronunciation peculiar to the dialect of Jerusalem. On the shekels, however, which have the same inscription without the Yod and He, the letters Shin and Daleth do not appear above the urn; instead there is Aleph. This is either because the name of the city where they were minted began with Aleph, or to signify ירושלם [Yerushalem], or the city in general, which was different from Hierosolyma. For it is common on coins to express the name of the place where they are struck.

units.la: Secundus eandem habet cum primo inscriptionem,sed in scriptione differt; sic enim scribitur קדשׁ ירושלם Jerusalem sanêta, sine Jod post Lamed, vel He in fine. & super urnam ponitur Aleph ob rationem fortasse supradictam.
units.tr: The second has the same inscription as the first, but differs in spelling: it is written קדש ירושלם [Yerushalem qadosh], Jerusalem holy, without the Yod after the Lamed or the He at the end. Above the urn is placed Aleph, perhaps for the reason mentioned above.

units.la: Tertius per omnia similis est primo, tantummodo virgam & urnam sculptor omisit, quia in primo satis exprimuntur.
units.tr: The third is in every respect like the first, except that the engraver omitted the rod and the urn, since these are sufficiently expressed on the first.

units.la: Quartum putat Vilalpandus fuisse sicli quadrantem , & legendum ex una parte [illegible, ~3 letters] ירושלם[?] appositâ litera Mem ad finem,quod interpretatur, ad scripturam Jerusalem, ab altera vero שמן unctionis tempus. Putat Morinus Amuletum Samaritanum fuisse non siclum.
units.tr: Vilalpandus thinks the fourth was a quarter shekel, and that on one side, with a Mem added at the end, the word [illegible] ירושלם should be read, which he interprets as for the writing of Jerusalem, and on the other שמן [shemen], the time of anointing. Morinus thinks the Samaritan amulet was not a shekel.

units.la: Quintus est hemisiclus, ex una parte habet eandem cum caeteris inscriptionem, literis quibusdam erasis, ירושלם קדשה Jerusalem sancta, scriptione cum secunda conveniente. Ex altera vero חצי השקל dimidium sicli, literae Tzade & Jod deletae sunt, & Coph media sua parte, urnae vero imponitur Aleph.
units.tr: The fifth is a half shekel. On one side it has the same inscription as the others, with some letters erased: ירושלם קדשה [Yerushalem qadshah], Jerusalem sancta, in a spelling agreeing with the second. On the other side is חצי השקל [chetzi hashekel], half a shekel; the letters Tzade and Yod have been erased, and Qoph has lost its middle part, while Aleph is placed above the urn.

units.la: Sextus ostendit Samaritanam aliquam literam figuram crucis habuisse.
units.tr: The sixth shows that some Samaritan letter had the figure of a cross.

units.la: Septimus; & octavus recentiores sunt, post reditum è captivitate Babylonica, literis Assyriis inscripti; eandem vero habent inscriptionem cum tertio & quinto. Sed de siclis haec satis sint: quae, si alia non essent argumenta, quemvis non pertinacem de vera literarum antiquarum Hebraicarum figura certum reddere possint.
units.tr: The seventh and eighth are more recent, dating from after the return from the Babylonian captivity, and are inscribed with Assyrian letters. They have the same inscription as the third and fifth. But let this be enough about the shekels. Even if there were no other arguments, they could make any unstubborn person certain about the true form of the ancient Hebrew letters.

units.la: Syrorum literæ, ut numero , sic potestate cum Hebræis conveniunt: nominibus quædam, ac figura pleræque variant.
units.tr: The letters of the Syrians agree with the Hebrews in their numerical value and in their phonetic value, just as they do in number; some of their names differ, and their shapes mostly vary.

units.la: Figuram habent duplicem, expeditiorem & usitatiorem, quæ in Tabula: Alteram magis difficilem & inusitatam, quam & Estrangelam quidam vocant; quæ in titulis & inscriptionibus librorum & capitum à quibusdam usurpantur: qui tamen priorem probè callet, facile alteram etiam cognoscet, à quâ prior derivatur.
units.tr: They have a twofold form: the more convenient and more common one, which is in the table, and another that is more difficult and unusual, which some also call Estrangela. The latter is used by some in the titles and inscriptions of books and chapters. Yet whoever knows the former well will easily recognise the latter too, since the former is derived from it.

units.la: Connectuntur literæ maximè in basi:

units.la: Dividuntur ut apud Hebraeos, in Gutturales, Linguales, Palatinos, Dentales & Labiales, & eædem sunt apud utrosque. Quiescentes apud Syros sunt tres tantùm, [illegible, ~5 letters] non quiescit, ideo nec mappic unquam habet. quiescit in [ɣ] in medio & fine, ut [illegible, ~8 letters] Laloho deo, [illegible, ~6 letters] baja consolatus est.
units.tr: They are divided, as among the Hebrews, into Gutturals, Linguals, Palatals, Dentals and Labials, and these are the same in both languages. Among the Syrians there are only three quiescent letters. … does not quiesce, and therefore never takes a mappiq. It is quiescent in [ɣ] in the middle and at the end, as in … Laloho (God), … baja (he was consoled).

units.la: In [ɵ] in medio & fine, ut [illegible, ~5 letters] arnanum, [illegible, ~5 letters] Deus.
units.tr: It is quiescent in [ɵ] in the middle and at the end, as in … arnanum, … (God).

units.la: Waw quiescit in vocali [ɬ] idque tantum in medio & fine, ut [illegible, ~9 letters] malcutho et [illegible, ~6 letters] malcu regnum.
units.tr: Waw is quiescent in the vowel [ɬ], and only in the middle and at the end, as in malcutho and malcu (kingdom).

units.la: In vocali ɵ tantum in nominibus peregrinis, cum (ω) vel (o) aut interdum (υ) Graecum exprimenda sunt, ut [illegible, ~6 letters] παῦλος[?].
units.tr: The vowel ɵ is used only in foreign names, when they must be expressed by the Greek ω, o, or sometimes υ, as in Paulos [Παῦλος].

units.la: Jod quiescit in [ɣ] & [ɲ,] ut [illegible, ~3 letters] mihi, [illegible, ~4 letters] duo.
units.tr: Jod is quiescent in [ɣ] and [ɲ], as in … (to me), … (two).

units.la: SECT. III.
units.tr: SECT. III.

units.la: De Vocalibus & Dipthongis.
units.tr: On the Vowels and Diphthongs.

units.la: Vocales sunt quinque, quas exprimunt tum per figuras tum per puncta. Nomen, | Figura, | Potestas. [illegible, ~3 letters] Pethoco. | a | [illegible, ~2 letters] | Pathac Hebr. [illegible, ~3 letters] Revotfo. | e | [illegible, ~3 letters] | Tfere & fegol. [illegible, ~3 letters] Chevotfo. | i | [illegible, ~2 letters] | Chirekutrumque [illegible, ~3 letters] Zequafo. | o | [illegible, ~2 letters] | ] vel Cametz Chatuph [illegible, ~3 letters] Otfotfo. | u | [illegible, ~3 letters] vel [illegible, ~2 letters] | ] vel Kibbuts.
units.tr: Vowels are five, and they express them both by figures and by points. Name, Figure, Power: Pethoco | a | Pathac (Hebrew) ... Revotfo | e | Tsere and segol ... Chevotfo | i | Chirek, either ... Zequafo | o | Cholem or Kamets Chatuph ... Otfotfo | u | Shureq or Kibbuts.

units.la: Olim punctum unicum omnes vocales repræ-sentabat, quod supra literam significabat a, o, vel u; sub litera, e vel i: at postea vocales à Græcis mutuatæ.
units.tr: Formerly a single point represented all the vowels: placed above the letter it signified a, o, or u, and placed below the letter it signified e or i. Later, however, the vowels were borrowed from the Greeks.

units.la: Figuræ vocalium pro libitu nunc infra, nunc supra literam collocantur: Puncta vero situm. non mutant, utraque sæpe miscentur in eadem dictione ita ut una syllaba hanc, alia illam habeat : nec semper vocales adduntur, sed una dictio sæpe habet, altera caret, & in eadem dictione una syllaba notatur, altera non, quem defectum ex analogia Grammatica supplere oportet. Otsotso sine o non scribitur ; excipe [illegible, ~3 letters] omnis, & [illegible, ~4 letters] propter, & subscriptum punctum habens refert Hebr. Schurec ; impositum vero Kibbuts.
units.tr: The vowel figures are placed at will, sometimes below and sometimes above the letter, but the points never change their position. The two are often mixed together in the same word, so that one syllable has one vowel and another has a different one. Vowels are not always added: one word often has one and another lacks it, and within the same word one syllable is marked and another is not. This deficiency must be supplied from the analogy of grammar. Otsotso is not written without o; excepting all, and because, which has a point placed underneath and corresponds to the Hebrew Schurec; a point placed above is Kibbuts.

units.la: Kamets Hebr. longum per Sekopho exprimitur, & interdum etiam Cholem, quod alio quin in dipthongum au mutatur, unde pro [illegible, ~2 letters] dicunt [illegible, ~2 letters] & [illegible, ~3 letters] lau, non. Dipthongi fiunt per literas Wau & Jud, valorem consonantium amittentes, & cum præcedente vocale in unam syllabam coalescentes. Wau efficit 4. dipthongos, (au) Initio, medio & fine præcedente Pthocho, ut [illegible, ~3 letters] auled, genuit. (eu) præcedente [illegible, ~1 letter] & interveniente Jud, ut [illegible, ~5 letters] bibam illud. Mat. 26. 29. (iu) in medio, præcedente Chirek longo, ante wau, ut [illegible, ~6 letters] perdet eum, (ou) post alterum Wau cum vocali [illegible, ~1 letter] ut [illegible, ~5 letters] Schioudoio promissio, quidam tamen non legunt secundum [illegible, ~1 letter].
units.tr: Kamets, long in Hebrew, is expressed by Sekopho, and sometimes also by Cholem, which otherwise changes into the diphthong au; whence they say lau, not, for the Hebrew word. Diphthongs are formed by the letters Wau and Jud, which lose their consonantal value and coalesce with the preceding vowel into one syllable. Wau forms four diphthongs: (au) at the beginning, middle and end, after a preceding Pthocho, as in auled, he begot; (eu) after a preceding [vowel] and with Jud intervening, as in bibam illud, Matt. 26. 29; (iu) in the middle, after a long Chirek, before wau, as in perdet eum, he will destroy him; (ou) after a second Wau with a vowel [following], as in Schioudoio, promissio; some, however, do not read it according to [the rule].

units.la: Jod facit duos dipthongos,oi & ai: oi cum [illegible, ~2 letters] ante [illegible, ~1 letter], cùm in medio tum in fine, ut [illegible, ~3 letters] primâ, [illegible, ~3 letters] nudus: ai per [illegible, ~1 letter] ut [illegible, ~3 letters] malkai reges mei, idque in principio medio & fine.
units.tr: Jod makes two diphthongs, oi and ai. Oi occurs with [a vowel] before it, both in the middle and at the end, as in primâ, and nudus. Ai is formed through [a vowel], as in malkai, my kings, and this occurs at the beginning, middle and end.

units.la: SECT. IV.
units.tr: SECT. IV.

units.la: de Daghes & Mappic.
units.tr: Of Daghes and Mappik.

units.la: Syri Daghes forte non habent, sed in literis Begadkephat, punctum supra literam valet Daghes lene, & vocatur [illegible, ~2 letters] kufchoi durities: sub litera valet Hebræorum Raphe, & vocatur [illegible, ~3 letters] Ruchoch mollities.
units.tr: The Syriac may not have Daghes, but in the letters Begadkephat a point above the letter has the value of soft Daghes, and it is called kufchoi, hardness. Under the letter it has the value of the Hebrew Raphe, and it is called ruchoch, softness.

units.la: Ubi verò Ruchoch, ubi Kufchoi locum habent, de quo intricata admodum sunt Grammaticorum Syrorum præcepta, ex Hebraico Daghes & ejus regulis facile est judicare. Itaque literæ Begadkephat habent Kufchoi, seu Daghes lene.
units.tr: Where Ruchoch and where Kufchoi apply, concerning which the rules of the Syriac grammarians are very intricate, can easily be judged from Hebrew Daghes and its rules. Therefore the letters Begadkephat have Kufchoi, or soft Daghes:

units.la: 1o. In initio dictionis, ut [illegible, ~3 letters] talmidho, discipulus.
units.tr: (1) At the beginning of a word, as talmidho, his disciple.

units.la: 2. In medio post scheva quiescens, ut [illegible, ~3 letters] malke rex ejus. Molles vero sunt,vel Ruchoch habent in media dictione vel in fine.
units.tr: (2) In the middle, after a quiescent sheva, as malke, his king. But they are soft, or have Ruchoch, in the middle of a word or at its end.

units.la: 1. Si efferantur ipsæ per scheva quiescens, ut חָכְמָתוֹ [?] sapientia; si vero eas in fine schevatas præcedat aliud scheva quiescens, asperæ fiunt, ut אֶתְחַרְקְ [?] ethkark, non ethkarch circunda; בַּזְתּ [?] bazt, non bazth, rapuisti.
units.tr: (1) If they are sounded with a quiescent sheva, as [chokhmato] wisdom; but if a quiescent sheva precedes them at the end of a word that has a sheva, they become hard, as ethkark, not ethkarch, circumcised; bazt, not bazth, you have plundered.

units.la: 2. Si sequantur Scheva mobile, ut בּוּרְכְּתוֹ [?] burktho, non burkto.
units.tr: (2) If a movable sheva follows, as [burktho] burktho, not burkto.

units.la: 3. Post quasvis vocales, ut in אֲכִילוֹ [?] achilo comesus, יָד [?] manus, nisi ratio conjugationis vel defectus alicujus compensatio, vel peculiaris aliqua emphasis,vel euphonia,Daghes forte postulet;quo in casu Syri ejus analogia imitantur, non aliter quàm si geminarent, duriùs scilicet pronuntiando.
units.tr: (3) After any vowels, as in achilo, eaten, and yad, hand, unless the form of the conjugation, the making up of some defect, some peculiar emphasis, or euphony calls for Daghes; in which case the Syrians follow its analogy, no differently than if they doubled the letter, that is, by pronouncing it more harshly.

units.la: 4. Quæ apud Hebræos daghessantur, apud Syros etiam(etsi non [illegible, ~2 letters] literæ Begad-kephat nec habeant Kuschoi expressum) in pronuntiatione tamen leges Daghes imitantur, id est, literam sequentem, si sit Begadkephat, faciunt moveri,ut מַלְפּוֹנוֹ [?] malphono doctor, non malpono.
units.tr: (4) Letters which among the Hebrews take Daghes, the Syrians also (although they do not have an expressed Kuschoi in the letters Begad-kephat) nevertheless imitate the rules of Daghes in pronunciation; that is, they make the following letter, if it is a Begadkephat, be pronounced with a stronger sound, as malphono, his teacher, not malpono.

units.la: Mappik Syri non habent in He finali, ut Hebræi: et ubi Hebræi per mappik designant assixum singularis numeri tertiae personae foem. praecedente Camets, ut in ܦܝܫ pes ejus foem. ibi Syri illud punctum quod notat foem. genus, ponunt supra ܥ, praecedente [ܝ] in singulari, ut ܥܝ ܩ ܝ pes ejus foem.
units.tr: The Syrians do not have Mappik in final He as the Hebrews do. And where the Hebrews use Mappik to mark the suffix of the third person singular feminine after a preceding qamets, as in pes, her foot, there the Syrians put over the letter ʿ, after a preceding yod in the singular, that point which marks the feminine gender, as in ʿīqī, her foot.

units.la: SECT. V.
units.tr: SECT. V.

units.la: De scheva.
units.tr: Concerning the scheva.

units.la: Syri scheva non exprimunt, sed intelligunt, cùm scilicet syllaba pluribus literis constat: quae enim litera vocali caret, intelligitur habere scheva quiescens vel mobile, ut ܒܘܪ bur-ktho, benedictio: ubi ܝ intelligitur habere scheva quiescens, quo trahitur litera ad praecedentia; ܕ vero scheva mobile, quo trahitur ad sequentia.
units.tr: The Syrians do not express the scheva but understand it, namely when a syllable consists of several letters. For a letter without a vowel is understood to have either a quiescent or a mobile scheva, as in bur-ktho, benediction. Here y is understood to have a quiescent scheva, by which the letter is drawn back to what precedes it, but d has a mobile scheva, by which it is drawn forward to what follows.

units.la: Eadem vero est Scheva quiescentis & mobilis ratio, quae apud Hebraeos, nisi quòd saepiùs post vocalem longam Scheva fit quiescens apud Syros quam apud Hebraeos, quod usu discendum: hoc tamen observatur, quòd post [ܝ] vocalem, ortam ex quiescentibus media vau, & quietis istius indicem, Scheva fit mobile, ut ܛܘܒܐ tovtho, bona.
units.tr: The reasoning behind the quiescent and mobile scheva is the same as among the Hebrews, except that among the Syrians a scheva becomes quiescent after a long vowel more often than among the Hebrews, and this must be learned by practice. It is observed, however, that after the y vowel, which arises from a quiescent medial vav and is a sign of that quiescence, the scheva becomes mobile, as in tovtho, good.

units.la: SECT. VI.
units.tr: SECTION VI.

units.la: De aliis punctis quæ Syris peculiaria.
units.tr: Concerning the other points peculiar to the Syrians.

units.la: Usurpant Syri præter Ruchoch & Kufchoi, aliapuncta diacritica, quæ vel solitaria vel socia.
units.tr: Besides Ruchoch and Kufchoi, the Syrians use other diacritical points, some standing alone and some paired.

units.la: 1. Solitarium, seu punctum unicum.
units.tr: 1. The solitary point, or single point.

units.la: 1. Infra literam, notat primò omnes personas præteriti, exceptâ primâ singulari: tertia vero singularis habet punctum supra ad latus sinistrum ultimi Tau, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] visitavit illa. 2, Infinitivum & imperativum sæpe; aliquando tamen omittitur: cum apponitur tamen infra scribitur, ut [illegible, ~3 letters] da: Joh. 4. 15. 3, Omnes personas suturi, exceptis primis utriusque numeri.
units.tr: 1. Placed below a letter, it marks first all the persons of the past tense except the first singular. The third singular, however, has a point above, on the left side of the final Tau, as [illegible] she visited. 2. It often marks the infinitive and the imperative, though sometimes it is omitted. When it is added, it is written below, as [illegible] give: John 4. 15. 3. It marks all persons of the future except the first of each number.

units.la: 2. Supra literam, in verbis notat 1, primam præteriti; ut [illegible, ~4 letters] visitavi. 2, Benoni, seu participium præsens, ut, [illegible, ~3 letters]: at in Benoni Aphel quiescentium media wau, puncto hoc non supra sed infra Jud ponitur, ut [illegible, ~5 letters] constituit. 3, Primam personam sing. & plur. futuri, ut, [illegible, ~3 letters] ædificabo. [illegible, ~3 letters] ædificabimus, quod sic distinguitur à [illegible, ~3 letters] ædificabit.
units.tr: 2. Placed above a letter, in verbs it marks (1) the first person of the past, as [illegible] I visited; (2) the Benoni, or present participle, as [illegible]. In the Benoni of the Aphel of quiescent verbs with a middle waw, however, this point is placed not above but below the Jud, as [illegible] he constituted. (3) the first person singular and plural of the future, as [illegible] I will build and [illegible] we will build, which is thus distinguished from [illegible] he will build.

units.la: 3. Ad latus literæ apponitur vocib9 ambiguis, ut, [illegible, ~4 letters] signum, & [illegible, ~4 letters] veniens: apponitur & tertiæ fæm. sing, ut supra.
units.tr: 3. It is placed at the side of a letter in ambiguous words, as [illegible] sign and [illegible] coming. It is also placed on the third feminine singular, as above.

units.la: Puncta socia, scil. duo supra vocem notant pluralem numerum: 1. in nominibus tam masculinis quàm fœmininis, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] Ktobe, libri [illegible, ~4 letters] tovotho, bona.
units.tr: Paired points, that is, two points above a word, mark the plural number: 1. in nouns, both masculine and feminine, as [illegible] Ktobe, books, and [illegible] tovotho, good things.

units.la: 2. In verbis fœm. gen. ut [illegible, ~4 letters] pekadh, visitaverunt fœm. Ubi verò adest litera [illegible, ~1 letter] quæ ex se habet punctum unicum, alterum ipsi additur, ut, [illegible, ~4 letters] sepulchra: si verò tertium addatur, id vocalem, aut Kufschoi aut tempus designat: imò cùm duplex est punctum supra [illegible, ~1 letter] non semper pluralis numerus notatur, sed primum notat literam, alterum verò primam præteriti aut Benoni, aut primam futuri, ut in [illegible, ~4 letters] Kryt vocavi. Et sic dicendum de duplici puncto sub [illegible, ~1 letter]; unum Dolath denotat, alterum personas vel tempora, ut supra.
units.tr: 2. In feminine verbs, as [illegible] pekadh, they (fem.) visited. Where, however, a letter that by itself has a single point is present, another point is added to it, as [illegible] sepulchres. If a third point is added, it designates a vowel, either Kufschoi or a tense. Indeed, when there is a double point above [illegible], it does not always mark the plural number; the first point marks the letter, and the other marks the first person of the past or the Benoni, or the first person of the future, as in [illegible] Kryt, I called. The same must be said of the double point below [illegible]: one denotes Dolath, the other the persons or tenses, as above.

units.la: SECT. VII.
units.tr: SECT. VII.

units.la: De Lineolis.
units.tr: On the Little Lines.

units.la: Lineolam habent Syri, quæ aliquando supra, aliquando infra dictionem ducitur.
units.tr: The Syrians have a little line, which is sometimes drawn above a word and sometimes below it.

units.la: 1. Supra
units.tr: 1. Above the word.

units.la: I. Supra, idque, 1, literis numeralibus, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] 12 : 2, vocibus contractis, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] pro [illegible, ~7 letters] sanctus : 3, particulæ vocativæ [illegible, ~3 letters], ô, ut notet literam o non pronunciandam, & ut distinguatur à particula [illegible, ~3 letters] : aut 4, ad indicandum quòd litera subjecta quiescit, & per scheva efferenda sit sequente alterâ quiescente, ut [illegible, ~8 letters] à quo usu appellatur [illegible, ~7 letters] Marhtono quasi currere faciens, quòd litera subjecta cursim proferatur.
units.tr: Above the word, and this is used (1) with numeral letters, as [illegible] 12; (2) with contracted words, as [illegible] for [illegible], "holy"; (3) with the vocative particle [illegible], "O", so that it marks the letter o as not to be pronounced, and so that it is distinguished from the particle [illegible]; or (4) to indicate that the letter beneath it is quiescent and is to be pronounced with a shewa when the following letter is quiescent, as [illegible]. From this use it is called Marhtono, as it were "making to run", because the letter beneath it is pronounced quickly.

units.la: 2. Infra literam, notat 1, otium quarundam literarum, quæ non leguntur, ut [illegible, ~5 letters] chrojo postremus : 2, In Imperativis formæ passivæ,abscentiam vocalis, ut [illegible, ~6 letters] eftakl intellige, [illegible, ~5 letters] ethbattn concipitor : 3, In carmine pro metri necessitate, priori quiescentium subductâ, dicitur [illegible, ~6 letters] meditari faciens ; & notat literam tardius legendam,vim habens vocalis[ʼn][?] vel (quòd in verbis frequentius) vocalis[ ʼ ]:apponitur itaq; τῷ [illegible, ~6 letters] marhtono, de quo suprà.
units.tr: 2. Below the letter, it marks (1) the idleness of certain letters, which are not read, as in chrojo, "last"; (2) in the imperatives of the passive form, the absence of a vowel, as in eftakl, "understand", and ethbattn, "is conceived"; (3) in verse, for the necessity of the metre, when the preceding quiescent letter is dropped, as [illegible], "making to meditate". It also marks a letter to be read more slowly, having the force of a vowel, either [ʼn] or, more often in verbs, [ʼ]. It is therefore placed in the same position as the Marhtono, of which we have spoken above.

units.la: In prosa verò,nisi difficilis obstet prolatio,apponitur ejus loco Marhtono, & cursim legitur. Vide Amyram.
units.tr: In prose, however, unless difficult pronunciation stands in the way, the Marhtono is put in its place and read quickly. See Amyram.

units.la: SECT. VIII.
units.tr: SECT. VIII.

units.la: De Accentibus.
units.tr: On Accents.

units.la: Apud Syros semper omittuntur accentuum notae: quae autem syllaba inter legendum tono affici debeat, ex hisce regulis observare licet.
units.tr: Among the Syrians the accent marks are never written. Which syllable should be stressed in reading may nevertheless be learned from the following rules.

units.la: 1 In diffyllabis, si prima syllaba esseratur per Scheva quiescens, vocalis Scheva illud antecedens accentum habet, ut, [illegible, ~5 letters] málcho Rex: si secunda, tunc illa afficitur, ut [illegible, ~5 letters] halécḥ ivit: si utraque sic se habeat, at utraque afficitur, ut [illegible, ~6 letters] lémdéth didici. Si neutra habeat scheva quiescens, prima afficitur, ut [illegible, ~5 letters] kthóvo liber.
units.tr: 1. In two-syllable words: if the first syllable is formed with a quiescent Shewa, the Shewa vowel that comes before it bears the accent, as in [illegible] málcho king. If the second syllable is so formed, that one is accented, as in [illegible] halécḥ he went. If both are so formed, both are accented, as in [illegible] lémdéth I learned. If neither has a quiescent Shewa, the first is accented, as in [illegible] kthóvo book.

units.la: 2 In trisyllabis, secunda plerunque afficitur, ut in [illegible, ~8 letters] mazmúro psalmus.
units.tr: 2. In three-syllable words the second syllable is generally accented, as in [illegible] mazmúro psalm.

units.la: 3 In quadrisyllabis, &c.: penultima afficitur, ut [illegible, ~9 letters] martyonútho admonitio.
units.tr: 3. In four-syllable words, etc., the penultimate is accented, as in [illegible] martyonútho admonition.

units.la: SECT. IX.
units.tr: SECT. IX.

units.la: De Distinctionibus.
units.tr: Concerning Punctuation.

units.la: Distinctionum notas habent Syri, puncto uno crassiori, vel duobus, vel asterisco adhibitis, quae incisa, colon, vel periodum designant: aliquando ad periodum adhibent quatuor puncta, ut ·✜ vel ::; & ad interrogationem puncta duo sinistrorsum inflexa, ut ↖ vide Georg. Amyram, lib. 1. c. ult. Notæ tamen istæ non ubique exactè observantur, ut in libris tum impressis, tum MSS. videre licet.
units.tr: The Syrians have marks of punctuation: a single thicker point, or two, or an asterisk, used to designate a clause (incisum), a colon, or a period. Sometimes for a period they use four points, as ·✜ or ::; and for a question two points bent to the left, as ↖ (see Georg. Amyram, book 1, last chapter). These marks, however, are not everywhere observed exactly, as one may see both in printed books and in manuscripts.

units.la: SECT. IX. [?]
units.tr: SECT. IX. [?]

units.la: De Grammaticis, & Lexicis Syriacis.
units.tr: On the Syriac Grammars and Lexicons.

units.la: Inter multos qui præcepta Grammatica Syriaca conscripserunt, ut Masius, Waserus, Trostius, Buxtorfius junior: cujus Grammatica propter defectum characterum Syriacorum (Hebraicis enim utitur) minus aptus est ad usum. Absolutissimè præcepta tradidit Georg. Amyra Maronita è monte Libano, & ex ipso & aliis Lud. de Dieu in comparatione trium linguarum ubi licet Hebraica, & Chaldaica, Syriacis conjunxit, maximam tamen ἀκρίβειαν [?] adhibuit in Syriacis: at cùm prolixè & copiosè agunt isti authores, nec facile comparari possunt, consultius est tyronibus epitomen aliquam Grammaticæ Syriacæ primò addiscere. Et quia Chaldæa cum Syriaca magnam habet affinitatem, Andreæ Sennerti Wittenbergensis Chaldaismus & Syriasmus, qui utriusque linguæ præcepta methodicè & breviter conjunxit, & Lexici Chald. Syriaci epitomen complectentem vocabula usitatiora N. Testamenti Syriaci adjecit, incipientibus utilis esse potest.
units.tr: Among the many who have written Syriac grammatical rules are Masius, Waserus, Trostius, and Buxtorf the younger, whose grammar is less suitable for use because of the lack of Syriac characters (he uses Hebrew ones). The most thorough rules were given by Georg Amira the Maronite of Mount Lebanon, and Lud. de Dieu, in his comparison of three languages, joined Hebrew and Chaldee with Syriac, though he showed the greatest exactness in the Syriac. But since these authors treat the subject at great length and in detail, and cannot easily be compared, it is better for beginners first to learn some epitome of Syriac grammar. And because Chaldee has a great affinity with Syriac, the Chaldaismus and Syriasmus of Andreas Sennertus of Wittenberg, which joins the rules of both languages in a methodical and brief way, and which adds to a Chaldee-Syriac lexicon an epitome containing the more common words of the Syriac New Testament, can be useful to beginners.

units.la: Necessarium verò est, linguæ Hebraicæ præcepta callere, antequam ad Chaldaicæ vel Syriacæ cognitionem se quis accingat, post jaćta vero Hebraica fundamenta, brevi in Chaldæa & Syriaca magnos progressus faciet, adeo ut miretur se tam esse doctum antequam didicit, & nota fertur regione viarum.
units.tr: It is indeed necessary to know well the rules of the Hebrew language before a person sets himself to learn Chaldee or Syriac. Once the Hebrew foundations are laid, he will soon make great progress in Chaldee and Syriac, so that he will marvel at how learned he has become before he has learned it, and he is said to know the roads of the region.

units.la: Inter Lexica vero Syriaca quæ ad huc extant, sunt, Buxtorfii junioris Lexic. Syriacum & Chaldaicum, Trostii item & Crinesii Lexica Syriaca, Ferrarii quoque nomenclator Syriacus in 4. Romæ impressus, quorum hic multa habet vocabula (ut qui Maronitæ operâ usus est) quæ in aliis desiderantur. Post editum vero vetus Testamentum Syriacum Parisiense nemo est qui Lexicon Syriacum ex eo; collegit, quod mihi adhuc videre contigit: adeo ut absoluta Lexica inde extrahendi & conficiendi labor, docto alicui adhuc relinquitur.
units.tr: Among the Syriac lexicons still extant are Buxtorf the younger's Syriac and Chaldee Lexicon, likewise the Syriac lexicons of Trostius and Crinesius, and also the Syriac nomenclator of Ferrarius, printed in quarto at Rome, which has many words (since it made use of a Maronite) that are missing in the others. But since the Old Testament in Syriac was published at Paris, no one, as far as I have yet had the chance to see, has compiled a Syriac lexicon from it. So the labour of extracting and completing a full lexicon from it is still left to some learned person.

units.la: In Columnis, prima exhibet literas initiales, secunda medias, quæ plerunq; aliis connectuntur, tertia finales quæ non connectuntur cum præcedentibus, quarta finales connexas cum præcedentibus: sex tamen sunt literæ quæ sequenti conjungi non possunt, scil. [illegible, ~6 letters] ideóque initiales post eas usurpantur etiam in medio dictionis.
units.tr: In the columns, the first gives the initial forms, the second the medial forms, which are generally joined to other letters; the third gives the final forms, which are not joined to the preceding letters; the fourth gives the final forms joined to the preceding letters. There are six letters, however, that cannot be joined to a following letter, namely [illegible], and so the initial forms are used after them even in the middle of a word.

units.la: Elif & Lam conjunguntur ut in tabula ; & quidem cùm alteri literæ non connectuntur, sic Ȳ. cùm connectuntur hoc modo ȝ, aliquando sic [illegible, ~2 letters], vel sic [illegible, ~2 letters]
units.tr: Elif and Lam are joined as in the table. When they are not joined to other letters, Ȳ is written thus; when they are joined, thus ȝ, sometimes thus [illegible], or thus [illegible].

units.la: Quæ litera, Te, The, Nun, & Je, mutatis punctis inservit, sæpè invertitur ante Gjim, Hha, & Cha, sic [illegible, ~2 letters]
units.tr: The letter which serves as Te, The, Nun, and Je, when its points are changed, is often inverted before Gjim, Hha, and Cha, thus [illegible].

units.la: Eædem literæ Gjim, Hha, & Cha, cùm literæ præcedenti conjunguntur, illum supra lineam plerunque (non semper) attollunt, ut in [illegible, ~8 letters] &c.
units.tr: The same letters Gjim, Hha, and Cha, when joined to the preceding letter, raise it above the line, usually though not always, as in [illegible] etc.

units.la: He finale interdum duo habet punĉta supernè, ut [illegible, ~2 letters] & tunc pronuntiatur ut Te, & numerum pluralem, vel genus fœm. notat.
units.tr: Final He sometimes has two points above it, as [illegible]; it is then pronounced like Te, and marks the plural number or the feminine gender.

units.la: Dictiones non dividunt Arabes in fine linearum, sed ne spatium fit vacuum, lineam extendunt sic [illegible, ~6 letters]
units.tr: The Arabs do not divide words at the ends of lines; but so that no blank space is left, they extend the line thus [illegible].

units.la: Punĉta diacritica literarum in scriptis vulgaribus sæpe omittuntur; & ubi punĉta adhibentur, sæpe in He finali omittuntur.
units.tr: The diacritical points of letters are often omitted in common writings; and where points are used, they are often omitted on final He.

units.la: In libris quibusdam, licèt punctorum absentia literas quasdam ab aliis distinguat, scil. [illegible, ~8 letters] ne tamen quis opinetur omissa esse puncta ex scriptoris incuria riâ, vel casu, alias notas adhibent, scil. super v v v hoc (v), ut [?] [illegible, ~6 letters]
units.tr: In some books, although the absence of points distinguishes certain letters from others, lest anyone think that the points were omitted through the writer's carelessness or by chance, they use other marks, namely above v v v this (v), as [?] [illegible].

units.la: reliquis verò eandem literam inferné minori formâ, at He finali aliud interdum superponitur indicans absentiam punctorum supradictorum: hœc autem alii omittunt, ut merè superfluum & inane Grammaticorum figmentum; absentia enim punctorum satis has literas distinguit ab aliis similibus quæ punctis afficiuntur, scil. â [illegible, ~6 letters]
units.tr: On the remaining letters the same letter is written below in a smaller form, and on final He something else is sometimes placed above it, indicating the absence of the aforesaid points. Others, however, omit these, regarding them as a mere superfluous and empty invention of the grammarians; for the absence of points already distinguishes these letters sufficiently from other similar letters which are marked with points, namely â [illegible].

units.la: Cæteros supplent ut Hebræi. Ut [illegible, ~6 letters] 11, 12, &c.
units.tr: The remaining numbers are supplied as the Hebrews supply them: for example, [illegible] 11, 12, and so on.

units.la: Distinguunt etiam literas ut reliqui Orientales in 5 classes : Gutturales | [illegible, ~6 letters] Labiales | [illegible, ~5 letters] Palatinas | [illegible, ~5 letters] Dentales | [illegible, ~8 letters] Linguales | [illegible, ~8 letters]
units.tr: They also divide the letters into five classes, as the other Orientals do: gutturals [illegible], labials [illegible], palatals [illegible], dentals [illegible], and linguals [illegible].

units.la: Dentales & linguales solares vocantur, Reliquæ lunares.
units.tr: The dentals and linguals are called solar, the rest lunar.

units.la: Difficultas est in pronunciatione ح & ع; illa est profunda aspiratio, hæc cùm difficillimæ fit pronunciationis, sæpè per (a) à noftratibꝰ effertur ; imò plerumque omittitur, & secundum vocalem adjunctam pronunciatur, ut [illegible, ~3 letters] Abda.
units.tr: The difficulty lies in pronouncing ḥa and ʿayin. The former is a deep aspiration; the latter, since it is the most difficult of all to pronounce, is often rendered by (a) by our people, and indeed is mostly left out and pronounced with the vowel attached to it, as in [illegible] Abda.

units.la: Kaf & Kef, eodem feré modo pronuntiantur, sed plerunque ex adjuncta vocali discriminantur, uti etiam [illegible, ~2 letters] & [illegible, ~2 letters], & [illegible, ~2 letters] & [illegible, ~2 letters]. At quatuor hæ [illegible, ~6 letters] ut (d) sine discrimine pronuntiari solent.
units.tr: Kaf and Kef are pronounced in almost the same way, but they are usually distinguished by the vowel attached to them, as also [illegible] and [illegible], and [illegible] and [illegible]. These four, however, [illegible], are customarily pronounced as (d) without any distinction.

units.la: SECT. III. De Vocalibus.
units.tr: SECT. III. Of the Vowels.

units.la: Vocales sunt tres, Fatha (a,) vel (e) بَ ba vel be : Damma (o) vel (u) بُ bo vel bu : Kefra (i) بِ bi.
units.tr: There are three vowels: Fatha (a, or e), written ba or be; Damma (o, or u), written bo or bu; and Kefra (i), written bi.

units.la: Mauri pingunt Fatha & Kefra jacentes hoc modo بُ بِ
units.tr: The Moors draw Fatha and Kefra lying on their side, in this way: bu, bi.

units.la: Valet Fatha secundum Erpenium (a) clarum, vel (a) ad (e) declinans : Damma (o) obscurum, vel (u) clarum ; priorem sonum habent semper supra literas dictionum ultimas, & ut plurimùm supra [illegible, ~12 letters] & ante easdem cùm vocali carent: alibi plerunque posteriorem; quod usus docebit.
units.tr: According to Erpenius, Fatha has the clear sound of a, or a sound inclining from a towards e; Damma has the obscure sound of o, or the clear sound of u. They always take the first sound above the final letters of words, and usually above [illegible] and before the same when they lack a vowel; elsewhere they usually take the second sound. Use will teach this.

units.la: Secundum verò Gabr. Sionitam Fatha pronuntiatur ut (a) ante | quiescens, alias ut (e). Damma ut (u) ante و[?] quiescens, alias ut (o). Et Kefra ut (i) ante Je quiescens, alias ut (e), de hoc verò dubitatur.
units.tr: According to Gabriel Sionita, however, Fatha is pronounced as a before a quiescent alef, and otherwise as e. Damma is pronounced as u before a quiescent waw, and otherwise as o. Kefra is pronounced as i before a quiescent yod, and otherwise as e; but about this there is doubt.

units.la: Accidunt hisce vocalibus Productio; & Nunnatio.
units.tr: Lengthening and nunation affect these vowels.

units.la: Productio est cum sonus producitur, vel duplicatur, quod fit cum aliqua ex literis ي[?] vocali destitutis ideoque quiescentibus, immediatè vocalem sequitur. Fatha producitur ante ا[?] quiescens, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] xāp.[?] Damma ante و[?] quiescens, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] xŭp.[?] Kefra, ante ي[?] quiescens ut [illegible, ~4 letters] xŭp.
units.tr: Lengthening occurs when the sound is prolonged or doubled. This happens when one of the letters that lacks a vowel, and is therefore quiescent, immediately follows the vowel. Fatha is lengthened before a quiescent alef, as [illegible] xāp. Damma is lengthened before a quiescent waw, as [illegible] xŭp. Kefra is lengthened before a quiescent yod, as [illegible] xŭp.

units.la: Sæpe ا[?] quiescens omittitur, & tunc Fatha præcedens est perpendicularis, ut ـ[?] vel hāc notâ (~) quæ Medda dicitur, supra literam usurpatur. Sic etiam Kefra ante ج[?] fit perpendicularis, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] judicium.
units.tr: Often the quiescent alef is omitted, and then the preceding Fatha becomes a straight upright stroke, written with the mark called Medda placed over the letter. In the same way Kefra before jim becomes an upright stroke, as in [illegible] judicium.

units.la: Pro ا[?] quiescente sæpe ponuntur و[?] & ي[?] cum ipsæ vocali carent, & notâ (ɔ) quæ Giesma dicitur, & immediatè eas præcedat Fatha, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] rama [illegible, ~4 letters] salâton.
units.tr: In place of a quiescent alef, waw and yod are often used when they lack their own vowel, marked with the sign called Giesma, and Fatha immediately precedes them, as in [illegible] rama [illegible] salâton.

units.la: Nunnatio est cum in fine dictionis duplicatur figura vocalis, quo fit ut ad proprium sonū addatur fonus [illegible, ~2 letters] Nun ut [illegible, ~6 letters] ban. bon. bin.
units.tr: Nunation occurs when the sign of the vowel is doubled at the end of a word, so that the sound of nun is added to its proper sound, as in [illegible] ban, bon, bin.

units.la: sed nisi Fatha nunnatum sit supra [illegible, ~1 letter] aut ([illegible, ~1 letter]) poftponitur ipsi semper [illegible, ~1 letter] aut [illegible, ~2 letters] quiescens infar [illegible, ~1 letter] fine ullo foni augmento, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] daraban, [illegible, ~3 letters] Hudan.
units.tr: But unless Fatha is nunated above [illegible] or [illegible], it is always followed by a quiescent [illegible] or [illegible] at the end, without any increase of sound, as in [illegible] daraban, [illegible] Hudan.

units.la: Duplex Damma, sæpe sic pingitur ⁊, vel sic [illegible, ~3 letters].
units.tr: A double Damma is often written in one of two ways, shown here as [illegible] or [illegible].

units.la: Dividuntur & literæ in Radicales quæ semper sunt de Radice, quales sunt [illegible, ~6 letters] & ferviles, quæ derivatis formandis, & accidentibus radici inducendis sæpe inserviunt, quales reliquæ.
units.tr: Letters are also divided into radicals, which are always part of the root, such as [illegible], and servile letters, which often serve to form derivatives and to introduce accidents into the root, such as the remaining ones.

units.la: SECT. IV.
units.tr: SECT. IV.

units.la: De Hamza, Wesla, Medda, Gjezma, & Tesdid.
units.tr: On Hamza, Wesla, Medda, Gjezma, and Tesdid.

units.la: HAbent & Arabes alias quasdam notas, quas literis apponunt, scil. Hamza ([illegible, ~1 letter]) Wesla ([illegible, ~1 letter]) Medda ([illegible, ~1 letter]) Gjesma ([illegible, ~1 letter]) & Tesded ([illegible, ~1 letter]).
units.tr: The Arabs also have certain other marks, which they attach to letters: namely Hamza, Wesla, Medda, Gjesma, and Tesded.

units.la: 1. Hamze
units.tr: 1. Hamze

units.la: 1. Hamza (ء) est servus Elif mobilis, cui cum vocali appositum, motum ejus actualem significat, ut أن، أن، أن an, on, in, & sine vocali motum ejus indicat potentialem, sil. quod | sit radicale, & naturâ suâ mobile, ut [?]لمين jamen. Sæpè tamen omittitur ut superfluum, quia motus | ex vocali adjecta facilè percipitur, sicut & posita Hamza, illud | sæpè omittitur, ita ut pro eodem usurpatur, & in pronuntiatione idem valet : idque
units.tr: 1. Hamza is the servant of mobile Elif. When it is joined to a vowel, it marks that vowel's actual motion, as in an, on, in. Without a vowel it indicates potential motion, that is, when it is radical and mobile by its own nature, as in jamen. Yet it is often omitted as superfluous, because the motion is easily perceived from the added vowel. Just as when Hamza is written, it is often left out, so that the one is used for the other and they have the same value in pronunciation, and this

units.la: 1, In sine, cum Hamza habet ante se unam ex literis [illegible, ~3 letters] ut [?]مـاون maon, pro [?]سـاون, [?]سـاون pro [?]سـاون, [?]سـيون shaion, pro [?]سيون.
units.tr: 1. At the end of a word, when Hamza has before it one of the letters [illegible], as in maon for saon, saon for saon, and shaion for syon.

units.la: 2, In medio post literam vocali carentem, ut [?]سـول pro [?]سـول, vel post aliud | ut [?]اَندرا aandera pro [?]اَندر ; cum tamen duplex occurrit | quarum prius movetur, in quibusdam libris utrumque | exprimitur, ut [?]الدر. [?] vel prius per Hamza, & posterius per [?] ut [?]
units.tr: 2. In the middle of a word, after a letter lacking a vowel, as in sul for sul, or after another letter, as in aandera for andar. When, however, a double letter occurs, of which the first is moved, some books express both, as in alder. Or the first is expressed by Hamza and the second by a letter.

units.la: Si vero fit supra literas [?] & [?] notat eas pro | suâ natura mobili poni, ut [?] joumino, pro [?] & [?] izir, pro [?]
units.tr: But if it stands above the letters, it marks that they are placed in their mobile nature, as in joumino for [illegible], and izir for [illegible].

units.la: 2, Wefla (~) est signum unionis inter ultimam literam dictionis praecedentis & primam post | initiale sequentis, ubi | initiale abjectâ vocali suâ otiosum est, & in signum unionis Wefla super | pingitur, ut in [?] Kalbo-Imeliki cor regis.
units.tr: 2. Wefla (~) is the sign of union between the last letter of the preceding word and the first letter of the following word, where the initial letter, having lost its vowel, is superfluous. As a sign of the union, Wefla is written above it, as in Kalbo-Imeliki, the heart of the king.

units.la: Est autem Elif initiale triplex :
units.tr: The initial Elif is of three kinds:

units.la: 1, Verbale; 2, Nominale; 3, Articulare.
units.tr: 1. Verbal; 2. Nominal; 3. Articular.

units.la: 1. Verbale, cùm format imperativum primae conjugationis, ut [?] idrib verbera, vel fit characteristicum in praeteritis imperativis & infinitivis Pentagrammatorum & Hexagrammatorum, ut [?] congregatus est, &c.
units.tr: 1. Verbal, when it forms the imperative of the first conjugation, as in idrib, strike; or when it becomes the characteristic in the preterite imperatives and infinitives of the Pentagrammata and Hexagrammata, as in ... was gathered, etc.

units.la: 3. Articulare est articuli ال ὁ ἡ τὸ [?], quo pertinet relativum الذي [?] alladi, cum casi-bus suis,
units.tr: 3. The article is al, corresponding to the Greek [ὁ ἡ τὸ], and with its cases belongs to it the relative alladi.

units.la: In hisce omnibus initiale privatur vocali sua, nisi sententiam inchoat, aut initio assumit literas servile: quo casu Elif sæpè exci-dit, ut [?] pro [?], & perpetuum est in particula ال quoties Lam servile præfigitur, ut الله lillahi, pro الله Deo.
units.tr: In all these, the initial loses its vowel, unless it begins a sentence or takes servile letters at the beginning. In that case Elif often drops out, as [obscure] for [obscure]. It is constant in the particle al whenever servile Lam is prefixed, as lillahi, for allahi, "to God."

units.la: Si dictio praecedens terminetur consona ea adsumit Kesram, ut [illegible, ~8 letters] darabati Iommo, verberavit mater. Sed terminationes verbales, [illegible, ~3 letters] & [illegible, ~3 letters] itemque affixa [illegible, ~5 letters] & [illegible, ~3 letters] assumunt Damma, ut [illegible, ~6 letters] gazawo ladova, oppugnarunt hostem. Praepositio [illegible, ~4 letters] a & affixa [illegible, ~2 letters], & [illegible, ~2 letters] pri-mae personae singularis Fatham, ut [illegible, ~8 letters] darabania Imuallimo verberavit me praeceptor.
units.tr: If the preceding word ends in a consonant, that consonant takes Kesra, as in darabati Iommo, the mother struck. But verbal endings, [illegible], and likewise the affixed [illegible] and [illegible], take Damma, as in gazawo ladova, they attacked the enemy. The preposition [illegible] and the affixed [illegible] and the [illegible] of the first person singular take Fatha, as in darabania Imuallimo, the teacher struck me.

units.la: Si vocalis nunnata praecedat ante articulum [illegible, ~3 letters] abjicit Nun, ut [illegible, ~9 letters] beito Imukaddafo, domus sanctificata, pro [illegible, ~5 letters] beiton. Alibi vero retinet, & Elif unionis licet vocalem non habeat adscriptam, tamen pronuntiatur cum vocali, ut مَدِينَةٌ medinaton iftetahat.
units.tr: If a nunated vowel precedes the article [illegible], it removes the Nun, as in beito Imukaddafo, the sanctified house, for beiton. Elsewhere, however, it retains it, and although the Elif of union has no vowel written over it, it is pronounced with a vowel, as in medinaton iftetahat.

units.la: Literæ quiescentes [?]اوي unioni non obstant, ut [?]نَصَرُوا الْمَلِكَ nafarou Imelika opem tulerunt regi.
units.tr: Quiescent letters, [illegible], do not hinder the union, as in nafarou Imelika, they brought aid to the king.

units.la: 3, Medda sic pingitur (~) & apponitur super Elif quiescens autem (ś) idque producit, ut [?]سَامَعُون famâon: usurpatur etiam supra notas Arithmeticas, & dictionum compendia, ut apud Hebræos (\ ). Elif tamen quiescens sæpè omittitur brevitatis causâ, ut [?]أُولَئِكَ pro [?]أُولَاكَ illi.
units.tr: 3. Medda is written thus (~) and placed over a quiescent Elif, and it lengthens the sound, as in famâon. It is also used above arithmetical signs and abbreviations of words, as among the Hebrews (\ ). Yet a quiescent Elif is often omitted for brevity's sake, as in ulâika for ulâka, those.

units.la: Elif etiam quiescens post Elif cum Fatha, excidit, & hoc casu ut sciatur Fatha esse longum, apponitur Medda, ut [?]آمِنُونَ ipso Fatha sæpè omisso, ita ut Medda pro ipso, & Elif subintellecto, adeóque pro (a) longo veniat: aliquando tamen ponitur Fatha perpendicularis, ut [?]آمِنُ, vel [?]آمِنُ.
units.tr: A quiescent Elif after an Elif with Fatha also falls out. In this case, so that it may be known that the Fatha is long, Medda is placed, the Fatha itself often being omitted, so that Medda takes its place and the Elif is understood, and so it stands for a long (a). Sometimes, however, an upright Fatha is written, as in amin, or amin.

units.la: 4. Gjezma, vel Gjezmon indicat literam cui superponitur cum praecedente vocali debere copulari, & sic mixtā syllabam constituere, ut Scheva quiescens apud Hebraeos : pingitur
units.tr: 4. Gjezma, or Gjezmon, indicates a letter over which it is placed, which must be joined to the preceding vowel and so form a mixed syllable, like the quiescent Sheva among the Hebrews. It is written

units.la: [illegible, ~3 signs] verò sic (o) vel (o) vel sic (o) ut [illegible, ~4 letters] darbo.
units.tr: [illegible] thus (o), or (o), or thus (o), as in darbo.

units.la: Literis omnibus appingitur nisi | quiescenti in fine post [illegible, ~1 letter]. Quiescentibus verò [illegible, ~3 letters] licet à multis apponitur, haud rectè tamen nisi radicales sint, & naturâ suâ mobiles, ut [illegible, ~3 letters] joulado, nascetur, [illegible, ~3 letters] jameno credet, &c.
units.tr: It is placed over all letters, except a quiescent letter at the end after [illegible]. Over quiescent letters [illegible] it is often placed by many, but not correctly, unless they are radical and mobile by nature, as in joulado, he will be born, and jameno, he will believe, etc.

units.la: 5. Tefdid, omnibus literis, excepto | superscribitur, eásque duplicat, ad modum daghes fortis apud Hebraeos : pingitur sic (w): Mauris verò seu Occidentalibus infra literam sic (ᴧ), supra verò sic (v) & subinde sic (ᴧ); vsurpatur euphoniae gratiâ, aliquando post literam vocali carentem, quae litera tunc non pronuntiatur, sed ejus vicem supplet litera sequens, per Tefdid geminata, ut [illegible, ~3 letters] walatta, non waladta.
units.tr: 5. Tefdid is written over all letters, except [illegible], and doubles them, after the manner of the Hebrew dagesh forte. It is written thus (w). The Moors, or Westerners, write it below the letter thus (ᴧ), and above it thus (v), and at times thus (ᴧ). It is used for the sake of euphony, sometimes after a letter lacking a vowel. That letter is then not pronounced, but the following letter, doubled by Tefdid, takes its place, as in walatta, not waladta.

units.la: Estque Tefdid hoc euphonicum triplex: Deltale, Lamdale, vel Initiale.
units.tr: This euphonic Tefdid is of three kinds: Deltale, Lamdale, or Initial.

units.la: Deltale adscribitur literæ ت post ذ, ut وَجَدْتُ wajatto inveni.
units.tr: A deltale is added to the letter ta after dhal, as wajatto, "I found."

units.la: Lamdale, post ل articuli اَلْ, ut اَلرَّبِّ arrabbo Dominus, اَللّٰه allaho ὁ Θεὸς.
units.tr: A lamdale, after the lam of the article al, as arrabbo, "the Lord," and allaho [ὁ Θεὸς], "God."

units.la: Lam vero articularis sæpè omittitur, cùm solaris eum sequitur ٱلَّيْلُ ut ٱللَّيْلُ allailo, pro ٱللَّيْلِ: & hoc perpetuum est in relati-vis, ٱلَّذِي ٱلَّتِي & ٱلدِّينِ, & cùm ar-ticulo præfigitur ل datívi casûs nota, ne tria Lam concurrant, ut لِلَّهِ Deo, pro لِلَّهِ[?].
units.tr: The articular Lam is often omitted when a solar letter follows it, as in allailo for alylo... and this is constant in the relatives "alladhi" and "allati" and in "addin". When the dative case sign Lam is prefixed to the article, so that three Lams do not meet, it is written as li-llahi, to God, for lillahi.

units.la: - Initiale est quod apponitur literis لَوْمِين[?] dictionem inchoantibus post Nun gjesmatum[?], vel expressum, ut مِن رَبِّ[?] mirrabbi-hi à domino suo, vel latens in vocali nunna-ta, ta, ut [illegible, ~6 letters] baitom mukaddafon.
units.tr: The initial is that which is placed on the letters beginning a word after Nun gjesmatum, either expressed, as in mirrabbihi, from his lord, or hidden in a nunated vowel, as in baitom mukaddafon [illegible].

units.la: SECT. V.
units.tr: SECT. V.

units.la: De Accentibus.
units.tr: On the Accents.

units.la: Accentus nulla est nota apud Arabes; Regula tamen generalis est, quód Dissyllaba attollunt penultimam, ut [illegible, ~5 letters] ónfur: Polysyllaba antepenultimam, ut [illegible, ~5 letters] jánfuro, nisi penultima producatur per [illegible, ~3 letters] quiescentia, ut supra; tunc enim illa habet accentum, ut ilåhon, &c.
units.tr: The Arabs have no accent mark. Yet the general rule is that disyllables raise the penultimate, as [illegible] ónfur, and polysyllables the antepenultimate, as [illegible] jánfuro, unless the penultimate is lengthened by a quiescent [illegible] letter, as above. In that case the penultimate takes the accent, as ilåhon, etc.

units.la: Distinctionum notæ communiores sunt,
units.tr: The more common marks of distinction are

units.la: SECT. VI.
units.tr: SECTION VI.

units.la: De radicalibus & servilibus literis.
units.tr: On radical and servile letters.

units.la: Radix est tertia praeteriti persona singularis masculina, quæ literis nunquam constat paucioribus quàm tribus, ut [illegible, ~5 letters] juzit,
units.tr: The root is the third person singular masculine of the past tense. It never consists of fewer than three letters, as [illegible, ~5 letters] juzit,

units.la: [illegible, ~6 letters] extendet, nec pluribus quàm quatuor; ut [illegible, ~4 letters] volvit.
units.tr: [illegible] extends, nor to more than four; as [illegible] volvit.

units.la: Literæ quæ radicem constituunt, vocantur Radicales : quæ verò ad formationem nominum & verborum accedunt, septem scil. hâc voce inclusæ [illegible, ~7 letters] pinguefient ; vel ad consignificationem, quatuor scil. in hac voce expressæ, [illegible, ~5 letters] in navi, appellantur serviles.
units.tr: The letters that constitute the root are called radicals. Those that are added to the formation of nouns and verbs, namely the seven included in this word pinguefient, or to the consignification, namely the four expressed in this word in navi, [illegible, ~5 letters], are called servile.

units.la: SECT. VII.
units.tr: SECT. VII.

units.la: De Grammaticis & Lexicis Arabicis.
units.tr: On Arabic Grammars and Lexicons.

units.la: Qui Arabicæ linguæ cognitionem desidèrat, legat inter alios, (ut Gabrielis Sionitæ & Johannis Efronitæ) maximè Erpenii Rudimenta Arabica, qui omnium accuratissimè Grammaticæ præcepta tradidit : postea verò ipsius Grammaticam Arabicam conferat, ex cujus collatione quædam plenius quàm in Rudimentis explicata inveniet.
units.tr: Whoever desires a knowledge of the Arabic language should read, among others (such as Gabriel Sionita and John Hesronita), above all Erpenius's Arabic Rudiments, who set out the precepts of grammar most accurately of all. Afterwards he should compare Erpenius's Arabic Grammar itself, from which comparison he will find some points explained more fully than in the Rudiments.

units.la: Inter Lexica verò, Schindleri Lexicon Pentaglotton, scil. Hebraicum;Chaldaicum, Syriacum, Arabicum & Rabbinicum, ut maximè utile linguarum Orientalium studiosis commendatur. Scripserunt etiam Lexica, Germanus Arabico-Latino-Italicum in folio, quod valdè mancum, Raphalengius Arabico-Latinum, in quo plurima desiderantur, Giggæus Thesaurü linguæ Arabicæ in 4. Vol. in sol. in quo licet magna sit verborum & phrasium copia, tamen præter magnum prætium, haud ita discentium usui accommodatus est. Lexicon autem Arabicum omnium absolutissimum nuper edidit Doctiss. Golius in sol. ejusque epitomen brevi se editurum promittit: fundamenta etiā Lexici ab ipso Erpenio dudum jacta erat, quod si ipsi Deus vitā produxisset, longè ante hac perfecisset & in lucem emisisset, prout ex Consilio ejus de studio Arabico fœliciter instituendo, quod hic subjungitur, patet.
units.tr: Among the lexicons, Schindler's Pentaglot Lexicon, that is, Hebrew, Chaldee, Syriac, Arabic and Rabbinic, is especially commended to students of the Oriental languages as very useful. Others have also written lexicons: Germanus, an Arabic-Latin-Italian lexicon in folio, which is very defective; Raphelengius, an Arabic-Latin lexicon, in which very many things are lacking; and Giggeius, a Thesaurus of the Arabic language in four volumes in folio, which, although it has a great abundance of words and phrases, is apart from its high price not very well suited to the use of learners. But the most complete Arabic lexicon of all was lately published by the very learned Golius in folio, and he promises to bring out an epitome of it shortly. The foundations of the lexicon were also laid long ago by Erpenius himself; had God granted him life, he would have completed and published it long before now, as is clear from his plan for the successful pursuit of Arabic study, which is appended here.

units.la: SECT. VIII.
units.tr: SECT. VIII.

units.la: Consilium Erpenii, de studio Arab. felici- ter instituendo.
units.tr: Erpenius's counsel on how to begin the study of Arabic happily.

units.la: QUum in eo totus sim, ut nobilissima literarum Arabicarum studia, hactenus apud Christianos fere neglecta, pro virilimea promoveam: & in eum finem haud exiguis impensis, elegantem excitaverim Typographiam, librosque nonnullos jam ediderim, pluresque et nobiliores ad editionem indies exornem; non possum non eorum quoque desiderio satisfacere, qui quomodo fœliciter studio hæc instituì possint, atque debeant, discere ex me gestiunt.
units.tr: Since I have devoted myself entirely to promoting, to the best of my strength, the most noble study of Arabic literature, which among Christians has until now been almost neglected, and since to that end I have at no small expense set up a handsome printing press and already published some books, with more and nobler ones being prepared for the press day by day, I cannot fail to satisfy the wishes of those who are eager to learn from me how this study may and should be begun successfully.

units.la: Habeant ergo, nobilis hujus Linguae studiofi, consilium bonum, atque sincerum quale ipse ego mihi cuperem dari; & certi sint, id fi fequantur, fore, ut paucis admodum mensibus majores in ejus cognitione progressus faciant, quam plerique hactenus pluribus etiam annis fieri posse sunt arbitrati.
units.tr: Let the students of this noble language therefore take a good and sincere counsel, such as I myself would have wished to be given to me. And let them be assured that if they follow it, they will make greater progress in knowing the language within a very few months than most people have hitherto thought possible even in several years.

units.la: In manus itaque primum fumantur haec quae nunc damus Rudimenta; quorum primus liber diligenter & attente legatur, & discatur: Eo cognito, progrediendum est ad fecundum de verbis: nam quod ad appendicem primi libri attinet, ea non tota uno tempore discenda est. Continet ea 24 nobilissimos Canones, ad folidam Arabifmi intelligentiam ita necessarios, ut frustra omnino fit futur⁹, qui fine eorum cognitione feliciter volet Arabicari. Sunt autem illi Canones singuli per fe facillimi, & nullo negotio intelliguntur, ac memoriae mandantur; multitudo tamen eorum ob materiae affinitatem confusionem aliquam facile inducit. Ea propter, confultum ego judico, ut singulis Canonibus singuli dentur dies & unus tantum quotidie accurate perpendatur, & firmiter memoriae imprimatur Canon, aut summum duo. Id qui fecerit, nec confusionem aliquam fentiet, & paucissimis diebus plus in solida Arabifmi notitia proficiet quam ego pluribus mensibus feci. Dum sic paulatim pergitur in aurea illa, & nunquā satis æstimanda appendice, possunt & conjugationes verborum perfectorum memoriæ mandari: ac primo quidem tabella illa tredecim Conjugationum, quam exhibet lib. 2. cap. 1. diligenter discenda est, eaque cognitā, verba quædam alia trilitera, ut [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] & alia quælibet per eam diduci debent, ut oblatæ cujusque radicis conjugationem quamlibet nullo negotio formare discas. Hinc progrediendū ad Paradigma primæ conjugationis Activæ, quod benè memoriæ est imprimendum, cum ab eo reliqui omnia dependeant: mox præcepta ei adjuncta legenda quoque & discenda sunt:
units.tr: Let these Rudiments, which we now offer, be taken into hand first. Let the first book be read and learned diligently and attentively. Once that is known, one should go on to the second, on verbs. As for the appendix to the first book, however, it should not all be learned at one time. It contains 24 most noble Canons, so necessary for a solid understanding of Arabic that anyone who wishes to become proficient in Arabic without knowing them will labour entirely in vain. These Canons are each very easy in themselves and are understood and committed to memory without any trouble, but their number, on account of the affinity of the subject matter, can easily produce some confusion. For this reason I judge it advisable that each Canon be given its own day, and that only one be carefully weighed each day and firmly fixed in memory, or at most two. Whoever does this will feel no confusion and will advance in solid knowledge of Arabic in a few days more than I did in several months. While one proceeds thus gradually through that golden appendix, which can never be valued highly enough, the conjugations of the regular verbs can also be committed to memory. First, the table of the thirteen conjugations, which the second book, chapter 1, sets out, must be learned diligently; once that is known, certain other triliteral verbs [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] and any others should be inflected by it, so that you may learn to form the conjugation of any root put before you without any trouble. Then one must go on to the paradigm of the first active conjugation, which must be firmly fixed in memory, since all the rest depend on it. Soon the precepts attached to it must also be read and learned.

units.la: Deinde differentiæ conjugationum derivativarum à primâ, sequentibus duobus capitibus traditæ, memoriæ quoque infigi debent, & radices plures per primas tantum temporum voces in prima conjugatione, & reliquis diducendæ sunt; nec ante pergendum ad verba imperfecta quàm perfectorum conjugationes omnes tum primitivæ tum derivativæ benè persectæ & cognitæ sint. Hinc ad imperfecta fiat progressus, et singulis speciebus singuli dentur dies, confusionis evitandæ gratiâ, beneque considerentur, & memoriæ mandentur generales imperfectionis rationes, quæ sub initium singulorum capitum proponuntur: iis enim intellectis & cognita verbi Perfecti conjugatione, facile erit formare Imperfectum: nam ut minori hoc molestia facias, omnino confultum est, ut quamlibet vocem verbi imperfecti ita formes, ac fi verbum perfectum fit. Ita formata cum erit, facile videbis an contra generales illas imperfectionis regulas, aut speciales peccet. Videbunt in hisce verbis studiosi quanti momenti sint aurei illi appendicis primi libri Canones, quos ut hic sæpe consulant & applicent rogatos eos volo. Verbis cognitis, pergatur ad Nomina; & ab his ad reliqua: de quibus nihil peculiare habeo quod moneam; est enim tractatus eorum facilis. Rudimentis hisce totis lectis & intellectis, exerceat fe studiosus in praxi Grammatica iis annexa, locaque citata diligenter inquirat, ut omnia melius memoriæ inhæreant.
units.tr: Next, the differences of the derived conjugations from the first, set out in the following two chapters, should likewise be fixed in the memory, and several roots should be inflected through the first tense forms only, in the first conjugation and the others. One should not proceed to imperfect verbs until all the conjugations of the perfect verbs, both primitive and derived, are well mastered and known. Then progress should be made to the imperfect verbs, giving each species its own days, to avoid confusion; the general rules of imperfection, which are set out at the beginning of each chapter, should be carefully considered and committed to memory. For once these are understood, and the conjugation of the perfect verb is known, it will be easy to form the imperfect. And so that you may do this with less trouble, it is wholly advisable that you form any imperfect verb as if it were a perfect one. Once it has been so formed, you will readily see whether it offends against those general rules of imperfection or against the special ones. Students will see in these verbs how great is the importance of those golden Canons of the appendix to the first book, which I ask them to consult and apply here often. When the verbs are known, let them proceed to the nouns, and from these to the rest. I have nothing peculiar to advise about these, since their treatment is easy. When these Rudiments have been read and understood in full, let the student exercise himself in the grammatical practice attached to them, and diligently look up the cited passages, so that everything may cling better to the memory.

units.la: Praxi illā absolutā, in manus sumat Historiam Josephi, ex Alchorano à me cum duplici versione Latina & notis editam: singulas voces ad normam Grammatices diligenter examinet, ut ego feci in ista praxi; notasque ad difficiliores voces consulat, & semel atque iterum egregii illius opusculi lectionem repetat; certus id maximo fine fructu facturum se non esse: nam & res Grammaticæ, & communiores quæque voces fœlicius memoriæ imprimentur. Deinde velim totum Alcoranum à capite ad calcem studiosè & attente perlegi, solius linguae gratiâ, quae in eo libro elegans est, & perfectissimè consonantibus ac vocalibus, aliisque notis orthographicis expressa. Sed quia exemplaria ejus manu exarata haberi vix possunt, multisque in locis eam difficultatem habet, ut sine interprete intelligi non queat, operam ego dabo, ut brevi elegantissimis typis prodeat, cum versione accurata Latina, notisque ad voces & sententias difficiliores; & ubi necesse id erit, solidâ mendaciorum & nugarum ejus confutatione atque explosione. Interim poterunt studiosi ejus loco se exercere in libello illo proverbiorum Arabicorum qui cum versione latina, & notis Josephi Scaligeri ac meis prodiit ex officina Raphelengiana: item in Psalterio Savariano Romae edito, in quibus libris vocales quoque satis accuratè adjectæ sunt. Si autem fuliorem [?] Doctrinam Grammaticam requirant, legant Thesaurum nostrum Grammaticum brevi edendum: quem utique talem speramus fore, ut forte nihil in eo sint desideraturi. Adjungant & Gjarumiam [?] noftram, libellum elegantissimum ac lectu dignissimum.
units.tr: When that practice is complete, let him take in hand the History of Joseph, which I have published from the Alcoran, with a double Latin version and notes. Let him examine each word diligently according to the rules of grammar, as I did in that practice, and let him consult the notes on the more difficult words, and read again and again that excellent little work, being certain that he will not do so to no great profit, for both the grammatical matters and the more common words will be impressed on the memory more successfully. Then I would like the whole Alcoran to be read through carefully and attentively from beginning to end, for the sake of the language alone, which is elegant in that book and expressed most perfectly with consonants, vowels and other orthographic signs. But since manuscript copies of it can hardly be had, and in many places it is so difficult that it cannot be understood without an interpreter, I shall take care that it appears shortly in very elegant type, with an accurate Latin version and notes on the more difficult words and passages, and where necessary with a solid refutation and exposure of its lies and trifles. Meanwhile, students may exercise themselves in its place with that little book of Arabic proverbs, which came out with a Latin version and the notes of Joseph Scaliger and of myself from the Raphelengian press, and also with the Savary Psalter published at Rome, in which books the vowels too are added quite accurately. If they require a fuller grammatical teaching, let them read our Grammatical Treasury, to be published shortly, which we hope will be such that they will perhaps find nothing lacking in it. Let them also add our Gjarumia [?], a most elegant little book and well worth reading.

units.la: Cognitâ benè re Grammaticâ; & lectis hisce libris qui vocalium figuras appositas habent; tuto se accingent ad lectionem eorum, qui iis destituuntur. Neque est quod infœlicem hîc metuant successum : non enim ea res difficultatem tunc ullam habebit.
units.tr: When the grammar is well mastered, and when they have read those books which have the vowel signs added, they may confidently set themselves to reading those which lack them. Nor need they fear an unhappy outcome here, for the task will then present no difficulty at all.

units.la: Duo autem omnino sunt præter Alcoranum, de quo jam diximus, libri, quos Arabismi studiosis maximopere hîc commendatos volo ; quippe ex quibus (aut ego vehementer fallor) brevi haurire poterunt ejus linguæ notitiam, & talem quæ ad communes quosque auctores intelligendos, abundè fit suffectura. Nam ut libri Medici, Mathematici, similefq; intelligantur, terminos eorum hîc, ut in omni alia lingua, necesse est discere. Sunt autem illi libri, Geographia illa anonyma, quæ Romæ é Typographia Medicæa in quarto prodiit: & Historia Saracenica, quæ ex mea nunc prodit Typographia. Prior longè elegantissimo stylo liber est, & cujus elaboratissimâ versionem Latinam tantopere hactenus à viris doctis expetitam, nunc dant viri undequaque doctissimi, & rerum Arabicarum peritissimi, Gabriel Sionita, & Johannes Hefronita, Maronitæ, & harum literarum insignes promotores in celeberrima Parisiorum Academia: quæ versio viam omnino sternet ad facilem præstantissimi libri lectionem, & intelligentiam. Posterior liber haud minoris est dignitatis tantaque elegantiâ, & rerum ac verborum varietate; ut nescisam quid in eo possit ulterius desiderari. Prodiit ea cum versione Latina, & notis meis in folio, & Arabicè tantùm in octavo, ac Latinè tantùm in quarto. Hisce auctoribus, ij qui rem medicā tractant, adjungant Avicennam, qui stylo scripsit ita eleganti, ut palmam hac in parte reliquis feré scriptoribus dicatur præripuisse. Sed de Dictinario nihil adhuc dixi. Extat Francisci Raphelengii Lexicon Arabicū : verū in quo meritò majorem vocū copiā, & vocalium appositionem desiderant studiosi ; itaque adjungi ei poterit Valentini Schindleri Lexicon Pentaglotton (quod merito suo omnibus Linguarum Orientalium studiosis sit commendatiffimum) tantisper dum meum quoque prodeat Lexicon, in quo nec vocum copia, aut accurata explicatio, nec vocales desiderabuntur. Faxit Linguarum Auctor, ut vita mihi & valetudo suppetant, ad ea quæ in manibus habeo, feliciter absolvenda. Scripsi hæc Ifelmundæ, die 22 Martii 1620, cùm iter Gallicum ingressus essem.
units.tr: Apart from the Alcoran, of which we have already spoken, there are altogether two books which I want to be strongly commended here to students of Arabic. From them (unless I am greatly mistaken) they will be able to draw in a short time a knowledge of that language sufficient for understanding the common authors. For, in order to understand medical and mathematical books and the like, it is necessary, here as in any other language, to learn their terminology. These books are that anonymous Geography, which came out in quarto at Rome from the Medici press, and the Saracen History, which is now coming out from my own press. The former is a book of a very elegant style, and its most elaborate Latin version, so long eagerly sought by learned men, is now provided by Gabriel Sionita and John Hesronita, Maronites, most learned men on every side and most expert in Arabic matters, and distinguished promoters of these letters in the famous Academy of Paris. That version will certainly pave the way to easy reading and understanding of this most excellent book. The latter book is of no less distinction and of such elegance and variety of matter and words that I do not know what could be further desired in it. It was published with a Latin version and my notes in folio, in Arabic only in octavo, and in Latin only in quarto. To these authors, let those who deal with medicine add Avicenna, who wrote in a style so elegant that he is said to have snatched the palm in this respect from almost all other writers. But I have not yet said anything about a dictionary. There exists the Arabic Lexicon of Francis Raphelengius, but in it students rightly miss a greater abundance of words and the addition of vowels; so Valentin Schindler's Pentaglot Lexicon may be added to it (which by its own merit is most highly commended to all students of the Oriental languages), until my own Lexicon also appears, in which neither abundance of words, nor accurate explanation, nor vowels will be missed. May the Author of Languages grant that life and health hold out for me to bring to a successful conclusion what I have in hand. I wrote this at Ifelmunda, on 22 March 1620, when I was about to set out on the French journey.
