units.tr: Section XI.

units.la: Exercitatio lectionis Arabicæ, ex Cap. sive Surata 58 Alchorani.
units.tr: Exercise in reading Arabic, from Chapter or Surah 58 of the Alcoran.

units.la: fi ma jaalamo llaha ana tara Alam ألم تر أن الله يعلم ما في in quod novit De quod attenditis Annon ma lardi[?] fi wama affamawati ما الأرض في وما السماوات enim non ? terra in quod & cælis illa thalathati nagfwa min jakuno إلا ثلاثة نجوى من يكون nisi tres conventu in sunt rabiohom howa رابعهم هو quartus fit ille
units.tr: Do you not see that God knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth? No secret conversation takes place among three but that He is their fourth. [alam tara anna llaha yaʿlamu ma fi s-samawati wa ma fi l-ardi; ma yakunu min najwatin thalathatin illa huwa rabiʿuhum]

units.tr: The consonants, as they are called, are the same for the Persians as for the Arabs, with the same shapes and order and, in most cases, the same values. The Persians, however, add four letters to the Arabic alphabet, as the table below makes clear. Name. | Form. | Value. At end | In middle | At beginning. 1 Elif | | | | soft breathing (spiritus lenis). 2 Be | | | | B. 3 Pe | | | | P. 4 Te | | | | T. 5 Se | | | | S. 6 Gjim | | | | G. 7 Che

units.la: SECT. II. De literarum pronuntiatione, &c.
units.tr: SECT. II. On the pronunciation of letters, etc.

units.la: Literæ [illegible, ~8 letters] in dictionibus verè Persicis raro inveniuntur, adeò ut ubi usurpantur, dictiones Arabicæ ferè omnes habendæ sunt, ut monet Lud. de Dieu.
units.tr: The letters [illegible] are rarely found in words that are truly Persian, so that wherever they are used, almost all the words should be regarded as Arabic, as Lud. de Dieu observes.

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] facilè Persis cōfunduntur, ut & [illegible, ~2 letters] & [illegible, ~2 letters]. In Libris MSS. magnam difficultatem parit tum punctorum Diacriticorum tum vocalium absentia, quum multæ dictiones punctis solùm & vocalibus distinguuntur.
units.tr: [illegible] are easily confused by the Persians, as are [illegible] and [illegible]. In manuscript books, the absence of both the diacritical points and the vowels causes great difficulty, since many words are distinguished only by their points and vowels.

units.la: Primà dictionis vocalis, sequente immediate vocali alterâ, vix pronuntiatur, & idem ferè valet quod fcheva mobile apud Hebræ. ut [illegible, ~5 letters] criften flere.
units.tr: The first vowel of a word, when another vowel immediately follows, is hardly pronounced, and this is almost the same as the mobile shewa among the Hebrews; e.g. criften flere (to weep).

units.la: In [illegible, ~2 letters] & [illegible, ~1 letter] sæpe duo ex tribus punctis omittuntur, præcipuè si [illegible, ~1 letter] immediatè sequatur, & tunc 5 puncta in tria coalescunt, ut fe-
units.tr: In [illegible] and [illegible] two of the three points are often omitted, especially if [illegible] immediately follows, and then the five points coalesce into three, as in fe-

units.la: ut [illegible, ~3 letters] pîr senex : aliquando verò sepa-rantur.
units.tr: as in [illegible] pîr old man; but sometimes they are separated.

units.la: Aliquando etiam duo illa puncta in unam curvam lineam extenduntur, quod & in [illegible, ~1 letter] & reliquis punctatis sæpè accidit: [illegible, ~1 letter] & [illegible, ~1 letter] sæpè in curvam lineam exten-duntur, & tria puncta in [illegible, ~1 letter] sæpè in lineo-lam etiam convertuntur.
units.tr: Sometimes also those two points are extended into one curved line, which often happens also in [illegible] and the other pointed letters: [illegible] and [illegible] are often extended into a curved line, and three points in [illegible] are often also converted into a little line.

units.la: Magna est discrepantia in pronuntiatione literarum [illegible, ~8 letters] inter Europæos & Orientales ; ex Tabella tamen vera pronuntiatio aliquatenus intelli-gi potest.
units.tr: There is great discrepancy in the pronunciation of the letters [illegible] between Europeans and Orientals; nevertheless, from the table the true pronunciation can be understood to some extent.

units.la: Literæ [illegible, ~4 letters] à Persis vulgò efferuntur, ut z apud nos : Ideoque in Pentateucho Persico Constantinopoli à Judæis edito, eas omnes per ץ[?] Hebræum exprimit Tawafius : at [illegible, ~1 letter] paulò fortius quasi zh, vel tz pronuntiatur.
units.tr: The letters [illegible] are commonly pronounced by the Persians as z is among us. Therefore, in the Persian Pentateuch printed at Constantinople by the Jews, Tawafius expresses all of them by the Hebrew letter tsade [ץ]; but [illegible] is pronounced a little more strongly, as zh or tz.

units.la: [illegible, ~1 letter] Ghaf Persicum (nam sine punctis [illegible, ~1 letter], Kaf Arabicum dicitur) à Turcis pronuntiatur ut (ng)vel ut vulgò [illegible, ~1 letter]; à Persis verò ut [illegible, ~1 letter], ut [illegible, ~2 letters] Gul rosa. Ideoque in in dicto Pentat. Persico, sæpius per [illegible, ~1 letter] effertur; quo etiam [illegible, ~1 letter] efferri solet.
units.tr: The Persian Ghaf (for without points it is called the Arabic Kaf) is pronounced by the Turks as ng, or as is commonly [illegible]; but by the Persians as [illegible], as in [illegible] Gul, a rose. Therefore in the said Persian Pentateuch it is more often expressed by [illegible]; by which also [illegible] is usually expressed.

units.la: Ordo literarum idem est Persis & Arabibus, & numerus etiam; exceptis quatuor [illegible, ~4 letters] quas Arabes non habent.
units.tr: The order of the letters is the same for Persians and Arabs, and the number too, except for four [illegible], which the Arabs do not have.

units.la: Olim Hebræorum ordo observabatur, reiectis ad finem literis asperioris soni, quod ex Epistolis Avicennæ Astrologicis, tum ex ipsius Canone medicinæ Romæ edito, lib.2, sen.2. ubi simplicia medicamenta secundum Hebræorum ordinem in Classes suas digeruntur; tum ex Euclidis propositionibus Arabicè editis, & ex tabulis omnibus, tum Persarum tum Arabum, Astronomicis, probat Doctissimus Joh. Gravius in Gram. Pers.p.9.10. Probabile autem est ad scripturæ venustatem, & ad sublevandam legendi & scribendi molestiam, ab iis qui pueros instituerunt, vel ab Alcorani scribis, consuetudinem hodiernam introductam fuisse.
units.tr: Formerly the Hebrew order was observed, with the letters of harsher sound put at the end. This the most learned Joh. Gravius proves in his Persian Grammar, pp. 9–10, from the astrological Epistles of Avicenna, and from his Canon of Medicine published at Rome, book 2, section 2, where simple medicines are arranged in their classes according to the Hebrew order; also from the Arabic edition of Euclid's propositions and from all the astronomical tables, both Persian and Arab. It is probable, however, that the present custom was introduced by those who taught boys, or by the scribes of the Koran, for the beauty of the script and to ease the labour of reading and writing.

units.la: SECT. III. De vocalibus aliisque notis.
units.tr: SECT. III. Of the vowels and other signs.

units.la: Vocales habent tres, eafdem scil. quas Arabes. Fatha [Arabic fatha sign] a vel e. Damma [Arabic damma sign] o vel u. Kefra [Arabic kesra sign] i, Sæpè e brevisimum.
units.tr: There are three vowels, the same ones that the Arabs use: fatha, which is a or e; damma, which is o or u; and kesra, which is i. Often it is a very short e.

units.la: Tres consonæ quiescentes, scil. [Arabic ا و ي letters] naturam vocalium præcedentium induunt, & in unam longam coalescunt, scil. [Arabic alif] cum Fatha, [Arabic] cum Damma, & [Arabic] cum Kefra, ut suprà diximus in Arabicis, quò lectorem remittimus. Hoc tamen addendum quod Fatha cum [Arabic alif], sequente [Arabic] vel [Arabic waw], tanquam o obscurum effertur, ut [Arabic word: adamion] adamion Homines; Idemque valet interdum cùm [Arabic alif] initio dictionis habet hanc notam (~), quæ Medda dicitur,
units.tr: The three quiescent consonants, namely alif, waw and ya, take on the nature of the vowel before them and coalesce into one long vowel: alif with fatha, waw with damma, and ya with kesra, as we said above in the section on Arabic, to which we refer the reader. This should be added, however: fatha combined with alif, when followed by waw, is pronounced like an obscure o, as in adamion, "men." The same holds at times when alif begins a word and carries this sign (~), which is called medda,

units.la: Fatha subintellecto, ut [illegible, ~6 letters] ofmon Cœlum, quod ex usu petendum.
units.tr: with fatha understood, as in [...] ofmon, "heaven," which must be learned from usage.

units.la: Hoc etiam observat dictus Gravius, Persas in scribendo literas istas quiescentes & [illegible, ~1 letter] in vocis incremento, vel omittere, vel inter se commutare; unde eadem dictio in eodem libro diversimodè scribitur: Et quod inter loquendum addunt Persæ vocales quasdam Euphoniæ causâ, quas non raro in scribendo omittunt, ut in Madere man Mater mea, quod sic scribitur [illegible, ~8 letters]
units.tr: Gravius also observes that the Persians, in writing, either omit these quiescent letters or interchange them when lengthening a word, so that the same word is written in different ways within the same book. He notes too that the Persians add certain vowels in speaking for the sake of euphony, which they often leave out in writing. For example, Madere man, "my mother," is written thus [...]

units.la: Mader man.
units.tr: Mader man.

units.la: Notas etiam quas usurpant Arabes inter legendum, scil. Gjefma Tefdid Hamza & Medda, habent etiam Persæ,eundemq; feré usum obtinent. Elifunionis non agnoscunt Persæ, unde Weslon non habent.
units.tr: The Persians also have the signs the Arabs use in reading, namely gjefma, tefdid, hamza and medda, and they keep nearly the same use of them. The Persians do not recognize elision, so they have no weslon.

units.la: Medda & Gjefmon frequentioris usus sunt apud Persas. Medda in principio quarundam dictionum super Elif adscribitur, illudque producit: licet enim apud Arabes Medda apponitur tantum supra [illegible, ~3 letters] quiescens ante (ꞩ), idque producit, ut [illegible, ~5 letters] Samaon Cœlum; apud Persas tamen frequenter ponitur super [illegible, ~1 letter] in principio dictionis loco vocalis quæ non apponitur, & idem valet quod Camets Hebr. sive duplex Fatha; ut è contrà quæ ab [illegible, ~1 letter] incipiunt & carent Meddâ, efferuntur per patach, seu a breve.
units.tr: Medda and gjefmon are in more frequent use among the Persians. Medda is written over alif at the beginning of certain words, and it lengthens the sound. Among the Arabs, medda is placed only over a quiescent alif after a [...], and it lengthens it, as in [...] samaon, "heaven." Among the Persians, however, it is often placed over [...] at the beginning of a word in place of a vowel that is not written, and it has the same value as the Hebrew camets, or a double fatha. Conversely, words that begin with [...] and lack medda are pronounced with patach, that is, a short a.

units.la: In medio etiā dictionis apponitur, ad indicandum elisionem ʼ quiescentis, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] pro [illegible, ~3 letters]. Gjesmon eodem modo adhibetur ut apud Arabes, nisi quòd cùm duæ concurrant consonæ vocalibus destitutæ, Gjesma alterutri indifferenter apponitur, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] gjenc bellum, [illegible, ~4 letters] dest manus. Hamza autem aliter se habet quam apud Arabes; hic enim ʼ mobili non inservit, sed in fine vocum usurpatur, præcipuè earum quæ terminantur in ḍ, & ferè valet [illegible, ~2 letters]. Reliquæ notæ à Persis plerunque omittuntur.
units.tr: It is also placed in the middle of a word to mark the elision of a quiescent letter, as [...] for [...]. Gjesmon is used in the same way as among the Arabs, except that when two consonants without vowels meet, the gjesma is placed indifferently on either of them, as in [...] gjenc, "war," and [...] dest, "hand." Hamza, however, is used differently from the Arabs. Here it is not used for a mobile consonant, but at the end of words, especially those ending in ḍ, where it has roughly the value of [...]. The other signs are mostly omitted by the Persians.

units.la: SECT. IIII.
units.tr: SECT. IIII.

units.la: De Grammaticis, & Lexicis Persicis.
units.tr: On Persian Grammars and Lexicons.

units.la: Præcepta Grammatica Persica primus Edidit Lud. de Dieu. in 4°. Lugd. Bat. 1639. Idem postea plenius præstitit Joh. Gravius; Cujus Elementa Persica prodierunt Londini in 4°. anno 1649.Hisce lectorem, qui penitiorem hujus linguæ cognitionem desiderat, remittimus: primò tamen necesse est, ut præceptis linguæ Arabicæ imbutus sit, qui Persicam addiscere velit. Lexicon Persicum nemo hactenus edidit; promittit tamen Doctissimus Golius in præf. ad Lex Arab.
units.tr: Ludovicus de Dieu was the first to publish Persian grammatical rules, in quarto, at Leiden in 1639. Johannes Gravius later did the same more fully, and his Persian Elements appeared in London in quarto in 1649. We refer the reader who wants a deeper knowledge of this language to these works. First, however, anyone who wishes to learn Persian must be trained in the rules of the Arabic language. No one has yet published a Persian lexicon, though the most learned Golius promises one in the preface to his Arabic lexicon.

units.la: se brevi Lexicon quod paratum habet editurum: Interim quisque ex libris Persicis, ut Rofario Persico, Pentateucho Persico, aliisque libris Lexicon in proprium usum, per collationem locorum conficiat.
units.tr: He says he has a short lexicon ready and will publish it soon. Meanwhile, anyone who wants a lexicon for his own use can compile one by comparing passages in Persian books, such as the Persian Rosary, the Persian Pentateuch, and other books.

units.la: Exercitatio lectionis Persicae, ex Gen. 1. ver. 1.
units.tr: Exercise in reading Persian, from Genesis 1:1.

units.la: cælum Deus creavit principio In در اول آفريد خدا مر آن آسمان [?] ofomân ân mer Chodâ aphrîd âwal Der erat terra Et .terram & بود زمین و آن زمین [?] ان ومر [?] boud zemîn vôân zemîn ân vomèr faciem super tenebra & ,desolata &,vacua روی و ویران و تاریکی ابر [?] roui aber votarîchi vovirân tibî super spirabat Dei ventus & ,abysi نهوم وادی هدایی و روح سوا آب [?] aber schovâ vezîdeh Chodâji vobâdi tehoum .aqua faciem روی ان اب [?] âb ân roui
units.tr: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. And the earth was without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters. Persian, transliterated word by word: dar avval (in the beginning) Khodâ (God) âfarîd (created) ân âsmân (that heaven) va (and) ân zamîn (that earth); ân zamîn būd (that earth was) va (and) virân (desolate) va (and) khālī (empty) va (and) tārīkī (darkness) bar (upon) rūy-i (the face of) āb (the water) va (and) rūḥ-i Khodâ (the Spirit of God) bar (upon) rūy-i āb (the face of the water) ravān būd (moved).

units.la: INTRODUCTIO AD lectionem LINGUÆ ÆTHIOPICÆ. SECT. I.
units.tr: INTRODUCTION TO THE READING OF THE ETHIOPIC LANGUAGE. SECT. I.

units.la: De Æthiopum Characteribus.
units.tr: On the Characters of the Ethiopians.

units.la: Characteres quibus hodiè utuntur Æthiopes, quique ipsis proprii sunt ex Potkenii Psalterio, maximè verò ex Wemmeri Insti-tutionibus Grammat. Æthiop. descripta Tabula sequens exhibet.
units.tr: The following table presents the characters that the Ethiopians use today and that are peculiar to them, described from Potken's Psalter and especially from Wemmer's Institutions of Ethiopic Grammar.

units.la: Scribunt verò Æthiopes non ut reliqui Orientales à dextra ad sinistram, sed ut nos Europæi, incipiendo à sinistra.
units.tr: The Ethiopians do not write from right to left as the other Orientals do, but as we Europeans do, beginning from the left.

units.la: Consonantes verò & vocales non à se invicem separant ut Græci, Latini, reliquíque Europæi;nec punctis vocalibus utuntur ut Hebræi, Syri[?] Chaldæi, & Arabes, sed simul jungunt, adeo ut consona cum vocali, una eademque litera esse videatur, cùm tamen unaquæque litera syllabam constituat. Unde etiam consonantes 26 per vocales quas habent septem multiplicati, figuras faciunt 182; quibus adjungunt viginti alias, extra Alphabetum, syllabas certas constituentes, & sic in toto habent
units.tr: They do not separate consonants and vowels from one another as the Greeks, Latins and other Europeans do, nor do they use vowel points as the Hebrews, Syrians, Chaldeans and Arabs do. Instead they join them together, so that a consonant and its vowel appear to be one and the same letter, although each letter constitutes a syllable. Hence the 26 consonants, multiplied by the seven vowels they have, make 182 figures. To these they add twenty other characters, outside the alphabet, which constitute certain syllables, and so in total they have 202 characters.

units.la: Characteres 202 quorum nomina, figuras & potestatem sequens exhibet tabula.
units.tr: The following table shows the names, forms and values of these 202 characters.

units.la: Tabula syllabarum.
units.tr: Table of syllables.

units.la: A U J A
units.tr: A U I A

units.la: SECT. II.
units.tr: SECT. II.

units.la: De pronunciatione quarundum literarum.
units.tr: On the pronunciation of certain letters.

units.la: In tabula prima septem sunt columnæ, quas stantias vocant, secundum vocalium numerum 1. Gheez. 2. Chaab. 3. Sals. 4. Erâb. 5. Hams
units.tr: In the first table there are seven columns, which they call stantiae, according to the number of vowels: 1. Gheez, 2. Chaab, 3. Sals, 4. Erâb, 5. Hams, 6. Sads, 7. Sab.

units.la: 6. Sads. 7. Sab. Dum itaque Alphabetum recitatur, primò literæ, tum stantiæ nomen proferunt, ut Hoi Gheez Ha, Hoi Chaab Hu,&c. Cum verò literæ extra orationem scribuntur sextam stantiam scribunt.
units.tr: So when the alphabet is recited, they first pronounce the letter and then the name of the stantia, as Hoi Gheez "Ha", Hoi Chaab "Hu", and so on. But when the letters are written apart from a sentence, they write them in the sixth stantia.

units.la: Apud Æthiopes quatuor literis Caf, Kaf, Geml,& Hharm, diphthongi quos agnoscunt scil. uo, uu, ui, ua, & ue, solent appingi, ut in præcedenti tabella.
units.tr: In Ethiopic, the four letters Caf, Kaf, Geml, and Hharm are usually marked with the diphthongs they recognise, namely uo, uu, ui, ua, and ue, as in the preceding table.

units.la: Dividunt etiam literas in Quinque classes, Gutturales, Linguales, Palatinas, Dentales, et Labiales, ut alii Orientales. Hoi, Haut, & Hharm, aspirationes sunt & pronunciantur ut Heb. ה[?] & Arab. ح[?] Saut & Saat. eundem sonum habent. scil. f.
units.tr: They also divide the letters into five classes: gutturals, linguals, palatals, dentals, and labials, as other Orientals do. Hoi, Haut, and Hharm are aspirations, and they are pronounced like Hebrew ה and Arabic ḥ. Saut and Saat have the same sound, namely f.

units.la: Alph & Aain, per A potius quam per Heb. ע[?] vel Arab. ع[?] proferantur.
units.tr: Alph and Aain should be pronounced with A rather than with Hebrew ע or Arabic ʿayn.

units.la: Caf. ut K. effertur.
units.tr: Caf is pronounced like K.

units.la: Waw. ut v consonans, vel w.
units.tr: Waw is pronounced as consonantal v, or w.

units.la: Zadai, & Zzap. ut z, vel ut Hebr. ז[?].
units.tr: Zadai and Zzap are pronounced like z, or like Hebrew ז.

units.la: Pa & Pfa vix in vsu sunt, nisi in lingua vulgari & nominibus peregrinis
units.tr: Pa and Pfa are hardly in use, except in the vernacular and in foreign names.

units.la: Vocales literis affixae omnes longae sunt, & cum latinis a. e. i o. u. in sono couveniunt, excepto a. primae stantiae quod ut Hebr. -: pronunciatur citissime, & (e) sextae classis, quod sono medio quasi inter (e) & (o) raptiffime profertur instar Scheva, cujus regulas inter legendum servare videtur.
units.tr: All the vowels attached to letters are long, and they agree in sound with the Latin a, e, i, o, u, except that the a of the first stantia is pronounced very quickly, like the Hebrew patah, and the e of the sixth class is pronounced very rapidly, with a sound midway between e and o, like the Hebrew shewa, whose rules it seems to observe in reading.

units.la: Juxta Potkenium sub Gutturalibus, post socium post longam vocalem, & ab initio per (o) breve effertur, at fecundam Reatinum, Caninium et alios per (e) breve, ut Scheva.
units.tr: According to Potkenius, under the gutturals, after the consonant that follows a long vowel, and at the beginning, it is pronounced with a short o; but Reatinus, Caninius and others pronounce it with a short e, like shewa.

units.la: SECT. III.
units.tr: SECT. III.

units.la: De Accentibus.
units.tr: On Accents.

units.la: Nullas accentuum notas habent, sed vocales (a) quartæ stantiæ ubique syllabam producunt, reliquæ primam tantum & penultimam etiamsi per (e) sextæ classis efferuntur.
units.tr: They have no marks for accents. Instead, the vowels of the fourth station (a) always lengthen the syllable, and the rest lengthen only the first and the penultimate, even when these are pronounced with (e) of the sixth class.

units.la: Omnes dictiones, etiam Monosyllabas, duobus punctis distinguunt, majores vero distinctiones per puncta duplicata notantur.
units.tr: They divide all words, even monosyllables, by two points, while the greater divisions are marked by doubled points.

units.la: SECT. IV.
units.tr: SECT. IV.

units.la: De Grammaticis & Lexicis Æthiopicis.
units.tr: On the Ethiopic Grammarians and Lexicographers.

units.la: Primus à quo in Europam illata est hæc lingua fuit Potkenius, qui Psalterio Hebraicè, Græcè & Æthiopicè (vel, ut ipse mavult, Chaldaicè) edito, singularum linguarum Alphabeta & introductiunculas quasdam legendi ad calcem libri adjecit, grammaticam non dedit.
units.tr: The first man through whom this language was brought into Europe was Potkenius. When he published the Psalter in Hebrew, Greek and Ethiopic (or, as he himself preferred, Chaldee), he added to the end of the book the alphabets of each language and some short introductions to reading them, but he did not give a grammar.

units.la: Post eum viginti supra centum annos Jac. Wemmerus Lexicon omnium vocabulorum quæ in Psalmis, Canticis & N. Testamento continentur, adjectis etiam institutionibus Grammaticis utilissimis, edidit. Scripsit etiam præcepta Grammaticalia Gerhardus in Harmonia linguarum quatuor cum Hebraea, juxta Schickardi methodum, quædam etiam Crinesius, Reatinus &c. quos consula qui volet, mihi Wemmerus solus sufficere videtur, si tamen quis linguæ hujus cum aliis comparationem instituere velit (quod magno cum fructu fieri potest) utiliter Gerhardi Harmonam legere potest. hoc vero singularum Linguarum cognitionem aliquam adeptus faciat qui enim omnes simul addiscere velit addiscet nullam.
units.tr: After him, a little over a hundred and twenty years later, Jac. Wemmer published a lexicon of all the words contained in the Psalms, the Canticles and the New Testament, with very useful grammatical rules added. Gerhard also wrote grammatical precepts in his Harmony of four languages with Hebrew, following Schickard's method, and Crinesius, Reatinus and others did some too; whoever wishes may consult them. For my part, Wemmer alone seems sufficient. If anyone, however, wishes to compare this language with the others (which can be done with great profit), he may read Gerhard's Harmony with advantage. But whoever wishes to gain some knowledge of each language separately should do so; for whoever wants to learn them all at once will learn none.

units.tr: SECT. V.

Quoniam confirmata est ኵሎሙ፡ ሕዝብ፡ እስመ፡ ጽንዓት [?] cuulomu ehezb efma zan-at misericordia ejus super nos, & veritas ምሕረቱ፡ ላዕሌነ፡ ወጽድቁ [?] mech-rato la-lena wez-dekusa Domini manet in æternum. ለእግዚአብሔር፡ ይነብር፡ ለዓለም [?] laegdziabcher johelu laalam
units.tr: Praise the Lord [sabchewo laegzjabcher]: all nations, and praise him [cuulcemu ach-zab waifeb-chewo], all peoples. For his mercy is confirmed toward us [efma zan-at; ehezb], and the truth of the Lord remains for ever [laegdziabcher johelu laalam]. ## Nomen | Figura | Potestas

units.la: Vocales sunt quatuor [illegible, ~4 letters], quae Latinorum A, E, I, U, respondent, vocalem (O) non habent.
units.tr: There are four vowels [illegible], which correspond to the Latin A, E, I, U; they have no vowel O.

units.la: Semivocales sunt 5. [illegible, ~4 letters] & sequuntur vocales, reliquae sunt consonan-tes.
units.tr: There are five semivowels [illegible], and they follow the vowels; the rest are consonants.

units.la: Dipthongi sunt septem;
units.tr: There are seven diphthongs:
ay, aw, ea, iw, oy, u.

units.la: Grammaticam Armenam nemo (uno excepto Calano) hactenus composuit. Extant vero Lexicon Armeno-Latinum, in quarto, & Institutiones Religionis itidem in quarto in Lingua Armena cum Latina translatione, in usum Armenorum{*}& aliorum jussu Cardinalis Ducis Richlieu Parisiis impressæ, quæ magno adjumento esse possunt iis qui linguæ hujus cognitionem desiderant.
units.tr: No one (except Calanus) has hitherto composed an Armenian grammar. There are, however, an Armenian-Latin lexicon in quarto, and likewise the Institutes of Religion in quarto, in the Armenian language with a Latin translation, printed at Paris by order of Cardinal Duke Richelieu for the use of Armenians and others; these can be of great help to those who desire a knowledge of this language.

units.la: Ebsi | [illegible, ~2 letters] | Ps Numerant Copti per literas ut reliqui Orientales, & hos numeros ut & literarum fere omnium nomina & figuras à Graecis Ptolomaeorum tempore mutati sunt, addunt virgulam supra literam ut Arabes; in millenariis vero infra, habent & alias numerorum notas sibi proprias.
units.tr: Ebsi | [illegible, ~2 letters] | Ps. The Copts number by letters, as the other Orientals do. Like almost all the names and figures of the letters, these numerals were changed from the Greek forms at the time of the Ptolemies. They put a small stroke above the letter, as the Arabs do; for thousands, however, they put it below, and they also have other numeral signs of their own.

units.la: De Pronunciatione literarum quarundam.
units.tr: On the Pronunciation of Certain Letters.

units.la: Vida, seu v consona, effertur ut b.
units.tr: Vida, or the consonant v, is pronounced like b.

units.la: Hida, similis est Graecae literae (η) & sonat ut I declinans ad E, at cum habet accentum sonat ut I clarum.
units.tr: Hida resembles the Greek letter eta [η] and sounds like I inclining towards E; but when it bears the accent it sounds like a clear I.

units.la: Ni in fine dictionis formam mutat, & extenditur infra lineam, ut Hebraicum mun in fine ן[?].
units.tr: Ni changes its form at the end of a word and extends below the line, as the Hebrew final nun [ן] does.

units.la: Thida ut Θ effertur.
units.tr: Thida is pronounced like theta [Θ].

units.la: Bi, ut P.
units.tr: Bi is pronounced like P.

units.la: Dau, ut D:
units.tr: Dau is pronounced like D.

units.la: He, aliquando ut I, & (y) & post Alpha ut (v) vocalis.
units.tr: He sometimes sounds like I, and like Y, and after alpha like the vowel V.

units.la: Phi, aliquando P. declinans ad B.
units.tr: Phi is sometimes P, inclining towards B.

units.la: Chi, absque aspiratione ut χ Graecum à Gallis.
units.tr: Chi, without aspiration, is pronounced like the Greek chi [χ] as the French pronounce it.

units.la: Ebsi, ut [illegible, ~1 letter].
units.tr: Ebsi is pronounced as [illegible].

units.la: Scei, ut Sc. ut ש[?] Hebræum & ش Arab-cum. Chei,ut ח Hebræum & [?] Arabum.
units.tr: Scei is pronounced like Sc, as the Hebrew shin [ש] and the Arabic shin. Chei is pronounced like the Hebrew chet [ח] and the Arabic kha.

units.la: CHori, H. ut Heb. [?] & Arab. [?] Giangia. ut I. Jota Hispanica. Scima. pronunciatur ut Scei.
units.tr: CHori, H, is pronounced like the Hebrew and Arabic letter [?]. Giangia is pronounced like I, as the Spanish jota. Scima is pronounced like Scei.

units.la: Dei idem cum Hebræorum [?], simile est Tau Samaritanorum seu antiquæ literæ Tau Hebrææ, à quibus Ægyptii & ab iis Æthiopes mutuarunt.
units.tr: Dei is the same as the Hebrew [?], and resembles the Tau of the Samaritans, or the ancient Hebrew Tau, from which the Egyptians, and through them the Ethiopians, borrowed.

units.la: Distinguunt etiam literas ut reliqui Orientales in Gutturis, Linguæ, Palati, Dentium & Labiorum.
units.tr: They also distinguish their letters, as the other Orientals do, into gutturals, linguals, palatals, dentals and labials.

units.la: Dictionum genera distinguuntur apud Coptos non ex terminatione, ut apud Heb. Græcos, Latinos, nec per articulos, sed ex præfixis quibusdam literis seu signis, ut ipsi vocant, quæ ipsis sunt instar articulorum.
units.tr: Coptic nouns are distinguished by gender not by their endings, as in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, nor by articles, but by certain prefixed letters or signs, as they call them, which serve them in place of articles.

units.la: In Lexicis vero, ut in Kircheri Thesauro Copto-Arabico-Latino, ordinantur dictiones singulæ à fine, ut enim nos dictiones in lexicis investigamus à literis cujusque vocis primis, sic Copti ab ultimis, quem modum etiam servavit Kamus in Celebri illo Arabico Lexico, quod in suum nuper transtulit Golius.
units.tr: In lexicons, however, as in Kircher's Coptic-Arabic-Latin Thesaurus, the words are arranged each from its end. For just as we look up words in lexicons by the first letters of each word, so the Copts go by the last ones. Kamus also kept this method in the famous Arabic lexicon, which Golius has lately translated into Latin.

units.la: Plura qui volet legat dicti Kircheri Prodromum Coptum una cum ejusdem Grammatica Coptica ad finem Prodromi annexa, ejusdem etiam Linguam Ægyptiacam restitutam. In qua,
units.tr: Whoever wishes for more should read Kircher's Coptic Prodromus, together with his Coptic Grammar appended at the end of the Prodromus, and also his Restored Egyptian Language. In it are:

units.la: 1. Institutiones Grammaticæ Coptæ, Elsumenadi, & Aben Kateb Keisar.
units.tr: 1. The Institutes of Coptic Grammar, by Elsumenadi and Aben Kateb Keisar.

units.la: 2. Thesaurus ille supra dictus, seu Nomenclator Ægyptiaco-Arabico-Latinus, quem scalam magnam vocant.
units.tr: 2. The Thesaurus mentioned above, or Egyptian-Arabic-Latin Nomenclator, which they call the Great Ladder.

units.la: 3. Prodromi & Lexici supplementum, in quibus multæ de Lingua hac antiquissima scitu digna inveniuntur.
units.tr: 3. The supplement to the Prodromus and Lexicon, in which many things worth knowing about this most ancient language are found.

units.la: P.53. lin.28. addantur hæc verba, Scripsit etiam Dilherus Grammaticam Syriacam in duodecimo, non indignam quam consulant studiosi; unà cum Eclogis quibusdam, sive Exercitationibus in illam linguam.
units.tr: P. 53, line 28: add these words: Dilherus also wrote a Syriac grammar in duodecimo, not unworthy of the study of students, together with certain Eclogues, or exercises, in that language.
